def: loud and too sure of oneself, in a self-important way that annoys others
ex: The bumptious new hire kept correcting his manager in front of clients.
Yuki found the bumptious tour guide far more irritating than informative.
A bumptious fan behind us shouted advice at the players all game, as if he were the coach.
The bumptious freshman told the professor, in front of everyone, that her lecture was out of date.

cloze.s: The ___ young executive bragged about his bonus to everyone at the party and talked over anyone who disagreed.

def: split into rival groups that argue, or likely to stir up conflict between groups within an organization
ex: The factious club spent more time arguing over rules than playing chess.
Historians blamed the empire's decline partly on its factious, feuding nobility.
The factious neighborhood association split bitterly over what color to paint the playground.
Years of factious fighting among the band members finally broke the group apart.

cloze.s: The board was so ___ that every vote split into the same two hostile camps.

note: Not the same as fractious (irritable, unruly) or factitious (artificial, invented).

def: persistent in asking or demanding something, to the point of being annoying
ex: The importunate salesman called four times in one afternoon.
Diego finally agreed to the interview just to quiet the importunate reporter.
Importunate seagulls circled the beach picnic, begging for French fries.
The toddler's importunate requests for a cookie went on for the whole drive home.

cloze.s: The ___ fundraiser kept knocking on our door every week, even after we had already donated twice.

def: cautious and reluctant, especially about trusting someone or giving something away
ex: After losing money in a scam, Olga is chary of any offer that sounds too good.
The coach was chary with praise, so a single nod from her meant a lot.
Wei is chary of giving his phone number to companies he doesn't know.
Dr. Okafor is chary of prescribing strong painkillers for minor injuries.

cloze.s: Having been burned by a bad business partner before, Hannah was ___ of signing anything without a lawyer reading it first.

note: Usually followed by of or with: 'chary of strangers,' 'chary with compliments.'

def: extremely unpleasant or offensive, especially in having a foul smell
ex: A noisome odor drifted from the dumpster behind the restaurant.
The hikers held their breath as they crossed the noisome swamp.
Health inspectors closed the market after finding noisome piles of spoiled meat in the back room.
Fumes from the factory gave the river a noisome smell that drove swimmers away.

cloze.s: When the refrigerator broke during the heat wave, the ___ smell of rotting fish filled the entire apartment.

note: Has nothing to do with noise. It comes from an old shortened form of annoy.

def: old-fashioned in attitude or style and unwilling to change; out of date
ex: The new principal swept away the school's fusty rules about hats and hair length.
Visitors found the museum's fusty displays dull compared with modern interactive exhibits.
Critics called the opera's staging fusty, with painted backdrops that had not changed since the 1950s.
The bank updated its fusty logo and dark offices to appeal to younger customers.

cloze.s: The magazine hired younger writers to shake off its ___ image and attract readers under forty.

also: smelling stale and damp, like a room that has been closed up too long (“the fusty smell of the attic”)

def: dark and serious in mood or looks, seldom cheerful or smiling
ex: The saturnine detective rarely smiled, even when he solved a case.
Behind his saturnine expression, Malik had a dry and generous sense of humor.
Fatima's saturnine brother sat silently through the wedding, barely cracking a smile.
The painter's saturnine self-portraits show a man with heavy eyes and a deep frown.

cloze.s: The actor's dark brows and ___ face made him perfect for playing brooding villains.

note: From the old astrological belief that people born under Saturn were gloomy. Compare jovial, from Jupiter (Jove).

def: extremely loud and powerful, used especially of a person's voice
ex: The drill sergeant's stentorian voice carried across the entire parade ground.
Without a microphone, the auctioneer relied on her stentorian delivery to reach the back rows.
The coach's stentorian shout of “Hustle!” could be heard from the parking lot.
The town crier read the news in a stentorian voice that echoed through the square.

cloze.s: Even over the roar of the crowd, the referee's ___ announcement reached every corner of the gym.

note: Named after Stentor, a Greek in Homer's Iliad whose voice was as loud as fifty men's.
story: In Homer's Iliad (Book 5), the goddess Hera takes the form of Stentor, a Greek with a voice of bronze who could shout as loudly as fifty other men.

def: showing nervousness, fear or a lack of confidence
ex: The timorous puppy hid under the bed whenever visitors arrived.
Priya gave a timorous knock on her boss's door before asking for a raise.
The timorous deer froze at the edge of the field, then fled at the slightest sound.
His timorous voice on the phone made it clear he was nervous about the job interview.

cloze.s: The ___ student whispered her answer so quietly that the teacher had to ask her to repeat it.

def: slow and inactive in mind or body; lacking energy or movement
ex: After the huge holiday meal, the whole family sat torpid in front of the television.
Economists worried that the torpid economy would not recover without new investment.
In the summer heat, the dogs lay torpid in the shade all afternoon.
Without coffee, Malik's mind felt torpid during his early morning class.

cloze.s: In the cold months, the lizards become ___ and barely move from their sheltered rocks.

def: bitterly abusive and full of harsh, insulting criticism
ex: The chef answered the bad review with a vituperative post insulting the critic.
Moderators removed the most vituperative comments from the forum.
The neighbors’ dispute over the fence grew vituperative, with insults shouted across the yard.
Hannah deleted her vituperative reply to her landlord before she could send it.

cloze.s: The coach's ___ outburst, full of insults aimed at the referee, earned him a two-game suspension.

def: having very little or no money; regularly short of cash
ex: As an impecunious graduate student, Wei lived on rice, beans and free conference snacks.
The impecunious artist paid his rent with paintings.
The impecunious young couple furnished their first apartment with chairs found on the curb.
The scholarship was created for impecunious students who could not otherwise afford college.

cloze.s: Too ___ to afford a hotel, the backpackers slept on a friend's floor for the whole trip.

note: Formal, often lightly humorous.

def: not respectable and a bit immoral, often in a way that still seems glamorous or attractive
ex: The novel is set in a louche nightclub full of gamblers and fading movie stars.
His louche charm made him popular at parties but distrusted by bankers.
The film's louche hero spends his days at the racetrack and his nights in expensive hotels.
Hannah's grandparents remember the neighborhood as a louche district of late-night clubs, long before it became family-friendly.

cloze.s: The jazz bar had a(n) ___ reputation, with rumors of backroom card games and shady deals, which only made tourists more curious.

note: Borrowed from French, where it originally meant 'squinting.'

def: transparently clear; also, of writing or speech, very easy to understand
ex: Fish darted through the pellucid water of the mountain lake.
Sofia's pellucid explanation of compound interest finally made it click for her students.
The jeweler held up a pellucid diamond with no visible flaws or cloudy spots.
The judge's pellucid ruling left no doubt about why the contract was invalid.

cloze.s: Her ___ prose makes even complicated legal ideas easy for ordinary readers to follow.

def: impossible to avoid or escape; certain to happen
ex: The novel builds steadily toward the hero's ineluctable downfall.
Aging is ineluctable, but Fatima believes how we age is partly up to us.
Hannah felt the ineluctable pull of sleep as the long train ride went on.
The ineluctable fact that summer would end did not stop the kids from enjoying every day of it.

cloze.s: The scientist argued that further sea-level rise was now ___: no policy could stop it entirely, only slow it.

def: extremely generous, especially in giving large gifts of money
ex: A munificent gift from a former student funded the school's new science lab.
The munificent host paid for every guest's hotel room.
The museum thanked a munificent collector who donated hundreds of paintings worth millions of dollars.
Kwame's munificent grandfather paid off the college loans of all six of his grandchildren.

cloze.s: Thanks to a(n) ___ donor who gave ten million dollars, the hospital could open a new children's wing.

def: relaxed and not worried, in a casual way, when others might be anxious
ex: Jamal gave an insouciant shrug when the flight was canceled and simply booked a hotel.
Her insouciant attitude toward deadlines alarmed the rest of the team.
With an insouciant wave, Sofia left the dishes in the sink and headed to the beach.
The young driver's insouciant attitude toward speed limits earned him three tickets in a month.

cloze.s: Despite the storm warnings, the surfers remained ___, joking on the beach as the waves grew larger.

def: unwilling to accept new ideas because of rigid devotion to tradition or old habits
ex: The hidebound firm refused to let employees work from home, even during the snowstorm.
Young researchers challenged the hidebound assumptions of their field.
Hidebound fans complained loudly when the baseball league added a pitch clock.
The hidebound restaurant still refuses to take reservations by email or text.

cloze.s: The ___ committee rejected the proposal simply because things had never been done that way before.

def: showing poor judgment and likely to cause trouble for yourself, especially by offending people
ex: It would be impolitic to criticize the client's logo during the sales pitch.
Liam made the impolitic remark that his boss's plan would never work.
It was impolitic of Sofia to mention her raise in front of coworkers who hadn't gotten one.
The ambassador's impolitic joke about the host country's food caused an uproar.

cloze.s: Announcing layoffs on the same day as the executive bonuses was a deeply ___ move that angered the whole staff.

def: calm and even-tempered, not easily upset; also, of climate, mild and steady
ex: Aisha's equable temperament made her the ideal person to handle angry customers.
The island's equable climate rarely drops below sixty degrees.
As a nurse in a busy emergency room, Jamal relies on his equable nature to stay calm with frightened families.
San Diego's equable weather makes it popular with people who dislike harsh winters.

cloze.s: Even when the project fell apart, our ___ team leader never raised his voice or lost his composure.

note: Not the same as equitable, which means fair and just.

def: impossible to doubt or question; clearly and certainly true
ex: The security footage offered indubitable proof that the package had been delivered.
Her indubitable talent earned her a scholarship to the conservatory.
Diego's indubitable skill at the grill made him the family's official barbecue cook.
It is an indubitable fact that water boils at a lower temperature high on a mountain.

cloze.s: The fingerprint match was ___ evidence, leaving the jury with no reason to question who had been in the room.

def: harmful, destructive or poisonous in effect
ex: Parents worried about the baneful influence of gambling ads on teenagers.
The weed is baneful to livestock and must be cleared from the pasture.
Doctors warned about the baneful effects of smoking on the heart and lungs.
Many gardeners consider the invasive vine baneful, since it chokes out native plants.

cloze.s: Years of pollution had a(n) ___ effect on the river, killing most of its fish.

def: clumsy or awkward in movement or in handling situations; lacking skill
ex: The maladroit waiter spilled soup on two guests in one evening.
The company's maladroit apology only made customers angrier.
Liam's maladroit attempt to dance at the wedding sent him crashing into the cake table.
The puppy was charmingly maladroit, tripping over its own paws on the stairs.

cloze.s: The official's ___ handling of the press conference, stumbling over answers and contradicting himself, became a national joke.

def: existing only in the imagination; wildly unrealistic or impossible to achieve
ex: The startup's promise of free, unlimited energy proved chimerical.
Tomás chased the chimerical dream of a perfect, error-free novel for twenty years.
The idea of a diet that lets you eat anything and still lose weight is chimerical.
Their plan to cross the ocean in a homemade rowboat turned out to be chimerical.

cloze.s: Hopes of finishing the bridge in six months were ___, since the steel had not even been ordered.

note: From the Chimera, a fire-breathing monster of Greek myth made of parts of several animals.

def: to begin to grow or develop quickly; to flourish and expand
ex: Small farms have burgeoned around the city as demand for local produce grows.
Maria's burgeoning career as a photographer left her little time for weekends off.
Wildflowers burgeoned across the hills after the spring rains.
The friendship that began in a chemistry lab burgeoned into a lifelong business partnership.

cloze.s: After the new highway opened, the sleepy town's population began to ___, doubling in just five years.

note: Originally meant 'to put out buds.' Most often seen as the adjective burgeoning.

def: to analyze and explain an idea, text or work of art in careful detail
ex: In her thesis, Hannah explicates a single poem line by line.
The professor spent the whole seminar explicating Kant's theory of duty.
The museum guide explicated the painting, pointing out the hidden symbols in each corner.
In a long article, the economist explicated the new tax rules for small business owners.

cloze.s: The literature teacher asked each student to ___ one stanza, explaining every image and its meaning.

note: Formal; used mostly for academic analysis of texts and ideas.

def: to formally and seriously give up a belief, claim or habit, sometimes under oath
ex: Under pressure from the authorities, the scientist was forced to abjure his theory in public.
Kwame abjured sugar for a month and, to everyone's surprise, stuck to it.
On joining the monastery, Brother Tomás abjured all personal possessions and took a vow of poverty.
In a signed statement to the court, the former hacker abjured his old tricks and promised to work legally.

cloze.s: To become citizens of some countries, applicants must ___ allegiance to any other nation.

note: Not the same as adjure, which means to urge someone solemnly.

def: to forbid or ban something officially, especially by law or rule
ex: The new regulations proscribe smoking anywhere on hospital grounds.
The league proscribes betting by players on any game.

The contract proscribes hiring away the other company's employees for two years.

cloze.s: Many countries ___ the sale of ivory in an effort to protect elephants.

note: Nearly the opposite of prescribe (to order or recommend). Don't mix them up.

def: to cut back spending or reduce operations, usually because of financial difficulty
ex: When sales slumped, the company retrenched by closing three stores.

After the drought cut his harvest in half, the farmer retrenched, selling two tractors and hiring no summer help.

cloze.s: Facing a budget shortfall, the university had to ___, freezing hiring and postponing new buildings.

def: to protest or argue strongly against something, often while telling someone they are wrong
ex: The player remonstrated with the umpire after being called out at home plate.
Neighbors remonstrated against the plan to cut down the old oaks.
Parents remonstrated with the principal over the sudden cancellation of the class trip.
When the airline gave away his seat, Kwame remonstrated with the gate agent for twenty minutes.

cloze.s: When the waiter tried to clear her half-finished plate, Olga began to ___ with him, insisting she was still eating.

note: Usually followed by with a person or against a thing.

def: to express loud, angry and bitter protest or criticism
ex: Columnists fulminated against the new parking fees for weeks.
Grandpa still fulminates about the price of coffee every single morning.
Fans fulminated online after the team traded away its most popular player.
The landlord fulminated against tenants who left trash bags in the hallway.

cloze.s: On his radio show, the host would ___ against modern architecture, calling every glass tower an eyesore.

note: Usually followed by against or about.

def: to feel or show great joy, especially in triumph or success
ex: Fans exulted in the streets after their team won its first championship.
Aisha exulted when she finally learned she had passed the bar exam.
The scientists exulted when the rover sent back its first clear pictures.
Liam exulted over the final payment on his student loans, dancing around the kitchen.

cloze.s: The climbers ___ at the summit, hugging and shouting after six days of struggle.

def: to exclude someone from a group or society and refuse to associate with them
ex: The whistleblower was ostracized by coworkers who saw her as disloyal.

The book club ostracized members who criticized its leaders, leaving them off every invitation.

cloze.s: After he cheated in the tournament, the other players ___ him, refusing to sit at his table or speak to him.

def: to show reluctance or raise an objection, often politely or mildly
ex: When asked to chair the committee, Wei demurred, saying she was too busy.

cloze.s: Offered the last slice of cake, Malik ___ politely, insisting his guest should have it instead.

def: to make someone feel deeply embarrassed, ashamed or humiliated
ex: Liam was mortified when his phone rang loudly during the funeral.

Diego was mortified to discover he had given his whole presentation with his shirt on inside out.
Her father's loud singing at the school concert mortified Aisha, who hid behind her program.

cloze.s: Priya's parents ___ her by showing her new boyfriend her baby photos from the bathtub.

def: to keep changing one's mind between different opinions or actions, unable to decide
ex: Hannah vacillated for weeks between taking the job in Denver and staying in Chicago.

Priya vacillated between the pasta and the curry until the waiter came back a third time.

cloze.s: Unable to decide between the two apartments, Jamal continued to ___ until both were rented by someone else.

def: to persuade someone gently by using charm, praise, pleading or sweet talk
ex: The children wheedled an extra hour of screen time out of their babysitter.
Diego tried to wheedle a discount from the salesman by praising his taste in cars.
Liam wheedled his roommate into doing the dishes with a flood of compliments about her cooking.
The cat wheedled treats from the guests by rubbing against their legs and purring.

cloze.s: With compliments, pleading and a sweet smile, my niece managed to ___ twenty dollars out of her grandfather.

def: to weaken or spoil the quality or effectiveness of something; to make it faulty
ex: A single biased sample can vitiate the results of an entire study.
Errors in the translation vitiated the force of the author's argument.
Poor lighting vitiated the photographer’s otherwise beautiful portraits.

cloze.s: One careless measurement error was enough to ___ the whole experiment, so the team had to start over.

also: in law, to make a contract or agreement no longer valid (“Fraud can vitiate the whole contract.”)
note: Formal; often used of arguments, evidence and results.

def: to keep something within strict limits, restricting its range or power
ex: The new rules circumscribe the mayor's power to approve contracts alone.
Her illness circumscribed her travel to short trips near home.
A tight budget circumscribed what the school could offer, so art and music classes were cut.
The new league rules circumscribe how much teams may spend on players' salaries.

cloze.s: The court ruled that the agency's authority was narrowly ___ and did not extend to private companies.

also: in geometry, to draw one shape around another so that they touch at points but do not cross (“Students had to circumscribe a circle around the triangle.”)

def: to calm someone's anger or win them over through friendly gestures or concessions
ex: The manager tried to conciliate the angry customer with a refund and a free dinner.
Negotiators worked to conciliate both unions before the strike deadline.
The airline tried to conciliate stranded passengers with hotel vouchers and free meals.
The coach conciliated the benched star by naming him team captain for the next game.

cloze.s: Hoping to ___ the neighbors after the loud party, Fatima brought them a basket of homemade cookies and an apology.

def: to give, grant or reveal something, often reluctantly or as if doing a great favor
ex: The famously private author vouchsafed only a few words to reporters.

cloze.s: The spokesperson refused to ___ any details about the merger, saying only that talks were continuing.

note: Formal and somewhat old-fashioned; often used in the negative: 'vouchsafed no answer.'

def: to solemnly promise to give up or stop doing something
ex: After the accident, Tomás vowed to forswear driving after even one drink.

After losing money at the casino, Aisha forswore gambling for good.
Guests at the silent retreat had to forswear their cell phones for the entire week.

cloze.s: Each New Year, Kwame vows to ___ fast food, but he is back at the burger stand by February.

also: to lie after swearing to tell the truth (“The witness had forsworn himself on the stand.”)

def: to make someone more humble or restrained, usually through criticism, failure or hardship
ex: Chastened by the defeat, the team spent the off-season working on fundamentals.

A semester of failing grades chastened Jamal, who started going to every study session.
The speeding ticket chastened Priya, and she now drives right at the limit.

cloze.s: The failed product launch ___ the overconfident founders, who finally began listening to their engineers.

note: Not the same as chastise, which means to scold or punish severely.

def: to involve someone deeply in a conflict, argument or difficult situation
ex: The company became embroiled in a lawsuit over its patents.

Sofia regretted sharing her opinion, which embroiled her in a week-long argument in the group chat.
A border dispute embroiled the two neighboring countries in years of tense negotiations.

cloze.s: The mayor's office was ___ in a scandal over missing funds for most of the year.

note: Most often used in the passive: 'embroiled in a dispute.'

def: to speak vaguely or ambiguously in order to avoid committing oneself or telling the truth
ex: When asked directly about the budget cuts, the director equivocated and changed the subject.

When the doctor asked whether he still smoked, Malik equivocated, saying he had “mostly” quit.
The coach equivocated about who would start at quarterback, refusing to name either player.

cloze.s: Pressed by reporters about the delays, the spokesman chose to ___, giving answers that could mean either yes or no.

def: to make up for a wrong or sin by accepting punishment or making amends
ex: He volunteered at the shelter for years to expiate his guilt over the accident.
Medieval pilgrims often traveled great distances to expiate their sins.
To expiate his mistake of missing her recital, Jamal took his daughter out for a special dinner.
The company paid a large fine and funded the cleanup to expiate its role in the oil spill.

cloze.s: Hoping to ___ her earlier rudeness, Olga sent the host flowers and a long handwritten apology.

def: to claim or take something for oneself without having the right to it
ex: The committee chair arrogated to herself the power to approve all spending.

The landlord's nephew arrogated the title of building manager, though no one had ever hired him.
The team captain arrogated the right to choose every play, ignoring the coach completely.

cloze.s: The new manager tried to ___ the credit for the project, even though he joined after it was finished.

note: Related to arrogant; usually 'arrogate something to oneself.'

def: to cite something as evidence or proof in support of an argument
ex: The lawyer adduced phone records showing the defendant was across town that night.
Researchers adduced data from twelve countries to support their theory.
Asked why the bridge needed repairs, the engineer adduced photos of the cracks and rust.
Malik adduced his excellent grades as proof that he was ready for a later curfew.

cloze.s: In her essay, Priya was able to ___ several studies showing that sleep improves memory.

note: Formal. Not the same as deduce (reach a conclusion) or induce (bring about).

def: to secretly plot with others to do something wrong or harmful

cloze.s: The two executives ___ with a supplier to inflate prices and split the extra profit between them.

def: to criticize someone or something very severely, especially in public

The coach excoriated his team in front of reporters after their careless loss.
Online shoppers excoriated the company in thousands of reviews after the toy broke within days.

cloze.s: In a scathing editorial, the newspaper ___ the city council for ignoring warnings about the water supply.

also: in medicine, to scrape or rub away the surface of the skin (“The rough rope excoriated his palms.”)

def: of facts or circumstances, to act as a powerful factor working against something happening
ex: His lack of experience militated against his promotion.

The thin snow cover militated against opening the ski slopes for the holiday weekend.

cloze.s: Several factors, including the bad weather and the tight budget, ___ against holding the festival outdoors this year.

note: Almost always followed by against. Often confused with mitigate, which means to make less severe.

def: to deny something or say that it is not true; to speak against it
ex: No one can gainsay her dedication; she hasn't missed a practice in ten years.

The coach's record of five straight league titles is hard to gainsay.

cloze.s: Few critics would ___ the singer's extraordinary vocal range, even if they dislike her songs.

note: Formal; usually used with a negative: 'there is no gainsaying her talent.'

def: to win or regain someone's favor, or calm their anger, by doing something that pleases them
ex: Ancient farmers offered grain to propitiate the gods of rain.
Hannah bought her sister concert tickets to propitiate her after missing her birthday.
Hoping to propitiate the angry customer, the manager offered a full refund and a free meal.
Diego cleaned the whole kitchen to propitiate his roommate after their argument.

cloze.s: In the myth, the villagers sacrificed a goat to ___ the angry storm god.

def: to persuade someone to do something by using tricks, sweet talk or lies
ex: The scammers inveigled retirees into handing over their bank details.
Malik inveigled his way into the VIP area by pretending to be the drummer's cousin.
Sofia inveigled her little brother into doing her chores by promising him her dessert.
The salesman tried to inveigle Grandpa into buying an expensive warranty he didn't need.

cloze.s: The con artist managed to ___ several investors into funding a gold mine that did not exist.

def: to erase or wipe out something, such as a mark, memory or trace
ex: Centuries of rain had effaced the inscription on the old gravestone.

The company tried to efface every record of its failed product from its website.

cloze.s: The new owners painted over the mural, ___ every trace of the artist's work.

def: of an insult or injustice, to keep causing lasting resentment or irritation

Her brother-in-law's comment about her cooking rankled Grandma for the rest of the holiday.
Being left out of the group email rankled Tomás more than he would admit.

cloze.s: Even years later, being passed over for the promotion continued to ___ with Fatima whenever her old boss was mentioned.

def: to treat someone as a celebrity and give them great public attention and admiration
ex: After her Olympic gold, the town lionized the young swimmer with parades and murals.
The tech press lionized the founder until the company collapsed.
Fans lionized the rookie quarterback after just three good games.
Literary circles lionized the young poet, inviting her to every festival and party.

cloze.s: Hollywood tends to ___ young directors after one hit film and then forget them after one flop.

def: to put forward an idea, theory or question for others to consider
ex: The economist propounded a theory linking housing prices to commuting times.
At the town meeting, Jamal propounded a plan for a community garden.
In class, Professor Tanaka propounded a new way to think about the causes of the war.
The young philosopher propounded a question that kept the seminar arguing for hours.

cloze.s: Darwin was not the first to ___ a theory of evolution, but his was far better supported by evidence.

def: cheerful, relaxed, friendly good nature, especially among a group of people
ex: The bonhomie at the office picnic made everyone forget about deadlines for a day.

cloze.s: The restaurant owner's warm ___ made every customer feel like an old friend.

note: From French, literally 'good-man-ness.' Pronounced bah-nuh-MEE.

def: pushing a dangerous situation to the edge of disaster to force an opponent to back down

Benjamin Franklin is known for aphorisms such as "Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise."

cloze.s: 'Actions speak louder than words' is a familiar ___ about judging people by what they do.

def: a leader who wins support by appealing to people's emotions and prejudices rather than reason
ex: History offers many warnings about demagogues who exploit public fear.
The novel's villain is a demagogue who blames every problem on outsiders.
The crowd cheered the demagogue's angry speeches, though he never explained how he would fix anything.
Good teachers warn students to watch out for demagogues who blame every problem on one group of people.

cloze.s: The ___ whipped up the crowd with false claims and scapegoats instead of offering real solutions.

def: excessive boldness or nerve, especially in a way that seems rude or disrespectful
ex: He had the temerity to ask for a raise on his second day.
Nobody could believe the intern had the temerity to correct the CEO in public.
The rookie reporter had the temerity to interrupt the governor in the middle of a sentence.
Tomás had the temerity to borrow my car without asking and return it with an empty tank.

cloze.s: After arriving two hours late, Malik had the ___ to complain that dinner was cold.

def: calmness and emotional balance, especially in a difficult or stressful situation
ex: She accepted the difficult diagnosis with remarkable equanimity and asked about next steps.
The pilot's equanimity during the emergency landing reassured the passengers.
Kwame lost his luggage, missed his connection and still handled the trip with equanimity.
Daily walks help Fatima keep her equanimity during stressful weeks at work.

cloze.s: Even when the project collapsed, Wei faced the setback with ___, calmly planning her next steps.

def: eager, cheerful readiness and speed in doing something
ex: Jamal accepted the job offer with alacrity, calling back within minutes.
The children cleaned their rooms with surprising alacrity once ice cream was promised.
When the coach asked who wanted to carry the trophy, Fatima stepped forward with alacrity.
The dog responded with alacrity whenever anyone picked up its leash, racing to the door.

cloze.s: When the boss offered free tickets to anyone who stayed late, the staff volunteered with surprising ___, every hand going up at once.

def: a complicated, confusing situation that is very hard to escape or make progress in
ex: The new manager inherited a morass of unpaid invoices and angry clients.
The project got stuck in a morass of paperwork and approvals.
After the divorce, Hannah spent a year stuck in a legal morass over who owned the house.
Talks between the two companies sank into a morass of lawyers, delays and changing demands.

cloze.s: Fatima spent months trying to get out of a(n) ___ of conflicting regulations before she could open her bakery.

also: an area of soft, wet, muddy ground (“the path disappeared into a morass”)

def: completely and directly, used to stress that two things are exact opposites
ex: The two candidates hold diametrically opposed views on taxes.
Their parenting styles are diametrically opposite: one strict, the other relaxed.
The roommates keep diametrically opposed sleep schedules: one goes to bed at nine, the other at three.
The two reports reached diametrically opposite conclusions about whether the bridge was safe.

cloze.s: The siblings have ___ opposite tastes in music: one loves heavy metal, the other only classical.

note: Almost always used with 'opposed' or 'opposite'.

def: up to this point in time; until now
ex: The study revealed a heretofore unknown species of frog.
The company entered a market it had heretofore ignored.
The detective uncovered heretofore hidden records in the basement of the old courthouse.
The new drug offers hope to patients who have heretofore had no treatment options.

cloze.s: The newly found letters shed light on a(n) ___ secret chapter of the author's life.

note: Formal; common in legal and academic writing.

def: in a calm, relaxed way that shows no worry, excitement or concern
ex: Aisha nonchalantly mentioned that she had won the lottery.
The cat walked nonchalantly past the barking dog.
Malik nonchalantly sipped his coffee while everyone else panicked about the missed deadline.
The skateboarder nonchalantly landed a difficult trick, as if it were nothing at all.

cloze.s: Trying to look cool, Liam leaned ___ against the wall as his crush walked by.

def: according to what people generally say or believe, though it has not been proven
ex: The old house is reputedly haunted by a sea captain.
The tiny restaurant reputedly serves the best tacos in the city.
The old oak reputedly sheltered soldiers during the war, though no records prove it.
Hannah’s grandmother reputedly never lost a card game in sixty years.

cloze.s: The painting, ___ worth millions, turned out to be a skillful copy.

def: later than it should have happened or been done
ex: The company belatedly apologized for the data breach, three months after it happened.
Hannah belatedly realized she had left her passport at home.
The referee belatedly waved off the goal after watching the replay several minutes later.
Wei belatedly thanked her favorite teacher in a letter written ten years after graduation.

cloze.s: The birthday card arrived a week after the party, ___ wishing Tomás a happy fortieth.

def: in a careless way, without any plan, order or system
ex: Books were stacked haphazardly on every surface of the apartment.
The new rules were applied haphazardly across departments.
After the party, shoes were thrown haphazardly into a pile by the front door.
The budget was put together haphazardly, with numbers copied from old reports without checking.

cloze.s: Instead of following a schedule, Jamal studied ___, opening whichever textbook happened to be closest.

def: in a sudden, rough or rude way, without the politeness or respect people expect
ex: The coach was unceremoniously fired after a single losing season.
The bouncer unceremoniously pushed the rowdy guests out the door.
Our old couch was unceremoniously dragged to the curb the day the new one arrived.
A sudden storm unceremoniously ended the outdoor graduation, sending families running for their cars.

cloze.s: After twenty years in the town square, the old statue was ___ dumped in a junkyard.

def: boldly and openly, without any shame, about behavior that is wrong
ex: The thieves brazenly stole the car in broad daylight.
He brazenly lied to the inspector, even with the evidence in front of him.
The student brazenly copied his neighbor's answers while the teacher stood right beside him.
The store brazenly tripled the price of bottled water during the storm, when families needed it most.

cloze.s: The shoplifter ___ walked out with a television, waving at the security camera on the way.

def: in an embarrassed way, because you know you have done something foolish or wrong
ex: Diego sheepishly admitted he had forgotten their anniversary.
The puppy looked up sheepishly from the chewed shoe.
Yuki sheepishly raised her hand when the teacher asked who had left the lab door open.
Malik sheepishly returned the library book, which was three months overdue.

cloze.s: Caught eating cookies right before dinner, the kids grinned ___ and put them back in the jar.

def: with great care, close attention and steady hard work
ex: Priya assiduously practiced the piano every evening for years.
The archivist assiduously cataloged every letter in the collection.
Wei assiduously checked every number in the report before sending it to the bank.
During flu season, the nurses assiduously followed the hospital's handwashing rules.

cloze.s: The restorer ___ cleaned the painting inch by inch with tiny swabs, careful not to damage a single brushstroke.

def: wisely and carefully, with good thought about how much or when to use something
ex: Use the hot sauce judiciously; a few drops are plenty.
The editor cut the manuscript judiciously, keeping all of its best scenes.
Kwame spends his small savings judiciously, buying only what he truly needs.
A good speaker uses humor judiciously, so the jokes support the message instead of distracting from it.

cloze.s: With a tight budget, the school had to spend its grant money ___, choosing only the most urgent repairs.

def: cautiously and suspiciously, watching out for possible danger or trouble
ex: The cat eyed the new dog warily from under the couch.
Investors reacted warily to the surprising earnings report.
The hikers stepped warily across the icy bridge, testing each board before trusting it.
Tomás read the too-good-to-be-true job offer warily, looking for hidden fees.

cloze.s: Unsure whether the stranger at the door was really from the gas company, Olga watched him ___ through the window.

def: with stubborn determination, refusing to give up despite difficulty or failure
ex: The reporter doggedly pursued the story for three years.
Kwame doggedly practiced free throws until he made fifty in a row.
The detective doggedly followed every clue until the case was solved.
Fatima doggedly climbed the steep trail despite her aching knees.

cloze.s: Despite repeated rejections, Yuki ___ reapplied to medical school every year until she was finally accepted.

def: in a way that shows dry, slightly mocking humor, often about something disappointing
ex: 'Well, that went well,' she said wryly as the cake collapsed.
The author wryly describes her many failed attempts at gardening.
When rain began the moment the picnic started, Kwame wryly noted that the forecast had promised sunshine.
Asked about the team's tenth straight loss, the coach wryly said they were 'building character.'

cloze.s: Looking at the flooded basement, Wei smiled ___ and said at least they finally had the indoor pool he always wanted.

def: very carefully and cautiously, so as to avoid causing pain, damage or danger
ex: Maria gingerly lowered herself into the hot bath.
The technician gingerly removed the cracked phone screen.
Fatima gingerly picked up the antique teacup, afraid it might crack in her hands.
The firefighter stepped gingerly across the old wooden floor, which creaked with every step.

cloze.s: With a sprained ankle, Liam stepped ___ down the stairs, testing each one before putting weight on it.

note: Can also be an adjective: 'a gingerly step.'

def: with a sad, longing feeling, often for something in the past or out of reach
ex: Grandpa spoke wistfully about the farm where he grew up.
Stuck in her office, Sofia looked wistfully at her beach vacation photos.
Leaning on the fence, the injured player watched wistfully as his teammates practiced without him.
Watching the teenagers skateboard, the retired athlete smiled wistfully at the memory of his younger days.

cloze.s: Watching the other kids leave for summer camp, Jamal stared ___ out the window, wishing he could go too.

def: bad-tempered, always ready to argue, and hard to deal with, often as a lasting habit
ex: The cantankerous old landlord complained about every repair request Priya submitted.
After a sleepless night, Diego was cantankerous with everyone at the morning meeting.
The cantankerous patient argued with every nurse about when to take his medicine.
The cantankerous food critic seemed to hate every restaurant he visited.

cloze.s: The ___ neighbor yelled at kids for stepping on his lawn and argued with the mail carrier daily.

note: Often used humorously, especially about older people.

def: easily upset and hard to control, often arguing or causing trouble; also used of groups that keep fighting among themselves
ex: The fractious toddler refused his nap and threw his cup across the kitchen.
Negotiations stalled because the coalition was fractious, with each group distrusting the others.
The fractious horse kicked and refused to let anyone near it.
The neighborhood association had grown fractious, splitting into groups that refused to speak to each other.

cloze.s: The committee meetings grew so ___ that members shouted over one another and two of them resigned.

def: deeply embarrassing and shameful, especially in a public way that damages someone's dignity
ex: The champion suffered an ignominious defeat, losing in the first round to an unranked player.
After the scandal, the executive made an ignominious exit, escorted out of the building by security.
The ad campaign was an ignominious failure, mocked online and pulled within a week.
Tripping and falling on the stage at graduation felt ignominious to Amara, though now she laughs about it.

cloze.s: The team's ___ season ended with zero wins and a last-place finish that fans still joke about.

def: having a long-established habit or trait that is very unlikely to change
ex: Malik is an inveterate gambler who visits the casino every weekend despite his losses.
My aunt, an inveterate optimist, insisted the rain would clear before the picnic started.
Grandpa Wei is an inveterate storyteller who can't let a dinner pass without a tale from his youth.
An inveterate traveler, Sofia has visited a new country every summer for thirty years.

cloze.s: After forty years of smoking two packs a day, Olga was a truly ___ smoker who doubted she could ever quit.

note: Usually describes a person by a habit (inveterate liar, inveterate traveler); often, but not always, negative.

def: made or used in place of the real thing and usually not as good; fake or imitation
ex: During the wartime shortage, people brewed ersatz coffee from roasted chicory and acorns.
The theme park's ersatz Venice had canals and gondolas but none of the real city's charm.
The diner served ersatz maple syrup made mostly of corn syrup and brown coloring.
Rafael's ersatz leather jacket started peeling after only one winter.

cloze.s: The restaurant served ___ crab made from processed white fish, though the menu implied it was the real thing.

note: From the German word for 'substitute'; usually implies lower quality.

def: willing to act dishonestly in exchange for money or bribes; open to corruption
ex: The venal inspector approved unsafe buildings for anyone who slipped him cash.
Reporters exposed a venal system in which some judges sold favorable rulings to wealthy clients.
The film's villain is a venal police chief who lets criminals go free for a share of their profits.
Reformers vowed to clean up the venal customs office, where bribes were needed to clear any shipment.

cloze.s: The ___ official was arrested for accepting bribes to award city contracts to his friends.

note: Not the same as *venial* (minor and forgivable), as in 'a venial sin.'

def: happening by lucky chance in a way that turns out to be good or useful
ex: Their serendipitous meeting on a delayed train led to a successful business partnership.
Aisha made a serendipitous discovery: a rare first edition sitting in a thrift-store bin.
A serendipitous wrong turn led Kwame to a tiny bakery that became his favorite.
In a serendipitous twist, the roommate Liam was randomly assigned turned out to share his hometown.

cloze.s: Finding my lost wedding ring while planting tomatoes was a(n) ___ surprise I never expected.

def: full of noble but unrealistic hopes and plans that have little chance of working in the real world
ex: His quixotic campaign to abolish all homework in the district never gained any support.
Sofia launched a quixotic plan to restore the old sailboat by herself in a single summer.
Malik's quixotic plan to grow bananas in his Chicago backyard ended with the first frost.
The town's quixotic attempt to build a ski resort on a small hill failed within a year.

cloze.s: Trying to read every book in the city library before retiring was a noble but ___ goal.

note: From Don Quixote, Cervantes's idealistic hero who attacks windmills he believes are giants.
story: In Miguel de Cervantes's Don Quixote (1605 and 1615), a Spanish gentleman obsessed with tales of chivalry sets out as a knight to right the world's wrongs, with absurd results.

def: relevant and appropriate to the subject being discussed
ex: The judge ruled that the witness's comments were not germane to the case.
Please keep your questions germane to the budget; we'll discuss hiring next week.
In the job interview, Nkechi kept her answers germane to the skills the role required.
The teacher asked students to include only germane facts in their history essays.

cloze.s: Her personal travel stories, though entertaining, weren't ___ to the workplace safety training.

def: confident, stylish, and charming, usually describing a well-dressed man
ex: In a tailored navy suit, the debonair host greeted every guest by name.
Kwame looked debonair at the wedding, cracking jokes and dancing with easy grace.
Grandpa Luis was still debonair at eighty, wearing a silk scarf and a perfectly pressed jacket to every family dinner.
The debonair pilot strolled through the airport in his crisp uniform, charming everyone waiting at the gate.

cloze.s: With his slicked-back hair and smooth charm, the ___ actor seemed born to play a gentleman spy.

def: living a careless, immoral life devoted to heavy drinking, gambling, or other excess
ex: The novel follows a dissolute heir who wastes his fortune on parties and card games.
After years of dissolute living, he quit drinking and began rebuilding his health.
His parents feared that their son's dissolute friends would draw him into gambling and late-night drinking.
The film portrays a dissolute king who empties the treasury on wild feasts while his people go hungry.

cloze.s: The biography describes the poet's ___ youth of nightly drinking binges and mounting gambling debts.

def: showing no emotion or reaction, especially on the face; calm and hard to read
ex: The defendant remained impassive as the jury foreperson read the verdict aloud.
Yuki kept an impassive face throughout the poker game, giving nothing away.
The goalkeeper remained impassive as the crowd booed and threw paper cups onto the field.
Her impassive expression gave no hint about whether she liked the gift.

cloze.s: The palace guard stood ___ while tourists made silly faces and tried to make him laugh.

note: Not the same as *impassioned*, which means full of passion, nearly the opposite.

def: sharp, biting, and harsh in speech or humor; critical in a clever, mocking way
ex: The critic's acerbic review called the film 'two hours I will never get back.'
Tomás is known for his acerbic wit, which delights some coworkers and stings others.
The judge on the cooking show is famous for acerbic remarks that make contestants cringe.
Grandma's acerbic letters to the local paper mocked every pothole on her street.

cloze.s: Her ___ comments about his cooking left him embarrassed in front of all the dinner guests.

def: clever and skilled, especially in handling difficult situations or using the hands
ex: The adroit negotiator found a deal that both companies could accept.
Fatima was adroit at calming angry customers before small problems escalated.
The adroit goalkeeper caught the ball with one hand while falling backward.
Maria proved adroit at keeping the peace between her feuding aunts at family dinners.

cloze.s: The surgeon's ___ hands tied the tiny stitches faster than the students could follow.

def: traveling from place to place, especially for work, rather than staying in one location
ex: As a peripatetic music teacher, Liam visits five different schools each week.
Her peripatetic childhood as the daughter of a soldier meant changing schools almost every year.
The circus performers led a peripatetic life, moving to a new town every week.
A peripatetic nurse, Aisha drives to patients' homes across three counties.

cloze.s: The ___ journalist filed stories from a dozen countries in a single year, living out of one suitcase.

def: too sweet or too sentimental, to the point of becoming unpleasant or almost making you feel sick
ex: The frosting was so cloying that Hannah scraped most of it off her slice of cake.
The movie's cloying ending, with everyone hugging in the rain, made the critics groan.
The greeting card's cloying poem about friendship made Malik roll his eyes.
The waiter's cloying flattery, calling every dish perfect for such lovely guests, made Hannah uneasy.

cloze.s: The perfume in the crowded elevator was so heavy and ___ that Wei felt slightly sick.

def: too ready to believe what people say, which makes one easy to trick
ex: Scammers target credulous investors with promises of guaranteed huge returns.
Only the most credulous viewer would believe the late-night commercial for a miracle diet pill.
The credulous child believed his brother's story that spaghetti grows on trees.
Wei was credulous enough to believe an email saying she had won a free cruise.

cloze.s: The ___ tourists paid fifty dollars for a 'genuine' gold watch from a street vendor.

note: Not the same as *credible* (believable): a credulous person believes too easily; a credible story deserves belief.

def: overly dramatic and theatrical in behavior, especially in order to get attention
ex: His histrionic sighs every time he was asked to help annoyed his roommates.
The coach dismissed the player's histrionic fall as an attempt to draw a penalty.
Leo's histrionic groans about doing his homework made his parents laugh.
The reviewer said the actor's histrionic performance, full of shouting and wild gestures, distracted from the story.

cloze.s: She burst into loud sobs over a tiny scratch on her phone, a(n) ___ display that embarrassed her friends.

def: refusing to change one's views or to compromise, even when others want agreement
ex: Talks collapsed because both sides remained intransigent about the overtime rules.
The intransigent landlord refused every request to delay the rent increase.
Negotiators called the other country's position intransigent after it rejected every proposal.
Hannah's father remained intransigent about her curfew, even after she offered to text him every hour.

cloze.s: Despite hours of debate, Jamal stayed ___, insisting on his plan with no changes at all.

def: easily made angry; having a quick, hot temper
ex: The irascible chef shouted at anyone who touched his knives.
Lack of sleep made Malik irascible, and he snapped at his kids over small things.
The irascible old landlord yelled at tenants who parked even an inch over the line.
Our irascible parrot screeches and bites whenever anyone moves its food bowl.

cloze.s: The ___ coach threw his clipboard after the very first missed free throw of the game.

def: strongly bringing something to mind, or smelling strongly of something
ex: The old farmhouse was redolent of woodsmoke and freshly baked bread.
Her speech was redolent of an earlier era, full of hope and old-fashioned moral urgency.
After the beach trip, the car was redolent of sunscreen and wet towels.
The old diner's neon signs and jukebox are redolent of the 1950s.

cloze.s: The kitchen was ___ of garlic and basil after Sofia spent the afternoon making sauce.

note: Usually followed by 'of' or 'with.'

def: eager to fight or start a war; aggressive and hostile
ex: The general's bellicose speeches alarmed the neighboring countries.
After losing the game, a few bellicose fans started shoving people outside the stadium.
The bellicose neighbor threatened to sue anyone whose tree dropped leaves on his yard.
The hockey player's bellicose attitude earned him more penalty minutes than goals.

cloze.s: The ruler's ___ threats of invasion sent diplomats rushing to calm the crisis.

note: Close to *belligerent*; bellicose stresses an eagerness for war or fighting.

def: done secretly and quietly so that others will not notice
ex: Kwame cast a surreptitious glance at his phone during the wedding toast.
The company made surreptitious changes to its privacy policy without notifying users.
With a surreptitious flick of his hand, Liam dropped a piece of chicken to the dog under the table.
Investigators found surreptitious recordings the manager had made of private staff meetings.

cloze.s: During the exam, she made a(n) ___ attempt to read her neighbor's answers without the teacher noticing.

def: describing conflict within a group or organization that harms its own members
ex: Internecine feuds within the club distracted it from its real goals.
The band split up after years of internecine squabbling over songwriting credits and royalties.
Internecine fights among the board members left the charity without a budget for months.
The rebel movement weakened itself through internecine struggles between its rival leaders.

cloze.s: The family business collapsed amid ___ battles among the founder's three children.

note: First meant simply 'deadly'; Samuel Johnson's dictionary recast it as 'mutually destructive.' Today it usually describes infighting within a group.

def: making false, insulting claims meant to damage someone's reputation
ex: The tabloid printed scurrilous rumors about the actor's private life.
Priya sued the blogger for spreading scurrilous accusations about her bakery.
Someone spread a scurrilous rumor that Olga had faked her test results to win the science award.
The coach dismissed the magazine article as a scurrilous attack, full of invented quotes.

cloze.s: The anonymous flyer made ___ claims that the school principal had stolen money from a charity.

def: lazy and unwilling to work or make an effort
ex: The indolent cat spent the whole afternoon sprawled in a patch of sunlight.
Critics called the new manager indolent because he rarely answered emails or attended meetings.
The indolent teenager left his dirty dishes in the sink for days.
Jamal felt pleasantly indolent on vacation, spending whole days lying in a hammock.

cloze.s: After a(n) ___ summer of sleeping late and watching TV, Diego struggled to get back to studying.

also: of a disease, developing slowly and causing little pain or few symptoms (“an indolent tumor”)

def: favorable; showing a good chance of success
ex: With interest rates low, it seemed a propitious time to buy a house.
The clear skies and calm winds were a propitious sign for the rocket launch.
The smooth first meeting was a propitious start to their business partnership.
Farmers waited for propitious weather before planting the corn.

cloze.s: Investors waited for a more ___ moment, when markets had calmed, to announce the merger.

def: silly and pointless, often in a self-satisfied way that shows little thought; foolish
ex: The interviewer asked fatuous questions about the scientist's favorite color.
He wore a fatuous grin while ignoring every warning his friends gave him.
The ad made the fatuous claim that buying a new phone would make your whole life happier.
Stop offering fatuous advice like “just relax” to someone who is clearly in pain.

cloze.s: The host's ___ remarks, smugly stating the obvious, made the panel of experts roll their eyes.

def: ordinary and everyday; happening daily and often dull
ex: The novel finds beauty in quotidian details like washing dishes and catching the bus.
After the vacation, the quotidian routine of commuting to work felt especially gray.
Her diary is full of quotidian notes about groceries, bus schedules, and the weather.
For astronauts, quotidian tasks like brushing teeth become tricky in space.

cloze.s: Her paintings turn ___ objects, such as coffee cups and house keys, into striking works of art.

def: lacking enthusiasm and effort; careless in a relaxed way, as if it does not matter
ex: The team's lackadaisical defense allowed three easy goals in the first half.
Kwame's lackadaisical approach to filing his taxes earned him a late fee.
The restaurant's lackadaisical service meant we waited forty minutes for a glass of water.
Doctors warned that a lackadaisical attitude toward blood pressure medicine can be dangerous.

cloze.s: Her ___ attitude toward homework, finishing it only whenever she felt like it, worried her parents.

def: extremely unwilling to spend money or use resources, even when spending is needed
ex: The parsimonious owner refused to replace the office's broken chairs.
Our parsimonious grandmother saved every rubber band, twist tie, and paper bag.
The parsimonious city council refused to buy new books for the library for a decade.
Diego's parsimonious boss gave each worker a single candy bar as a holiday bonus.

cloze.s: Liam was so ___ that he reused tea bags three times and never turned on the heat.

note: Stronger and more negative than *frugal*.
also: of an explanation or theory, as simple as possible while still fitting the facts (“the most parsimonious explanation”)

def: very cheerful and bursting with energy and enthusiasm
ex: The ebullient host greeted everyone at the door with hugs and laughter.
Fatima was ebullient after hearing she had passed her nursing exams.
The ebullient tour guide sang and joked as she led us through the old town.
Despite the early hour, the ebullient students chattered and laughed all the way to the science museum.

cloze.s: The ___ crowd cheered and danced in the streets after the team won the championship.

def: too eager to please or obey people with power; excessively flattering
ex: The obsequious waiter kept bowing and praising the wealthy diners.
Jamal disliked the obsequious way his coworker agreed with every word the boss said.
The obsequious salesman complimented every outfit Liam tried on, even the ugly ones.
The new intern's obsequious emails to the CEO embarrassed the rest of the team.

cloze.s: The ___ assistant laughed loudly at all of the director's jokes, even the ones that weren't funny.

def: eager to argue or fight, and quick to start a conflict
ex: The pugnacious little terrier barked at dogs three times its size.
Her pugnacious interviewing style made guests nervous on the talk show.
The pugnacious lawyer objected to nearly every question the other side asked.
Kwame's pugnacious attitude at meetings made coworkers dread disagreeing with him.

cloze.s: Known for his ___ temperament, the boxer picked arguments even at polite press conferences.

def: talking far too much, especially about things that do not matter
ex: The garrulous taxi driver told us his whole life story on the way to the airport.
Normally garrulous, Hannah fell silent when the exam results were announced.
Our garrulous neighbor kept me on the porch for an hour talking about his lawn.
Grandma becomes garrulous after her afternoon coffee, telling long stories nobody asked for.

cloze.s: Our ___ seatmate chatted nonstop for the entire six-hour flight.

def: lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; jumping from one thing to another without a clear aim
ex: They made desultory conversation while waiting for the delayed train.
After a desultory search of the parking lot, the guard gave up looking for the lost keys.
Rafael made a few desultory attempts at cleaning his room before giving up and turning on the TV.
The meeting drifted in a desultory way from parking problems to holiday plans, and nothing was decided.

cloze.s: Bored and tired, Wei flipped through the magazine in a(n) ___ way, barely reading a single page.

def: shy and lacking self-confidence; hesitant to speak up or assert oneself
ex: The diffident student rarely raised her hand, though she usually knew the answers.
Malik gave a diffident smile when his colleagues praised his presentation.
Though diffident in class, Ravi became confident and funny once he joined the drama club.
The diffident new employee waited until everyone else had finished speaking before quietly offering her idea.

cloze.s: Too ___ to ask for a raise, Olga waited years for her manager to offer one.

def: very hard to understand because the ideas are complex, specialized, or far from everyday knowledge
ex: The professor's abstruse lecture on quantum theory left most students lost.
Tax law is so abstruse that many people hire an accountant just to file.
The instruction manual was so abstruse that Hannah watched a video online instead.
The lawyer turned the abstruse terms of the contract into plain language for her client.

cloze.s: The philosopher's ___ arguments required several careful readings before Diego could follow them.

def: to put someone or something in danger
ex: Cutting the safety budget could imperil workers at the chemical plant.
The long drought has imperiled crops across the entire region.
Overfishing has imperiled cod in parts of the North Atlantic.
Texting while driving imperils not only the driver but everyone else on the road.

cloze.s: Ignoring the doctor's advice could ___ your recovery after surgery.

def: to go beyond a limit, or to break a moral rule or law
ex: Players who transgress the league's code of conduct will be suspended.
The comedian's jokes transgressed the boundaries of good taste, and the audience fell silent.
By reading her sister's diary, Maria knew she had transgressed an important boundary.
The ancient myth tells of a hero punished for transgressing the laws of the gods.

cloze.s: The monks believe that anyone who ___ the vow of silence must perform extra chores.

def: to reject an offer, request, or friendly approach in a sharp or rude way
