ex: The talk-show host was known for her sharp repartee with guests.
Their dinner-party repartee had everyone at the table laughing.
Sofia and her grandfather enjoy a gentle repartee over breakfast every morning.
The movie's witty repartee between two rival lawyers keeps every scene lively.

cloze.s: The two detectives' playful ___ was the best part of the TV series.

def: the use of clever tricks or dishonest methods to get what one wants
ex: Accounting chicanery hid the company's debt from investors for years.
The lawyer's legal chicanery delayed the trial again and again.
The used-car dealer's chicanery included turning back the mileage on old cars.
The chess club accused the visiting team of chicanery after a player was caught using a phone.

cloze.s: The game show was canceled after viewers discovered the ___ used to fix the results.

def: a generous, forgiving attitude, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful
ex: The winner showed great magnanimity by praising her opponent's courage.
Their magnanimity in forgiving the old debt surprised everyone in the family.
With surprising magnanimity, Diego shared the award money with the coworker who had doubted him.
The general's magnanimity toward the defeated soldiers helped bring a lasting peace.

cloze.s: In a show of ___, the champion invited the defeated challenger to share the stage.

def: a relaxed, calm manner showing little concern, worry, or interest
ex: With practiced nonchalance, he leaned against the wall as if nothing had happened.
Her nonchalance about the final exam annoyed her nervous classmates.
Kwame accepted the award with a nonchalance that hid how excited he really was.
The cat watched the barking dog through the window with complete nonchalance.

cloze.s: The pilot announced the engine trouble with such ___ that the passengers barely worried.

def: an excessive amount of something, more than is needed or wanted
ex: A surfeit of holiday sweets left the children cranky and sick.
The market now has a surfeit of cheap smartphones.
A surfeit of rain this spring has left the farmer's fields too muddy to plant.
With a surfeit of volunteers, the animal shelter had to turn some helpers away.

cloze.s: After a(n) ___ of meetings all week, Jamal had no time left to do any actual work.

def: a bad-tempered, grumpy person, often an older one, who complains a lot
ex: The local curmudgeon writes angry letters to the newspaper every week.
Despite his reputation as a curmudgeon, he secretly fed all the neighborhood cats.
Even the office curmudgeon smiled when the puppy visited on Friday.
Grandpa plays the curmudgeon, grumbling about phones, but he loves video calls with the grandkids.

cloze.s: Our neighbor, a lovable old ___, grumbles about everything from the weather to modern music.

def: reckless waste, especially spending money or resources far too freely
ex: The family fortune vanished through decades of profligacy.
Auditors blamed the city's debt on years of profligacy and poor planning.
The team's profligacy with its salary budget left no money to sign young players.
Fatima's parents warned that her profligacy with her first paycheck would leave nothing for rent.

cloze.s: His ___ with credit cards, buying designer clothes every week, left him deeply in debt.

also: wild, immoral living devoted to pleasure (“a life of profligacy and excess”)

def: an accusation made in response to someone else's accusation; mutual blaming
ex: The project's failure led to weeks of bitter recrimination among the team.
Instead of recriminations, the couple focused calmly on solving the problem.
Their divorce dragged on for years amid bitter recrimination.
After the failed rocket launch, the engineers avoided recriminations and studied what went wrong.

cloze.s: After the loss, the locker room filled with angry ___, each player blaming the others.

note: Often plural: 'mutual recriminations.'

def: a person who praises powerful people too much, in order to gain favor or advantage
ex: The king surrounded himself with sycophants who never told him the truth.
Don't be a sycophant in meetings; give the director your honest opinion.
Tomás refused to become a sycophant just to win a promotion from the vice president.
The movie star's inner circle was full of sycophants who agreed with everything she said.

cloze.s: The executive fired the only adviser who disagreed with her and kept every ___ who praised her ideas.

def: a feeling of guilt or moral hesitation about doing something wrong
ex: He felt no compunction about taking the last slice of pizza.
She lied to her manager without compunction, then blamed a coworker for the mistake.
The cat showed no compunction about knocking my glass off the table.
Diego felt a twinge of compunction after snapping at his little brother.

cloze.s: The con artist had no ___ about taking money from elderly victims.

note: Usually used in the negative: 'no compunction about...'

def: a thing that keeps causing irritation, worry, or fear, often over a long time
ex: Slow internet is the biggest bugbear of people who work from home.
Misplaced apostrophes are a particular bugbear of my English teacher.
Paperwork is the biggest bugbear of nurses, who would rather spend time with patients.
Traffic jams on the bridge are a daily bugbear for commuters heading downtown.

cloze.s: Rising grocery prices have become the main ___ for families trying to stick to a budget.

def: a person with wide and deep knowledge across many different subjects
ex: Leonardo da Vinci, a famous polymath, was a painter, engineer, and inventor.
Our polymath neighbor fixes cars, plays the cello, and teaches physics.
Benjamin Franklin was a polymath who worked as a printer, writer, scientist, and diplomat.
At trivia night, every team wanted Mei, a polymath who seemed to know the answer in every category.

cloze.s: A true ___, Aisha published research in biology, wrote two novels, and composed music.

def: the appearance of being true or real, especially in fiction, film, or art
ex: The novelist used real street names to give the story verisimilitude.
The film's verisimilitude came from shooting in actual hospitals with real nurses.
To add verisimilitude, the video game designers recorded the sounds of real city streets.
The actor lived on a fishing boat for a month to bring verisimilitude to his role as a sailor.

cloze.s: The set designers carefully aged the props to give the period drama greater ___.

def: a remark used so often that it has become dull and meaningless
ex: The graduation speech was full of platitudes about following your dreams.
'Everything happens for a reason' is a platitude that rarely comforts anyone.
When Diego lost his job, his uncle offered only platitudes like “When one door closes, another opens.”
The company's apology was a string of platitudes with no actual plan to fix anything.

cloze.s: Instead of real advice, the coach offered the tired ___ that hard work always pays off.

def: clever-sounding but false or misleading reasoning, often used to trick people
ex: The essay's argument was clever sophistry, sounding logical while hiding a basic error.
Students learned to spot sophistry in advertisements and online debates.
The lawyer's argument that her client had “only borrowed” the money for ten years was sheer sophistry.
Debate coaches teach students to win with solid evidence, not sophistry.

cloze.s: The salesman's claim that spending more would save us money was pure ___.

def: likely to cause resentment or hurt feelings, especially by making unfair comparisons between people
ex: Ranking the volunteers by hours worked put the manager in an invidious position with her team.
Priya refused to make invidious comparisons between her two children's report cards.
The coach had the invidious job of cutting one of two close friends from the final roster.
Posting everyone's salaries on the wall would invite invidious comparisons and resentment in the office.

cloze.s: Choosing just one of three equally deserving nurses for the award was a(n) ___ task that was sure to hurt feelings.

note: Formal; common in 'invidious comparison' and 'invidious position.' Not the same as insidious (harmful in a gradual, hidden way).

def: dishonest and two-faced; ready to break promises and betray people who trust you
ex: The novel's perfidious advisor smiles at the queen while secretly plotting with her enemies.
Fans called the star's sudden move to their rival a perfidious betrayal of the city.
In the legend, a perfidious servant opens the castle gates to the enemy at night.
Hannah never forgave her perfidious friend for sharing her secrets with the whole class.

cloze.s: The ___ business partner secretly sold their client list to a competitor while swearing he was loyal.

note: Formal and strongly negative.

def: showing eager, caring concern for someone's comfort, health or well-being
ex: The nurse was solicitous of Mr. Okafor, checking on his pain every hour through the night.
Our host was so solicitous that she refilled our glasses before we noticed they were empty.
The flight attendant was solicitous toward the nervous passenger, checking on her throughout the trip.
Malik became especially solicitous of his grandmother after her fall, calling her every evening.

cloze.s: After Diego's surgery, his ___ neighbors brought meals daily and kept asking whether he needed anything else.

note: Often followed by 'of' or 'about'; can hint at attention that is a little excessive.

def: sweet, soft and pleasant to hear
ex: The dulcet sound of a flute floated across the quiet garden party.
Wei teased his roommate, who woke everyone at dawn with the dulcet tones of a blaring alarm.
The radio host's dulcet voice made the late-night show feel calm and soothing.
Birds filled the morning with dulcet songs as Hannah drank her coffee on the porch.

cloze.s: The harpist's ___ melody was so soft and sweet that the baby fell asleep within minutes.

note: Often used ironically, as in 'the dulcet tones of' something loud or unpleasant.

def: happening by lucky chance at exactly the right moment, as if arranged by fate
ex: A providential break in the storm let the hikers reach the shelter safely.
Running into an old classmate who worked at the bank proved providential for Aisha's loan application.
Spotting a gas station just as the tank hit empty was a providential stroke of luck on our road trip.
The star player returned from injury on the eve of the final, a providential bit of timing for the coach.

cloze.s: The ___ arrival of an off-duty doctor at the scene of the crash saved the cyclist's life.

also: relating to God's care and guidance of the world (“Many settlers saw their survival as a sign of providential care.”)

def: ridiculously old-fashioned or outdated; literally, from the time before the biblical Flood
ex: The office still runs on an antediluvian computer system that crashes every afternoon.
Sofia rolled her eyes at her uncle's antediluvian ideas about who should cook dinner.
Hannah's antediluvian cell phone could make calls but could not send photos.
The company finally dropped its antediluvian rule that every woman on staff must wear a skirt.

cloze.s: The museum's ___ fax machine, older than most of its staff, finally broke down for good.

note: Usually humorous or mocking. From Latin for 'before the flood.'

def: so unhappy or disappointed that nothing can comfort or cheer you
ex: The disconsolate fans sat in silence long after the final whistle.
Malik was disconsolate for days after his dog ran away.
Yuki was disconsolate when rain washed out the garden party she had planned for months.
The disconsolate boy clutched his popped balloon and would not stop crying.

cloze.s: After missing the deadline by a single day, Hannah sat ___ at her desk, refusing every attempt to cheer her up.

def: full of bitter, long-lasting resentment or hostility
ex: The divorce became rancorous once the couple began fighting over the house.
After a rancorous debate, the town council voted to close the public pool.
The rancorous breakup of the band left the former members refusing to speak for twenty years.
Months of rancorous emails between the two departments finally ended when the boss called a meeting.

cloze.s: Years of ___ feuding over a property line left the two families unable to share a single holiday.

def: too eager to give orders or unwanted help, interfering in other people's business, especially about small matters
ex: An officious security guard insisted on checking every bag twice, even the empty ones.
Olga found her officious coworker exhausting, since he corrected everyone's emails without being asked.
An officious neighbor called the city to complain that Diego's grass was half an inch too long.
The officious waiter kept interrupting our conversation to refold our napkins.

cloze.s: The ___ hall monitor scolded students for walking too slowly and reported them for every tiny rule breach.

note: Not the same as 'official.' Negative: describes someone who overuses a little authority.

def: insisting on being obeyed at once, in a short, rude way that allows no discussion
ex: The manager's peremptory email simply said, 'Be in my office at nine.'
Tomás bristled at the peremptory tone the clerk used with elderly customers.
With a peremptory knock, the landlord demanded to be let in at once.
The coach's peremptory “Sit down!” silenced the arguing players.

cloze.s: With a(n) ___ wave of her hand, the director dismissed the question and ordered everyone back to work.

also: in law, final and not open to debate or appeal (“The court issued a peremptory order to the city.”)

def: joking about sex or bodily functions in a crude but playful, humorous way
ex: The comedian's ribald jokes made some guests laugh and others blush.
Old sailors' songs are full of ribald verses about life ashore.
The audience roared at the comedian's ribald story about an embarrassing trip to the doctor.
Shakespeare's plays include many ribald puns that teachers sometimes skip in class.

cloze.s: Grandma was shocked when the best man's toast turned ___, full of crude, cheeky jokes about the honeymoon.

def: calm by nature and showing little feeling; not easily excited, upset or stirred to action
ex: Jamal's phlegmatic manner made him a steady presence in the chaotic newsroom.
Even when the flight was canceled, the phlegmatic traveler simply opened a book and waited.
The phlegmatic farmer barely looked up when the storm blew his barn door off.
Tour guides need a phlegmatic temperament to handle lost passports and missed trains.

cloze.s: Unlike his excitable brother, the ___ Kwame rarely showed strong feelings of any kind, even at weddings.

note: Neutral or mildly negative (can suggest dullness). Comes from the old medical theory of four 'humors,' one being phlegm.

def: staying calm and in control even during a crisis or under great pressure
ex: The unflappable pilot calmly guided the plane through heavy turbulence.
As a teacher, Fatima is unflappable, no matter how loud the class gets.
The unflappable nurse calmly organized the emergency room during the power outage.
Even when the toddler spilled juice on her laptop, Hannah remained unflappable.

cloze.s: Even when the stage lights failed mid-speech, the ___ host kept talking as if nothing had happened.

note: Informal and positive; from 'flap,' meaning a state of panic.

def: only just beginning to form, so not yet fully developed, clear or organized
ex: Priya had an inchoate idea for a business but no real plan yet.
The protest movement was still inchoate, with no leaders or clear demands.
The committee's plans for the park were still inchoate, with no map, budget or schedule.
Yusuf felt an inchoate sense of unease before he could even say what was bothering him.

cloze.s: His thoughts about the novel were still ___, a jumble of images without a plot or main characters.

note: Pronounced in-KOH-it. Comes from Latin for 'begin,' not from 'chaos.'

def: so closely linked or tangled together that the parts cannot be separated
ex: For Kwame, music and memory are inextricable; every song recalls a moment from his past.
The city's history is inextricable from the river that runs through it.
In the old mill town, the fortunes of the factory and its workers were inextricable.
In the novel, the twins' lives are so inextricable that neither can make a decision alone.

cloze.s: Money worries and health problems had become ___ for the family, so fixing one without the other was impossible.

def: lying regularly, or deliberately false; not telling the truth
ex: The company's mendacious ads claimed the drink could cure the common cold.
Reporters exposed the mendacious claims in the official statement within hours.
The mendacious salesman swore the car had never been in an accident.
Fact-checkers labeled the viral post mendacious, pointing out three invented statistics.

cloze.s: The witness's ___ testimony fell apart when security footage showed she had been home all night.

def: highly relevant and well suited to the situation or topic being discussed
ex: Liam opened his speech with an apposite quote about courage.
The lawyer's apposite question exposed the gap in the witness's story.
The teacher chose an apposite poem about change to read on graduation day.
Fatima's apposite example from her own job helped the class understand the theory.

cloze.s: Her remark about the dangers of overconfidence was especially ___, given that the team had just lost to the last-place side.

note: Formal. Not the same as 'opposite.'

def: having an extreme, selfish desire for money or possessions
ex: The avaricious landlord raised the rent every year while ignoring repairs.
In the old story, an avaricious king wished that everything he touched would turn to gold.
The avaricious heirs fought for years over every piece of their uncle's furniture.
Fans accused avaricious ticket resellers of charging ten times the printed price.

cloze.s: The ___ collector bought every rare coin he could find, never satisfied with what he already owned.

def: completely clear and transparent, like still, clean water
ex: We could see fish darting over the sand in the limpid lagoon.
The pond was so limpid that every pebble on the bottom was visible.
In the limpid tide pools, Amara could see crabs scuttling between the stones.
After the snow melted, the creek ran limpid and cold over smooth gray rocks.

cloze.s: Yuki snorkeled in the ___ mountain lake, where the water was as clear as glass.

also: of writing or music, clear and easy to follow (“Her limpid prose is a pleasure to read.”)

def: talking easily, quickly and at great length; always ready to chat
ex: Our voluble tour guide kept up a stream of stories for three hours.
Usually voluble, Hannah went oddly quiet when asked about her new job.
My voluble seatmate on the flight told me her whole life story before we even took off.
The voluble host of the morning radio show can talk for an hour without needing a guest.

cloze.s: The ___ salesman talked nonstop through the entire test drive, barely pausing to breathe.

def: excessively flattering and smoothly polite in a way that seems fake and self-serving
ex: The unctuous waiter praised every single order as 'an excellent choice.'
Guests grew tired of the host's unctuous smile and endless empty compliments.
The unctuous salesman called Hannah “my dear friend” within thirty seconds of meeting her.
Staff disliked the new manager's unctuous praise of the CEO at every single meeting.

cloze.s: The ___ realtor gushed over every room, calling a cramped closet 'charming,' which made us trust him less.

note: Strongly negative. Its literal meaning is 'oily or greasy.'

def: looking or sounding very sad and serious, often in an exaggerated way
ex: The basset hound gazed up at us with its lugubrious, droopy eyes.
The band's lugubrious ballads made the birthday party feel like a funeral.
The undertaker in the old comedy spoke in such a lugubrious voice that the children giggled.
Even after the team's big win, Coach Ahmed wore his usual lugubrious expression at the press conference.

cloze.s: The old movie's slow, ___ theme music had half the audience feeling gloomy before the opening scene ended.

def: grossly unfair and morally wrong; wicked
ex: Critics called the tax that fell hardest on the poorest families iniquitous.
The report described iniquitous working conditions inside the factory.
Workers protested the iniquitous system that paid them half as much as coworkers doing the same job.
The court struck down the iniquitous rule that let landlords evict tenants without any notice.

cloze.s: Charging desperate patients ten times the normal price for basic medicine was a(n) ___ practice.

def: stubbornly refusing to change your mind or behavior, no matter what others say or do
ex: Despite every appeal, the obdurate official refused to reopen the case.
Diego remained obdurate, insisting the restaurant had gotten his order wrong.
The obdurate landlord refused to return the deposit, even after seeing photos of the spotless apartment.
Despite his doctor's warnings, Grandpa remained obdurate about eating salty food.

cloze.s: No matter how many engineers explained the risks, the ___ owner would not delay the bridge's opening.

def: eager to argue or fight; aggressive and ready for conflict
ex: The truculent customer was shouting at staff before the manager even arrived.
Teenagers can turn truculent when they feel they are being treated unfairly.
The truculent neighbor threatened to call the police over a single leaf on his lawn.
The talks stalled because the truculent negotiator answered every offer with insults.

cloze.s: When the referee warned him, the ___ player squared up as if he wanted to fight the official too.

def: in keeping with good taste and proper behavior; calm, polite and correct
ex: The wedding guests remained decorous until the dancing started.
Students were asked to keep a decorous silence during the ceremony.
The courtroom was decorous and quiet as the judge entered.
The diplomats exchanged decorous handshakes, even though their countries were bitter rivals.

cloze.s: Even at the noisy family reunion, Grandma Sofia expected a(n) ___ dinner, with napkins on laps and no shouting.

def: deliberately one-sided, presenting a biased view in order to promote a particular cause or opinion
ex: The documentary was so tendentious that it ignored every expert who disagreed.
Reviewers criticized the history book as tendentious for cherry-picking its evidence.
The museum's tendentious exhibit showed only the factory's benefits and none of its pollution.
Teachers asked students to compare a balanced news article with a tendentious opinion blog.

cloze.s: The pamphlet's ___ summary of the study left out every finding that weakened its argument.

note: Not the same as 'tenuous' (weak or flimsy).

def: so light, delicate and thin that you can almost see through it, usually of fabric
ex: The dancer wore a diaphanous scarf that fluttered as she spun across the stage.
Diaphanous curtains let soft morning light fill the bedroom.
Yuki sewed a diaphanous white costume for the ghost in the school play.
The dragonfly's diaphanous wings let the sunlight shine through.

cloze.s: A(n) ___ veil of fine silk floated over the bride's face without hiding her smile.

def: severely critical of others; quick to find fault and to judge
ex: A censorious neighbor complained about every paint color on the street.
Maria worried that her censorious mother-in-law would criticize the holiday dinner.
Liam dreaded posting photos online because of his censorious classmates, who mocked every flaw.
The new coach was censorious, pointing out every tiny error but never praising a good play.

cloze.s: The ___ critic found fault with nearly every film he reviewed and rarely gave more than one star.

note: Related to 'censor,' but means harshly critical, not banning things.

def: behaving as if you are better than others; proud and looking down on people
ex: The sommelier gave a supercilious smile when Liam asked for ice in his wine.
Her supercilious tone made the new interns afraid to ask questions.
The supercilious food critic sniffed at the diner's menu before tasting a single dish.
Kwame's older cousin gave him a supercilious glance when he admitted he had never read any classics.

cloze.s: Raising one eyebrow, the ___ clerk looked down at our muddy boots as if we were beneath his notice.

def: sentimental in an exaggerated, too-sweet way that feels false or embarrassing
ex: The movie's mawkish ending, with swelling violins and tearful hugs, made critics groan.
Kwame avoided mawkish greeting cards and wrote his own simple note instead.
Critics praised the novel for handling grief honestly without ever becoming mawkish.
The best man's speech turned mawkish as he sobbed for ten minutes about true love and destiny.

cloze.s: The ad was so ___, with slow-motion puppies and syrupy music, that viewers found it more cringeworthy than moving.

def: innocent, open and trusting, sometimes too much so; lacking cunning or worldly experience
ex: Her ingenuous question about who pays for the free samples made the whole room laugh.
Aisha had an ingenuous faith that everyone at her new job wanted to help her.
Lena's ingenuous belief that every online review was honest led her to a terrible hotel.
With an ingenuous smile, the five-year-old told the guests exactly how much the new couch had cost.

cloze.s: The ___ young tourist believed the stranger's story and handed over his wallet for 'safekeeping.'

note: Not 'ingenious' (clever). Its opposite, 'disingenuous,' means insincere.

def: too large, strong or difficult to be overcome
ex: Lack of funding proved an insuperable obstacle for the small museum.
To the exhausted team, a ten-goal deficit seemed insuperable.
What once looked like insuperable problems in the bridge design were solved by a young engineer.
Without a visa or any savings, moving abroad seemed an insuperable challenge to Amara.

cloze.s: Without roads or bridges, the jagged mountains posed a(n) ___ barrier to the invading army.

def: showing far too much confidence or pride; arrogant and expecting more than one deserves
ex: His overweening ambition eventually cost him every friendship he had.
Analysts blamed the company's collapse on its overweening confidence in a single product.
The general's overweening pride led him to ignore his scouts' warnings.
Lena's overweening confidence in her cooking ended when the soufflé collapsed in front of her guests.

cloze.s: Her ___ pride made her ignore all advice, certain she could win the marathon without ever training.

note: Usually before 'ambition,' 'pride' or 'confidence.'

def: minor and easily forgiven; not seriously wrong
ex: Forgetting to return a borrowed pen is a venial offense, not a betrayal.
The editor overlooked venial slips in style but never factual errors.
Leaving dishes in the sink overnight is a venial sin in Olga's house, but lying is not.
The coach forgave venial mistakes in practice, such as a dropped pass, but never laziness.

cloze.s: Compared with stealing the money, his habit of arriving five minutes late was a(n) ___ fault.

note: In Catholic teaching, a venial sin is less serious than a mortal sin. Don't confuse with 'venal' (open to bribery).

def: producing many offspring, crops or new ideas; highly fertile or productive
ex: The fecund river valley grew enough grain to feed the entire region.
Wei's fecund imagination produced a new story idea almost every week.
The fecund tomato plants gave us more fruit than we could eat all summer.
Those early years were a fecund time for the band, which wrote dozens of songs.

cloze.s: Rabbits are famously ___, with a single pair able to produce dozens of young in one year.

def: easily annoyed and bad-tempered; grumpy and hard to please
ex: The crotchety cat hissed at anyone who sat in its favorite chair.
Malik gets crotchety when he hasn't had his morning coffee.
The crotchety bus driver refused to wait even five seconds for passengers running to catch up.
After two weeks with a bad cold, Wei was crotchety and complained about everything.

cloze.s: Short on sleep after the overnight flight, Priya was ___ all day, snapping at anyone who spoke to her.

note: Informal; often used of older people, but fits anyone in a grumpy mood.

def: done carelessly, without enough attention to detail or quality
ex: The slipshod repair job left water leaking under the sink within a week.
The teacher would not accept slipshod essays full of spelling errors.
The auditor criticized the company's slipshod record keeping, with receipts missing for whole months.
Slipshod cleaning in a hospital can let germs spread from one patient to the next.

cloze.s: Inspectors blamed the collapse on ___ construction, with missing bolts and badly mixed concrete.

def: so ridiculous or poor that it deserves to be laughed at
ex: The team's risible defense allowed six goals in the first half alone.
Tomás called the offer of a one-dollar raise risible and walked out of the meeting.
Critics found the movie's special effects risible, with monsters that looked like rubber bath toys.
The landlord's risible claim that we had caused the roof leak was quickly rejected by the court.

cloze.s: The thief's excuse, that the TV had somehow fallen into his car by accident, was frankly ___.

note: Usually scornful.

def: extremely bad or unpleasant; of terrible quality
ex: The hotel's food was execrable, so we ate at the diner every night.
Olga apologized for her execrable handwriting on the birthday card.
Critics called the sequel execrable, with a plot that made no sense and wooden acting.
The phone reception at the cabin was execrable; calls dropped every few seconds.

cloze.s: The coffee at the bus station was ___: bitter, burnt and served lukewarm in a leaky cup.

def: extremely badly; to a terribly low standard or degree
ex: The team played abysmally and lost by thirty points.
Wages at the old factory were abysmally low, even for the region.
Fatima did abysmally on her first driving test, failing to stop at two signs.
The new phone's battery life is abysmally short, lasting barely half a day.

cloze.s: The new restaurant was so ___ run that orders took two hours and half of them were wrong.

def: in a gradual, hidden way that causes harm before anyone notices
ex: Mold had spread insidiously behind the walls for years before anyone noticed the smell.
Chronic stress can insidiously damage health over many years.
Doubt crept insidiously into the team, and by midseason no one believed they could win.
The scam worked insidiously, taking a few dollars a month so that customers never noticed.

cloze.s: High blood pressure works ___, causing serious damage for years without obvious symptoms.

def: in a smooth, easy way that sounds too quick or shallow to be sincere or well thought out
ex: The spokesperson glibly promised the problem would be fixed by Friday.
It's easy to glibly tell someone to 'just relax' when you aren't the one worrying.
The salesman glibly assured Tomás that the used car had never been in an accident.
Doctors should never glibly promise that a treatment will work.

cloze.s: He answered the tough question ___, with a quick joke that showed he hadn't really thought about it.

def: in a joking, not serious way, often about a serious matter when humor may be inappropriate
ex: Jamal facetiously suggested selling his car to pay for one fancy dinner.
She was speaking facetiously, but her boss took the comment literally.
“I'll just quit and become a pirate,” Hannah said facetiously after a terrible day at work.
The coach facetiously thanked the thunderstorm for giving his tired players a day off.

cloze.s: When asked how the exam went, Yuki ___ replied that she had probably invented a new branch of math.

def: in a grim, mocking or cynical way, as if bitterly amused
ex: 'Great, another meeting about meetings,' Liam said sardonically.
The critic smiled sardonically as the actor forgot his lines yet again.
When the fourth bus in a row drove past full, the waiting commuters began to applaud sardonically.
The exhausted nurse laughed sardonically when asked whether she ever got a lunch break.

cloze.s: Stuck in traffic for the third hour, Maria ___ remarked that at least they would get to see the sunrise.

def: without showing any emotion or reaction on your face or in your manner
ex: The judge listened impassively as the verdict was read aloud.
The palace guard stared impassively ahead while tourists tried to make him laugh.
Rosa listened impassively as her brother begged for another loan, then simply said no.

def: said privately and not to be officially reported, published or quoted
ex: The official spoke to reporters off the record about the investigation.
Off the record, the coach admitted the team was exhausted.

The mayor's aide asked that her comments about the budget stay off the record.

cloze.s: The source agreed to talk only ___, so her name won't appear in the article.

def: people have not yet reached a decision or agreement about something
ex: The jury is still out on whether the new diet actually works.
Two months after the launch, the jury is still out on the app's success.
Hannah likes her new job so far, but the jury is still out on her long commute.
The jury is still out on whether the new traffic lights have reduced accidents.

cloze.s: Some early studies look promising, but ___ on whether the supplement prevents colds.

def: the existing state of affairs, especially in social, political or business matters
ex: Many employees are comfortable with the status quo and resist the new software.

The new coach shook up the status quo by benching two veteran players.
Workers voted to keep the status quo rather than switch to a four-day week.

cloze.s: The reformers pushed for change, while the old guard defended the ___.

def: created or done for one particular purpose or situation, not planned in advance
ex: The neighbors formed an ad hoc committee to deal with the flooding.

When the regular coach got sick, the parents set up an ad hoc schedule for practices.
The airline set up an ad hoc help desk in the terminal after the storm canceled hundreds of flights.

cloze.s: There was no formal policy, so decisions were made on a(n) ___ basis as problems came up.

def: existing in reality, even if not officially or legally recognized
ex: Because few people use the official app, group texts became the de facto way to share news.
With no formal rules, the longest-serving employee became the de facto office manager.
With her parents working late, Yuki became the de facto cook for her younger brothers.
The wide hallway outside the library became the students' de facto study room.

cloze.s: While the director was on leave, Kwame became the ___ head of the department, though he had no official title.

origin: Latin for 'from the fact,' meaning in fact.
note: Contrasts with de jure, 'by law': what is so in practice versus what is so officially.

def: something given or done in exchange for something else; a favor for a favor
ex: The deal was a simple quid pro quo: free advertising in exchange for sponsoring the event.

cloze.s: She agreed to help him move, but only as a(n) ___: he'd babysit her kids next weekend.

def: a public admission that you are at fault or have made a mistake
ex: The CEO issued a mea culpa after customer data was exposed in a breach.

The restaurant posted a mea culpa online after dozens of customers got sick from spoiled food.
The airline's president delivered a televised mea culpa after a computer failure stranded thousands of travelers.

cloze.s: The newspaper published a front-page ___ admitting its story contained serious errors.

origin: Latin for 'through my fault,' from a prayer of confession used in the Catholic Mass.

def: repeated or continued so much that it becomes annoying or boring
ex: My uncle discusses his golf scores ad nauseam at every family dinner.
The same car commercial played ad nauseam throughout the playoffs.
On the long drive to Ohio, the twins sang the same camp song ad nauseam.
The manager repeated the safety rules ad nauseam until every worker could recite them in their sleep.

cloze.s: The radio station played the same three songs ___ until the whole office was sick of them.

origin: Latin for 'to the point of sickness.'
note: Often misspelled 'ad nauseum.'

def: the central purpose that justifies someone's or something's existence
ex: Helping new immigrants find jobs is the charity's raison d'être.
For Olga, playing the cello was her raison d'être.
The festival's raison d'être is to raise money for the children's hospital.
After retiring, Malik found a new raison d'être in coaching youth soccer.

cloze.s: Teaching children to read is the program's entire ___; without it, there would be no point to the organization.

def: a policy of minimal interference, letting people or markets act freely without control
ex: The manager's laissez-faire style let each team set its own schedule.
Laissez-faire economists argue that governments should rarely regulate business.
The city's laissez-faire attitude toward street vendors let food carts pop up on every corner.
The school's laissez-faire approach to the dress code means students wear almost anything they like.

cloze.s: The parents took a(n) ___ approach, letting their teenagers set their own curfews.

origin: French for 'let do,' meaning let people act as they choose.

def: in strong, ongoing disagreement or conflict with someone
ex: The two departments have been at loggerheads over the budget for months.
Residents are at loggerheads with the city about the planned highway expansion.
Wei and his sister have been at loggerheads over who should care for their aging father.
The coach and the star player were at loggerheads about his role on the team.

cloze.s: The union and management remain ___, and neither side is willing to compromise.

def: a result that is certain and obvious even before it happens
ex: With their star player injured, the team's loss seemed a foregone conclusion.

cloze.s: Everyone expected the popular senior to be elected class president; her victory was ___.

note: Spelled fore- ('before'), not 'forgone.'

def: something that has both helpful and harmful effects
ex: Fame is a double-edged sword: it brings money but destroys privacy.
Working from home can be a double-edged sword for people who struggle to switch off.
A big promotion can be a double-edged sword: more money, but much longer hours.

cloze.s: A strong currency is ___: imports become cheaper, but exporters lose sales.

def: to issue a challenge, especially one inviting someone to compete or fight
ex: The new airline threw down the gauntlet with fares half the price of its rivals.
Aisha threw down the gauntlet: whoever sold fewer raffle tickets would buy lunch.

cloze.s: By announcing a cheaper, faster phone, the small startup ___ to the industry giants.

origin: A medieval knight challenged an opponent by throwing down his gauntlet, an armored glove.

def: to refuse to change your opinion or decision despite opposition or pressure
ex: Despite harsh criticism, the director stuck to her guns and kept the controversial ending.
Wei stuck to his guns and refused to sign the unfair contract.
The referee stuck to his guns, refusing to change the call despite boos from the crowd.
Aisha's parents wanted a big wedding, but she stuck to her guns and kept it small.

cloze.s: Her whole family urged Hannah to switch her major to business, but she ___ and stayed with art.

def: to argue or come into conflict with someone
ex: The critic and the director crossed swords in a heated public exchange.
Olga crossed swords with the board over the hiring plan.
Wei and his father-in-law cross swords every Thanksgiving over football.
The two scientists crossed swords at the conference over how to read the data.

cloze.s: The two chefs had ___ many times before, so nobody was surprised when they argued at the competition.

def: to make an obvious query arise; traditionally, to assume in an argument the very thing being proved
ex: The team spent its whole budget by March, which begs the question of how it will operate until December.

cloze.s: Rents have doubled downtown, which ___: who can still afford to live there?

note: Purists insist on the traditional logic sense (circular reasoning, Latin 'petitio principii'); the 'raise the question' use is now far more common.

def: to try to persuade people who already agree with you
ex: Sharing the article in a group of fellow cyclists is just preaching to the choir.
The speaker realized she was preaching to the choir and rewrote her talk for skeptics.
The nurse knew she was preaching to the choir when she told the marathon runners to drink water.
You're preaching to the choir, Hannah; I already canceled my cable TV.

cloze.s: Telling a room full of environmental activists to recycle is ___; they already do.

note: Also 'preach to the converted.'

def: a situation in which one side's gain exactly equals the other side's loss
ex: Trade isn't always a zero-sum game; both countries can benefit.

cloze.s: Promotions here feel like ___: if Diego moves up, someone else is left behind.

origin: From game theory, the mathematical study of strategic decision-making.

def: a personal stake, usually money, in an outcome, so that you share the risk
ex: Investors trust founders more when the founders have their own skin in the game.
Requiring a down payment ensures that buyers have skin in the game.
Since Liam paid half the cost of his car, he has skin in the game and drives carefully.
Coaches who own part of the team have more skin in the game than hired staff.

cloze.s: The managers invested their own savings in the company, so they have real ___.

def: a long struggle in which each side tries to wear the other down gradually
ex: The price fight between the two airlines became a war of attrition.
The lawsuit turned into a war of attrition, with each side hoping the other would run out of money.
The strike became a war of attrition as workers and owners waited each other out.
Our fight against the ants in the kitchen turned into a war of attrition that lasted all summer.

cloze.s: Neither candidate could land a decisive blow, so the long primary became ___.

def: a final cutting remark made just as someone is leaving
ex: As he left the meeting, Kwame fired a parting shot about the manager's poor planning.

As she left the party, Yuki's parting shot was a sharp comment about the host's cooking.
In his final broadcast before retiring, the news anchor took a parting shot at his old bosses.

cloze.s: On his way out the door, the fired coach delivered ___ aimed at the team's owners.

def: to unite defensively to protect a group from outside criticism or attack
ex: After the scandal broke, the company's leaders circled the wagons and refused to comment.
The family circled the wagons when reporters started calling the house.
When a reporter questioned the school's test scores, teachers and parents circled the wagons.
Hospital staff circled the wagons after a news story criticized their emergency room.

cloze.s: When fans attacked the team's star after the loss, the players ___ and defended him publicly.

def: a prominent public position that gives someone a strong platform to promote their views
ex: The mayor used her bully pulpit to promote free vaccination clinics.
Coaches of famous teams have a bully pulpit for speaking about youth fitness.
The famous chef used her bully pulpit to push for healthier school lunches.
The talk show host used his bully pulpit to encourage viewers to donate blood.

cloze.s: As a famous athlete, Malik used his ___ to raise money for children's hospitals.

origin: Coined by Theodore Roosevelt, when 'bully' was slang for 'excellent.'
note: Has nothing to do with bullying.

def: describing a quick, rough calculation done informally rather than carefully or precisely
ex: A back-of-the-envelope estimate suggests the project will cost about two million dollars.

Kwame's back-of-the-envelope budget showed he could afford the apartment if he cooked at home.

cloze.s: Using a quick ___ calculation, the engineer guessed the old bridge could hold forty trucks.

def: a win that brings little real benefit or satisfaction
ex: Winning the lawsuit was a hollow victory after legal fees swallowed the entire settlement.

cloze.s: Beating his brother at chess was ___ for Tomás, since his brother had barely paid attention.

note: Close to a 'Pyrrhic victory,' which stresses that the win cost too much.

def: the principle that buyers are responsible for checking quality before purchasing
ex: At flea markets, caveat emptor applies, so inspect everything before you pay.
Buying a used car from a stranger online is a classic case of caveat emptor.
Caveat emptor: concert tickets bought from strangers online may turn out to be fake.
The used-book seller's sign read, 'All sales final, caveat emptor.'

cloze.s: The seller offers no refunds or guarantees, so the rule here is ___.

def: as an automatic, direct result of that very act or circumstance
ex: Under the club's rules, missing three meetings ipso facto ends your membership.

cloze.s: Under the treaty, signing it ___ makes a country subject to the court's rulings.

def: something already done or decided, leaving those affected no choice but to accept it
ex: By the time residents heard about the new highway, it was a fait accompli.

cloze.s: The manager signed the contract before consulting the team, presenting them with a(n) ___.

def: the general spirit, mood and ideas typical of a particular period of history

def: pleasure felt at someone else's misfortune or failure

cloze.s: When the arrogant player tripped over his own feet while celebrating, the crowd couldn't hide its ___.

def: someone who is unwelcome or not accepted, especially a diplomat expelled by a host country
ex: After leaking the club's secrets, Liam became persona non grata at its meetings.

cloze.s: After selling the team's playbook to a rival, the former coach was ___ at the stadium.

def: an outstanding performance or achievement that shows great skill

origin: French for 'feat of strength' or 'feat of skill.'

def: a final blow or event that ends something already weakened or failing

def: a typical way of working or doing something, especially a criminal's characteristic methods

def: harmed or defeated by the very scheme one devised to hurt someone else

def: to criticize indirectly by praising so weakly that the approval actually sounds negative

def: to gain an advantage over a rival by acting earlier or more quickly than they do

def: to be in the position of control or advantage over others in a situation

def: to keep resisting a change or defeat that will probably happen anyway
ex: Video rental stores fought a rearguard action against streaming before most of them closed.

def: advice that is ideal in theory but too demanding to follow in practice

def: to act or speak mainly to win popular applause rather than to achieve something serious
ex: The lawyer's dramatic speech played to the gallery but did little to persuade the judge.

def: a small sign that hints at what is likely to happen in the future

cloze.s: The first few empty storefronts downtown were ___, signaling the slowdown to come.

term: nail one's colors to the mast
def: to declare one's position publicly and firmly, making it impossible to back down later

cloze.a: nailed her colors to the mast

origin: A warship whose flag, or colors, was nailed to the mast could not lower it to surrender.

def: to take risks by acting near the limits of what is legal or acceptable
ex: The accountant's aggressive tax strategies sailed close to the wind, and auditors soon noticed.

def: a difficult, awkward situation that is hard to handle without causing offense or harm
ex: Telling a major client that their project is over budget is a sticky wicket.

cloze.s: Explaining to both families why the wedding was suddenly postponed was ___.

origin: From cricket: a pitch drying after rain makes the ball bounce unpredictably, making batting difficult.

def: to behave carelessly or dishonestly, especially with facts, rules or other people's trust
ex: The documentary played fast and loose with history, inventing entire conversations.

def: a law, rule or agreement that formally still exists but is no longer enforced or obeyed
ex: The town's ban on Sunday shopping has been a dead letter for decades.

def: an essential condition; something absolutely necessary, without which another thing cannot exist

def: unique; so unusual that it forms a category of its own
ex: The musician's blend of jazz and folk was sui generis, impossible to imitate.

cloze.s: Critics struggled to label the novel; it was truly ___, unlike anything written before it.

def: a statement or conclusion that does not logically follow from what came before it
ex: 'It's raining, so we should buy a new car' is a classic non sequitur.

cloze.s: Asked about rising prices, the spokesperson praised the company's new logo, an obvious ___.

def: a passionate, heartfelt appeal or protest
ex: The teacher's open letter was a cri de coeur for smaller class sizes.

The farmers' letter to the governor was a cri de coeur about the long drought.

def: a person or thing that someone especially dislikes, dreads or finds troublesome
ex: Spelling tests were Diego's bête noire throughout elementary school.

For the famous chef, soggy French fries are a personal bête noire.

cloze.s: Long, pointless meetings are Hannah's ___; she avoids them whenever she possibly can.

def: a powerful adviser who shapes decisions from behind the scenes without holding official authority
ex: Though she held no title, the founder's sister was the company's éminence grise.

The coach's quiet assistant was the éminence grise behind every trade the team made.

cloze.s: Officially just a consultant, he was the ___ who quietly shaped every major decision the CEO made.

origin: French for 'gray eminence,' first used of Father Joseph, the gray-robed friar who advised Cardinal Richelieu.

def: a comprehensive philosophy or outlook on the world and humanity's place in it
ex: The novelist's Weltanschauung, shaped by years of war, colors every chapter of her work.
A year studying abroad reshaped Aisha's entire Weltanschauung.
Growing up on a farm gave Kwame a Weltanschauung built on patience and hard work.
The professor argued that every major religion offers its followers a complete Weltanschauung.

cloze.s: To understand the philosopher's ethics, you must first grasp her broader ___.

origin: German, from Welt 'world' and Anschauung 'view, perception.'
note: Capitalized because all German nouns are; 'worldview' is the everyday English equivalent.

def: the shared pride, loyalty and team spirit felt among members of a group
ex: The demanding training camp built a strong esprit de corps among the rookies.
Weekly team lunches helped restore esprit de corps after the painful layoffs.
The firefighters' esprit de corps kept them going through the long wildfire season.
Winning the robotics contest together gave the class a new esprit de corps.

cloze.s: The nurses' ___ was obvious: they covered each other's shifts and celebrated each other's wins.

origin: French for 'spirit of the body,' meaning the group as a whole.

def: to offer unwanted advice or comments, especially while watching others play a game
ex: Grandpa loves to kibitz at the chess tables in the park, critiquing every move.
Please don't kibitz while I'm working on the crossword; I want to solve it myself.
During the video game tournament, Mateo's friends kibitzed behind him, shouting which buttons he should press.
Ana couldn't concentrate on her putt with her brother kibitzing about her grip from the edge of the green.

cloze.s: Onlookers crowded around the card table to ___, suggesting plays no one had asked for.

origin: Yiddish, from German kiebitzen 'to look on at cards,' from Kiebitz, the lapwing, a noisy bird.
note: Also means to chat or joke casually; a person who does it is a kibitzer.

story: In a later legend, best known from the Roman poet Statius, the sea goddess Thetis dipped her baby son Achilles in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, holding him by the heel. That one untouched spot was where an arrow later struck and killed him at Troy.
def: a small but serious weakness in someone or something that is otherwise strong
ex: Priya is a brilliant surgeon, but her Achilles' heel is paperwork, which she always leaves until the last minute.
The team's defense is excellent; its Achilles' heel is a lack of speed on the counterattack.
Wei did well in every subject at school, but spelling was her Achilles' heel.
The old bridge's Achilles' heel was a single rusty support beam that could fail in a flood.

cloze.s: Strong sales, low debt, loyal customers — the company's one ___ is that it depends on a single supplier.

story: In Greek myth, Pandora, the first woman, opened a jar that released sickness, toil, and other evils into the world; only hope remained inside. Later retellings turned the jar into a box.
def: an action that unleashes a whole series of unexpected problems that cannot be undone
ex: Changing the tax code without studying it first could open a Pandora's box of legal challenges.
Diego worried that asking about the old family feud would open Pandora's box at Thanksgiving dinner.
Allowing phones in class opened a Pandora's box of cheating and distractions for the teachers.
Changing one line of old code opened a Pandora's box of bugs across the whole website.

cloze.s: Once the city allowed one exception to the zoning rules, it opened a(n) ___, and dozens of developers demanded the same treatment.

story: In Greek legend, after ten years of besieging Troy, the Greeks built a huge wooden horse, hid soldiers inside, and pretended to sail away. The Trojans brought the horse into their city, and that night the hidden soldiers opened the gates to the Greek army.
def: something that looks harmless or welcome but secretly brings in danger or an enemy from within
ex: The free app was a Trojan horse that quietly collected users' contacts and location data.
Critics called the small amendment a Trojan horse for much bigger changes to the law.
The rival company's offer to share office space was a Trojan horse that let it copy the startup's ideas.
Some parents saw the free school tablets as a Trojan horse for ads aimed at their children.

cloze.s: The friendly-looking email attachment was a(n) ___: once opened, it let hackers into the hospital's network.

note: In computing, a “Trojan” is malicious software disguised as a useful program.

story: In Greek myth, King Midas of Phrygia was granted his wish that everything he touched would turn to gold. He soon regretted it when even his food turned to gold, and he begged to have the gift taken away.
def: the ability to make money or succeed at almost everything one attempts
ex: Kwame seems to have the Midas touch; every restaurant he opens is packed within a month.
The producer's Midas touch faded after three expensive flops in a row.
The coach seems to have the Midas touch, turning every losing team she takes over into a winner.
Every clothing line the young designer launched sold out, and magazines began writing about her Midas touch.

cloze.s: Investors lined up behind her new startup, convinced that her ___ would make it another success.

note: The myth is a warning about greed, but the modern phrase is usually admiring.

story: Hercules (Heracles in Greek) was the strongest of the Greek heroes. As penance he performed twelve famously difficult labors, such as killing the many-headed Hydra and capturing the three-headed dog Cerberus.
def: requiring enormous strength, effort, or determination; extremely hard to accomplish
ex: Cleaning up the flooded basement was a Herculean job that took the whole family two weekends.
Wei made a Herculean effort to finish her nursing degree while working night shifts.
Getting all forty relatives to agree on one vacation date was a Herculean task.
The volunteers made a Herculean effort, filling ten thousand sandbags before the river rose.

cloze.s: Rebuilding the bridge in just three months would take a(n) ___ effort from every crew in the region.

story: Cupid was the Roman god of love, usually shown as a winged boy with a bow. Anyone struck by one of his golden arrows fell in love.
def: to try to bring two people together romantically; act as a matchmaker
ex: Aisha played Cupid by seating her two single friends next to each other at her wedding.
Grandpa loves to play Cupid, always mentioning the nice young doctor down the street.
The dog park regulars played Cupid, making sure the two shy dog owners always ended up on the same bench.
Yuki's mom keeps playing Cupid, inviting her friends' single sons over for dinner.

cloze.s: Malik decided to ___ and invited both of his lonely coworkers to the same dinner party.

story: In a parable told by Jesus in the Gospel of Luke, a man is robbed and left injured by the road. A priest and a Levite pass him by, but a Samaritan, from a group the listeners were hostile toward, stops, treats his wounds, and pays for his care.
def: a stranger who helps someone in trouble without expecting anything in return
ex: A good Samaritan changed Olga's flat tire on the highway and drove off before she could thank him.
Many states have laws protecting good Samaritans who give first aid at accident scenes.
Fatima lost her wallet on the train, and a good Samaritan mailed it back with every dollar inside.
A good Samaritan saw smoke pouring from the building and knocked on every door until the neighbors got out.

cloze.s: When the elderly man collapsed at the bus stop, a(n) ___ called 911 and stayed with him until help arrived.

story: In the Hebrew Bible (1 Samuel), the young shepherd David faces Goliath, a giant Philistine warrior. Armed only with a sling and stones, David strikes Goliath in the forehead and defeats him.
def: a contest in which a small, weak side faces a far larger, more powerful opponent
ex: The lawsuit between the family bakery and the global food company was a classic David and Goliath battle.
Fans loved the David and Goliath story of the tiny college beating the national champions.
Residents saw the zoning fight as David and Goliath: a tiny neighborhood group against a giant shipping company.
In the chess final, the twelve-year-old faced the grandmaster in a true David and Goliath match.

cloze.s: The small-town newspaper's fight against the media giant was a true ___ struggle, and readers rooted for the underdog.

story: In the Book of Genesis, God tells Adam and Eve they may eat from any tree in the Garden of Eden except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Tempted by a serpent, they eat its fruit and are driven out of the garden.
def: something desired all the more because it is not allowed or is considered wrong
ex: For the teenagers, the locked liquor cabinet was forbidden fruit, which only made it more tempting.
Dessert became forbidden fruit for Tomás once his doctor told him to cut back on sugar.
At the strict boarding school, candy was forbidden fruit, and students traded it like treasure.
Once the boss declared the top shelf of snacks off-limits, those cookies became forbidden fruit for the whole team.

cloze.s: Because her parents banned video games, they became a kind of ___ that Yuki thought about constantly.

note: Genesis never says the fruit was an apple; that idea came later in European tradition.

story: In the Sermon on the Mount (Gospel of Matthew), Jesus teaches that if someone strikes you on the right cheek, you should turn the other to them as well, rather than seeking revenge.
def: to respond to an insult or attack calmly, without striking back or seeking revenge
ex: When a rival posted mean comments about her, Hannah turned the other cheek and simply ignored them.
It's hard to turn the other cheek when a coworker takes credit for your work.
When her sister mocked her new haircut, Fatima turned the other cheek and just smiled.
The coach told his players to turn the other cheek whenever opponents taunted them.

cloze.s: Instead of shouting back at the rude driver, Jamal chose to ___ and drove on.

story: This principle of equal punishment appears in the laws of the Hebrew Bible (Exodus, Leviticus, Deuteronomy) and in the even older Code of Hammurabi. Jesus later quotes it in the Sermon on the Mount, telling his followers not to retaliate.
def: the idea that punishment or revenge should match the harm that was done
ex: The debate over the death penalty often comes down to whether justice means an eye for an eye.
Fatima told her sons that an eye for an eye just keeps a fight going forever.
When his little brother broke his toy, Liam wanted an eye for an eye and broke one of his brother's toys.
The war movie showed how an eye for an eye turned a small border fight into years of revenge.

cloze.s: The two neighbors lived by ___: when one blasted music late at night, the other did the same the next evening.

story: In the Sermon on the Mount (Gospel of Matthew), Jesus says that if someone forces you to go one mile, you should go with them two. The saying came to mean doing more than is required.
def: to make more effort than is expected or required of you
ex: The hotel staff went the extra mile, leaving a birthday cake in our room after overhearing us.
Liam always goes the extra mile for his students, staying late to help anyone who's struggling.
Dr. Okafor goes the extra mile for her patients, calling them at home to check on their recovery.
To win the contract, Tomás went the extra mile and built a working model of his design.

cloze.s: Customers keep coming back because the shop's employees ___, even delivering orders on their way home.

term: by the skin of your teeth
story: The phrase comes from the Book of Job in the King James Bible, where the suffering Job says, “I am escaped with the skin of my teeth,” describing how narrowly he has survived.
def: only just; by the narrowest possible margin
ex: Sofia passed her driving test by the skin of her teeth, scraping through with the minimum score.
We caught the last train home by the skin of our teeth, jumping on as the doors closed.
The team won the final game by the skin of their teeth, scoring in the last second.
Kwame finished his tax forms by the skin of his teeth, filing them minutes before the midnight deadline.

cloze.s: Diego and Maria made their connecting flight ___, sprinting up to the gate just before it shut.
cloze.a: by the skin of their teeth

story: In Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Sikhism, karma is the principle that a person's intentional actions shape their future experiences, including future lives in the cycle of rebirth.
def: the idea that good or bad actions eventually bring matching consequences back to the person who did them
ex: He cut in line and then spilled coffee all over himself — instant karma, Olga joked.
Priya believes that good karma comes from treating everyone with kindness.
Liam laughed when his sister tripped, then fell down the stairs himself, and Maria called it karma.
The driver who splashed people at the bus stop got a flat tire a block later, and onlookers called it karma.

cloze.s: After years of helping neighbors, Kwame felt it was ___ when a stranger returned his lost wallet with every dollar inside.

note: Everyday English often treats it as quick payback or luck; in its original traditions it is a long-term moral law that can span lifetimes.

story: In Hinduism, Buddhism, and Sikhism, a guru is a spiritual teacher or guide; the word is Sanskrit. In Sikhism, the title belongs to the ten human Gurus, from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh, and to the scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib.
def: an expert or trusted adviser in a particular field whom others look to for guidance
ex: The company hired a marketing guru to help relaunch its tired brand.
Ask Jamal about your phone settings — he's the tech guru of the family.
Fatima became the office's spreadsheet guru, and everyone brought her their formula questions.
The fitness guru's videos teach millions of people how to exercise at home.

cloze.s: Thousands of investors hang on every word of the self-styled financial ___, who claims his system never fails.

note: In its religious sense the word carries deep reverence; in casual English it can sound playful or mocking (“a self-styled guru”).

story: In one of Aesop's fables, a fox tries again and again to reach a bunch of grapes hanging high on a vine. When he fails, he walks away saying they were probably sour anyway.
def: pretending to dislike or look down on something only because you could not get it yourself
ex: When Liam said he never wanted the promotion anyway, everyone knew it was sour grapes.
The losing team's complaints about the referees sounded like sour grapes to most fans.
After not making the team, Diego claimed soccer was boring, but his mom knew it was sour grapes.
The losing bidder said the house was overpriced anyway, which sounded like sour grapes.

cloze.s: Calling the award “meaningless” right after losing it sounded like ___ to the other nominees.

story: In Aesop's fable “The Boy Who Cried Wolf,” a shepherd boy repeatedly fools villagers by shouting that a wolf is attacking his flock. When a wolf really comes, no one believes him.
def: to raise false alarms so often that people stop believing you when a real problem comes
ex: Maria has cried wolf about quitting so many times that her boss no longer takes it seriously.
If the weather service keeps issuing storm warnings that never pan out, it risks crying wolf.
Ben cried wolf about stomachaches to skip school so often that his mom stopped believing him.
If you call every small problem an emergency, you're crying wolf, and your team will ignore you when it really matters.

cloze.s: Our smoke detector goes off every time we make toast, and I worry it's ___ so often that we'll ignore a real fire.

term: slow and steady wins the race
story: In Aesop's fable “The Tortoise and the Hare,” a speedy hare mocks a slow tortoise and agrees to race it. The overconfident hare naps along the way, and the tortoise, plodding on without stopping, crosses the finish line first.
def: consistent, patient effort usually succeeds better than speed combined with carelessness or overconfidence
ex: Aisha paid off her student loans a little each month, proving that slow and steady wins the race.
When it comes to losing weight safely, slow and steady wins the race.
Kwame studied twenty minutes every night instead of cramming, since slow and steady wins the race.
Many financial advisers say that in investing, slow and steady wins the race, not quick, risky bets.

cloze.s: Wei's coach reminded her that in a marathon, ___, so she shouldn't sprint the first mile.
cloze.a: slow and steady wins the race

story: In Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale “The Ugly Duckling,” a homely young bird is teased by the ducks and other animals. After a hard winter it grows up and discovers it is actually a beautiful swan.
def: someone or something considered unattractive or unpromising at first that later becomes impressive or beautiful
ex: The run-down warehouse was the ugly duckling of the block until artists turned it into a gallery.
Tomás was the ugly duckling of his class but grew into a confident, striking adult.
The puppy nobody wanted at the shelter was an ugly duckling that grew into a beautiful dog.
Once the ugly duckling of the city's restaurants, the tiny diner now wins awards for its food.

cloze.s: Once the plainest car in the lineup, the boxy hatchback turned out to be the ___ that became the company's bestseller.

story: In the folk tale of Cinderella, best known from the versions by Charles Perrault and the Brothers Grimm, a mistreated young woman forced to work for her stepfamily gets magical help to attend a royal ball and ends up marrying the prince.
def: an unexpected success by an unknown or overlooked person or team that rises from obscurity to fame
ex: The low-ranked college's run to the championship game was the Cinderella story of the tournament.
Her rise from mailroom clerk to company president is a real Cinderella story.
The small family bakery that won the national baking contest became a Cinderella story in the local news.
Fans loved the Cinderella story of the soccer club that rose from the lowest league to win a championship.

cloze.s: No one expected the unknown singer from a small town to win the national contest, making hers the ___ of the season.

story: In the English folk tale “The Three Little Pigs,” a wolf blows down the houses that two pigs built of straw and sticks but cannot blow down the third pig's house of bricks. A 1933 Disney cartoon made “Big Bad Wolf” a familiar label.
def: a person or thing portrayed as a frightening villain or threat, often more than it deserves
ex: Local shop owners treat the new superstore as the big bad wolf that will drive them out of business.
In the movie, the greedy landlord is the big bad wolf who threatens to evict everyone.
Many students treat the final exam as the big bad wolf, but it is really just a review of the course.
For years, newspapers painted video games as the big bad wolf behind every problem with teenagers.

cloze.s: Some economists argue that automation isn't the ___ it's made out to be and will create new jobs.

story: In Old Norse sagas and poems, berserkers were warriors said to fight in a wild, trancelike fury, seemingly unaware of pain or danger.
def: to become wildly out of control with anger, excitement, or frenzy
ex: The crowd went berserk when the home team scored in the final second.
Our dog goes berserk every time the mail carrier walks up the driveway.
The kids went berserk with excitement when the snow day was announced on the radio.
When the referee made a bad call, the coach went berserk and threw his clipboard onto the field.

cloze.s: When the store announced a 90 percent off sale, shoppers ___ and rushed the doors.

story: Homer's epic poem the Odyssey tells of the Greek hero Odysseus's ten-year journey home after the Trojan War, full of monsters, storms, and detours.
def: a long, eventful journey or experience full of adventures and changes of fortune
ex: Getting a visa turned into a six-month bureaucratic odyssey for Malik's family.
Their road trip became an odyssey of flat tires, wrong turns, and unforgettable diners.
Finding a doctor who could explain her rare illness became a two-year odyssey for Fatima.
Moving the family piano across three states turned into an odyssey of broken ramps and borrowed trucks.

cloze.s: After three canceled flights and a night in a bus station, Hannah's trip home had become a true ___.

story: In Homer's Odyssey, Mentor is the old friend Odysseus leaves in charge of his household, and the goddess Athena takes Mentor's form to guide Odysseus's young son, Telemachus. A popular 1699 French novel about Telemachus helped make the name a word for a wise guide.
def: an experienced, trusted person who advises and guides someone less experienced over time
ex: Dr. Patel became Yuki's mentor during residency, teaching her far more than any textbook.
The program pairs each new employee with a mentor from another department.
Kwame's high school coach became his mentor, guiding him through college applications and his first job.
After retiring, Olga became a mentor to young business owners, meeting them monthly to review their plans.

cloze.s: Throughout her first year of teaching, Maria met weekly with her ___, a veteran teacher who helped her plan lessons.

story: In Greek myth, the Sirens were creatures whose beautiful singing lured sailors to wreck their ships on the rocks. In the Odyssey, Odysseus has his crew plug their ears with wax and has himself tied to the mast so he can hear the song safely.
def: a tempting appeal that is hard to resist but likely to lead to trouble or ruin
ex: Many investors fell for the siren song of quick profits and lost their savings.
Sofia resisted the siren song of the sofa and went for her evening run.
For many retirees, the siren song of a beachfront condo led to debts they couldn't afford.
The siren song of video games kept Kwame from studying, and his grades slipped all semester.

cloze.s: Despite promising to save money, Diego couldn't resist the ___ of the holiday sales and maxed out his credit card.

story: In Greek myth, the Titans were a race of giant, powerful gods who ruled before Zeus and the Olympian gods overthrew them.
def: a person of enormous power, importance, or achievement, especially in business or a particular field
ex: The museum was funded by a steel titan of the early 1900s.
When the two tech titans met in court, the case drew worldwide attention.
The retiring surgeon was a titan of heart medicine, training hundreds of doctors over forty years.
The documentary profiles a titan of the fashion world who built her label from a single sewing machine.

cloze.s: As a(n) ___ of the shipping industry, she controlled ports on three continents.

story: In Ovid's version of the Greek myth, the beautiful young man Narcissus falls in love with his own reflection in a pool and wastes away gazing at it; a flower that bears his name grows where he died.
def: a person excessively absorbed in themselves who craves admiration and shows little real concern for others
ex: Her ex was such a narcissist that every conversation somehow ended up being about him.
The talk-show host came across as a narcissist, constantly steering questions back to his own career.
The narcissist on the dating app posted forty selfies and never asked anyone a single question.
When Malik shared news of a family emergency, his roommate, a true narcissist, changed the subject back to his own workout.

cloze.s: Liam realized his new boss was a(n) ___ when she took credit for the team's work and demanded constant praise.

note: Also a clinical term (narcissistic personality disorder); in everyday speech it is often used loosely as an insult.

story: In ancient legend, told by Greek and Roman writers, the phoenix was a sacred bird that lived for centuries and then was reborn; in the best-known version it bursts into flames and rises again from its own ashes.
def: a person or thing that makes a powerful comeback after being destroyed or seeming finished
ex: After the fire, the bakery rose like a phoenix from the ashes, reopening bigger than before.
Critics hailed the singer as a phoenix after a comeback album that many had thought impossible.
The soccer club rose like a phoenix, going from last place to champions in a single season.
Written off after the flood, the riverside neighborhood proved a true phoenix, reopening with new shops and families.

cloze.s: The bankrupt airline seemed finished, but under new owners it rose like a(n) ___ from the ashes.

term: fly too close to the sun
story: In Greek myth, the craftsman Daedalus made wings of feathers and wax so he and his son Icarus could escape Crete. Icarus ignored his father's warning, flew too close to the sun, the wax melted, and he fell into the sea.
def: to become dangerously overambitious or reckless and suffer disaster as a result
ex: The founder flew too close to the sun, expanding into ten countries before the business could support it.
Olga's coach warned her not to fly too close to the sun by training through injuries.
The young singer flew too close to the sun, booking a world tour before she had a single hit.
Wei knew she was flying too close to the sun by taking six classes while working full-time.

cloze.s: Analysts said the hedge fund had ___ by borrowing huge sums on a single risky bet.
cloze.a: flown too close to the sun

story: In a parable told by Jesus in the Gospel of Luke, a younger son wastes his inheritance in reckless living, then returns home in shame. His father joyfully welcomes him back and throws a feast, to the resentment of the dutiful older brother.
def: a person who leaves home or a group, behaves irresponsibly, and later returns regretful and is welcomed back
ex: When the star player rejoined his first club after years abroad, fans hailed the return of the prodigal son.
Jamal felt like the prodigal son, coming home broke after his failed music career.
After years of partying abroad and ignoring calls, Malik came home humbled, and his parents threw a party for their prodigal son.
The founder who quit the company in anger came back ten years later, humbled, and was greeted as a prodigal son.

cloze.s: After a decade of ignoring the family, Uncle Ray showed up at the reunion, and Grandma welcomed him like the ___.

note: Prodigal alone means wastefully extravagant; it does not mean “returning,” a common misunderstanding.

story: In the Gospel of John, the apostle Thomas refuses to believe the other disciples' report that Jesus has risen until he can see and touch the wounds himself.
def: a person who refuses to believe something without direct, personal proof
ex: Even after seeing the test results, a few doubting Thomases on the board wanted another study.
Don't be a doubting Thomas; the bus really does stop right outside the hotel.
Diego was a doubting Thomas about the new recipe until he tasted it himself.
The magician invited the doubting Thomases in the audience to come up and inspect the empty box.

cloze.s: Aisha was the office ___, refusing to believe the new software worked until she tested it herself.

story: In the Gospels, Judas Iscariot, one of Jesus's twelve apostles, betrayed him to the authorities for thirty pieces of silver, identifying him with a kiss.
def: a person who betrays a friend or ally, especially someone who pretends to be loyal
ex: Fans called the striker a Judas when he signed with their bitterest rivals.
She felt she'd been betrayed by a Judas when her business partner sold their idea to a competitor.
When his best friend told the teacher about their prank, Liam called him a Judas.
In the spy novel, the agent's most trusted partner turns out to be a Judas working for the enemy.

cloze.s: After leaking the team's plans to a rival company, Mark was branded a(n) ___ by his former colleagues.

story: In the Book of Daniel, during a feast held by King Belshazzar of Babylon, a mysterious hand writes words on the palace wall. Daniel interprets them as a sign that the king's reign is ending, and Belshazzar is killed that night.
def: clear signs that something bad, such as failure or an ending, is about to happen
ex: When the store cut its hours and stopped restocking, employees saw the writing on the wall.
The writing was on the wall for the old factory once its biggest customer moved overseas.
When Kwame's manager stopped inviting him to meetings, he saw the writing on the wall and started job hunting.
Ignoring the writing on the wall, the camera company kept making film long after everyone switched to phones.

cloze.s: After three straight losing seasons and empty stands, the coach could read ___ and resigned.

story: In the Sermon on the Mount (Gospel of Matthew), Jesus tells his followers, “Ye are the salt of the earth,” praising them as valuable and good for the world.
def: a decent, honest, unpretentious person who is kind and dependable
ex: Our neighbors are salt of the earth; they shoveled our driveway every morning while I was in the hospital.
The farmer was the salt of the earth, always the first to help anyone in town.
The school janitor, who fixed kids' bikes for free and never missed a day, was the salt of the earth.
