cloze.s: Raising government spending to boost a weak economy is an example of expansionary ___.

note: Contrast with *monetary policy*, which works through interest rates and the money supply.

def: a central bank's management of interest rates and the money supply to control inflation and support employment
why: Changes in it ripple through mortgage rates, savings yields, stock prices, and the value of a currency.
ex: In the early 1980s, tight US monetary policy helped bring down very high inflation.
The central bank's statement on monetary policy caused stock markets to jump.
Hannah's mortgage rate went up after the central bank tightened monetary policy to slow inflation.
In the United States, monetary policy is set by the Federal Reserve, not by Congress.

cloze.s: When the Federal Reserve lowers interest rates to encourage borrowing, it is loosening ___.

def: the observation that roughly 80 percent of effects often come from about 20 percent of causes
why: Managers use it to focus effort, for example on the few customers or defects behind most revenue or problems.
ex: Applying the Pareto principle, Wei focused on the handful of clients who generated most of the firm's sales.
The Pareto principle suggests that most complaints may come from a small number of product defects.
Using the Pareto principle, Sofia cleared out her closet after noticing she wore a few favorite outfits most of the time.
The software team applied the Pareto principle by fixing the few bugs that caused most of the crashes.

cloze.s: The 80/20 rule, formally called the ___, is named after an Italian economist.

note: Named after Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto, who studied how unevenly wealth and income were spread. A rule of thumb, not a law.

def: the ability to produce something at a lower opportunity cost than others, which makes specialization and trade mutually beneficial
why: Described by David Ricardo in 1817, it is the core argument for why countries gain from trading with each other.
ex: Even though Maria types faster than her assistant, comparative advantage says she should delegate typing and focus on clients.
Ricardo illustrated comparative advantage with England trading cloth for Portugal's wine.
Because its workers give up less to grow rice than to build cars, the country has a comparative advantage in rice.
Making slides costs Lena less research time than it costs her teammates, so the group used her comparative advantage in design.

cloze.s: A country with no edge in making anything can still gain from trade by specializing according to its ___.

note: Differs from *absolute advantage*, which means simply producing something more efficiently than others.

def: a policy in which a central bank creates money to buy large amounts of bonds, pushing down long-term interest rates
why: Major central banks used it heavily after the 2008 financial crisis and during the COVID-19 pandemic.
ex: Through quantitative easing, the central bank bought billions of dollars in government bonds each month.
Economists still debate how much quantitative easing helped the economy after 2008.
During the 2020 pandemic, the Federal Reserve restarted quantitative easing to keep borrowing cheap.
Critics of quantitative easing warn that creating so much money can push up the prices of stocks and homes.

cloze.s: With interest rates already near zero, the Federal Reserve turned to ___, buying bonds on a massive scale.

note: Often shortened to QE. Japan's central bank was an early user in the early 2000s.

def: an economic condition combining rapidly rising prices with weak growth and high unemployment
why: It hit many Western economies in the 1970s and is hard to fix, since cures for one problem can worsen the other.
ex: The oil shocks of the 1970s pushed the United States into stagflation.
Economists warned that rising costs and falling output could bring stagflation.
Stagflation is hard to fix, because raising interest rates to fight rising prices can deepen the slump.
With prices climbing and layoffs spreading, Diego's family felt the squeeze of stagflation.

cloze.s: In the 1970s, prices soared while unemployment also rose, a painful mix known as ___.

note: A blend of *stagnation* and *inflation*.

def: a cost or benefit of an activity that falls on people not directly involved in it
why: Pollution is a classic negative example, which is why governments use taxes or rules to make producers account for wider harm.
ex: Traffic noise from the new warehouse was an externality borne by the whole neighborhood.
A neighbor's beautiful garden creates a positive externality for everyone who walks by.
Secondhand smoke is an externality, because nonsmokers nearby pay a health cost for someone else's habit.
When Sofia's neighbors got vaccinated, the protection they gave others was a positive externality.

cloze.s: Because the factory doesn't pay for the smoke it releases, the pollution is a negative ___.

def: Adam Smith's metaphor for how individuals pursuing self-interest in free markets can unintentionally benefit society as a whole
why: It is a foundational image in economics, from Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776), and is often cited in debates about markets.
ex: The lecturer explained the invisible hand with a baker who sells bread to earn a living, not out of kindness.
Some economists note that the invisible hand works poorly when there is pollution or monopoly.
Adam Smith mentioned the invisible hand only a few times, yet the phrase became one of the most famous in economics.
Maria's economics teacher said the invisible hand explains why phone repair shops pop up wherever people need them, with no central planner.

cloze.s: Adam Smith used the image of a(n) ___ to describe how self-interested trade can serve the public good.

def: the theory that government spending and tax policy should be used to boost demand and fight recessions
why: Developed by John Maynard Keynes in the 1930s, it shaped stimulus policies during many later downturns.
ex: Supporters of Keynesian economics argued for public works spending to put the unemployed back to work.
Keynes laid out his ideas in a 1936 book, and Keynesian economics guided many governments for decades after World War II.
Diego's professor explained that Keynesian economics supports cutting taxes during a slump so that families have more money to spend.
Critics of Keynesian economics worry that heavy spending during slumps can lead to large government debts.

cloze.s: The idea that governments should spend more during a slump to make up for weak private demand is central to ___.

note: Pronounced KAYN-zee-un.

def: the tendency to take bigger risks when someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong
why: It comes up in insurance, bank bailouts, and guarantees, where protection can unintentionally encourage reckless behavior.
ex: Some economists warned that bailing out the banks would create moral hazard by encouraging future risk-taking.
Insurers use deductibles partly to reduce moral hazard, so drivers still have a reason to be careful.
Hannah's landlord worried about moral hazard: tenants who never pay for repairs may treat the appliances carelessly.
Drivers of rental cars sometimes treat them roughly, knowing the company pays for wear, a familiar example of moral hazard.

cloze.s: If a company knows the government will rescue it, it may gamble more freely, a problem known as ___.

def: a statistical measure of income or wealth inequality, ranging from 0 for perfect equality to 1 for maximum inequality
why: Developed by Italian statistician Corrado Gini, it is widely used to compare inequality across countries and over time.
ex: A Gini coefficient of 0 would mean every household had exactly the same income.
The report used the Gini coefficient to track how inequality changed over twenty years.
The news report said the country's Gini coefficient had risen, meaning income had become less evenly shared.
In Diego's economics class, students calculated a Gini coefficient for a tiny pretend town of ten families.

cloze.s: Economists measure how unevenly income is spread in a country using a number called the ___.

note: Sometimes shown on a 0–100 scale instead of 0–1.

def: the extra satisfaction a person gains from consuming one more unit of a good or service
why: It explains why the first slice of pizza feels better than the fifth, and underlies how economists model demand.
ex: By the third cup of coffee, the marginal utility for Jamal had dropped close to zero.
Economists use marginal utility to explain why people spread their spending across many goods.
For a thirsty hiker, the marginal utility of the first bottle of water is far greater than that of the fifth.
Before adding a second streaming service, Fatima asked herself whether its marginal utility was worth the extra monthly fee.

cloze.s: The law of diminishing ___ says each additional slice of cake brings less enjoyment than the last.

note: “Marginal” in economics means “one more” or “additional,” not “minor.”

def: the principle that when two forms of money circulate, people hoard the more valuable one and spend the less valuable
why: Often summarized as “bad money drives out good,” it explains why coins with more precious metal vanish from circulation.
ex: Gresham's law explains why US silver dimes vanished from circulation after cheaper coins were introduced in 1965.
Historians cite Gresham's law to explain how debased coins pushed purer coins out of everyday trade in Tudor England.
Gresham's law is named after Sir Thomas Gresham, a financier who advised Queen Elizabeth I.
Gresham's law is often summed up as “bad money drives out good,” since people hold on to the better coins.

cloze.s: People kept the old silver coins and spent the new cheaper ones, just as ___ predicts.

note: Named after Thomas Gresham, a 16th-century English financier, though the idea is older.

def: a figure of speech that describes something by saying it is something else, without using “like” or “as”
why: It is everywhere in speech and writing, from “time is money” to song lyrics and political speeches.
ex: When Kwame called his office a zoo, he was using a metaphor for its noise and chaos.
Shakespeare's line “All the world's a stage” is a famous metaphor.
Coach Rivera's metaphor, “This team is a family,” stuck with the players all season.
Saying “time is money” is a common metaphor in business for how valuable every hour is.

cloze.s: Emily Dickinson's line “Hope is the thing with feathers” is a(n) ___ comparing hope to a bird.

note: Differs from *simile*, which compares using “like” or “as.”

def: a figure of speech that compares two different things using “like” or “as”
why: It is common in poems, songs, and everyday speech, such as “busy as a bee” or “sleeping like a log.”
ex: “Her smile was like sunshine” is a simile because it uses the word “like.”
The coach's simile, “They hit like a freight train,” made the whole team laugh.
In her essay, Yuki described the calm morning with the simile “The lake was as smooth as glass.”
Asked to describe the storm with a simile, Diego wrote, “The thunder roared like a lion.”

cloze.s: Robert Burns's line “O my Luve is like a red, red rose” is a famous ___.

note: Contrast with *metaphor*, which compares without “like” or “as.”

def: a dramatic work in which the story is told mainly through singing, accompanied by an orchestra
why: It developed in Italy around 1600 and includes famous works by Mozart, Verdi, and Puccini.
ex: Sofia saw her first opera, Puccini's La Bohème, on a school trip to the city.
Most of the dialogue in an opera is sung rather than spoken.
At the opera, screens above the stage showed English words so the audience could follow the Italian singing.
Malik's sister trained for years to sing opera, building a voice strong enough to fill a theater without a microphone.

cloze.s: Verdi's Aida, with its soloists, chorus, orchestra, and elaborate sets, is a famous Italian ___.

def: a long piece of music for a full orchestra, usually in four sections called movements
why: Composers such as Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven made it a central form of Western classical music.
ex: Beethoven's Ninth Symphony ends with a choir singing the “Ode to Joy.”
The city's orchestra will perform a symphony by Dvořák on Saturday night.
Mozart wrote his first symphony when he was only eight years old.
The radio station played a full symphony, and Hannah listened to all four movements on her drive home.

cloze.s: Haydn wrote 104 numbered examples of the ___, a large orchestral work usually in four movements.

note: Also short for a *symphony orchestra*, as in “the Chicago Symphony.”

def: an account of a person's life written by that person
why: It is a major genre in which public figures, from Benjamin Franklin to Maya Angelou, tell their own stories.
ex: Frederick Douglass recounted his years in slavery and his path to freedom in his autobiography.
Priya's grandmother is writing an autobiography for her grandchildren.
In his autobiography, the retired pilot described his first solo flight at age seventeen.
The library shelved the singer's autobiography next to books that others had written about her.

cloze.s: Unlike a biography, a(n) ___ is written by the person whose life it describes.

note: A *memoir* is similar but usually focuses on particular experiences rather than a whole life.

def: the use of humor, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose and criticize foolishness or wrongdoing, especially in politics and society
why: From Jonathan Swift to late-night comedy, it is a long-standing way to criticize powerful people and institutions.
ex: Gulliver's Travels is a satire that mocks the politics and science of Jonathan Swift's England.
The newspaper's satire column pokes fun at office culture and corporate jargon.
The cartoon used satire, showing lawmakers asleep at their desks while a budget deadline passed.
Some readers took the satire website's made-up headline seriously and shared it as real news.

cloze.s: The comedy show's ___ mocked politicians of every party by exaggerating their habits.

def: a poem of fourteen lines with a set rhyme scheme, often about love
why: Shakespeare wrote 154 of them, and poets have used the form from Petrarch to the present day.
ex: Shakespeare's sonnet beginning “Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?” is one of the most quoted poems in English.
For her poetry class, Hannah wrote a sonnet with exactly fourteen lines.
Samir ended his sonnet with a rhyming pair of lines, just as Shakespeare did in his.
For their anniversary, Rosa wrote her husband a sonnet about the day they first met.

cloze.s: Petrarch's love poems helped make the fourteen-line ___ popular across Europe.

note: A Shakespearean one ends with a rhyming couplet.

def: a short Japanese poetic form of three lines, traditionally of five, seven, and five syllables, often about nature
why: Masters like Matsuo Bashō made it famous, and it is widely taught and written in English today.
ex: Bashō's haiku about a frog jumping into an old pond is one of the most famous poems in Japanese.
Yuki's students each wrote a haiku about the first snowfall.
Diego's class counted syllables to make sure each haiku had lines of five, seven and five.
Hannah's favorite haiku describes a single leaf falling on a quiet autumn evening.

cloze.s: In just three short lines, the ___ captures a single moment, often with a seasonal reference.

note: Japanese poets count sound units rather than English syllables, so the 5-7-5 pattern is approximate in English.

def: a 19th-century French painting movement that captured light and fleeting moments with visible brushstrokes and bright color
why: Artists such as Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir changed how painters approached light, color, and everyday subjects.
ex: Monet's water lily paintings are among the most famous works of Impressionism.
Diego's favorite museum room is the one devoted to French Impressionism.
Critics first used the name Impressionism as an insult, borrowing it from Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise.
Olga's art class tried Impressionism by painting the pond quickly with short dabs of bright color.

cloze.s: Painting outdoors to catch shifting light was a hallmark of ___, the movement of Monet and Renoir.

note: The name came from a critic mocking Monet's 1872 painting *Impression, Sunrise*.

def: the main character of a story, play, or film, whose goals usually drive the plot
why: Talking about stories, from novels to video games, often starts with identifying this central figure.
ex: Elizabeth Bennet is the protagonist of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice.
The film's protagonist is a nurse who uncovers a scandal at her hospital.
In the video game, the protagonist is a young mapmaker searching for her missing brother.
Ethan's writing teacher told him to give his protagonist a clear goal by the end of the first page.

cloze.s: Harry Potter is the ___ of the series, while Voldemort is his main enemy.

def: a category of art, music, or writing defined by shared style, form, or subject, such as mystery or jazz
why: Bookstores, streaming services, and critics organize works this way to help audiences find what they like.
ex: Science fiction is Malik's favorite genre, especially stories about space travel.
The band mixes several genres, blending reggae with hip-hop.
Priya writes in the fantasy genre, creating stories full of dragons and magic.
Country is the genre of music Kwame's father likes to play on long drives.

cloze.s: Horror, romance, and westerns are each a different film ___.

note: Pronounced ZHAHN-ruh; from French for “kind.”

def: a story, poem, or picture in which characters and events stand for deeper moral, political, or spiritual meanings
why: Works like Orwell's Animal Farm and Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress use it to teach lessons or make criticism.
ex: Animal Farm is an allegory of the Russian Revolution told through farm animals.
Aisha's essay read the film as an allegory about grief and letting go.
Samir's teacher explained that Plato's story of the cave is an allegory about learning to see the truth.
The children's movie works as an allegory, with the dragon who hoards gold standing for greed.

cloze.s: In The Pilgrim's Progress, a traveler named Christian journeys toward the Celestial City in a(n) ___ of the Christian life.

note: Plato's “Allegory of the Cave” is a famous philosophical example.

def: a dramatic, richly ornamented style in European art, architecture, and music from about 1600 to 1750
why: It includes the music of Bach and Vivaldi and the art of Caravaggio and Bernini.
ex: Bach's fugues are high points of Baroque music.
The church's gilded ceilings and swirling sculptures are typical of the Baroque style.
The orchestra's concert of Baroque music featured works by Handel and Vivaldi.
Amara's tour of Rome included Baroque fountains with twisting marble figures and splashing water.

cloze.s: The era of European music that produced Vivaldi's The Four Seasons is called the ___ period.

def: an early 1900s art movement that broke objects into geometric shapes and showed several viewpoints at once
why: Founded by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, it transformed modern art and paved the way for abstraction.
ex: Picasso's Les Demoiselles d'Avignon is often seen as a forerunner of Cubism.
Wei's design class studied how Cubism influenced modern graphic design.
At the museum, Samir stood puzzled before a work of Cubism that showed a guitar broken into sharp, flat shapes.
Georges Braque and Pablo Picasso developed Cubism together in Paris.

cloze.s: Paintings in which a face is seen from the front and the side at the same time are typical of ___.

def: the repetition of the same first consonant sound in nearby words, as in “Peter Piper picked”
why: Writers, poets, advertisers, and headline editors use it to make phrases catchy and memorable.
ex: Tongue twisters like “She sells seashells by the seashore” rely on alliteration.
The headline “Bears Battle Back” used alliteration to grab readers' attention.
The shop's name, Busy Bee Bakery, uses alliteration to make it easy to remember.
Rosa added alliteration to her campaign speech for class president with the phrase “safe streets and strong schools.”

cloze.s: Cartoon names like Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck use ___, repeating the same starting sound.

note: The related term *assonance* means repeated vowel sounds.

def: a traditional Japanese theater form known for stylized acting, elaborate costumes, bold makeup, and live music
why: Dating from the early 1600s, it is recognized by UNESCO as part of the world's intangible cultural heritage.
ex: In kabuki, all roles, including women's, are traditionally played by men.
Tomás bought tickets to a kabuki performance during his trip to Tokyo.
Kabuki began in Japan in the early 1600s and is still performed in Tokyo today.
Ethan's favorite part of the kabuki show was a lightning-fast costume change done right on stage.

cloze.s: Actors in ___ wear striking white makeup and perform on a stage with a walkway running through the audience.

note: Its founder is traditionally said to be a woman, Izumo no Okuni, but women were banned from performing in 1629.

def: a long narrative work in verse about heroic deeds and events central to a culture's identity
why: Examples like the Epic of Gilgamesh, Homer's Iliad, and India's Mahabharata are foundational works of world literature.
ex: Homer's Odyssey is an epic poem about a hero's ten-year journey home after the Trojan War.
The Mahabharata, an epic poem from ancient India, is one of the longest ever written.
Rosa's class read Beowulf, an Old English epic poem about a hero who fights a monster.
The Epic of Gilgamesh, from ancient Mesopotamia, is one of the oldest epic poems known.

cloze.s: Virgil's Aeneid is a Latin ___ about the legendary Trojan ancestor of the Romans.

def: a 1920s art and literary movement that used dreamlike, illogical images to explore the unconscious mind
why: Salvador Dalí's melting clocks and René Magritte's visual puzzles made it famous, and its influence runs through film and advertising.
ex: Dalí's The Persistence of Memory is a classic work of Surrealism.
The film's floating furniture and talking shadows felt like Surrealism brought to the screen.
René Magritte's painting of a pipe with the words "This is not a pipe" in French is a famous work of Surrealism.
Followers of Surrealism tried automatic writing, jotting down words as fast as they came, without stopping to think.

cloze.s: André Breton launched ___ with a 1924 manifesto inspired by Freud's ideas about dreams.

note: The adjective *surreal* now means bizarre or dreamlike in everyday speech.

def: the use of strong contrasts between light and dark in painting or drawing to create depth and drama
why: It is a signature of artists like Caravaggio and Rembrandt and is used today in photography and film lighting.
ex: Caravaggio's chiaroscuro makes his figures seem to emerge from total darkness.

The film's director borrowed chiaroscuro from old paintings, lighting each scene with a single lamp in the dark.

cloze.s: Rembrandt's portraits use ___, with faces glowing against deep shadow.

note: From Italian *chiaro* (light) and *scuro* (dark).

def: a line of verse with ten syllables in five pairs, each pair an unstressed beat followed by a stressed one
why: It is the rhythm of most of Shakespeare's verse and much English poetry, close to the natural flow of speech.
ex: The line “But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?” is written in iambic pentameter.
Our teacher had us clap out the beats of iambic pentameter: da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM.
Liam tried writing a love poem in iambic pentameter, counting ten syllables on his fingers for each line.
Actors learn to stress every second syllable when speaking Shakespeare's iambic pentameter.

cloze.s: Shakespeare's sonnets are written in ___, with five da-DUM beats per line.

def: a flowering of African American literature, music, and art centered in a New York City neighborhood in the 1920s and 1930s
why: It produced writers like Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston and helped bring jazz into the mainstream.
ex: Langston Hughes's poems about jazz and Black life are landmarks of the Harlem Renaissance.
Jamal's book club is reading Zora Neale Hurston, a major voice of the Harlem Renaissance.
The museum's new exhibit features paintings by Aaron Douglas, a leading artist of the Harlem Renaissance.
Jazz clubs, art salons and poetry readings filled New York evenings during the Harlem Renaissance.

cloze.s: Duke Ellington's performances at the Cotton Club are often linked with the cultural boom known as the ___.

def: a literary style that weaves supernatural events into an otherwise true-to-life, everyday setting as if they were ordinary
why: Strongly associated with Latin American writers like Gabriel García Márquez, it influenced novelists around the world.
ex: In One Hundred Years of Solitude, magical realism lets a young woman rise into the sky while folding sheets.
Toni Morrison's Beloved is often read as magical realism, bringing a ghost into a story about slavery's aftermath.
Laura Esquivel's Like Water for Chocolate uses magical realism, as a cook's emotions pass into the people who eat her food.
Kwame's short story used magical realism, letting his grandmother's ghost sit quietly at family dinners as if nothing were strange.

cloze.s: In the novel's ___, no one in the village is surprised when a rain of tiny yellow flowers falls from the sky.

def: a Japanese genre of woodblock prints and paintings from the 1600s to 1800s showing landscapes, actors, and city life
why: Works like Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa influenced European artists, including Van Gogh and the Impressionists.
ex: Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa is a celebrated example of ukiyo-e.
Van Gogh collected ukiyo-e and copied several of the prints in oil paint.
At the museum gift shop, Sofia bought a copy of a ukiyo-e print showing a kabuki actor.
Ukiyo-e artists worked with carvers and printers, using a separate carved wooden block for each color.

cloze.s: Hiroshige's woodblock prints of travelers on the Tōkaidō road are classics of ___.

note: Means “pictures of the floating world,” referring to the pleasure districts of Edo, now Tokyo.

def: a novel following a young protagonist's growth from youth to maturity, especially their moral and psychological development
why: Classics such as Jane Eyre, Great Expectations, and The Catcher in the Rye are often described this way.
ex: Dickens's Great Expectations is a bildungsroman tracing Pip's journey from poor orphan to gentleman.
Literary critics often call coming-of-age films a modern version of the bildungsroman.
Aisha's book club chose a bildungsroman this month, following a shy farm girl until she becomes a confident adult.
Many readers treat the Harry Potter series as a bildungsroman, since Harry grows from a lonely boy into a mature young man.

cloze.s: Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre, which follows its heroine from a harsh childhood to independent adulthood, is a classic ___.

note: German for “novel of formation” or “novel of education.”

def: an unexpected, often implausible event or character that suddenly solves a story's seemingly impossible problem
why: Critics use it to fault lazy plotting; it comes from ancient Greek theater, where a crane lowered actors playing gods onto the stage.
ex: Readers complained that the sudden inheritance at the end of the novel was a deus ex machina.
The Greek playwright Euripides often ended his plays with a deus ex machina.
The screenwriter avoided a deus ex machina by showing the hero's hidden skill early in the film.
Sofia's writing teacher warned that a deus ex machina, like a sudden magic spell that fixes everything, can leave readers feeling cheated.

cloze.s: Just as the heroes seemed doomed, giant eagles swooped in to rescue them, a plot device some critics call a(n) ___.

note: Latin for “god from the machine.”

def: a West African storyteller, historian, and musician who preserves a community's history and genealogy through oral performance
why: They are keepers of traditions like the epic of Sundiata, founder of the Mali Empire, passed down for centuries.
ex: The griot accompanied his story of the ancient kings on a kora, a West African harp-lute.
At the wedding, a griot sang the family's history, naming ancestors going back many generations.
The documentary followed a griot in Senegal who could recite the history of local kings from memory.
In music class, Aisha learned that a griot traditionally passes family histories down through songs and spoken stories.

cloze.s: In Mali and Senegal, a(n) ___ might recite a family's genealogy at a naming ceremony or wedding.

note: Pronounced GREE-oh. In many communities the role is hereditary.

def: a German school of art, design, and architecture, open from 1919 to 1933, that united craft, fine art, and industrial production
why: Its clean, functional style shaped modern furniture, graphic design, and architecture worldwide.
ex: The Bauhaus was founded in Weimar by the architect Walter Gropius in 1919.
The minimalist steel-tube chairs in Yuki's office reflect Bauhaus design.
Sofia's design class studied Bauhaus posters, with their bold shapes, primary colors and simple lettering.
Tel Aviv's White City has thousands of buildings in the Bauhaus style.

cloze.s: The ___ school closed in 1933 under pressure from the Nazi government, and many of its teachers fled abroad.

def: the release of strong emotions, such as pity and fear, that an audience experiences through art, especially tragedy
why: Aristotle used the idea in his Poetics, and today it also describes any emotional release, such as a good cry.
ex: Watching the tragic ending gave the audience a powerful sense of catharsis.
For Olga, writing in her journal after a hard day at work was a kind of catharsis.
Many readers cried through the final chapter of the war novel, and several described the experience as a catharsis.
Sad movies can offer catharsis, letting viewers release grief they have been holding in.

cloze.s: Aristotle argued that tragedy stirs pity and fear in order to bring about their ___.

def: a late 1700s to mid-1800s movement in art, music, and literature that celebrated emotion, nature, imagination, and individual freedom
why: Figures such as Wordsworth, Mary Shelley, Delacroix, and Chopin defined it as a reaction against Enlightenment rationalism and industrialization.
ex: Wordsworth's poems about lakes and mountains are central works of English Romanticism.
Chopin's emotional piano music is often seen as a high point of musical Romanticism.
The museum's Romanticism gallery is filled with paintings of storms, ruins and lone travelers gazing at mountains.
Mary Shelley's Frankenstein is often studied as a novel of Romanticism, full of wild nature and strong emotion.

cloze.s: Rejecting cold reason, artists of ___ painted stormy seas, wild mountains, and intense personal feelings.

note: Not mainly about romantic love; it emphasizes feeling and imagination in general.

def: the study of right and wrong, and of the principles that guide how people should behave
why: It underlies debates in medicine, business, law, and technology, from patient consent to fair hiring.
ex: The hospital's committee on ethics reviews difficult cases about end-of-life care.
Malik's company requires every employee to complete training on workplace ethics.
Medical students study ethics before they begin treating real patients.
The reporter refused the gift because her newspaper's rules on ethics forbid accepting presents from sources.

cloze.s: Whether it is ever right to lie to protect someone is a classic question in ___.

def: the principle that you should treat others the way you would want to be treated
why: Versions of it appear in many traditions, including Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Confucianism.
ex: Diego's mom reminded him of the Golden Rule after he teased his little sister.
Confucius stated a form of the Golden Rule: do not impose on others what you do not want for yourself.
The coach asked her players to follow the Golden Rule and cheer for the other team too.
Before repeating gossip at work, Priya remembered the Golden Rule and stayed quiet.

cloze.s: “Do unto others as you would have them do unto you” is the classic wording of the ___.

def: the ability to make choices that are genuinely your own, not fully determined by outside forces or prior causes
why: It matters for questions of moral responsibility, punishment, and religious belief, and philosophers have debated it for millennia.
ex: The novel asks whether its hero acted out of free will or was simply following fate.
Philosophers and neuroscientists still argue about whether free will really exists.
Nobody forced Tomás to quit; he left the job of his own free will.
In philosophy class, the students debated whether a robot could ever have free will.

cloze.s: If every action is caused by earlier events, some philosophers ask, can we truly have ___?

def: basic freedoms and protections that belong to every person simply because they are a person
why: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations in 1948, set out a widely recognized list.
ex: Freedom from torture and slavery are among the most basic human rights.

The right to a fair trial is one of the human rights that many countries promise to protect.
Kwame's class discussed which human rights should be taught to every child in school.

cloze.s: In 1948, the United Nations adopted a Universal Declaration of ___ listing freedoms owed to everyone.

def: an economic system in which private individuals and businesses own property and production, with prices set mostly by markets
why: Most economies today are built on it, usually mixed with some government regulation and public services.
ex: Adam Smith is often described as the founding thinker of modern capitalism.
Under capitalism, entrepreneurs like Fatima can start a business and keep its profits.
In economics class, Wei compared capitalism with systems in which the government owns most businesses.
Under capitalism, competing shops often lower their prices to win customers.

cloze.s: In ___, factories, shops, and farms are mostly privately owned and run for profit.

def: an economic and political system in which the community or state owns or controls major industries and resources
why: Its ideas shaped labor movements, welfare states, and communist governments, and the word is used in many different senses today.
ex: Karl Marx's writings influenced many forms of socialism in the 1800s and 1900s.
The debate class compared socialism and capitalism using examples from several countries.
In economics class, Yuki read about how the Soviet Union called its system socialism, with the state running factories and farms.
Under socialism, the government might own the railroads, the power plants and the steel mills.

cloze.s: Supporters of ___ argue that key industries such as railways and utilities should be publicly owned.

note: Used loosely in everyday debate; “social democracy” usually means a market economy with a strong welfare state.

def: the ethical theory that the right action is the one producing the greatest good for the greatest number
why: Developed by Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, it shapes debates in public policy, economics, and medical triage.
ex: A strict utilitarianism might justify sacrificing one person to save five.
Kwame's essay criticized utilitarianism for ignoring individual rights.
Following utilitarianism, the committee chose to fund the clinic that would help the most patients.
John Stuart Mill defended utilitarianism, arguing that actions are right when they promote happiness.

cloze.s: Jeremy Bentham's ___ judged laws by whether they increased overall happiness.

def: an ancient Greek and Roman philosophy teaching calm acceptance of what you cannot control and a focus on virtue
why: Thinkers like Epictetus, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius remain widely read, and its ideas echo in modern cognitive therapy.

The Roman thinker Seneca wrote letters to a friend explaining the ideas of Stoicism.

cloze.s: Founded in Athens by Zeno of Citium, ___ taught that virtue is the only true good.

note: Lowercase *stoic* now means enduring hardship without complaint.

def: a Chinese ethical and social tradition, founded around 500 BCE, that stresses family duty, education, moral leadership, and social harmony
why: It has shaped values, education, and government in China, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam for more than two thousand years.
ex: Respect for parents and elders, called filial piety, is a central value in Confucianism.

Many Korean families still follow customs shaped by Confucianism, such as bowing to elders on New Year's Day.

cloze.s: Filial piety, rituals of respect, and the ideal of the virtuous scholar-official are all core ideas of ___.

def: the idea that people accept a government's authority and some limits on freedom in exchange for order and protection
why: Developed by Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau, it influenced modern ideas of democracy and the American founding.
ex: Rousseau's 1762 book The Social Contract famously declares: “Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.”

def: an attitude of doubt toward claims until they are supported by good evidence

def: the view that knowledge comes mainly from experience and observation through the senses

def: a philosophy holding that life has no built-in meaning, so individuals must create purpose through their own free choices

def: the belief that life has no meaning or value, or that moral principles have no real basis

def: a way of teaching or inquiry that uses a series of probing questions to examine beliefs and expose contradictions

def: a Chinese philosophy and religion teaching harmony with the natural way of the universe, simplicity, and effortless action

def: the view that reason, rather than sensory experience, is the main source of knowledge
why: Linked with René Descartes, Baruch Spinoza, and Gottfried Leibniz, it contrasts with empiricism in the history of philosophy.

Leibniz, a leading voice of rationalism, believed the mind holds some ideas before any experience.

def: Kant's principle that you should act only in ways you could will to become a universal rule for everyone
why: It is a cornerstone of duty-based ethics and is often contrasted with utilitarianism.
ex: According to the categorical imperative, lying is wrong because a world where everyone lied would make trust impossible.

def: a method of reasoning that seeks truth through the clash and resolution of opposing ideas or arguments
why: Found in Plato's dialogues and central to Hegel and Marx, it shapes how philosophers describe change through conflict.
ex: Plato's dialogues show dialectic in action, as Socrates tests each answer against objections.

def: the view that right and wrong are not absolute but depend on culture, era, or individual perspective
why: It is central to debates about whether practices can be judged across cultures and whether universal human rights exist.
ex: The anthropology student argued for moral relativism, saying each culture's customs should be judged on their own terms.

Studying customs around the world led Diego to wonder whether moral relativism is right, since cultures judge the same act so differently.

cloze.s: Someone who believes there is no single standard of right and wrong for all societies holds a form of ___.

def: an American philosophy that judges ideas by their practical consequences and usefulness rather than abstract truth
why: Developed by Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey, it influenced American education, law, and psychology.
ex: William James popularized pragmatism in a series of lectures published in 1907.
John Dewey's pragmatism led him to favor hands-on learning in schools.

Our philosophy professor said pragmatism asks what difference a belief makes in practice, not whether it is true in the abstract.

cloze.s: Charles Sanders Peirce founded ___, the view that an idea's meaning lies in its practical effects.

note: In everyday speech, *pragmatism* simply means a practical, realistic approach.

def: Plato's story of prisoners who mistake shadows on a wall for reality until one escapes into sunlight
why: From his Republic, it is a famous image of education and of the gap between appearance and truth.
ex: In the allegory of the cave, the freed prisoner is dazzled by the sun before he can see clearly.

Leaving her small town for college felt to Ana like the freed prisoner's journey in the allegory of the cave.
In the allegory of the cave, the escaped prisoner returns to free the others, but they mock him and refuse to believe him.

cloze.s: Plato's ___ compares people who never question appearances to captives watching shadows.

def: the branch of philosophy that studies knowledge: what it is, how we get it, and how we justify beliefs
why: It underlies questions about evidence, certainty, and expertise in science, law, and everyday reasoning.
ex: A classic question in epistemology is whether we can know anything with complete certainty.

In epistemology class, Sofia debated whether reading something on a trusted website counts as real knowledge.
Questions about how scientists justify their conclusions from evidence belong to epistemology.

note: From Greek *episteme*, “knowledge.”

def: the branch of philosophy that studies the basic nature of reality, including existence, time, causation, and mind
why: Questions such as whether the mind is separate from the body or whether time is real belong to it.
ex: Aristotle's work called Metaphysics gave the field its name, though the title was likely added by later editors.

Questions about free will, such as whether every event has a cause, are central topics in metaphysics.

cloze.s: Asking whether anything exists beyond the physical world is a question of ___.

note: Bookstores sometimes use the word for spiritual or New Age books, a different sense.

def: the idea that the mind at birth is a blank slate, with all knowledge coming from experience
why: Associated with John Locke, it shapes debates about how much of personality and intelligence comes from nature or nurture.
ex: Locke's view of the mind as a tabula rasa challenged the idea of inborn knowledge.
Modern psychologists reject a pure tabula rasa, since babies show some built-in abilities.
Behaviorists who claimed they could train any baby into any kind of adult were treating the mind as a tabula rasa.
In the novel, a robot begins as a tabula rasa and learns everything from the family it lives with.

note: Latin for “scraped tablet.”

def: a southern African philosophy of shared humanity, often summed up as “I am because we are”
why: Archbishop Desmond Tutu drew on it in South Africa's truth and reconciliation process after apartheid.

When neighbors rebuilt Fatima's house after the storm, she said their kindness was ubuntu in action.

cloze.s: The Nguni saying “a person is a person through other people” expresses the ethic of ___.

note: From Nguni languages such as Zulu and Xhosa. A computer operating system later borrowed the name.

def: Descartes's statement “I think, therefore I am,” meaning that the very act of thinking, even doubting, proves one's own existence
why: It was his starting point for rebuilding knowledge on certain foundations and is among the most famous lines in philosophy.
ex: Descartes arrived at cogito, ergo sum after trying to doubt everything he believed.
The poster in the philosophy department read “Cogito, ergo sum” in large letters.
When her roommate doubted that anything was real, Yuki answered with cogito, ergo sum: at least the doubter must exist.
The philosophy teacher explained cogito, ergo sum by asking students whether they could doubt that they were doubting.

cloze.s: Even if an evil demon deceived him about everything else, Descartes reasoned, ___ would still hold true.

note: It first appeared in French in his 1637 *Discourse on the Method* as “je pense, donc je suis.”

def: the view that the thinking self is a nonphysical substance, fundamentally distinct from physical matter like the brain
why: Most associated with René Descartes, it frames the long-running puzzle of how thought relates to the brain.
ex: Descartes's mind-body dualism held that the mind could exist without the body.
Many neuroscientists reject mind-body dualism, seeing the mind as what the brain does.
Hannah's psychology professor contrasted mind-body dualism with the view that thoughts are simply brain activity.
The science fiction film about uploading a person's mind into a robot plays with ideas from mind-body dualism.

cloze.s: Critics of Descartes's ___ asked how a nonphysical soul could move a physical arm.

def: misrepresenting someone's argument as a weaker or more extreme version, then attacking that distorted version instead
scenario: Maria suggests the office cut back on printing. Her coworker replies, "So you want us to stop using paper entirely and email everything, even signed contracts?"
fix: Restate the other person's actual claim in words they would agree with before responding to it.

tests.s: When Kwame said kids should get a little less homework, his neighbor answered, "Oh, so you think school shouldn't teach anything at all?"
Priya proposed adding one vegetarian dish to the cafeteria menu. A classmate told everyone she was trying to ban meat from campus.

def: attacking the character or traits of the person making an argument instead of addressing the argument itself
scenario: At a town meeting, Diego presents traffic data supporting a new crosswalk. Another resident says, "Why listen to him? He can't even keep his lawn mowed."
fix: Ask whether the personal remark has anything to do with whether the claim is true; usually it doesn't.

tests.s: Hannah points out a math error in the team budget, and a colleague responds that nobody should listen to someone who is always late to meetings.
A scientist presents data on river pollution, and a critic dismisses it by calling her rude and arrogant without ever mentioning the data.

def: presenting only two choices as if they were the only possibilities, when other options actually exist
scenario: "Either we cancel the company picnic or we go over budget," Liam says, ignoring the option of a cheaper venue.
fix: Ask whether other options, including combinations or middle paths, were left out.

tests.s: A coach tells his players, "You're either fully committed to this team, or you don't care about it at all."
A phone salesperson tells Jamal, "You either buy our top model, or you settle for a phone that can't do anything useful."

def: claiming that one small step will inevitably set off a chain of events ending in disaster, without showing why
scenario: "If we let students use calculators on one quiz, soon they'll use them on every test, forget basic math, and fail in college."
fix: Check each link in the predicted chain and ask what evidence shows one step must lead to the next.

tests.s: Yuki's dad says that if she stays up late this one Friday, she'll start skipping sleep every night, fail her classes, and never get into college.
A council member warns that allowing one food truck downtown will lead to dozens more, then to every restaurant closing, then to an empty, dying city center.

def: treating a claim as true mainly because a famous or respected person said it, especially outside their expertise
scenario: An actor who plays a doctor on TV recommends a vitamin in a commercial, and Jamal buys it because "a doctor said so."
fix: Ask whether the person is a genuine expert on this exact topic and whether other experts agree, then check the evidence itself.
note: Citing real experts on their own subject is reasonable; the problem is irrelevant expertise, or treating someone's status as proof.

tests.s: In a debate about tax policy, Malik ends the discussion by saying, "A Nobel Prize-winning chemist agrees with me, so I'm right."
A website claims a diet cures arthritis, and its only support is a quote from a famous physicist praising it.

def: arguing that something is true, good, or correct simply because many people believe it or do it
scenario: "Millions of people are buying this new digital coin, so it must be a smart investment," Tomás tells his sister.
fix: Remember that popularity shows what people believe, not whether it's true; look for evidence about the claim itself.

tests.s: "Everyone at school has this phone, so it has to be the best one," Aisha tells her parents.
A podcast host argues that a diet must work because it was the most searched diet online this year.

def: an argument whose conclusion is already assumed in its premises, so it offers no independent support
scenario: "This news site is trustworthy because it says it only publishes reliable stories."
fix: Ask what support exists for the claim that doesn't already assume the claim is true.
note: "Begging the question" traditionally names this fallacy; it does not originally mean "raising the question."

tests.s: "Olga is the best manager in the company because no one manages better than she does."
"You can trust my promise because I'm an honest person, and you know I'm honest because I always keep my promises."

def: drawing a broad conclusion about a whole category from too few or unrepresentative examples
scenario: After two of his flights on one airline were delayed, Wei declares that the airline is always late.
fix: Ask how many examples the conclusion rests on and whether they represent the whole category.

tests.s: Fatima met two rude shopkeepers on her first day in a new city and decided that everyone who lives there is unfriendly.
After his first two dates from an app were boring, Liam announces that everyone who uses dating apps is dull.

def: an irrelevant topic brought up to distract attention from the real issue being discussed
scenario: Asked why the project went over budget, the manager talks at length about how hard the team worked through the holidays.
fix: Notice when the conversation drifts and steer back: "That may be true, but how does it answer the original question?"

tests.s: When a reporter asks a company spokesperson about a product recall, she begins describing the company's charity work and its new logo.
Malik's roommate asks why he hasn't paid the electric bill, and Malik starts talking about how expensive groceries have gotten.

def: trying to win an argument by stirring up feelings like fear, pity, or guilt instead of giving good reasons
scenario: A fundraising letter shows photos of shivering puppies but gives no information about how donations are actually spent.
fix: Separate how the message makes you feel from the reasons it gives, and ask whether those reasons hold up.

tests.s: Instead of explaining why his grade should be changed, a student tells his professor how crushed his parents will be if he doesn't pass.
A salesperson tells Hannah that if she skips the extended warranty, she'll be heartbroken when her laptop dies and her family photos are lost forever.

def: continuing something because of the time, money, or effort already spent, even when quitting would be wiser
scenario: Jamal stays to watch a boring movie at the theater because he already paid for the ticket.
fix: Ignore what has already been spent and can't be recovered; judge only the future costs and benefits of each option.

tests.s: Priya has spent $3,000 repairing an old car that keeps breaking down, and she pays for another big repair because she can't bear to waste what she's already put in.
A company keeps funding a failing software project after five years, mainly because executives don't want the money already spent to have been for nothing.

def: believing a random outcome becomes more or less likely because of what happened in earlier independent trials
scenario: After a roulette wheel lands on red six times in a row, Diego bets heavily on black, convinced it is "due."
fix: Remember that independent events like coin flips have no memory; past results don't change the odds of the next one.

tests.s: Sofia flips a fair coin and gets heads five times in a row, so she tells her friend that tails is now almost certain on the next flip.
A lottery player avoids last week's winning numbers, sure they are now less likely to come up again in this week's random draw.

def: the tendency to seek out, notice, and remember information that supports what you already believe while dismissing the rest
scenario: Convinced his new running shoes make him faster, Kwame remembers every good run in them and forgets the slow ones.
fix: Deliberately look for the strongest evidence against your view and ask what would change your mind.

tests.s: Aisha believes her coworker dislikes her, so she reads every short email from him as cold and forgets the times he thanked her.
Sure that a certain stock will soar, Liam reads only the forums that agree with him and dismisses every critical analysis as uninformed.

def: the tendency, after learning an outcome, to believe you knew or could have predicted it all along
scenario: After the underdog team wins the final, Tomás insists he "always knew" they would, though he picked the favorite beforehand.
fix: Write down predictions before outcomes are known, then compare them honestly with what happened.

tests.s: When the stock market dropped, Olga told friends the crash had been obvious, even though she had bought more stocks the week before.
After a couple announced their breakup, several friends said they had seen it coming for months, though none had mentioned any concern before.

def: letting one positive trait, such as good looks or charm, color your judgment of a person's unrelated qualities
scenario: Because the new hire is friendly and well dressed, his manager assumes his reports must be accurate too.
fix: Judge each quality on its own evidence and ask whether the impressive trait is actually relevant.
note: The negative version, where one bad trait colors everything, is sometimes called the horn effect.

tests.s: Parents assume the school's star athlete must also be honest and hardworking, though they know nothing else about him.
Impressed by how attractive and well-spoken a job candidate is, the interviewer assumes he must also be organized and good with numbers.

def: the principle that two things occurring together, or rising and falling together, does not show one produces the other
scenario: A survey notes that people who own more books tend to earn more, and a blogger concludes that buying books will raise your income.
fix: Ask whether a third factor, a reversed direction, or chance could explain the link before assuming one thing drives the other.
note: A link can hint at a cause, but showing one usually takes experiments or careful controls.

tests.s: A survey finds that students who eat breakfast earn higher grades, and the principal announces that breakfast makes students smarter.
Countries where people eat more chocolate tend to have more Nobel Prize winners per person, so a website urges readers to eat chocolate to boost their intelligence.

def: relying on personal stories or isolated examples instead of systematic data to support a general claim
scenario: "My grandmother smoked her whole life and lived to 95, so smoking can't be that bad," says Malik.
fix: Ask what larger, carefully collected data show; one memorable story can't outweigh studies of thousands of people.

tests.s: Despite crash studies showing seatbelts save lives, Diego refuses to wear one because his uncle once survived a crash after being thrown from the car.
Large studies found a cold remedy does nothing, but Hannah keeps recommending it because her neighbor swears it cured her.

def: the number of people or cases a study examines; too few can make results unreliable or misleading
scenario: An app advertises that "90% of users lost weight," but its study included only ten people.
fix: Check how many cases a result is based on; small numbers can produce big swings by pure chance.

tests.s: A toothpaste ad announces that "4 out of 5 dentists recommend" it, but the fine print shows only five dentists were asked.
A poll of just 15 voters is reported on the evening news as showing which candidate the whole state prefers.

def: presenting only the facts or data that support your point while leaving out those that contradict it
scenario: A company's ad shows sales charts for its two best months, omitting the ten months of decline.
fix: Ask what the full data set looks like and what was left out, such as other time periods or studies.

tests.s: To argue that the town's streets are safe, a council candidate cites crime figures from the calmest month of the year and ignores the other eleven.
A hotel's website displays the twenty five-star reviews it received and hides the two hundred one- and two-star reviews.

def: the duty of the person making a claim to support it, rather than expecting others to show it is wrong
scenario: Yuki says a local lake has a monster in it, and when friends doubt her, she says, "Well, you can't prove there isn't one."
fix: Ask the person making the claim to provide evidence; doubting a claim doesn't require proving it false.

tests.s: Kwame claims his new supplement doubles memory and tells his skeptical friends it's up to them to show it doesn't work.
A user posts that a famous singer secretly owns his favorite pizza chain and insists critics must disprove it before he'll stop sharing it.

def: assuming that because one event followed another, the first event must have produced the second
scenario: Fatima's computer crashed right after she installed a game, so she blamed the game, though a failing hard drive was the real culprit.
fix: Ask whether there's a real mechanism linking the two events, and whether the second might have happened anyway.

tests.s: The lights went out in Liam's apartment right after he plugged in his new toaster, so he returned it, but the whole block had lost power.
A soccer fan wore a new jersey on Saturday, his team won, and now he insists the jersey brings victories.

def: dismissing criticism by pointing out that the critic is guilty of the same behavior, instead of answering it
scenario: When Olga's sister asks her to drive more carefully, Olga snaps, "You got a speeding ticket last year!"
fix: Remember that a critic's hypocrisy doesn't make their point wrong; respond to the criticism itself.
note: Latin for "you too." Closely related to whataboutism.

tests.s: When a teenager is told he spends too much time on his phone, he only points out that his mom checks hers at every meal.
A city council member criticized for missing votes responds only that her accuser missed even more votes last year.

def: protecting a broad claim from a counterexample by redefining the category so that the example no longer counts
scenario: "No real fan would leave a game early." "My cousin is a lifelong fan, and he left early." "Then he's not a real fan."
fix: Ask whether the definition was changed only to dodge the counterexample; if so, the original claim has been quietly abandoned.

tests.s: Wei says no serious chef uses store-bought pasta. Shown an award-winning chef who does, he replies that she can't be a serious chef, then.
"No genuine runner walks during a marathon," Sofia insists. Told that an Olympic marathoner walked part of a race, she says he isn't a genuine runner.

def: changing the standard of evidence or success after it has been met, so the demand can never be satisfied
scenario: Priya's boss said she'd get a raise if she landed three new clients. When she landed three, he said it would take five.
fix: Agree beforehand on what would count as success or proof, and point out when that standard keeps changing.

tests.s: Diego asked for proof that the new bus route was faster. When shown it saved ten minutes, he said it had to save twenty, every day for a full year.
A skeptic said he'd accept electric cars as practical if one could go 300 miles on a charge. When shown one, he said it must also recharge in five minutes.

def: arguing something is good or safe because it comes from plants or the wild, or bad because it is artificial
scenario: Aisha assumes an herbal supplement can't hurt her because it's made from plants.
fix: Remember that many natural things are harmful, like poisonous mushrooms, and many artificial ones are helpful; judge each by evidence.

tests.s: A shampoo ad promises the product is safe for babies simply because every ingredient is "all natural."
Malik says anything made in a lab must be worse for him than something that comes straight from a plant, so he avoids all artificial sweeteners.

def: treating two things as the same because they share some feature, while ignoring major differences in scale or kind
scenario: Hannah argues that forgetting to return a library book is as bad as stealing a car, since both involve keeping something that isn't yours.
fix: Ask how the two things differ in size, harm, and context, not just how they're alike.

tests.s: Kwame says jaywalking and drunk driving are equally serious because both are traffic violations.
A commentator says a restaurant with one minor health citation is no different from one that caused a food poisoning outbreak, since both "broke health rules."

def: a query built on an unproven assumption, so that any direct answer seems to admit that assumption
scenario: A reporter asks a coach, "Have you stopped favoring your star player?"
fix: Point out the hidden assumption and challenge it instead of answering yes or no.

tests.s: During a meeting, someone asks Olga, "Why do you always ignore customer complaints?" though she has never ignored one.
A survey asks shop owners, "How much has the new parking policy hurt your business?" with no option for "It hasn't."

def: arguing that something is right or best simply because it has been done that way for a long time
scenario: When Liam suggests online scheduling at the clinic, the office manager says, "We've used paper sign-in sheets for thirty years, so they're fine."
fix: Ask what reasons support the practice today, apart from how long it has existed.

tests.s: A school board member opposes a later start time, arguing that school has always started at 7:30 in this town, so that must be the right time.
Asked why the family recipe calls for boiling vegetables for an hour, Tomás's aunt says it must be correct because their family has made it that way for generations.

def: assuming a compromise between two opposing positions must be correct simply because it lies between them
scenario: One friend says the restaurant opens at 5 p.m. and another says 7 p.m., so Wei assumes it must open at 6.
fix: Judge each position on its evidence; sometimes one side is simply right and the halfway point is wrong.

tests.s: One engineer says the bridge can hold 10 tons and another says 2 tons, so the manager posts a 6-ton limit without checking either calculation.
Sofia's doctor says a medication is safe while an online forum calls it poisonous, so Sofia concludes the truth must be that it's "somewhat dangerous."

def: relying too heavily on the first number or piece of information you encounter when making later estimates
scenario: A car dealer first shows Jamal a $50,000 model, so the $35,000 car he sees next feels like a bargain.
fix: Form your own estimate from independent facts before hearing others' numbers, and question where the first figure came from.

tests.s: People first asked whether a city has more or fewer than 5 million residents later guess its population far higher than people first asked about 200,000.
Because the first salary mentioned in the negotiation was $40,000, Aisha countered at just $45,000, though similar jobs paid $60,000.

def: judging how common or likely something is by how easily examples of it come to mind
scenario: After seeing news coverage of a shark attack, Olga becomes afraid to swim in the ocean, though her daily drive is far riskier.
fix: Look up actual statistics rather than relying on the most vivid or recent examples you remember.

tests.s: After a week of headlines about a plane crash, Diego decides to drive across the country instead of flying, believing driving is safer.
Because she can easily recall several friends whose homes were burglarized, Hannah guesses that most homes in her city are broken into every year.

def: drawing conclusions only from the people or things that made it through some filter, ignoring those that failed
scenario: Noting that several famous tech founders dropped out of college, Malik concludes that dropping out is a path to success.
fix: Ask what happened to the cases you can't see, the failures that were filtered out, before drawing conclusions.

tests.s: Admiring the old houses in her town, Fatima concludes builders long ago did better work, not considering that poorly built old houses were torn down decades ago.
Looking only at investment funds still operating today, an analyst concludes funds generally do well, not counting the many that shut down after poor results.

def: making different choices depending on how the same information is worded, such as in terms of gains or losses
scenario: Patients are more willing to choose a surgery described as having a 90% survival rate than one described as having a 10% death rate.
fix: Restate the information the opposite way and see whether your decision still makes sense.

tests.s: Shoppers prefer ground beef labeled "80% lean" over the identical beef labeled "20% fat."
Students are more likely to sign up for a course when told 75% of past students passed than when told 25% of past students failed.

def: when a team's desire for harmony leads members to suppress doubts and reach a poor, unchallenged decision
scenario: Every member of a planning committee privately doubts the launch date, but no one speaks up because everyone else seems confident.
fix: Invite dissent openly, assign someone to argue the other side, and collect opinions privately before discussion.

tests.s: A hospital board approves an expensive new wing in one meeting; several members had serious concerns but stayed quiet so as not to seem disloyal to the director.
On a hiking trip, four friends all go along with a risky shortcut, each secretly worried but unwilling to spoil the upbeat mood by objecting.

def: the tendency to feel the pain of giving something up more strongly than the pleasure of an equal gain
scenario: Kwame refuses a coin-flip bet in which he would win $120 on heads and lose $100 on tails, even though on average he would come out ahead.
fix: Compare outcomes in plain numbers and ask whether a gain and a loss of the same size truly deserve such different weight.

tests.s: Tomás feels miserable for days after losing $100 on a bad trade, though winning $100 the month before barely lifted his mood.
Offered an even-odds bet to win $150 or lose $100, Fatima turns it down because losing $100 would sting more than winning $150 would please her.

def: the tendency to underestimate how long your own tasks will take, even when similar past tasks ran late
scenario: Every year Aisha expects to finish her taxes in one evening, and every year it takes her a full weekend.
fix: Base estimates on how long similar past projects actually took, then add a buffer.

tests.s: A contractor promises a kitchen remodel in three weeks, as he did for his last ten jobs, every one of which took more than two months.
Liam tells his professor the paper will be done by Friday, though each of his last five papers took twice as long as he expected.

def: a hidden third factor that influences both things being studied, creating a misleading link between them
scenario: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together, but hot weather drives both: people buy more ice cream and swim more.
fix: Ask what other factor could affect both things, and look for studies that measured and adjusted for it.

tests.s: A study finds coffee drinkers have higher lung cancer rates, but the coffee drinkers also smoked more; once smoking is accounted for, the link disappears.
Children with bigger shoe sizes score higher on reading tests, but that's because older children have both larger feet and more years of reading practice.

def: a distortion that occurs when the people or cases studied don't represent the larger population being described
scenario: A gym surveys its members at 6 a.m. and concludes that most people in town love early morning exercise.
fix: Ask how the participants were chosen and whether that process favored certain kinds of people.

tests.s: A poll on a gaming forum finds that 85% of respondents want video game classes in schools, and the forum reports this as national opinion.
To estimate how many books a typical resident reads, a researcher interviews only people walking out of the public library.

def: a real improvement in symptoms that comes from believing you are being treated, not from the treatment itself
scenario: Patients given sugar pills they think are painkillers often report that their pain has eased.
fix: Compare treatments against an inactive look-alike in blinded trials so that belief alone can't explain the results.
note: It mainly affects self-reported symptoms such as pain or nausea, not the underlying disease.

tests.s: In a trial, half the volunteers with headaches got an inactive pill, yet many of them said their headaches improved after taking it.
Malik feels much more alert after drinking what he thinks is strong coffee, though his roommate secretly served him decaf.

def: the principle that, among competing explanations, the one requiring the fewest assumptions is usually preferable
scenario: When cookies vanish from the jar, Hannah suspects her teenage son rather than a burglar who took only cookies.
fix: Prefer the simplest explanation that fits all the facts, but drop it if new evidence demands something more complex.
note: A rule of thumb, not proof: the simpler explanation is the better starting bet, not guaranteed to be true.

tests.s: When her car won't start on a freezing morning, Olga suspects a weak battery before considering sabotage by a neighbor.
Seeing a crop circle appear overnight, Wei concludes people made it with boards and rope rather than a spaceship, since that explanation needs far fewer assumptions.

def: judging an idea or practice as good or bad based on where it originated rather than on its current merits
scenario: Diego refuses to use a proven study technique because it was first developed for military training.
fix: Ask whether the idea's origin actually affects whether it is true or useful today.

tests.s: Jamal says the town's popular spring festival is worthless today because it was first started decades ago to promote a local car dealership.
Sofia won't try a popular dish because it was invented by accident when a cook made a mistake, so she says it "can't be any good."

def: shifting between two different meanings of the same word within an argument to reach a misleading conclusion
scenario: "A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. So a feather cannot be dark."
fix: Pin down what each key word means and check that it means the same thing every time it appears.

tests.s: "The sign said 'Fine for parking here,' so I figured it was fine to park here."
"Nothing is better than a long vacation. A cheap sandwich is better than nothing. So a cheap sandwich is better than a long vacation."

def: assuming that what is true of each part must also be true of the whole they make up
scenario: Every player on the all-star team is excellent, so Tomás assumes they will easily beat a squad that has practiced together for years.
fix: Ask whether the whole can behave differently from its parts because of interactions, combinations, or scale.

tests.s: Since chocolate, pickles, and garlic each taste great on their own, Aisha assumes mixing all three will make a great dish.
Because one person standing up at a concert gets a better view, Liam concludes that if everyone stood up, everyone would get a better view.

def: assuming that what is true of a whole must also be true of each of its parts or members
scenario: The university is world famous, so Olga assumes every professor there must be a world-class teacher.
fix: Remember that a whole's overall traits, like its average or reputation, may not apply to every member.

tests.s: The country has one of the highest average incomes in the world, so Malik assumes every family living there is wealthy.
A salad is healthy, so Wei assumes every ingredient in it, including the heavy creamy dressing, must be healthy too.

def: applying a rule or standard to others while exempting yourself or a favored case without good reason
scenario: Hannah says everyone must follow the no-phones-in-meetings rule, but checks hers because her messages are "different."
fix: Ask what relevant difference justifies the exception; if there is none, the rule should apply equally.

tests.s: Diego insists speeding is dangerous and reckless, but says it's fine when he does it because he's an experienced driver.
A manager requires every employee to submit receipts for expenses but exempts his own spending, saying he's "too busy for paperwork."

def: spotting a cluster or pattern in data after the fact and claiming it was meaningful or predicted all along
scenario: A reporter marks every case of a rare illness on a map, spots one neighborhood with several cases, and declares something there must be causing them.
fix: Ask whether the pattern was predicted before looking at the data, and how often similar clusters appear by chance.
note: Named for a joke about a man who fires at a barn, then paints a target around the tightest group of bullet holes.

tests.s: An investor tests 500 trading rules on past stock prices, finds the one that would have earned the most, and advertises it as a proven winning strategy.
After the season, a fan sifts through the schedule, notices his team won every game played on a date ending in 7, and declares the pattern meaningful.

def: the finding that people with little skill in an area often overestimate their own ability in it
scenario: After reading one article about investing, Jamal is sure he can outperform professional fund managers.
fix: Seek objective feedback and compare your results with skilled performers; the less you know, the harder your gaps are to see.
note: From a 1999 study by David Dunning and Justin Kruger. How large the effect is remains debated; some researchers argue part of it is a statistical artifact.

tests.s: After two chess lessons, Yuki is certain she could beat most players at the local club, though she can't yet spot basic tactics.
On a grammar quiz, the students who scored lowest predicted they had outscored most of the class.

def: ignoring how common something is in general when judging the probability of a specific case
scenario: A test for a rare disease is 99% accurate. Tomás tests positive and assumes he almost certainly has it, forgetting that only 1 in 10,000 people do.
fix: Start with how common the thing is overall, then adjust for the specific evidence.

tests.s: Told that a stranger is quiet and loves books, Fatima guesses he is more likely a librarian than a salesperson, forgetting that salespeople vastly outnumber librarians.
An airport scanner wrongly flags 1% of innocent travelers, yet Sofia assumes anyone it flags is almost surely a smuggler, though smugglers are extremely rare among millions of passengers.

def: explaining other people's behavior by their character while underestimating the role of their circumstances
scenario: When a driver cuts him off, Kwame decides the man is a selfish jerk, never considering he might be rushing to a hospital.
fix: Before judging someone's character, ask what situation might lead a reasonable person to act the same way.

tests.s: When a new cashier is slow, Olga decides she must be lazy, not noticing that the register keeps freezing.
Diego assumes a classmate who skipped the study session doesn't care about grades, without knowing she works night shifts to support her family.

def: a preference for keeping things as they are, even when a change would leave you better off
scenario: Malik has stayed on the same expensive phone plan for eight years without ever comparing it with cheaper ones.
fix: Imagine choosing from scratch today: would you pick your current option?

tests.s: When a company switches its retirement plan from sign-up to automatic enrollment, participation jumps, because most workers simply stick with whatever the default is.
Priya keeps her savings in an account earning almost no interest, though a similar account at the same bank pays far more and switching takes five minutes.

def: the tendency for an unusually extreme result to be followed by one closer to the average
scenario: A flight instructor praises a student after an exceptionally smooth landing, the next landing is worse, and he decides that praise backfires.
fix: Expect extreme results to drift back toward normal on their own, and don't credit or blame whatever happened in between.

tests.s: A baseball rookie has a spectacular first season and a much more ordinary second one, and fans blame the pressure of fame.
A student who got the top score on one quiz scores closer to the class average on the next, and her teacher concludes she has stopped trying.

def: the tendency for journals to print studies with striking positive results more often than studies finding no effect
scenario: Twenty labs test whether a supplement improves memory; the two that find an effect appear in journals, while the eighteen null results sit in file drawers.
fix: Look for preregistered trials and reviews that include unpublished studies, and be cautious when only positive results appear.

tests.s: A doctor reviewing the journals finds that nearly every study of a new therapy shows benefits, unaware that many trials showing no benefit were never submitted or accepted.
Researchers who find no link between a food and cancer rarely get their papers accepted, so readers hear only about studies that do find a link.

def: the difference between a percentage change in the chance of harm and the actual number of people affected
scenario: A headline says a new drug cuts stroke risk in half, but the actual drop is from 2 in 1,000 people to 1 in 1,000.
fix: Ask for the actual numbers before and after, such as how many people out of 1,000 are affected.

tests.s: A brochure says a new bike helmet "cuts your chance of a head injury by 50%," but the fine print shows it fell from 2 in 10,000 rides to 1 in 10,000.
A news story warns that a snack raises the risk of a rare cancer by 30%, without mentioning that the lifetime risk goes from 10 in 100,000 to 13 in 100,000.

def: a comparison set of subjects who don't receive the treatment, used to show whether the treatment made a difference
scenario: A company gives every employee a standing desk, sees productivity rise 8%, and credits the desks, without checking similar workers who kept their old desks.
fix: Ask "Compared to what?" and look for a similar set of people or places that didn't get the change.
note: Test scenarios for this concept show a conclusion drawn without one.

tests.s: A town installs new streetlights and burglaries fall 20%, but no one checks whether burglaries fell just as much in nearby towns without new lights.
