ex: Thanks to a timely warning from neighbors, the family left before the flood reached their street.

def: easy to understand or do; not complicated
ex: Setting up the new printer was more straightforward than Liam expected.

ex: The nurse was sympathetic and held Malik's hand while the doctor explained the results.

also: agreeing with or supporting an idea or group (“sympathetic to their cause”)

cloze.s: The patient needed a(n) ___ stay in the hospital after problems following surgery.

def: existing in large amounts; more than enough

def: together with one or more other people or groups, sharing the work or the responsibility

def: the act of moving down to a lower place, or a path or slope that goes down

also: the family or ethnic background that a person comes from (“She is of Korean descent.”)

def: the state of being successful and having plenty of money and good things

def: something nice you say to praise someone or show that you like what they did

def: respect and a high opinion of someone

def: a person who hates spending money, even when spending is fair or expected
ex: Liam's friends called him a cheapskate after he refused to chip in for the pizza.
Don't be a cheapskate; leave the waiter a proper tip.
The cheapskate boss gave everyone a single candy bar as a holiday bonus.
Wei is no cheapskate; he just refuses to pay for things he never uses.

cloze.s: My uncle is such a(n) ___ that he reuses paper towels to avoid buying new ones.

note: Informal and disapproving.

def: a careful feeling of not trusting someone or something because of possible danger or problems
ex: After the scam, Aisha treated every unexpected email with wariness.
There was some wariness among voters about the candidate's big promises.
New employees approached the strict manager with understandable wariness.
Investors showed growing wariness about the company after it missed its sales targets again.

cloze.s: The stray cat approached the bowl with great ___, ready to run at any sound.

def: a lack of courage or confidence; the quality of being shy and easily frightened
ex: His timidity kept him from speaking up during meetings.
Critics blamed the company's timidity for its failure to try new ideas.
The puppy's timidity faded once it learned that the children meant no harm.
Overcoming her timidity, Olga asked her new neighbor to join her for coffee.

cloze.s: Yuki overcame her ___ and sang a solo in front of the whole school.

def: a person's look or manner, especially as it shows their character or mood
ex: The judge's calm mien gave no hint of what she was thinking.
Despite his gentle mien, Tomás was a fierce competitor on the tennis court.
Kwame's cheerful mien made patients in the waiting room feel calmer.
Even after losing the match, the champion kept a dignified mien.

cloze.s: With her serious ___ and gray suit, the new principal seemed stern until she smiled.

note: Literary or formal; pronounced like “mean.”

def: a failure to show thanks for help, kindness, or gifts received
ex: Sofia was hurt by her brother's ingratitude after she lent him money for rent.
The coach was shocked by the ingratitude of players he had helped for years.
The volunteers felt stung by the town's ingratitude after weeks of cleaning up flood damage.
Ana scolded her son for his ingratitude when he complained about his birthday gift.

cloze.s: After all the help he gave them, their ___ left him angry and disappointed.

def: a sudden, brief feeling of excitement or fear that is like a thrill
ex: A frisson of excitement ran through the crowd as the lights went down.
Wei felt a frisson of fear when he heard footsteps behind him on the empty street.
Riding the roller coaster gave Amir a frisson of fear as the car tipped over the top.
A frisson ran through the courtroom when the surprise witness walked in.

cloze.s: Opening the old letter gave Maria a(n) ___ of excitement, as if a secret were about to be revealed.

note: From French. Usually in “a frisson of excitement” or “a frisson of fear.”

def: the quality of lasting only a short time
ex: The poem reflects on the transience of youth and beauty.
The transience of the city's population makes it hard to build strong neighborhoods.
Traveling constantly for work, Jamal grew tired of the transience of hotel life.
The artist builds sand sculptures to celebrate transience, knowing the tide will wash them away.

cloze.s: Cherry blossoms, which fall within days, are often seen as a symbol of the ___ of life.

def: something that looks like or copies something else, but is often a poor or empty imitation
ex: The theme park's main street is a simulacrum of a small town that never existed.
Critics called the reality show a simulacrum of real life, staged from start to finish.
The hotel lobby was a simulacrum of a Venetian palace, built of plastic and painted foam.
Hannah felt the video calls were only a simulacrum of the family dinners she missed.

cloze.s: The cheap restaurant offered only a(n) ___ of Italian food, with canned sauce and soggy pasta.

note: Formal; plural usually “simulacra.”

def: the fact of being able to make mistakes or be wrong
ex: Good scientists accept their own fallibility and test their ideas carefully.
The trial showed the fallibility of eyewitness memories.
The coach reminded the team of the referee's fallibility, saying even the best officials miss calls.
The famous chef laughed about her own fallibility after a dish went badly wrong on live TV.

cloze.s: The judge's honest admission of her own ___ made people trust her more, not less.

def: politics based on practical goals and power rather than on moral ideals or principles
ex: The treaty was a piece of cold realpolitik, uniting two countries that disliked each other.
Critics said the president's friendship with the dictator was realpolitik, not principle.
In history class, students debated whether the alliance was wise realpolitik or a betrayal of principles.
Realpolitik led the two rival countries to work together on stopping the spread of disease.

cloze.s: Choosing trade over human rights, the government defended its deal as necessary ___.

note: From German, roughly “practical politics.”

def: in a way that shows you think something is good or right
ex: Jamal's grandmother nodded approvingly as he cleared the table without being asked.
The critic wrote approvingly of the museum's new exhibit.
The crowd murmured approvingly when the mayor announced free buses on weekends.
Fatima's boss read the report and spoke approvingly of its clear charts.

cloze.s: The coach smiled ___ as the rookie made his first perfect free throw.

def: in a nervous or worried way, often because you feel something is wrong
ex: Hannah glanced uneasily at the dark clouds as the boat left the dock.
The witness shifted uneasily in his chair when the lawyer raised the question.
Priya laughed uneasily when the stranger seemed to know her name.
The dog paced uneasily around the house hours before the thunderstorm began.

cloze.s: The two former friends sat ___ across from each other, neither one sure what to say.

def: in a firm, determined way that will not accept no or be ignored
ex: The phone rang insistently until Malik finally picked it up.
The children asked insistently to stay up and watch the fireworks.
The nurse insistently reminded Tomás to finish all his antibiotics, even after he felt better.
Aisha knocked insistently on her neighbor's door until he came out to move his car.

cloze.s: The dog barked ___ at the door until someone finally let him in.

def: in a way that shows you cannot or will not believe what you see or hear
ex: “You won the lottery?” Olga asked incredulously.
The fans stared incredulously at the scoreboard after the last-second goal.
The teacher looked incredulously at the student who claimed a goat had eaten his homework.
Nadia read the hospital bill incredulously, sure there had been a mistake.

cloze.s: When the mechanic named the repair price, Diego laughed ___ and asked him to repeat it.

def: in a short and rude way, using very few words
ex: The receptionist curtly told the visitors to wait outside.
When asked about the scandal, the senator replied curtly, “No comment.”
The busy pharmacist answered curtly, 'One pill a day,' and turned away.
Kwame nodded curtly at his ex-girlfriend and kept walking.

cloze.s: Annoyed by the interruption, she ___ said “not now” and closed the door.

def: in a way that shows anger at something that seems unfair or insulting
ex: “I've never cheated in my life,” Aisha said indignantly.
The passengers complained indignantly when the airline canceled the flight without notice.
The customer indignantly demanded a refund after being charged twice for the same meal.
“I'm not too young to help,” the girl replied indignantly.

cloze.s: Accused of taking the last cookie, the boy ___ denied it and pointed at his sister.

def: in a way meant to show off, attract attention, and impress others
ex: The new owner ostentatiously parked his gold sports car right in front of the restaurant.
Kwame yawned ostentatiously to show how bored he was by the speech.
She ostentatiously paid for everyone's dinner with a thick stack of hundred-dollar bills.
The couple's new mansion was ostentatiously decorated with gold faucets and marble lions.

cloze.s: He checked his diamond watch ___ so that everyone at the table would notice it.

def: in a way that shows doubt about whether something is true or will work
ex: The investors listened skeptically to the founder's promise of quick profits.
Yuki raised an eyebrow skeptically when her son said he had finished all his homework.
The mechanic listened skeptically as Liam insisted the strange noise had started only that morning.
Shoppers eyed the “buy one, get three free” sign skeptically, looking for the catch.

cloze.s: The doctor looked ___ at the bottle of “miracle” pills her patient had bought online.

def: in a way that is surprising because it seemed unlikely to happen or be true
ex: The team improbably came back from twenty points down to win the game.
The tiny bakery has improbably become one of the city's most famous restaurants.
Improbably, the shy intern ended up giving the best speech at the company party.
A sunflower seed improbably sprouted in a crack in the sidewalk and grew taller than a fence.

cloze.s: The old car, which looked ready for the junkyard, ___ made it all the way across the country.

def: unable to keep still, moving the hands or body in a restless or nervous way
ex: The children grew fidgety during the long wedding ceremony.
Liam always gets fidgety before a job interview and taps his pen on the table.
Students get fidgety in the last minutes before the bell rings for summer break.
Waiting for her test results, Grace grew fidgety and kept twisting her ring.

cloze.s: After two hours on the plane, the ___ toddler kept kicking the seat in front of him.

def: not reduced or made weaker, even after time or difficulty
ex: At ninety, my grandfather's love of chess remains undiminished.
The team's popularity was undiminished despite three losing seasons.
Despite a knee injury, the dancer performed with undiminished grace.
The hurricane crossed the island with its strength undiminished.

cloze.s: Even after the long delay, the fans' excitement was ___ when the band finally took the stage.

def: not well known or praised, often despite being talented or important
ex: An unheralded rookie scored the winning goal in the championship game.
The book tells the story of the unheralded nurses who kept the hospital running during the flood.
The real hero of the project was an unheralded engineer who fixed the software the night before launch.
The museum finally gave the unheralded painter, who had worked in poverty for years, her first solo show.

cloze.s: Nobody had heard of the ___ young runner before she won the marathon.

def: not paying attention to possible danger or tricks, and so easy to catch or cheat
ex: The fake website was designed to trap unwary shoppers into giving away their card numbers.
An unwary hiker could easily slip on the wet rocks near the waterfall.
Pickpockets in the crowded station looked for unwary travelers busy checking their phones.
Hidden fees in the fine print can trap unwary renters into paying hundreds of dollars more.

cloze.s: Scammers often target ___ older people who trust callers claiming to be from the bank.

note: Often used as a noun phrase: “a trap for the unwary.”

def: unwilling to spend or give money, even when it is needed; also used for a very small amount
ex: Despite his wealth, Liam was so miserly that he refused to turn on the heat in winter.
The company offered a miserly raise of half a percent after a record year.
The miserly landlord refused to fix the broken heater until the tenants complained to the city.
Travelers often complain about the miserly legroom in economy seats on long flights.

cloze.s: Her ___ uncle reused tea bags three times and never once paid for a family dinner.

def: going against the beliefs or opinions that most people in a field or group accept
ex: Kwame's heterodox views on economics made him popular with students but unpopular with older professors.
The doctor's heterodox approach to treatment was later accepted as standard practice.
The coach's heterodox strategy of never punting went against decades of accepted football wisdom.
In a field where nearly everyone agreed, Tomás's heterodox opinion sparked a lively debate at the conference.

cloze.s: Her ideas were so ___ that the main scientific journals refused to publish them for years.

note: Formal; often used of religious, political or academic views.

def: noticeable in a way that is unpleasant, annoying, or not wanted
ex: The new cell tower is an obtrusive sight on the quiet hillside.
Waiters at the restaurant were attentive without being obtrusive.
Kwame removed the obtrusive logo from his slides so the charts would stand out.
The loud, obtrusive music in the hotel lobby made it hard to have a conversation.

cloze.s: The security cameras were so ___ that guests felt they were being watched every second.

def: willing to act dishonestly or unfairly to get what one wants; without moral standards
ex: The unprincipled landlord kept tenants' deposits by inventing damage that never happened.
Voters were angered by the unprincipled tactics used in the final weeks of the campaign.
The unprincipled car dealer secretly lowered the mileage shown on used cars before selling them.
Hannah refused to work for an unprincipled boss who told her to lie to customers.

cloze.s: Only a(n) ___ lawyer would hide evidence that proved his own client's victim was telling the truth.

def: good and quick at using the hands, or clever in handling hard problems
ex: The dexterous surgeon tied tiny knots that were almost too small to see.
Aisha's dexterous handling of the angry customers impressed her new manager.
The dexterous pianist raced through the fast passage without missing a single note.
A dexterous negotiator, Ana found a deal that pleased both the union and the company's owners.

cloze.s: It takes ___ fingers to repair the tiny gears inside an old watch.

note: Also spelled “dextrous.”

def: round and full in shape, used especially of a person with a large belly
ex: The rotund little man laughed so hard that his belly shook.
A rotund pumpkin sat on the front step beside the door.
The rotund cat could barely squeeze through the pet door after months of extra treats.
Mr. Delgado, a rotund man with a booming laugh, played Santa at the community center every December.

cloze.s: After years of rich meals, the once-thin chef had become quite ___.

note: Gentler and more humorous than “fat.”

def: so honest, reliable, or correct that it cannot be doubted or questioned
ex: The reporter refused to run the story until she had an unimpeachable source.
Hannah's record as a judge was unimpeachable after thirty years on the bench.
The scientist's methods were unimpeachable, so other labs quickly accepted her results.
Before hiring Malik, the company checked his references, which were unimpeachable.

cloze.s: With video, fingerprints and three witnesses, the evidence against him was ___.

def: so angry that one seems almost unable to control oneself
ex: The coach was apoplectic when the referee ignored a clear foul in the final minute.
Diego's father went apoplectic after seeing the dent in his new car.
Malik was apoplectic when the moving company lost every box of his books.
The chef went apoplectic after a critic called her famous soup bland.

cloze.s: When he learned his flight was canceled for the third time, the traveler was ___ with rage.

note: Stronger than “angry”; often used humorously for extreme anger.

def: able to bend easily without breaking or cracking
ex: Soak the willow branches overnight so they become pliant enough to weave.
The new running shoes have pliant soles that bend with each step.
The dentist pressed pliant plastic around Kwame's teeth to make a mold.
Young bamboo stems are pliant and sway in the wind without snapping.

cloze.s: Old leather turns stiff and cracks, but well-oiled leather stays soft and ___.

also: too easily controlled or influenced by other people (“a pliant board that approved every plan”)

def: in the habit of getting involved in other people's business when not wanted
ex: Our meddlesome neighbor reads our mail if it's left on the porch.
Wei asked his meddlesome aunt to stop giving advice about his marriage.
The meddlesome manager kept rewriting emails that Priya had already sent.
Malik's meddlesome roommate rearranged his desk and read his notes without asking.

cloze.s: Every family seems to have one ___ relative who keeps asking when you'll get married.

def: showing a playful wish to cause small, harmless trouble
ex: Yuki gave an impish grin before dropping the ice cube down her brother's shirt.
The comedian's impish sense of humor kept the audience laughing all night.
The impish students switched the labels on the teacher's coffee and tea jars before class.
Lena's impish smile told us she had planned the surprise water-balloon fight.

cloze.s: With a(n) ___ wink, Grandpa hid the TV remote inside the cookie jar.

note: Positive and affectionate; comes from “imp,” a small mischievous creature in folklore.

def: coming from very old, basic human instincts or habits that seem to return from early ancestors
ex: Some experts link our atavistic fear of snakes to dangers faced by early humans.
The crowd's atavistic roar as the fighters entered the ring was almost frightening.
Hearing thunder in the night, Liam felt an atavistic urge to hide under the blankets.
The hunters' atavistic thrill at the chase seemed to come from somewhere deep and ancient.

cloze.s: Sitting around a campfire seems to awaken a(n) ___ comfort that goes back thousands of years.

note: Formal; often describes fears, urges or behavior that feel ancient or primitive.

def: so surprised and confused that one does not know how to react
ex: Malik was nonplussed when the interviewer asked him to sing a song.
The teacher looked nonplussed by the strange answer and paused for a long moment.
Fatima was nonplussed when her toddler announced that he was now a dinosaur named Steve.
The referee looked nonplussed as both teams walked off the field at the same time.

cloze.s: Totally ___, the tourist stared at the menu, which had no prices and no English.

note: In American English it is often used to mean “calm, unbothered,” the opposite sense. Many careful writers still treat that use as a mistake.

def: not paying attention to a danger, warning, or advice
ex: Heedless of the storm warnings, the sailors headed out of the harbor.
Sofia rushed ahead, heedless of her parents shouting at her to slow down.
Heedless of the “wet paint” sign, the toddler pressed both hands on the fresh bench.
Some hikers wander off the trail, heedless of warnings about falling rocks.

cloze.s: ___ of his doctor's advice, he kept eating fried food every day.

note: Often followed by “of.”

def: dried up, thin, and full of lines, especially because of old age
ex: A wizened old fisherman sat on the dock mending his nets.
The forgotten apples in the bowl had turned brown and wizened.
The wizened old woman at the market had sold herbs from the same stall for sixty years.
Years in the desert sun had left the old rancher's hands wizened and brown.

cloze.s: The ___ face of the ninety-year-old farmer was lined like a map.

note: Not related to “wise” or “wizard.”

def: causing or tending to cause sleep; also so boring that it makes people sleepy
ex: The professor's soporific voice had half the class nodding off by noon.
A warm bath and herbal tea had a soporific effect on Priya after a long shift.
Some allergy pills are soporific, so the label warns against driving after taking them.
The long, soporific drive across the flat Kansas plains made Jamal pull over for coffee.

cloze.s: The two-hour budget presentation was so ___ that several people dozed in their seats.

def: never changing or becoming weaker, especially in loyalty or support
ex: Fatima thanked her coach for his unswerving support during her injury.
The dog's unswerving loyalty to its owner was the subject of a local news story.
The team's unswerving commitment to defense carried them through the playoffs.
Despite years of setbacks, the scientist kept an unswerving dedication to finding a cure.

cloze.s: Through every hard year, her ___ belief in her son never wavered.

def: rude and mean, especially by failing to be polite or thankful when you should be
ex: It would be churlish to refuse such a kind gift from your hosts.
The star's churlish behavior toward fans hurt his reputation.
Liam was churlish to the waiter who brought the wrong order, refusing even to look at him.
It seems churlish to criticize a free concert, but the sound really was terrible.

cloze.s: After the team won, it seemed ___ to complain about the coach's choices.

note: Often in the phrase “it would be churlish to…” meaning it would seem ungrateful.

def: lacking self-control, especially in using angry or extreme words
ex: The senator apologized for his intemperate remarks about the reporters.
Jamal's intemperate email to the whole office got him called into a meeting.
Late at night, Wei typed an intemperate review of the hotel, then deleted it the next morning.
Parents at the school board meeting were asked to avoid intemperate language and stay respectful.

cloze.s: Her ___ outburst at the meeting, full of shouting and insults, surprised everyone.

also: drinking too much alcohol, often as a habit (“an intemperate man who drank every night”)

def: dull, old-fashioned, and not willing to change or have fun
ex: The museum hired a young director to make its stodgy image more appealing to families.
Tomás found the law firm too stodgy and moved to a small startup.
Liam's stodgy uncle refused to try any restaurant that had opened after 1990.
Kwame expected the retirement party to be stodgy, but the guests danced until midnight.

cloze.s: The magazine tried to shed its ___ reputation by adding humor and bright photos.

also: heavy and filling, used of food (“a stodgy pudding”)

def: having lost hope and enthusiasm, often after failure or bad news
ex: The dispirited players walked off the field after their tenth straight loss.
After months of job rejections, Olga felt dispirited but kept applying.
The dispirited farmers stared at their dry fields after another month without rain.
Noor felt dispirited when her science project fell apart the night before the fair.

cloze.s: Volunteers grew ___ when the flood washed away all the work they had done.

def: done openly and without shame, even though it is clearly wrong
ex: The mayor's claim that he had never met the builder was a barefaced lie.
Diego was shocked by the barefaced cheating going on in the back row.
Liam's barefaced claim that the dog ate his homework made the teacher laugh out loud.
Raising prices a week after reporting record profits was barefaced greed, angry customers said.

cloze.s: Looking straight at the camera, the CEO told a(n) ___ lie about the company's losses.

note: Most often in “a barefaced lie.”

def: big, strong, and having large muscles
ex: Two brawny movers carried the piano up three flights of stairs.
The brawny lineman was surprisingly gentle with the children at the clinic.
The brawny farmer tossed hay bales onto the truck as if they weighed nothing.
Sofia's brawny shoulders showed her years of rowing practice.

cloze.s: It took four ___ firefighters to lift the fallen tree off the car.

def: having a pleasant, gently rising and falling rhythm, used of a voice or music
ex: Grandma sang a lilting lullaby until the baby fell asleep.
Everyone enjoyed the lilting accent of the tour guide from Dublin.
The waiter spoke in a lilting voice that made the menu sound like a song.
Sofia hummed a lilting tune as she watered the garden.

cloze.s: The ___ melody of the folk song made the dancers sway in time.

def: refusing to obey a boss or someone of higher rank
ex: The sergeant warned that insubordinate soldiers would be punished.
Kwame was fired for being insubordinate after he repeatedly ignored his manager's instructions.
The nurse was disciplined for being insubordinate when she refused her supervisor's direct order.
The ship's captain locked the insubordinate sailor in his cabin for refusing orders during the storm.

cloze.s: The player was benched for being ___ after he swore at the coach and refused to leave the field.

def: to give something respect or serious attention, or to make it seem more important or worthy than it is
ex: The mayor said she would not dignify the rumor with a response.
Calling his messy sketch “art” only dignifies a lazy afternoon.
The coach would not dignify the rival team's insults by even mentioning them at the press conference.
The fancy menu tried to dignify plain toast by describing it as “hand-crafted grilled bread.”

cloze.s: That insult is so silly that I refuse to ___ it with an answer.

note: Most often in the phrase “not dignify (something) with a response.”

def: to hit someone or something again and again, usually with the fists
ex: The boxer pummeled his opponent in the final round.
Heavy rain pummeled the coast for three days straight.
The baker pummeled the dough with her fists to knock out the air.
In the cartoon, the two brothers pummel each other until their mother steps in.

cloze.s: Frustrated, Liam began to ___ his pillow with both fists.

also: to defeat or criticize someone very heavily (“critics pummeled the new film”)

def: to drink something, especially alcoholic drinks
ex: Guests who imbibe too much at the party should take a taxi home.
Maria rarely imbibes, but she had a glass of champagne at her sister's wedding.
Under federal rules, airline pilots may not imbibe alcohol within eight hours of flying.
Grandpa liked to imbibe a small glass of brandy after dinner on holidays.

cloze.s: The sign at the stadium warned fans not to ___ too freely before driving.

also: to take in and absorb ideas or knowledge (“children imbibe their parents' values”)
note: Formal or humorous.

def: to list things one by one, often with the cost of each
ex: The mechanic itemized every repair on the bill so we could see each cost.
Many people itemize their deductions to lower their tax bill.
Before the move, Yuki itemized everything in each box so nothing would get lost.
The hospital agreed to itemize the bill after Malik questioned the huge total.

cloze.s: Please ___ your travel expenses—hotel, meals, and taxis—on separate lines.

def: to take away a person's right to vote, or to leave a group without power or a voice
ex: For decades, unfair literacy tests were used to disenfranchise Black voters in the American South.
Many workers felt disenfranchised when the union was shut out of the talks.
In many countries, women were disenfranchised until the twentieth century, when they finally won the right to vote.
Tenants felt disenfranchised when the building's owners made major changes without ever asking for their views.

cloze.s: Closing polling places in rural areas could ___ people who have no car.

def: to be filled with a loud sound, or for a sound to ring loudly through a place
ex: The hall resounded with cheers as the winner was announced.
Church bells resounded across the valley on Sunday morning.
The gym resounded with the squeak of sneakers and the shouts of the players.
Laughter resounded through the small apartment as the family played board games late into the night.

cloze.s: Applause began to ___ through the theater as the curtain fell.

note: “A resounding success” means a clear, complete success.

def: to move around the side of an enemy to attack, or to gain an advantage over a rival
ex: The general planned to outflank the enemy by marching through the hills.
The small company outflanked its larger rivals by launching online first.
The soccer team outflanked the defense by sending players wide down both wings.
In the board game, Yuki outflanked her brother's army and captured his capital.

cloze.s: By offering free shipping a week early, the store managed to ___ its main competitor.

def: to set aside money or something else for a particular purpose
ex: The city earmarked two million dollars for new bike lanes.
Hannah earmarks part of every paycheck for her daughter's college fund.
The hospital earmarked the large donation for a new children's play area.
Rosa earmarks one weekend each month for visiting her aging parents in the country.

cloze.s: The school board voted to ___ the grant money for new science labs only.

note: As a noun, “an earmark” is money in a bill set aside for a specific local project.

def: to combine two or more things, such as groups or companies, into one
ex: The two small banks amalgamated to compete with larger rivals.
The new album amalgamates jazz, hip-hop, and West African rhythms.
The two hospitals amalgamated last year and now share one name and one emergency room.
The school plans to amalgamate its two small art classes into one larger group next year.

cloze.s: The county plans to ___ its three fire departments into a single service to save money.

def: to put or keep someone in prison or jail
ex: The United States incarcerates more people than almost any other country.
He was incarcerated for five years before new evidence proved his innocence.
The judge decided to incarcerate the repeat offender for two years.
A local charity helps families stay in touch with relatives who are incarcerated far from home.

cloze.s: Judges must decide whether to ___ first-time offenders or give them probation.

note: Formal; common in news and legal writing.

def: to dig a dead body out of the ground after it has been buried
ex: Investigators got a court order to exhume the body for new tests.
The remains were exhumed and moved to a family grave in another state.
The family asked permission to exhume their grandfather's body so he could be buried beside his wife.
When the old cemetery had to make way for a highway, workers carefully exhumed the graves and reburied the remains elsewhere.

cloze.s: Police asked the court for permission to ___ the coffin and test for poison.

also: to bring back something long forgotten (“the documentary exhumes an old scandal”)

def: to divide something and give a share to each person or group
ex: The will apportioned the farmland equally among the four children.
It is not always easy to apportion blame when a project fails.
The teacher apportioned the classroom jobs so that each student had one task.
The family apportioned the cost of Grandma's care among the three siblings according to their incomes.

cloze.s: After the trip, Priya had to ___ the hotel bill fairly among six friends.

def: to state firmly that something is true
ex: The witness averred that she had seen the driver run the red light.
Malik averred that he had never touched the money, but no one believed him.
The company averred that customer data had never been shared with anyone.
Grandpa averred that he had caught a fish as long as his arm, though no one saw it.

cloze.s: In court, the defendant continued to ___ that he was at home all evening.

note: Formal; common in legal writing and older literature.

def: to pay out money from a fund, especially by a government or organization
ex: The charity disbursed more than a million dollars to flood victims last year.
Student loans are usually disbursed directly to the college at the start of each term.
The scholarship fund disburses money to students each fall once their grades are confirmed.
City officials disbursed the grant money to local food banks within a month of the storm.

cloze.s: The agency will ___ the relief payments to families within two weeks.

note: Not the same as “disperse,” which means to scatter.

def: to attack someone or something violently, or to criticize them strongly
ex: The new law was assailed by business groups and unions alike.
The protesters assailed the police line with rocks and bottles.
Reviewers assailed the new phone for its poor battery life.
Fierce winds assailed the coast for three days, tearing roofs off houses.

cloze.s: Critics continued to ___ the director for the film's confusing ending.

def: great force or strong feeling in what someone says or does

def: honest and morally correct behavior, especially in the way a person lives and works

def: a person, animal or plant that lives in, or is often found in, a particular place

def: the ability to know or correctly guess what will happen in the future

def: too high an opinion of your own importance, shown by thinking and talking mostly about yourself

def: saying the same thing twice in different words, without adding any meaning

def: talking in a loud, angry or proud way, often making threats that have little real effect

def: of or used by ordinary people, especially everyday spoken language rather than formal language
ex: The novelist mixed elegant description with the demotic speech of dock workers and street vendors.

note: Formal word, often used in writing about language, literature and culture.

def: saying the same thing twice in different words, so that nothing new is added
ex: Phrases like “free gift” and “new innovation” are tautological, since every gift is free.

def: extremely hard and impossible to break, or firm and impossible to change

def: quick to get angry and likely to act suddenly without thinking first

def: lazy and lacking ambition or any real purpose in life

def: unwilling to believe or rely on others; suspicious of their motives

def: unable to move because there is no wind, of a sailing ship

def: to say mean and critical things about someone, often behind their back

def: to charm or delight someone so strongly that they can think of little else

def: a wild, noisy party with a lot of drinking

def: a person who is not thankful for help, gifts or kindness

cloze.s: The border shooting was treated as a(n) ___, and within a week the two countries were at war.

def: out of action and unable to fight or take part, usually because of injury
ex: With their star striker hors de combat, the team struggled to score.

cloze.s: Two of our best players are ___ with knee injuries, so the coach is starting the rookies.

origin: French for 'out of the fight'; also a term in the laws of war for soldiers who can no longer fight.

def: loud, dramatic emotional struggle and conflict, full of strong feelings
ex: After all the Sturm und Drang of the divorce, Hannah longed for a quiet life.
The band's early albums are full of teenage Sturm und Drang.

cloze.s: Despite weeks of public ___ between the owners and players, the season started on time.

def: a sad, tired feeling that the world can never be as good as it should be

cloze.s: The young hero is not sad about anything in particular; he suffers from ___, a gloom about the state of the whole world.

def: a false belief or foolish idea shared by two close people who feed each other's thinking
ex: The couple's plan to sail around the world with no training was a folie à deux.

cloze.s: Psychiatrists describe the rare case of two sisters who shared the same delusion as a(n) ___.

origin: French for 'madness for two'; originally a psychiatric term for a delusion shared by two people.

def: thinking of the perfect clever reply only after the chance to say it has passed
ex: Hours after the argument, Tomás came up with a brilliant comeback: a classic case of l'esprit de l'escalier.

At the party, Wei said nothing to the rude guest; on the bus home, l'esprit de l'escalier struck.

cloze.s: Only in the elevator did Fatima think of the perfect answer to her rude boss, a painful case of ___.

origin: French for 'staircase wit'; from Diderot, who said he could only think of a reply once he had reached the bottom of the stairs.

def: a court case, issue or event that attracts wide public attention and strong debate
ex: The wrongful arrest of the teenager became a cause célèbre across the country.
The fight to save the old theater turned into a local cause célèbre.
The elderly woman's fight against eviction became a cause célèbre in the city's newspapers.

cloze.s: The jailed journalist's case became a(n) ___, with celebrities and world leaders demanding her release.

def: a sudden, dramatic action or turn of events that surprises everyone
ex: In a coup de théâtre, the witness pointed at the defense lawyer.

cloze.s: In a(n) ___ at the final meeting, the quiet intern revealed she had built the winning design herself.

def: required by fashion, custom or good manners
ex: At the gala, black tie was de rigueur, so Jamal rented a tuxedo.

At the ski lodge, a thick wool sweater is de rigueur after a day on the slopes.

cloze.s: At the summer weddings in that town, linen suits are ___, and anyone in wool looks out of place.

def: an idea or belief that takes over a person's mind and that they cannot stop thinking about
ex: Finding the lost family painting became an idée fixe for Olga.

The coach's idée fixe about running drills crowded out every other part of practice.

cloze.s: Building a perfect replica of his childhood home became a(n) ___ that consumed all of Wei's weekends.

def: the exactly right word or phrase for what one means
ex: Maria paused, searching for le mot juste to describe her grandmother's kitchen.

cloze.s: "Brave" was not quite right; after some thought, Kwame found ___: "reckless."

origin: French for 'the right word'; closely linked with novelist Gustave Flaubert, famous for laboring over every word.

def: ordinary people, the general public, often said by people who think they are better

note: Often misused to mean rich, fancy people; the standard meaning is the opposite.

def: said with full official authority, as if no one may question it

cloze.s: The professor delivered his opinions ___, as though they were laws no student could challenge.

def: taking a parent's role and responsibility for a child who is not one's own

cloze.s: Because summer camp staff act ___, they must make medical decisions when parents cannot be reached.

origin: Latin for 'in the place of a parent'; also a legal term.

def: a person or thing that is very unusual and hard to find

def: in a desperate situation or at the point of death

def: based on how things first appear, before closer study; accepted as true unless proved wrong

def: for an even stronger reason; used when a second claim follows even more surely than the first

cloze.s: If the rule bans phones during class, then ___ it bans phones during exams.

def: a practical arrangement that lets people or groups who disagree live or work together peacefully

def: a reminder that fame, power and success do not last

cloze.s: Last year's chart-topping band now plays to half-empty bars; ___.

def: an object or reminder, such as a skull in a painting, that everyone must die someday

def: alert and ready for danger or trouble at any moment

def: a complete change of opinion, plan or policy, to the opposite position

def: a person who loves fine food, drink and good company

def: politics based on practical power and interests rather than on moral principles or ideals

def: a year full of disasters and bad luck

def: a novel about real people and events, with the names changed

def: the characters in a play or story, or the main people involved in a real event

cloze.s: Before reading the long novel, Wei studied the list of ___ at the front so he could keep track of everyone.

term: the mills of God grind slowly

def: so many good things or choices that it is hard to decide or to use them all

def: a person who is used by someone else to do something risky or unpleasant for that person's gain

term: it's an ill wind that blows nobody any good

def: of the highest quality or most extreme kind

term: not to put too fine a point on it

term: on the side of the angels

term: let the cobbler stick to his last

origin: From a story told by Pliny: a shoemaker correctly pointed out a sandal error in a painting by Apelles, then criticized the leg, and was told to stick to shoes.

def: to be delayed, or to wait before deciding or acting

def: something that has some good parts and some bad parts

term: beard the lion in his den

def: a vacation or free time spent doing the same kind of thing you do at work

def: in good health, spirits or condition

def: to act much too dramatically, with big gestures and a loud voice, on stage or screen

def: to act in plays on a stage, especially as a career

def: in a state of confusion, disorder or disagreement

The plan was neither fish nor fowl, pleasing neither side.
Priya's job is neither fish nor fowl, part sales and part engineering, so no one knows whom she reports to.
Critics called the new museum neither fish nor fowl, since it could not decide whether it was an art gallery or a shopping mall.

cloze.s: The show was ___, too silly to be a drama and not funny enough to be a comedy.

def: a person who does whatever they want, ignoring rules and what others expect
ex: The star player was a law unto himself, skipping practice whenever he liked.
Our cat is a law unto herself and sleeps wherever she chooses.
In the kitchen, the head chef is a law unto himself and changes the menu on a whim.
Jamal's teenage son has become a law unto himself, coming and going as he pleases.

cloze.s: The surgeon was brilliant but ___, ignoring hospital rules and doing things her own way.

term: have the courage of one's convictions
def: to be brave enough to act on what one believes, even when others disagree
ex: Hannah had the courage of her convictions and refused to sign the false report.
If you think the plan is wrong, have the courage of your convictions and say so.
The young doctor had the courage of her convictions and questioned the senior surgeon's plan.
Malik thought the referee's call was wrong, but he didn't have the courage of his convictions to say so.

cloze.s: Only one council member ___ and voted against the popular but unfair law.
cloze.a: had the courage of her convictions

def: lost in deep, often sad thought and unaware of what is happening around you
ex: Wei sat in a brown study by the window, not hearing the phone ring.
Grandma was in a brown study after reading the old letters.
After the loss, the coach found the young pitcher sitting alone on the bench in a brown study.
In a brown study at her desk, Priya didn't hear her own name called in the meeting.

cloze.s: Lost ___, Fatima didn't notice that her coffee had gone cold an hour ago.

term: make a rod for one's own back
def: to do something that will cause problems for yourself later
ex: By answering work emails at midnight, Yuki made a rod for her own back; now everyone expects it.
Parents who give in to every tantrum are making a rod for their own backs.
By letting the puppy sleep in his bed just once, Diego made a rod for his own back.
A teacher who never sets deadlines is making a rod for her own back at grading time.

cloze.s: By promising to fix every customer's computer for free, the shop owner ___.
cloze.a: made a rod for his own back

def: growing in power, influence or success
ex: Electric cars are in the ascendant as gas car sales fall.
The young senator's career is clearly in the ascendant.
With three straight tournament wins, the young chess player is clearly in the ascendant.
After a record sales year, Maria's bakery is in the ascendant and opening a second shop.

cloze.s: After years of decline, the city's old downtown is ___ again, with new shops and crowds.

origin: From astrology, where the ascendant is the sign of the zodiac rising in the east, thought to have strong influence.

def: hard, useful, reliable work, done without making a show of it
ex: The volunteers did yeoman's work clearing the beach after the storm.
As backup goalie, Diego did yeoman's work all season.
Priya did yeoman's work organizing the school fundraiser, handling every detail without complaint.
The old pickup truck has done yeoman's work on the farm for twenty years.

cloze.s: The night nurses did ___ during the outbreak, quietly caring for patients through every shift.

origin: A yeoman was a small landowner or servant known for steady work; Shakespeare's Hamlet says something 'did me yeoman's service.'
note: Also 'yeoman's service' or 'yeoman work.'

def: to try too hard to please someone by doing everything they want
ex: The staff danced attendance on the visiting billionaire all week.
Liam got tired of dancing attendance on his demanding cousin.
Waiters danced attendance on the famous actor while other diners waited for their food.
After work hours, Hannah refused to dance attendance on her boss and ignored his late-night texts.

cloze.s: Three assistants ___ the pop star, fetching her water, her phone and her sunglasses.

def: to show clearly that a claim or belief is false
ex: The company's record profits give the lie to its claim that it can't afford raises.
Her quick recovery gave the lie to the doctors' gloomy predictions.
The long lines at the new bakery give the lie to claims that nobody buys fresh bread anymore.
Tomás's perfect test score gave the lie to the rumor that he never studied.

cloze.s: The packed stadium ___ the idea that nobody cares about women's soccer.

def: to not support or defend someone or something
ex: I hold no brief for the mayor, but this attack on her is unfair.
Aisha holds no brief for fast food, yet she admits the fries are good.
Let me be clear: I hold no brief for the landlord, who ignored our repair requests for months.
Malik holds no brief for students who copy homework, however tired they claim to be.

cloze.s: "I ___ the old manager," said Jamal, "but even he deserved a fair hearing."

origin: From law: a 'brief' is the case papers a lawyer is given in order to argue for a client.

def: in spite of strong opposition or danger, or directly against it
ex: The law passed in the teeth of fierce public protest.
The small boat sailed home in the teeth of a gale.
The marathon runners pushed on in the teeth of a freezing headwind.
Yuki opened her bookstore in the teeth of warnings that nobody reads printed books anymore.

cloze.s: The company launched the product ___ fierce criticism from its own engineers.

def: to keep one's thoughts, plans or opinions private
ex: During the debate, Olga kept her own counsel and let the others argue.
The coach keeps his own counsel about the starting lineup until game day.
Sofia kept her own counsel about the job offer until she had signed the contract.
In family arguments, Grandpa usually keeps his own counsel and just listens.

cloze.s: Asked whom she would vote for, the judge smiled and ___, saying nothing at all.

def: to break free of rules, control or duty and behave as one likes
ex: After years as a careful accountant, Tomás kicked over the traces and moved to a beach town.
Every so often, the quiet student kicks over the traces and skips school.
After years of strict training, the gymnast kicked over the traces and spent a summer backpacking.
When his parents left town, sixteen-year-old Liam kicked over the traces and threw a huge party.

cloze.s: At fifty, Hannah ___, quit her safe office job and started a rock band.

origin: From horses: 'traces' are the straps linking a horse to a cart, and a restless horse might kick over them to get free.

def: to keep annoying or upsetting someone because it seems unfair or wrong
ex: Losing the contest to a cheater really stuck in Priya's craw.
What sticks in my craw is that he never apologized.
The referee's bad call in the final minute still sticks in the coach's craw, years after the game.
Mei let most complaints go, but the hotel's hidden fees stuck in her craw for the rest of the trip.

cloze.s: It still ___ that the company gave my idea to someone else and never thanked me.

note: A 'craw' is the crop or throat of a bird.

def: an easy, pleasant way of living that leads to disaster or ruin
ex: Easy credit led the young couple down the primrose path to debt.
The novel follows a rich heir down the primrose path of parties and gambling.
Years of fast food and no exercise felt easy at the time, but for Ray they were the primrose path to heart disease.
Skipping classes for parties was the primrose path that led Diego to fail his first year of college.

cloze.s: The cheap, quick loans seemed harmless, but they led many families down ___ to bankruptcy.

origin: From Shakespeare's Hamlet, where Ophelia warns of 'the primrose path of dalliance.'

term: a consummation devoutly to be wished
def: an outcome that someone hopes for very much
ex: An end to the endless meetings would be a consummation devoutly to be wished.
For the tired parents, a full night's sleep was a consummation devoutly to be wished.
A week without rain during our camping trip would be a consummation devoutly to be wished.
For the striking workers, a fair contract was a consummation devoutly to be wished.

cloze.s: After years of delays, the opening of the new subway line is ___ for every commuter in the city.
cloze.a: a consummation devoutly to be wished

origin: From Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be' speech, where he speaks of death as 'a consummation devoutly to be wish'd.'
note: Often used humorously about everyday hopes.

def: a rallying call to make one more brave effort at a hard task
ex: Facing another night of tax forms, Diego sighed, "Once more unto the breach."
Before the final round of interviews, the team leader joked, "Once more unto the breach, friends."
Monday morning came, and Yuki opened her overflowing inbox with a sigh: once more unto the breach.
Before the third overtime period, the hockey captain shouted, "Once more unto the breach!"

cloze.s: Exhausted but determined, the movers lifted the piano one last time, muttering, "___."

origin: From Shakespeare's Henry V, where the king urges his soldiers back into a gap in a town's walls: 'Once more unto the breach, dear friends.'

def: to get ready for something hard, dangerous or tiring
ex: Malik girded his loins for a long day of meetings.
Shoppers girded their loins for the holiday crowds.
The students girded their loins for finals week, stocking up on coffee and snacks.
Before calling the cable company, Olga girded her loins for a long wait on hold.

cloze.s: With the inspectors arriving Monday, the restaurant staff ___ for a week of hard scrubbing.

origin: From the Bible, where people tucked their long robes into a belt so they could move freely to work, travel or fight.
note: Often used humorously; also 'gird up one's loins.'

term: a little learning is a dangerous thing
def: knowing only a small amount about a subject can make people too sure of themselves and lead to mistakes
ex: After one online video, Liam tried to rewire the house; a little learning is a dangerous thing.
The doctor sighed at the patient's internet diagnosis: a little learning is a dangerous thing.
After one cooking class, Wei tried to carve a whole fish; a little learning is a dangerous thing.
The new driver thought one lesson made him an expert, proving that a little learning is a dangerous thing.

cloze.s: Having read one article about investing, Uncle Ray bet his savings on a risky stock. As the saying goes, ___.
cloze.a: a little learning is a dangerous thing

origin: From Alexander Pope's 1711 poem 'An Essay on Criticism.'
note: Often misquoted as 'a little knowledge is a dangerous thing.'

term: fools rush in where angels fear to tread
def: foolish people with little experience rush into risky situations that smarter people avoid
ex: The new intern offered to settle the bosses' feud; fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
Sofia wanted to tell the couple how to fix their marriage, but fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
Liam offered to plan his sister's wedding all by himself; fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
Every new coach thinks he can fix the team overnight, but fools rush in where angels fear to tread.

cloze.s: Experts refused to predict the market crash, but a teenage blogger did. ___.
cloze.a: Fools rush in where angels fear to tread

origin: From Alexander Pope's 1711 poem 'An Essay on Criticism.'

def: people keep hoping for the best, even when there is little reason to
ex: The team hasn't won in years, but hope springs eternal every spring.
Kwame bought another lottery ticket; hope springs eternal.
Every January, Priya buys a new gym membership; hope springs eternal.
Nothing has ever grown in his shady garden, but hope springs eternal, so Tomás planted seeds again.

cloze.s: She has applied to the same company six times without success, but ___.

origin: From Alexander Pope's 'An Essay on Man' (1733–34): 'Hope springs eternal in the human breast.'

def: to pretend to be something one is not in order to fool or trick others
ex: The "charity" was sailing under false colors; it kept most of the money.
Critics said the politician was sailing under false colors, posing as an outsider.
The online seller sailed under false colors, posing as a small family business while shipping cheap copies.
Malik discovered that his new friend had been sailing under false colors, using a fake name all along.

cloze.s: The man claimed to be a doctor, but he had no degree; he had been ___ for years.

origin: From ships that flew another nation's flag ('colors') to trick enemies before attacking.

def: to think very hard, trying to remember or solve something
ex: Yuki cudgeled her brains for the name of the song but couldn't remember it.
We cudgeled our brains over the puzzle for an hour.
Tomás cudgeled his brains for a clever toast but ended up just saying thank you.
The detective cudgeled her brains over the missing clue all night.

cloze.s: Hannah ___ trying to recall where she had left the car keys.

origin: From Shakespeare's Hamlet, where a gravedigger says, 'Cudgel thy brains no more about it.'

def: the slow process by which kinds of living things change over many generations, giving rise to new kinds
why: It explains how the huge variety of life on Earth, including humans, came to be.
ex: Fossils of early horses show the evolution of a small forest animal into the large horse we know today.
In biology class, Aisha learned how the evolution of whales began with land animals millions of years ago.
Bacteria that become resistant to antibiotics show evolution happening fast enough for scientists to watch.
The museum's exhibit traces the evolution of birds from small, feathered dinosaurs.

cloze.s: Charles Darwin's 1859 book helped explain ___, the gradual change of living things over countless generations.

note: Natural selection is the main way this happens. In everyday speech the word can also mean any gradual development, as in the evolution of the car.

def: the smallest living unit that all plants, animals and other living things are built from
why: Understanding it is the starting point for understanding growth, health and disease.
ex: Under the microscope, Tomás could see each onion cell outlined like a tiny brick in a wall.
Your body is made of trillions of cells, and each type, such as a blood cell or a nerve cell, has its own job.
When you scrape your knee, new skin cells grow to close the wound.
Aisha's biology class stained cheek cells blue so they were easier to see under the microscope.

cloze.s: A bacterium is a living thing made of just one ___, while a human body is made of trillions.

note: Do not confuse it with an atom, which is far smaller and not alive.

def: a group of living things so alike that they can breed together and have young that can also breed
why: Scientists use it to name, count and protect the different kinds of life on Earth.
ex: The giant panda is a species that lives in the wild only in the mountains of central China.
Wei's team discovered a new species of frog in the rainforest and gave it a scientific name.
Dogs come in many shapes and sizes, but they all belong to the same species.
Volunteers protect the nests of several sea turtle species on Florida beaches every summer.

cloze.s: The snow leopard is a rare ___ of big cat that lives in the high mountains of Central Asia.

note: The word is the same in singular and plural: one species, many species. A horse and a donkey are different ones, which is why mules usually cannot have young.

def: the remains or print of a plant or animal from long ago, kept in rock over a very long time
why: These remains are our main record of dinosaurs and other life that existed before humans.
ex: On a beach walk, Hannah found a fossil of a tiny sea creature pressed into a flat gray stone.
The museum's dinosaur skeleton was rebuilt from fossils dug up in Montana.
Fossils of seashells found high in the mountains show that the land was once under the sea.
Priya's son spent the museum visit staring at a fossil of a giant ancient fish.

cloze.s: The scientist split the rock open and found a perfect ___ of a fern that grew millions of years ago.

note: Coal, oil and natural gas are called fossil fuels because they formed from the remains of ancient living things.

def: the Sun and everything that travels around it, including eight planets and their moons
why: It is our home in space and the first step to understanding the wider universe.
ex: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system, bigger than all the others put together.
Kwame built a model of the solar system for school, with a yellow ball for the Sun in the middle.
Pluto was once called the ninth planet of the solar system, but in 2006 it was reclassified as a dwarf planet.
Astronomers have found thousands of planets outside our solar system circling other stars.

cloze.s: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun, and Neptune is the farthest planet in our ___.

note: Pluto was counted as the ninth planet until 2006, when astronomers reclassified it as a dwarf planet.

def: a pure substance made of only one type of atom, such as gold, oxygen or iron
why: These are the basic building blocks of all matter, listed in the periodic table.
ex: Oxygen is the element we need to breathe, and it makes up about a fifth of the air.
Priya's chemistry teacher explained that water is not an element because it contains both hydrogen and oxygen.
The periodic table on the classroom wall lists every known element.
Helium, the element that fills party balloons, is much lighter than air.

cloze.s: Gold is a chemical ___, so it cannot be broken down into any simpler substance.

note: In everyday speech the word also means one part of something, as in an element of surprise.

def: a warm-blooded animal with hair or fur that feeds its babies with milk from its body
why: Humans belong to this group, along with dogs, whales, bats and many other animals.
ex: A whale lives in the ocean, but it is a mammal, not a fish, because it breathes air and nurses its young.
Diego was surprised to learn that the bat is the only mammal that can truly fly.
The zookeeper explained that a kangaroo is a mammal, even though its baby grows in a pouch.
Wei's daughter asked if a penguin was a mammal, and he explained it is a bird because it has feathers and lays eggs.

cloze.s: The dolphin has to come up to breathe air and feeds its calf milk, which shows it is a(n) ___.

note: Most give birth to live young, but the platypus and the echidna lay eggs.

def: tiny one-celled living things, seen only with a microscope, found almost everywhere; some cause illness
why: They cause infections like strep throat, but many also help us digest food and stay healthy.
ex: Washing your hands with soap removes many bacteria that could make you sick.
Yogurt is made when helpful bacteria turn milk thick and slightly sour.
Keeping raw chicken cold slows the growth of bacteria that cause food poisoning.
The doctor swabbed Wei's sore throat to see whether bacteria were causing the infection.

cloze.s: Antibiotics can kill ___, but they do nothing against viruses such as the common cold.

note: The word is plural; one is a bacterium. They are not the same as viruses, which are much smaller.

def: a possible explanation or prediction that can be tested with an experiment or careful observation
why: Making and testing these is the heart of the scientific method.
ex: Malik's hypothesis was that plants given more light would grow taller, so he set up an experiment to check.
The researchers rejected their first hypothesis when the test results did not match it.
Detectives work a bit like scientists: they form a hypothesis about the crime, then look for evidence.
Scientists tested the hypothesis that the new drug lowers fever by comparing it with a sugar pill.

cloze.s: Before the experiment, each student wrote down a(n) ___ predicting which paper towel would soak up the most water.

note: Not the same as a scientific theory, which is a broad explanation already supported by a great deal of tested evidence. Plural: hypotheses.

def: a building block in foods like meat, fish, eggs, beans and nuts that the body uses to build and repair muscle
why: Eating enough of it keeps muscles, skin and the immune system working well.
ex: After her workout, Sofia ate eggs and beans to get plenty of protein.
Lentils are a cheap source of protein for people who do not eat meat.
Diego adds peanut butter to his toast for extra protein before soccer practice.
Older adults need enough protein in their meals to help keep their muscles strong.

cloze.s: Chicken, tofu and Greek yogurt are all good sources of ___, which helps the body build muscle.

note: It is one of the three main nutrients that give the body energy, along with carbohydrates and fats.

def: one of several substances, found in food, that the body needs in small amounts to stay healthy
why: Lacking one can cause disease, which is why food labels and doctors pay attention to them.
ex: Oranges and peppers are rich in vitamin C, which helps the body heal cuts.
Yuki's doctor told her to take a vitamin D supplement during the dark winter months.
Carrots contain beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A.
Kwame takes a daily vitamin because a blood test showed his vitamin B12 level was low.

cloze.s: Sailors on long voyages once got scurvy because they went months without fresh fruit and the ___ it provides.

note: The skin makes vitamin D when exposed to sunlight; most others must come from food.

def: a long-lasting disease in which the body cannot make or properly use insulin, so blood sugar gets too high
why: It is very common and, if poorly controlled, can damage the heart, eyes, kidneys and nerves.
ex: Since he was told he had diabetes, Jamal checks his blood sugar every morning before breakfast.
Regular exercise and a healthy diet can lower the risk of type 2 diabetes.
Ana's doctor ordered a blood test to check for diabetes after she felt thirsty all the time.
People with type 1 diabetes need insulin because their bodies make little or none of it.

cloze.s: The nurse showed Olga how to give herself insulin shots to manage her ___.

note: Type 1 often starts in childhood when the body stops making insulin; type 2 is more common and usually develops in adults.

def: a sudden brain injury that happens when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a blood vessel there bursts
why: Fast treatment can save brain cells and lives, so everyone should know the warning signs.
ex: When her father's face drooped and his speech slurred, Fatima called 911 because she feared a stroke.
After his stroke, Liam worked with therapists to regain the use of his left hand.
Doctors say that high blood pressure greatly raises a person's risk of having a stroke.
Hospitals can often limit the damage from a stroke if the patient arrives within a few hours.

cloze.s: Sudden weakness on one side of the body and trouble speaking can be signs of a(n) ___, so call for help at once.

note: The letters FAST help people remember the signs: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911.

def: a medical emergency in which blood flow to part of the heart muscle is blocked, damaging it
why: It is a leading cause of death, and quick treatment greatly improves the chance of survival.
ex: Chest pain that spreads to the arm or jaw can be a sign of a heart attack.
After his heart attack, Mr. Okafor changed his diet and started walking every day.
Smoking, high blood pressure and high cholesterol all raise the risk of a heart attack.
Suspecting a heart attack, the paramedics rushed Mrs. Russo to the hospital with the siren on.

cloze.s: A blocked artery cut off blood to part of his heart, and doctors said he had suffered a(n) ___.

note: Not the same as cardiac arrest, when the heart suddenly stops pumping blood; a heart attack can lead to cardiac arrest.

def: a body temperature higher than normal, often a sign that the body is fighting an infection
why: It is one of the most common signs of illness that parents and doctors check for.
ex: Maria kept her son home from school because he had a fever and a sore throat.
The thermometer read 102 degrees, so the doctor said Kwame had a high fever.
A fever usually means the body is fighting off a germ, such as the flu virus.
Malik gave his daughter medicine to bring down her fever and kept her in bed all day.

cloze.s: Her forehead felt hot, and the thermometer confirmed she had a(n) ___ of 101 degrees.

note: In the United States, a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is commonly treated as one.

def: the process of breaking down food in the stomach and gut so the body can take in what it needs
why: It turns meals into the energy and building materials every part of the body uses.
ex: Chewing food well is the first step of digestion and makes the stomach's job easier.
Foods high in fiber, like beans and whole grains, help keep digestion regular.
The small intestine does most of the work of digestion, taking nutrients into the blood.
Kwame's doctor said that eating slowly and drinking enough water can help digestion.

cloze.s: Saliva starts breaking down food in the mouth, and ___ continues in the stomach and intestines.

note: The related verb is digest, and an upset stomach is often called indigestion.

def: the frame of bones that supports the body, protects organs and lets us move
why: It holds us up, shields the brain and heart, and makes blood cells inside the bones.
ex: An adult human skeleton has 206 bones, from the tiny ones in the ear to the long thighbone.
The science room had a plastic skeleton that students used to learn the names of the bones.
At the museum, Kwame's kids stared up at the huge skeleton of a dinosaur.
Weight-bearing exercise like walking helps keep the skeleton strong as people age.

cloze.s: The skull and ribs are parts of the ___ that protect the brain and the heart.

note: Babies are born with more bones than adults; many of them join together during growth.

def: emergency first aid for someone whose heart has stopped, done by pushing hard and fast on the center of the chest
why: Starting it right away can double or triple a person's chance of surviving cardiac arrest.
ex: When a runner collapsed at the finish line, a nurse in the crowd began CPR until the ambulance arrived.
Our office offered a free CPR class, and Priya practiced chest pushes on a dummy.
The 911 dispatcher talked Omar through CPR on his father, counting each push on the chest out loud.
Thanks to quick CPR from a coworker, Mr. Patel survived collapsing at his office.

cloze.s: The man was not breathing and had no pulse, so the lifeguard started ___ while someone called 911.

note: Short for cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Hands-only CPR, with chest pushes and no rescue breaths, is recommended for untrained bystanders helping an adult.

def: the amount of flat surface a shape covers, measured in square units such as square feet
why: You use it to figure out how much paint, carpet or land you need or own.
ex: To find the area of the rectangular room, Diego multiplied its length, 12 feet, by its width, 10 feet.
The apartment listing gave an area of 850 square feet.
Before buying carpet, Fatima measured the area of her bedroom in square feet.
The farmer's field has an area of about forty acres.

cloze.s: A square garden 5 meters on each side has a(n) ___ of 25 square meters.

note: Not the same as perimeter, which is the distance around the edge of a shape.

def: the amount of space an object takes up or a container holds, measured in units like cups or gallons
why: It tells you how much a box, tank or bottle can hold.
ex: The volume of the fish tank is 20 gallons, so Hannah bought enough water conditioner for that much.
To find the volume of a box, multiply its length, width and height.
Priya used a measuring cup to find the volume of water the pot could hold.
Olga bought a larger suitcase with twice the volume of her old one.

cloze.s: A cube that is 2 inches on each side has a(n) ___ of 8 cubic inches.

note: In everyday speech it also means how loud a sound is, or one book in a set.

def: a number written with a dot to show parts smaller than one, as in 2.5 or 0.75
why: Prices, measurements and sports statistics are almost always written this way.
ex: The price $4.99 is written as a decimal, with 99 hundredths of a dollar after the point.
Wei turned the fraction one-quarter into the decimal 0.25.
Aisha's calculator showed the answer as a decimal, 0.75, instead of the fraction 3/4.
The sprinter's time was 9.86 seconds, written as a decimal to show hundredths of a second.

cloze.s: The fraction one-half can also be written as the ___ 0.5.

note: Each place after the point is ten times smaller: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

def: the amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point, measured in degrees
why: It matters in building, design, sports and navigation, anywhere direction or slope counts.
ex: The corner of a sheet of paper is a right angle, which measures 90 degrees.
The skateboard ramp was built at a gentle angle so beginners could ride it safely.
Wei used a protractor to measure the angle between the two lines: exactly 45 degrees.
The carpenter cut each board at a 45-degree angle so the corners of the picture frame fit together.

cloze.s: The three corners of any triangle add up to 180 degrees, no matter how big each ___ is.

note: An acute one is less than 90 degrees; an obtuse one is between 90 and 180 degrees.

def: a straight line from one side of a circle to the other passing through the center, or its length
why: It is used to size pipes, wheels, pizzas and anything round.
ex: The large pizza has a diameter of 16 inches, measured straight across the middle.
Aisha measured the diameter of the tree trunk to estimate how old it was.
To buy the right lid, Wei measured the diameter of the pot across its top.
A circle's diameter is always exactly twice as long as its radius.

cloze.s: The radius of the wheel is 10 inches, so its ___ is 20 inches.

note: It is always twice the radius, which runs from the center to the edge.

def: a math statement showing that two amounts are the same, using an equals sign, as in 2 + 3 = 5
why: Solving them is how we work out unknown amounts in math, science and everyday budgeting.
ex: To find x in the equation x + 4 = 10, Malik subtracted 4 from both sides.
Einstein's famous equation E = mc² links energy and mass.
In the puzzle book, each equation had a missing number, like 7 + ? = 15.
Both sides of an equation must have the same value, like the two pans of a balanced scale.

cloze.s: The teacher wrote 3x = 12 on the board and asked the class to solve the ___ for x.

note: Whatever you do to one side of the equals sign, you must do to the other to keep it true.

def: a number less than zero, written with a minus sign in front, like −5
why: It is used for temperatures below zero, debts, losses and depths below sea level.
ex: On a winter morning in Minnesota, the thermometer showed a negative number: −12 degrees.
If Tomás spends more than he has in his account, his balance becomes a negative number.
When the submarine dove 50 meters below sea level, its depth showed as a negative number.
In the board game, Priya's score became a negative number after she lost more points than she had.

cloze.s: On a number line, any ___ sits to the left of zero.

note: Multiplying two of them together gives a positive result: −2 × −3 = 6.

def: the number system of ancient Rome, which writes numbers with letters such as I, V, X, L, C, D and M
why: You still see them on clocks, in movie dates, book chapters, Super Bowl titles and the names of kings.
ex: The clock in the train station uses Roman numerals, with XII at the top.
In Roman numerals, the year 2024 is written MMXXIV.
Old movie credits often show the year in Roman numerals, like MCMXCIX for 1999.
The chapters in Olga's old book are numbered with Roman numerals: I, II, III and IV.

cloze.s: King Henry VIII's number is written in ___, where V means five and each I adds one.

note: I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1,000. The system has no symbol for zero.

def: the quality of having two sides that match exactly, like an object and its mirror image
why: It appears throughout nature, art and design, from butterflies to buildings.
ex: A butterfly's wings show perfect symmetry, with the same pattern on the left and the right.
The architect gave the building strong symmetry, with identical towers on each side of the entrance.
The capital letter A has symmetry: draw a line down its middle, and the two halves match.
The Taj Mahal is famous for its symmetry, with matching towers and gardens on every side.

cloze.s: If you fold a paper heart down the middle and both halves match, the shape has ___.

note: The fold line that splits a shape into matching halves is called the line of symmetry.

def: the worldwide network that links billions of computers and phones so they can share information
why: Nearly all modern communication, shopping, banking and news runs over it.
ex: When the internet went down at the office, nobody could send files or join video calls.
Grandma Olga uses the internet to video chat with her grandchildren in another country.
Before the internet, students looked up facts in printed encyclopedias at the library.
Ana's smart doorbell connects to the internet, so she can see visitors on her phone from anywhere.

cloze.s: The village finally got cables for fast ___ service, so students could take classes online.

note: The World Wide Web is one service that runs on it; email and video calls are others. Often capitalized as Internet.

def: a secret word or set of characters you type to prove who you are and unlock an account
why: Strong, unique ones are a basic defense against hackers and identity theft.
ex: Jamal chose a long password mixing words, numbers and symbols for his bank account.
Never share your email password, even with someone who says they work for tech support.
The website asked Malik to create a password with at least eight characters and one number.
Hannah keeps every password in a password manager app so she does not have to remember them all.

cloze.s: After three wrong tries at her ___, Sofia was locked out of her account for an hour.

note: Using the same one on many sites is risky: if one site is hacked, all those accounts are exposed.

def: a program you put on a phone, tablet or computer to do a certain task, like a game or map
why: Most people use these every day for messaging, banking, shopping and travel.
ex: Yuki uses a weather app to check whether she needs an umbrella before leaving home.
The bank's new app lets customers deposit checks by taking a photo.
Malik orders dinner with a food delivery app on his phone.
Grandma Rosa learned to video-call her grandkids using an app on her new tablet.

cloze.s: Liam downloaded a language-learning ___ to his phone and practices Spanish on the bus.

note: Short for application. Phones get them from an online store such as Apple's App Store or Google Play.

def: to copy a file, program or other data from the internet or another computer onto your own device
why: It is how we get music, documents, updates and programs onto our devices.
ex: Before the flight, Hannah decided to download a few movies so she could watch them offline.
Only download files from websites you trust, because some contain harmful programs.
Kwame had to download the airline's app to get his boarding pass.
The free e-books took only seconds to download onto Fatima's tablet.

cloze.s: The video was too large to ___ on the slow hotel Wi-Fi, so Diego watched it later at home.

note: Also used as a noun for the file itself: The download took five minutes.

def: messages nobody asked for, sent in huge numbers to many people, usually ads or scams, often by email
why: Recognizing it protects you from wasted time, scams and harmful links.
ex: Priya's inbox filter catches most spam, like fake prize offers and ads for pills.
Kwame reported the text as spam after it asked him to click a link to claim a free phone.
Malik never opens spam, because some of those emails carry links that steal passwords.
The office's email filter blocks hundreds of spam messages every day.

cloze.s: The email promising a million dollars from a stranger went straight into the ___ folder.

note: The name comes from a Monty Python comedy sketch in which the word Spam is repeated over and over.

def: the address you type or click to reach a particular page on the web, such as https://www.example.com
why: Checking it carefully helps you avoid fake websites that copy real ones.
ex: Fatima typed the URL of the city library's website into her browser to renew her books.
Before entering her password, Maria checked that the URL really belonged to her bank.
The teacher wrote the URL for the class website on the whiteboard so students could find it.
Diego shortened the long URL before posting the link on social media.

cloze.s: To share the article, Wei copied the ___ from the address bar and pasted it into a message.

note: Short for Uniform Resource Locator. It is usually said letter by letter: U-R-L.

def: websites and phone programs where people post and share words, photos and videos and connect with others
why: It shapes how many people get news, keep up with friends and advertise businesses.
ex: The bakery promotes its daily specials on social media, posting photos of fresh bread each morning.
Malik decided to spend less time on social media and more time reading before bed.
Priya learned on social media that her old school friend had just had a baby.
News of the storm spread on social media before TV stations had even reported it.

cloze.s: The video of the dancing dog was shared millions of times on ___ within a day.

note: Usually treated as a plural or a collective noun: social media is or social media are both heard.
