def: a message sent over the internet from one person's account to another's, or the system for sending such messages
why: It remains the main way most workplaces send written messages and files.
ex: Aisha sent her manager an email with the report attached before the meeting.
Tomás checks his email every morning to see if any job offers have arrived.
Malik's grandmother learned to send an email so she could share photos with relatives abroad.
The school uses email to tell parents when classes are canceled for snow.

cloze.s: The airline sent Olga a(n) ___ with her boarding pass a day before her flight.

note: Short for electronic mail. Also spelled e-mail, and used as a verb: Please email me the file.

def: a mobile phone that works like a small computer, with a touch screen, internet access and apps
why: For many people it is now their camera, map, wallet and main computer.
ex: Jamal uses his smartphone to pay for coffee, check the bus schedule and read the news.
The hikers' smartphones showed their exact location on a map, even deep in the forest.
Fatima's grandson set up a smartphone for her so she could video chat and see family photos.
Many drivers now use a smartphone for directions instead of a paper map.

cloze.s: Diego took the photo, edited it and posted it online all from his ___.

note: Older mobile phones that mainly make calls and send texts are often called basic phones or feature phones.

def: the global war from 1914 to 1918 in which Britain, France, Russia and later the United States fought Germany and its partners
why: It redrew the map of Europe and helped set the stage for World War II.
ex: Millions of soldiers died in World War I, many in muddy trenches in France and Belgium.
Sofia's great-great-grandfather drove an army ambulance in France during World War I.
The fighting in World War I ended with an armistice on November 11, 1918.
Red poppies became a symbol of remembrance for the soldiers who died in World War I.

cloze.s: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914 set off ___, which lasted four years.

note: Germany's side, the Central Powers, also included Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria.

def: the global war from 1939 to 1945 in which the Allies defeated Germany, Italy and Japan
why: It was the deadliest war in history and shaped the modern world, including the United Nations.
ex: Germany's invasion of Poland in September 1939 marked the start of World War II in Europe.
Hannah's grandmother worked in a factory building airplanes during World War II.
Kwame's great-uncle served as a radio operator in the Pacific during World War II.
After World War II, the United Nations was founded in 1945 to help keep peace between countries.

cloze.s: The United States entered ___ after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941.

note: The main Allied powers were Britain, the Soviet Union, the United States and China; Germany, Italy and Japan were the Axis powers.

def: the 1775–1783 war and break with Britain through which thirteen American colonies won their independence
why: It created the United States and spread ideas about self-government around the world.
ex: The battles of Lexington and Concord in 1775 were the first fighting of the American Revolution.
France sent soldiers and ships to help the colonists during the American Revolution.
Paul Revere's famous midnight ride took place in 1775, at the very start of the American Revolution.
Kwame's history teacher asked the class to write a diary as a young soldier in the American Revolution.

cloze.s: George Washington led the Continental Army during the ___, the colonies' fight to break free from British rule.

note: The war formally ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783, in which Britain recognized American independence.

def: the 1861–1865 war between the U.S. government and Southern states that tried to break away, mainly over slavery
why: It kept the country united and ended slavery in the United States.
ex: More Americans died in the American Civil War than in any other war in the nation's history.
Abraham Lincoln was president during the American Civil War and issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863.
Diego's class visited Gettysburg, where one of the largest battles of the American Civil War was fought.
Aisha is reading letters that soldiers wrote home to their families during the American Civil War.

cloze.s: The Union's victory in the ___ in 1865 was followed by the Thirteenth Amendment, which ended slavery.

note: The Northern side was called the Union; the eleven Southern states that left formed the Confederacy.

def: the huge state ruled by emperors from Rome that controlled the lands around the Mediterranean Sea for centuries
why: Its roads, laws, Latin language and buildings still shape Europe and the Western world.
ex: At its largest, the Roman Empire stretched from Britain to Egypt and the Middle East.
Kwame's class studied how the Roman Empire built aqueducts to carry water into its cities.
Latin, the language of the Roman Empire, later grew into Spanish, French and Italian.
Tourists in Rome can still walk through ruins from the Roman Empire, such as the Colosseum.

cloze.s: Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC, beginning the ___ that would rule much of Europe for centuries.

note: The western half fell in AD 476; the eastern half, later called the Byzantine Empire, lasted until 1453.

def: the earliest and longest period of human history, when people made tools and weapons mainly from stone
why: It covers most of the human story, from the first tools to the start of farming and metalworking.
ex: Archaeologists found Stone Age arrowheads and scrapers in a cave near the river.
During the Stone Age, people lived by hunting animals and gathering wild plants.
The museum displays Stone Age hand axes that early humans used to cut meat and wood.
Yuki's class tried making fire and simple tools the way people did in the Stone Age.

cloze.s: Long before people learned to work bronze or iron, ___ hunters shaped flint into sharp blades.

note: In many regions it was followed by the Bronze Age and then the Iron Age, though the timing differed from place to place.

def: the first time humans walked on the Moon, on NASA's Apollo 11 mission in July 1969
why: It is one of the greatest achievements in exploration and a turning point of the space race.
ex: Hundreds of millions of people around the world watched the moon landing live on television.
Liam's grandfather still remembers staying up late as a boy to watch the moon landing.
Priya's science teacher showed the class grainy black-and-white footage of the moon landing.
Kwame's school celebrated the anniversary of the moon landing by building and launching model rockets.

cloze.s: Neil Armstrong's words "one small step for man" are the most famous line from the 1969 ___.

note: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the surface while Michael Collins stayed in orbit. Often capitalized as Moon landing.

def: a secret network of people and safe houses that helped enslaved people in the South escape to freedom before the Civil War
why: It is a powerful example of ordinary people risking their lives to resist slavery.
ex: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery and then returned many times to guide others north on the Underground Railroad.
The old farmhouse had a hidden cellar that once sheltered people traveling the Underground Railroad.
Historians estimate that thousands of enslaved people reached freedom through the Underground Railroad.
Many people escaping on the Underground Railroad traveled at night and followed the North Star.

cloze.s: Families who hid escaping people in their homes were part of the ___, though no trains were involved.

note: It was not a real railroad; it borrowed train words, so guides were called conductors and hiding places stations. Many escapees went on to Canada.

def: a very long series of walls and forts built over many centuries to protect China from attackers from the north
why: It is one of the largest building projects in human history and a symbol of China.
ex: Wei and his parents hiked a steep section of the Great Wall of China near Beijing.
Much of the Great Wall of China that tourists see today was built during the Ming dynasty.
The Great Wall of China is not one single wall but many walls built by different dynasties.
Kwame's class built a clay model of the Great Wall of China, with watchtowers along its length.

cloze.s: Stretching across mountains and deserts in northern China, the ___ was built to keep out raiders.

note: Despite a popular myth, it cannot be seen with the naked eye from the Moon.

def: an organized vote in which people choose who will hold a public office, such as mayor or president
why: It is the main way citizens in a democracy pick their leaders and hold them accountable.
ex: Fatima volunteered at the polling place on the day of the city election.
The school held an election for class president, and every student got one vote.
Diego turned eighteen just in time to vote in the election for mayor.
The local newspaper printed each candidate's views before the school board election.

cloze.s: Voters lined up early to cast their ballots in the ___ for governor.

note: Not the same as a referendum, where people vote directly on a law or question rather than on a person.

def: the elected body that makes national laws in the United States, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives
why: It writes federal laws, sets the national budget and can declare war.
ex: A bill must pass both the Senate and the House before Congress can send it to the president.
Diego's class visited the Capitol in Washington, D.C., where Congress meets.
Every state sends two senators to Congress, no matter how large its population is.
Malik wrote to his representative in Congress about a proposed highway bill.

cloze.s: Under the Constitution, only ___ has the power to declare war and to pass the federal budget.

note: Each state has two senators, while seats in the House are divided by population. Many other countries call a similar body a parliament.

def: the highest court in the United States, whose rulings all other courts in the country must follow
why: Its decisions settle what the Constitution means and can affect the whole nation.
ex: The case went all the way to the Supreme Court after two lower courts disagreed.
Brown v. Board of Education was a 1954 Supreme Court decision that ruled school segregation unconstitutional.
Thurgood Marshall became the first African American justice on the Supreme Court in 1967.
Reporters waited outside the Supreme Court on the morning the justices announced their decision.

cloze.s: Once the ___ decides a case, there is no higher court in the country to appeal to.

note: Its members are called justices, not judges, and are appointed by the president with the Senate's approval. Many other countries also have one.

def: a formal change or addition to a law, contract or constitution
why: It is how a constitution is updated, and it is how Americans gained many key rights.
ex: The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, gave American women the right to vote.
The city council approved an amendment to the parking rules after residents complained.
Hannah's landlord added an amendment to her lease allowing her to keep a cat.
The club voted on an amendment to its rules that raised yearly dues by ten dollars.

cloze.s: To change the U.S. Constitution, a(n) ___ must be approved by three-fourths of the states.

note: The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution are called the Bill of Rights.

def: the legal status of being a full member of a country, with its rights, such as voting, and its duties
why: It decides who can vote, hold a passport and receive a country's protection.
ex: After living in the United States for many years, Yuki passed her test and gained citizenship.
Some countries allow dual citizenship, so a person can belong to two nations at once.
Diego's grandmother studied American history for months before her citizenship interview.
With his new citizenship, Kwame voted in a national election for the first time.

cloze.s: At the ceremony, fifty immigrants took an oath and received U.S. ___.

note: People can gain it by birth or through a legal process called naturalization.

def: a system in which a king or queen is head of the country, usually taking the role from a parent or relative
why: Many countries still have one, though most kings and queens today have little real power.
ex: The United Kingdom is a monarchy, but elected members of Parliament make its laws.
France ended its monarchy during the French Revolution.
Tourists in London watch the guards at Buckingham Palace, a symbol of Britain's monarchy.
Nepal ended its monarchy in 2008 and became a republic.

cloze.s: When the old king died, his eldest daughter became queen, as the rules of the ___ required.

note: In a constitutional monarchy, such as Sweden or Spain, the king or queen is mostly a symbol and elected leaders govern.

def: a country where power belongs to the people and the leaders they elect, with no king or queen as head
why: Most countries today, including the United States, are organized this way.
ex: After the revolution, the country became a republic and held its first election for president.
India became a republic in 1950, when its new constitution took effect.
The United States is a republic, so citizens elect a president instead of crowning a king.
Italy voted in 1946 to end its monarchy and become a republic.

cloze.s: The country got rid of its king and became a(n) ___ led by an elected president.

note: The word comes from Latin res publica, meaning the public matter or the people's affair.

def: the right to say, write and share your ideas and opinions without being punished by the government
why: It lets people criticize leaders, debate ideas and share information openly.
ex: The protesters were exercising their freedom of speech when they marched peacefully downtown.
In the United States, freedom of speech is protected by the First Amendment.
Freedom of speech lets Malik write a blog criticizing the city's new bus routes.
Hannah's history class studied writers who were jailed in countries without freedom of speech.

cloze.s: The court ruled that arresting the writer for criticizing the mayor violated his ___.

note: In the U.S. it limits what the government can do; it does not stop private companies or employers from setting their own rules.

def: the 1776 document in which the thirteen American colonies announced they were no longer under British rule
why: It explained why the colonies broke from Britain and stated ideals of equality and natural rights.
ex: The Declaration of Independence states that all men are created equal and have rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
Americans celebrate July 4 because the Declaration of Independence was adopted on that day in 1776.
John Hancock's large signature on the Declaration of Independence made his name a slang word for any signature.
Visitors to the National Archives in Washington, D.C., can see the original Declaration of Independence.

cloze.s: Thomas Jefferson wrote most of the ___, which the Continental Congress adopted on July 4, 1776.

note: Not the same as the Constitution, which was written in 1787 and sets out how the U.S. government works.

def: money that people and businesses are required to pay to the government to fund public services
why: It pays for roads, schools, the military and other public services.
ex: The sales tax added a few dollars to the price of Malik's new shoes.
Every April, Maria files her income tax return to report what she earned last year.
The city raised the property tax to pay for new schools and roads.
Many states add a tax to each pack of cigarettes to discourage smoking and raise money.

cloze.s: Part of every paycheck goes to the government as income ___ to pay for public services.

note: Common kinds include income, sales and property ones.

def: an amount of money you borrow and must pay back over time, usually with interest added
why: People use them to pay for big things like houses, cars and college.
ex: Kwame took out a car loan and will make monthly payments for five years.
The bakery got a small-business loan to buy a new oven.
Olga asked her brother for a small loan to cover rent and promised to pay him back next month.
Before approving the loan, the bank checked how much Jamal earned and how much debt he already had.

cloze.s: Hannah borrowed $20,000 from the bank as a student ___ and must repay it after she graduates.

note: A mortgage is a specific kind used to buy a home.

def: money a person or business receives regularly, such as pay from a job or profit from sales
why: It determines what you can afford and how much tax you owe.
ex: Priya's income rose when she took a second part-time job on weekends.
Many families spend about a third of their income on housing.
Fatima's bakery had its highest income ever during the holiday season.
The apartment requires renters to have a monthly income of at least three times the rent.

cloze.s: Tomás tracks his monthly ___ and expenses so he never spends more than he earns.

note: Gross means the amount before taxes and deductions; net means what is left after them.

def: an arrangement in which you pay a company regularly and it agrees to pay for certain losses, like accidents or illness
why: It protects people from costs too large to pay alone, such as a hospital stay or a house fire.
ex: After the storm damaged their roof, the Garcias' home insurance paid for the repairs.
Liam's job comes with health insurance that covers most of his doctor visits.
Fatima's travel insurance paid for her hotel when a snowstorm canceled her flight home.
When Wei cracked his phone screen, the insurance he pays for each month covered most of the repair.

cloze.s: Driving without car ___ is illegal in most states, because accidents can cost thousands of dollars.

note: The regular payment is called a premium; the amount you pay yourself before the company starts paying is the deductible.

def: the system of money a country uses, such as the U.S. dollar or the euro
why: Travelers, importers and investors all deal with changing values between them.
ex: Before her trip to Mexico, Sofia changed some dollars into pesos, the local currency.
Many European countries share one currency, the euro.
At the airport, Kwame exchanged his leftover euros back into his home currency.
Travelers to the United Kingdom need British pounds, the country's currency, for small shops that refuse cards.

cloze.s: The yen is the ___ of Japan, so visitors must swap their dollars for it.

note: The exchange rate is how much of one is worth in another.

def: the state of not having a paid job while wanting one and actively looking for work
why: Its rate is one of the main measures of how well an economy is doing.
ex: When the factory closed, unemployment in the small town rose sharply.
While he searched for a new job, Diego received unemployment benefits from the state.
The government reports the unemployment rate each month to show how many people are looking for work.
After a year of unemployment, Olga finally found a job as a bookkeeper at a clinic.

cloze.s: During the Great Depression, ___ soared, and about a quarter of American workers could not find jobs.

note: Retirees and full-time students who are not looking for work are not counted in the official rate.

def: the lowest amount per hour that employers are allowed by law to pay their workers
why: It sets a floor on pay for millions of workers in jobs like retail and fast food.
ex: Aisha's first job at the movie theater paid minimum wage.
Some states and cities set a minimum wage higher than the national one.
Working 40 hours a week at minimum wage, Fatima still struggled to pay her rent and bills.
Employers who pay workers less than the minimum wage can be fined by the government.

cloze.s: The new law raised the ___, so the lowest-paid workers at the store got a raise.

note: The first U.S. national one was set in 1938 by the Fair Labor Standards Act, at 25 cents an hour.

def: a plastic card that lets you buy things with money borrowed from a bank and pay it back later
why: It is convenient, but unpaid balances can grow quickly because of high interest charges.
ex: Jamal pays off his credit card in full each month so he never owes interest.
Olga used her credit card to book the hotel, and the bill came a few weeks later.
Tomás lost his credit card at the mall and called the bank to cancel it right away.
The small taco stand only takes cash, so Yuki couldn't use her credit card there.

cloze.s: Because she paid only the smallest amount due, the interest on Hannah's ___ kept growing.

note: Not the same as a debit card, which takes money straight out of your own bank account.

def: a bank account for keeping money you do not plan to spend soon, which usually earns a little interest
why: It is a safe place to build an emergency fund or save for a goal.
ex: Wei puts part of every paycheck into a savings account for emergencies.
Maria opened a savings account for her daughter and adds birthday money to it each year.
Diego put money into his savings account for a year to pay for a trip to Peru.
When her car broke down, Hannah used money from her savings account to pay for the repairs.

cloze.s: Instead of keeping cash under the mattress, Malik moved it into a(n) ___ at the bank, where it earns interest.

note: Unlike a checking account, it is meant for storing money rather than for paying everyday bills.

def: an opening in Earth's surface, often a mountain, where melted rock, ash and gas burst out from deep below
why: Eruptions can destroy towns and change the weather, yet their ash makes some of the richest farmland.
ex: When the volcano erupted, a huge cloud of ash forced airlines to cancel flights for days.
The Hawaiian Islands were formed by volcanoes rising from the ocean floor.
Mount Vesuvius, a volcano in Italy, buried the Roman city of Pompeii in AD 79.
Scientists placed instruments on the volcano to warn nearby towns before it erupts again.

cloze.s: Lava poured down the sides of the ___ and slowly flowed toward the sea.

note: Melted rock is called magma while underground and lava once it reaches the surface.

def: a sudden shaking of the ground caused by huge blocks of rock shifting deep below Earth's surface
why: Strong ones can topple buildings, so earthquake-prone areas need special building rules and drills.
ex: During the earthquake, Yuki ducked under her desk and held on until the shaking stopped.
The earthquake was strong enough to crack roads and knock dishes off shelves.
California has frequent earthquakes because it sits where two giant plates of Earth's crust meet.
After the earthquake, workers inspected every bridge in the city for cracks.

cloze.s: The ground shook for thirty seconds, and scientists measured the ___ at magnitude 6.

note: Most happen along the edges of the huge plates that make up Earth's outer layer. One under the sea can cause a tsunami.

def: a very dry area of land that gets very little rain or snow during the year
why: About a third of Earth's land is this dry, and life there must survive with little water.
ex: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, covering much of North Africa.
Cactuses store water in their thick stems, which helps them survive in the desert.
The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth.
Diego packed plenty of water for his hike through the Arizona desert.

cloze.s: The camel can go days without drinking, which suits it to life in the ___.

note: It is defined by dryness, not heat: Antarctica is the largest one on Earth. Not to be confused with dessert, the sweet course after a meal.

def: a huge mass of ice that moves very slowly over land, formed from snow piled up over many years
why: They store much of the world's fresh water, and their melting adds to rising sea levels.
ex: On their trip to Alaska, Hannah and Kwame watched chunks of ice break off a glacier into the sea.
Thousands of years ago, glaciers carved out many of the valleys and lakes in the northern United States.
The guide warned the hikers not to walk on the glacier because of hidden cracks in the ice.
The lake was milky blue from fine rock dust ground up by the glacier above it.

cloze.s: The river was fed by a(n) ___ high in the mountains, a slow-moving river of ice.

note: An iceberg is a large piece that has broken off one and floats in the sea.

def: a huge, powerful spinning storm with very strong winds and heavy rain that forms over warm ocean water
why: These storms cause floods and severe damage along coasts, so forecasts and evacuations save lives.
ex: Residents boarded up their windows as the hurricane moved toward the Florida coast.
After the hurricane, Diego's neighborhood was without power for a week.
Hurricane season in the Atlantic Ocean runs from June through November.
Before the hurricane hit, Maria stocked up on water, canned food and batteries.

cloze.s: Winds of 150 miles per hour made the ___ one of the strongest storms to hit the Gulf Coast.

note: The same kind of storm is called a typhoon in the northwest Pacific and a cyclone in the Indian Ocean.

def: a thick forest of tall trees in an area that gets heavy rain throughout the year
why: Though they cover a small part of Earth's land, they are home to a huge share of its plant and animal species.
ex: The Amazon rainforest in South America is the largest tropical rainforest in the world.
Many medicines come from plants first found in the rainforest.
Yuki's class watched a film about the frogs and insects that live high in the rainforest treetops.
Large areas of rainforest are cut down every year to make room for farms and cattle.

cloze.s: Monkeys, parrots and jaguars live in the warm, wet ___, where it rains almost every day.

note: Most are tropical, near the equator, but cooler ones also exist, such as on the Pacific coast of the northwestern United States.

def: the number of people, or of a kind of animal or plant, living in a particular place
why: It guides decisions about schools, hospitals, housing and how many representatives an area gets.
ex: The town's population doubled after a new factory opened and brought thousands of jobs.
Scientists are counting the wolf population in the national park.
The city built two new schools because its population of young families kept growing.
After hunting was banned, the elephant population in the reserve slowly increased.

cloze.s: China and India each have a(n) ___ of more than a billion people.

note: In the United States, it is counted every ten years by the census.

def: the city where a country's or state's government is based
why: Knowing them helps you follow world news, where they often stand for a whole government.
ex: Ottawa, not Toronto, is the capital city of Canada.
Priya visited Washington, D.C., the capital city of the United States, to see the White House.
On her road trip, Aisha stopped in Austin, the capital city of Texas, to tour the state capitol.
Lawmakers from every corner of the state travel to the capital city when the legislature meets.

cloze.s: Canberra, not Sydney, is the ___ of Australia, where its parliament meets.

note: News writers often use one as shorthand for a government, as in "talks between Washington and Beijing."

def: something found in nature that people use, such as water, wood, soil, oil or minerals
why: Countries' wealth and trade often depend on them, and many can run out if overused.
ex: Saudi Arabia's most valuable natural resource is its oil.
Forests are a natural resource that can grow back if trees are replanted.
Wood from the nearby forests is the natural resource that keeps the town's sawmill busy.
In geography class, Diego listed copper as the most important natural resource of Chile.

cloze.s: Clean fresh water is a precious ___ that many dry regions must carefully share.

note: Renewable ones, like sunlight and wind, are replaced naturally; nonrenewable ones, like coal and oil, take millions of years to form.

def: a long written story about made-up people and events, published as a book
why: It is the main form of storytelling in modern literature, from classics to bestsellers.
ex: To Kill a Mockingbird is a famous novel by Harper Lee about justice in a small Southern town.
Fatima stayed up late to finish the last chapters of her mystery novel.
Wei's book club is reading a novel about a family that moves from Mexico to Chicago.
Jane Austen's novel Pride and Prejudice has been made into several films.

cloze.s: The author spent five years writing her first ___, a 400-page story about two sisters in Lagos.

note: As an adjective, the word means new and unusual, as in a novel idea.

def: stories about people and events that are imagined by the writer rather than real
why: Bookstores and libraries sort books by this label, and it helps you know whether to read something as true.
ex: The Harry Potter books are fiction, but they are set partly in real places like London.
Malik reads history books during the week and fiction on vacation.
Science fiction imagines future worlds, like cities on Mars or talking robots.
Although the movie felt real, the director said the story was fiction, not based on any true events.

cloze.s: The library keeps novels and short stories in the ___ section, separate from history and science books.

note: It can also mean any false story presented as true: His excuse was pure fiction.

def: writing that uses rhythm, sound and carefully chosen words, often in short lines, to express feelings or ideas
why: It is one of the oldest art forms and appears in songs, speeches, greeting cards and ceremonies.
ex: Maya Angelou's poetry speaks about strength, hope and dignity.
In English class, Sofia wrote poetry about her grandmother's garden.
Diego reads his poetry aloud at a café open mic on Thursday nights.
Fatima's grandmother can still recite poetry in Arabic that she learned as a young girl.

cloze.s: The poet Langston Hughes is known for ___ inspired by the rhythms of jazz and blues.

note: One piece is a poem; the person who writes it is a poet.

def: the matching of the ending sounds of words, like "cat" and "hat," often used in poems and songs
why: It makes poems, songs and slogans catchy and easy to remember.
ex: Many children's books use rhyme, so kids can guess the next word.
The songwriter struggled to find a rhyme for "orange."
The jump-rope chant had a catchy rhyme that the kids repeated all through recess.
The rapper is famous for packing rhyme after rhyme into a single fast verse.

cloze.s: The poem's lines end with "night" and "light," a simple ___ that is easy to remember.

note: Also a short poem for children, as in a nursery rhyme. Not all poetry uses it.

def: a work of art made by cutting, shaping or building materials like stone, metal, wood or clay into a solid form
why: It fills museums, parks and public squares and is one of the oldest forms of art.
ex: Michelangelo's David is a famous marble sculpture in Florence, Italy.
Kwame made a sculpture of a bird out of old bicycle parts.
The town square has a bronze sculpture of a jazz musician playing the trumpet.
In art class, Aisha shaped clay into a small sculpture of her cat.

cloze.s: The artist carved a large ___ of a horse from a single block of marble.

note: The artist who makes it is a sculptor.

def: a painting, drawing or photograph of a person, usually focused on the face
why: For centuries it was the main way to record what people looked like, and it remains a major art form.
ex: Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa is probably the most famous portrait in the world.
The family hired a photographer to take a portrait of all three generations together.
Tomás sketched a quick portrait of his daughter while she read on the couch.
Before the conference, Aisha had a professional portrait taken for her company's website.

cloze.s: The artist spent weeks painting a(n) ___ of the mayor, getting her face and smile just right.

note: A portrait an artist makes of himself or herself is a self-portrait. Phones also use the word for a tall, upright screen view.

def: a large group of musicians playing string, wind and drum instruments together, led by a conductor
why: It performs symphonies, operas and many movie soundtracks.
ex: The city orchestra played music from famous movies at the free summer concert.
Diego plays the cello in his high school orchestra.
The orchestra tuned their instruments while the conductor waited at the front of the stage.
Yuki's daughter joined the youth orchestra and practices the violin every evening.

cloze.s: The conductor raised her baton, and the whole ___ of violins, flutes and horns began to play.

note: Its four sections are strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion.

def: a formal style of dance, set to music, with exact, flowing movements that often tell a story
why: It is a major performing art and the training base for many other kinds of dance.
ex: Every December, the theater stages The Nutcracker ballet, with music by Tchaikovsky.
Yuki has taken ballet lessons since she was six and now dances on her toes in pointe shoes.
Kwame took his niece to her first ballet, and she copied the dancers' spins all the way home.
Ballet dancers train for years to leap and turn with perfect control.

cloze.s: The dancers in tutus leaped across the stage in a classic ___ called Swan Lake.

note: It began in the courts of Renaissance Italy and was developed in France, so many of its terms, like plié, are French. Pronounced bal-LAY in American English.

def: a style of music that began in African American communities in New Orleans, known for swinging rhythms and made-up-on-the-spot solos
why: It is one of America's great art forms and influenced rock, R&B, hip-hop and much other music.
ex: Louis Armstrong, a trumpeter from New Orleans, became one of the most famous jazz musicians ever.
On Friday nights, Jamal plays saxophone with a jazz band at a downtown club.
Hannah's grandfather loves jazz and plays old Duke Ellington records every Sunday afternoon.
New Orleans holds a famous jazz festival every spring, filling the city with brass bands and crowds.

cloze.s: The trumpeter made up a brand-new solo on the spot, as ___ musicians often do.

note: It took shape in the late 1800s and early 1900s, drawing on blues and ragtime.

def: the study of basic questions about life, knowledge, right and wrong, and what is real, using careful reasoning
why: It shapes law, science, politics and religion, and trains clear thinking.
ex: In her philosophy class, Hannah debated whether people are ever truly free to choose.
Plato and Confucius are two of the most influential thinkers in the history of philosophy.
Ana's favorite philosophy book asks whether we can ever be sure the world around us is real.
Over dinner, Wei and his son had a long talk about philosophy, wondering what makes a life truly good.

cloze.s: Socrates spent his life asking questions about justice and truth, and he is often called a founder of Western ___.

note: The word comes from Greek words meaning love of wisdom. It can also mean a personal guiding belief: My philosophy is to do my best.

def: fair treatment, in which people get what they deserve and laws and rules are applied fairly to all
why: It is a central goal of laws and courts and a key idea in debates about right and wrong.
ex: The victims' families wanted justice and asked the court to hold the company responsible.
Martin Luther King Jr. spoke often about justice and equal treatment for all people.
Malik became a lawyer to fight for justice for workers who had been cheated out of their pay.
Many people felt justice was not done when the drunk driver got off with a small fine.

cloze.s: When the innocent man was finally freed after years in prison, his lawyer said ___ had been done at last.

note: It can also be the title of a judge on a high court, such as a Supreme Court justice.

def: the state in which all people have the same rights, chances and treatment
why: It is a founding ideal in many constitutions and a goal of civil rights movements.
ex: The marchers carried signs calling for equality at work for people of every background.
Wei's school teaches that equality means everyone gets a fair chance to succeed.
The club's rules promise equality, so every member gets one vote no matter how long they have belonged.
Hannah's essay traced the long struggle for equality between women and men in the workplace.

cloze.s: The law guarantees ___ before the court, so rich and poor are judged by the same rules.

note: Equality of opportunity (same chances) and equality of outcome (same results) are different ideas.

def: clear, careful reasoning in which each step follows from the one before to reach a sound conclusion
why: It helps you test arguments, spot mistakes in thinking and solve problems.
ex: Detectives in mystery novels use logic to work out who committed the crime from small clues.
Sofia's logic was simple: if the store closes at nine and it is ten now, it must be closed.
The lawyer pointed out a flaw in the witness's logic, since her two claims could not both be true.
In math class, Yuki used logic to prove that the puzzle had only one possible answer.

cloze.s: If all birds have feathers and a robin is a bird, ___ tells us that a robin has feathers.

note: It is also the name of a branch of philosophy and math that studies correct reasoning.

def: a statement that can be checked with evidence and shown to be true
why: Telling these apart from opinions is a basic skill for reading news and judging arguments.
ex: It is a fact that water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit at sea level.
The reporter checked every fact in the story before it was published.
Kwame's teacher asked the class to sort each sentence into fact or opinion.
Before sharing the post, Olga checked whether its claim was a fact or just a rumor.

cloze.s: "Paris is the capital of France" is a(n) ___, but "Paris is the most beautiful city" is an opinion.

note: Contrasted with an opinion, which is a personal view that cannot be proved true or false.

def: a personal belief or judgment about something, which others may reasonably disagree with
why: Separating these from facts helps you read news, reviews and ads with a clear head.
ex: In Malik's opinion, the book was better than the movie, but his sister disagreed.
Newspapers print opinion pieces on a separate page from the regular news.
The movie critic gave her opinion that the film was too long, though many viewers loved it.
At the town meeting, each neighbor shared an opinion about where the new park should go.

cloze.s: Saying pizza is the best food is just a(n) ___, since many people prefer something else.

note: Also a formal written decision by a judge or an expert's official judgment, as in a second medical opinion.

def: a shared system of beliefs, worship and practices, often centered on God or gods and the meaning of life
why: It shapes the values, holidays, laws, art and history of cultures around the world.
ex: Christianity, Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism are among the largest religions in the world.
Priya's class visited a mosque, a temple and a church to learn about different religions.
The hospital chaplain visits patients of any religion who want comfort or someone to pray with.
Wei's college course compared how each major religion explains what happens after death.

cloze.s: The U.S. Constitution protects each person's right to practice any ___ or none at all.

note: Not all of them center on a god; many forms of Buddhism, for example, do not.

def: a set of reasons given to support a conclusion or persuade others that something is true
why: Judging whether reasons really support a claim is central to debate, law and science.
ex: Tomás made a strong argument for the four-day work week, backing it with data from other companies.
The lawyer's argument was that the evidence did not prove her client was at the scene.
In debate club, Yuki learned to support each argument with facts and examples.
The scientist's argument rested on twenty years of carefully recorded temperature data.

cloze.s: Her essay presented a clear ___: three reasons, each with evidence, leading to one conclusion.

also: an angry disagreement between people (“The neighbors had a loud argument about parking.”)
note: In logic and debate, it means reasoning, not a quarrel; a good one can be calm and polite.

def: the freedom to live, think and act as you choose, without unfair control by the government or others
why: It is a core ideal in many constitutions and in debates about the limits of government power.
ex: The Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor has welcomed immigrants since 1886.
The Declaration of Independence names life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness as basic rights.
Diego's grandmother left her homeland in search of the liberty to speak and worship freely.
The strict new dress code limited the students' liberty to choose their own clothes, and many complained.

cloze.s: After years in prison, the freed writer said nothing mattered more to him than his ___.

note: Often used in political writing about rights; in everyday speech, freedom is the more common word.

def: a tightly wound thread of DNA inside a cell that carries many genes; humans usually have 46
why: Counting and checking these threads helps doctors find conditions such as Down syndrome before or after birth.
ex: Each human egg and sperm cell carries 23 chromosomes, so a fertilized egg ends up with 23 pairs.
Under the microscope, Priya could see each chromosome as a small dark X shape in the dividing cell.
Biological females typically have two X chromosomes, while males typically have one X and one Y.
A genetic test counted each chromosome in the baby's cells to check that none was missing or extra.

cloze.s: People with Down syndrome have an extra copy of ___ 21 in their cells.

note: Biological sex in humans is usually linked to the X and Y pair: XX or XY.

def: the distance light travels in one year, about six trillion miles, used to measure space
why: Distances between stars and galaxies are so huge that miles or kilometers become impractical numbers.
ex: The nearest star beyond the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is a little over four light-years away from Earth.
When Kwame looks at a star 100 light-years away, he sees light that left it a century ago.
The Andromeda galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.
Astronomers estimate that our Milky Way galaxy is about 100,000 light-years across.

cloze.s: Despite the word “year,” a(n) ___ measures distance, not time.

note: A common mistake is to treat it as a unit of time; it is a unit of distance.

def: a region in space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape
why: Many form when giant stars collapse, and they help scientists test our deepest ideas about gravity.
ex: In 2019 astronomers released the first image of a black hole, a glowing ring around a dark center.
Scientists believe a supermassive black hole sits at the center of our own Milky Way galaxy.
Some black holes form when a giant star collapses at the end of its life.
Diego's daughter asked why a black hole looks black, and he explained that no light can escape it.

cloze.s: Because no light can get out of a(n) ___, astronomers find one by watching how nearby stars and gas behave.

def: a plant or animal brought to a new area where it spreads quickly and harms the local wildlife
why: Such newcomers cost farms, fisheries and cities huge sums and can wipe out native plants and animals.
ex: Zebra mussels, an invasive species in the Great Lakes, clog water pipes and crowd out native mussels.
Hikers are asked to clean their boots so they do not carry seeds of an invasive species to new trails.
Burmese pythons, an invasive species in Florida's Everglades, eat many native birds and mammals.
On weekends, Kwame volunteers pulling up kudzu, an invasive species that smothers native trees in the South.

cloze.s: Cane toads, brought to Australia to eat beetles, became a(n) ___ that poisons the native animals that try to eat them.

note: Not every non-native species is invasive; the label means it spreads and causes harm.

def: the moving of pollen from one flower part to another so the plant can make seeds and fruit
why: Many fruit, nut and vegetable crops depend on bees and other insects carrying pollen between flowers.
ex: Almond farmers rent beehives every spring because their trees need pollination to produce nuts.
Wind carries out the pollination of corn, scattering pollen from the tassels to the silks.
Rosa planted wildflowers in her yard to attract butterflies and help with pollination.
Without enough bees for pollination, the apple orchard produced far less fruit that year.

cloze.s: As the bee crawled into each blossom, dust stuck to its legs and moved on to the next flower, a process called ___.

def: an event in which the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun and blocks some or all sunlight
why: These rare events draw huge crowds, and looking at the Sun without special glasses can damage your eyes.
ex: During the total solar eclipse, the sky went dark at noon and the birds in the park fell silent.
Aisha bought certified glasses so her children could safely watch the solar eclipse from the backyard.
Looking straight at a solar eclipse without special glasses can permanently damage your eyes.
Omar's family drove six hours to stand in the path of the total solar eclipse.

cloze.s: A(n) ___ can only happen at new moon, when the Moon lines up directly between us and the Sun.

note: In a lunar eclipse it is the other way around: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

def: an electric charge that builds up on an object's surface, often from rubbing, and stays until released, sometimes as a spark
why: It explains the small shocks from doorknobs and why dry winter air makes hair stand up.
ex: After shuffling across the carpet in socks, Diego got a spark of static electricity from the metal doorknob.
Rubbing a balloon on your hair creates static electricity that lets it stick to the wall.
On dry winter days, static electricity makes Nadia's hair stand up when she pulls off her wool hat.
Workers who handle computer chips wear grounding wrist straps so static electricity does not damage the parts.

cloze.s: Clothes fresh from the dryer often cling together because of ___ built up as they tumbled.

note: Unlike current electricity, which flows steadily through wires, this charge stays put until it is released.

def: the scientific account that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in an extremely hot, dense state and has expanded since
why: It is the starting point for how scientists explain the age, history and expansion of the universe.
ex: Faint microwave radiation coming from every direction in the sky is leftover heat from the Big Bang.
In her astronomy class, Yuki learned that the Big Bang was not an explosion in space but an expansion of space itself.
Kwame's son asked what existed before the Big Bang, and his science teacher admitted no one knows for sure.
Most astronomers accept the Big Bang partly because distant galaxies are still moving away from us.

cloze.s: Scientists estimate that the universe began with the ___ roughly 13.8 billion years ago.

def: tiny parts inside most cells that turn food and oxygen into energy the cell can use
why: Often called the cell's power plants, they matter for exercise, aging and a group of inherited diseases.
ex: Muscle cells in a marathon runner's legs are packed with mitochondria to supply steady energy.
Liam's biology teacher explained that mitochondria have their own small set of DNA, passed down from the mother.
In biology class, Grace drew a cell and labeled the mitochondria as the parts that make energy.
Some rare inherited diseases weaken the mitochondria, leaving muscles tired after even light activity.

cloze.s: Known as the powerhouses of the cell, ___ release energy from the sugar we eat.

note: This is the plural; one of them is a mitochondrion.

def: a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart to the rest of the body
why: Blocked or narrowed ones cause heart attacks and strokes, which are leading causes of death.
ex: The nurse pressed two fingers on the artery in Malik's wrist to count his pulse.
Fatty buildup inside an artery can slowly narrow it and reduce the flow of blood through it.
During the checkup, the doctor listened to the large artery in Olga's neck with a stethoscope.
A blocked artery that feeds the heart muscle can cause a heart attack.

cloze.s: The aorta, the body's largest ___, carries blood straight out of the heart.

note: Veins carry blood back toward the heart; this vessel carries it away.

def: a mild brain injury caused by a blow to the head or a hard shake, often causing headache and confusion
why: Sports leagues now pull players from games after head hits, because repeated injuries can cause lasting harm.
ex: After falling off her bike, Sofia had a concussion and needed several days of rest away from screens.
The coach benched Jamal for the rest of the game until a doctor checked him for a concussion.
Doctors told Aisha to avoid sports until her concussion symptoms, like headaches and dizziness, went away.
After the car accident, Wei had a concussion and could not remember the drive home.

cloze.s: The football player felt dizzy and could not remember the play after the tackle, so trainers tested him for a(n) ___.

def: an outbreak of disease that spreads across many countries or continents and affects very large numbers of people
why: Such worldwide outbreaks, like the 1918 flu and COVID-19, reshape health care, work and daily life.
ex: The World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic in March 2020.
During the pandemic, Wei's office closed and everyone worked from home for more than a year.
The 1918 flu pandemic spread around the world and killed tens of millions of people.
Health agencies stockpile masks and medicines so they are ready for the next pandemic.

cloze.s: An outbreak limited to one region is an epidemic; once it spreads around the world, it becomes a(n) ___.

note: An epidemic is a sharp rise in cases in one area; this word means the spread has gone worldwide.

def: medicine that stops a patient from feeling pain during surgery, by numbing part of the body or putting them fully to sleep
why: Safe pain control made modern surgery possible, and patients are asked about it before most operations.
ex: Tomás was under general anesthesia for his knee surgery and remembered nothing afterward.
The dentist used local anesthesia, so Hannah stayed awake but felt no pain while her tooth was filled.
The vet put the dog under anesthesia before cleaning its teeth.
After waking up from anesthesia, Kwame felt groggy and was not allowed to drive himself home.

cloze.s: Before the operation, a doctor explained the ___ that would keep Maria asleep and pain-free.

note: General means fully asleep; local means only a small area is numbed.

def: an extra result of a medicine or treatment, usually one you do not want, beyond the change it is meant to cause
why: Every drug label lists them, and weighing them against benefits is part of choosing any treatment.
ex: Drowsiness is a common side effect of some allergy pills, so Aisha takes hers at night.
The doctor switched Kwame to a new drug because the first one had a side effect of constant coughing.
The pharmacist warned Amara that an upset stomach is a possible side effect of her new antibiotic.
Hair loss is a well-known side effect of some cancer treatments.

cloze.s: The medicine lowered his blood pressure well, but feeling dizzy when he stood up was an annoying ___.

def: the part of plant foods that the body cannot digest, which helps keep the gut healthy and regular
why: Most adults eat less of it than recommended, and getting more is linked to better heart and gut health.
ex: Beans, oats, berries and whole grains are good sources of dietary fiber.
Priya's doctor suggested more dietary fiber, like vegetables and brown rice, to help with constipation.
Eating apples with the skin on gives you more dietary fiber than eating them peeled.
Kwame added beans to his soup for more dietary fiber, which also helps him feel full longer.

cloze.s: White bread has had much of its ___ removed, while whole wheat bread keeps the bran that supplies it.

note: Found mainly in plant foods; meat, eggs and dairy contain none.

def: a long-lasting illness in which the body stops responding well to insulin, so blood sugar stays too high
why: It is the most common form of diabetes and is closely tied to weight, diet and physical activity.
ex: After his diagnosis of type 2 diabetes, Liam began walking daily and checking his blood sugar.
Doctors say regular exercise can lower the risk of developing type 2 diabetes.
Mateo's doctor said that losing some weight could help control his type 2 diabetes.
Many people with type 2 diabetes manage it with diet, exercise and a pill called metformin.

cloze.s: Unlike type 1, which often starts in childhood, ___ most often develops in adults and is linked to lifestyle.

note: In type 1 the body makes little or no insulin; in this form insulin is made but does not work well.

def: the distance all the way around the edge of a circle
why: You use it to measure belts, tires, tree trunks and tracks, and it equals pi times the width.
ex: Malik wrapped a tape measure around the oak tree to find its circumference.
The circumference of Earth at the equator is roughly 25,000 miles.
Hannah measured the circumference of the round lampshade to know how much ribbon to buy.
With each full turn, Malik's bike wheel rolls forward a distance equal to its circumference.

cloze.s: If a circle is 10 inches across, its ___ is about 31.4 inches, since you multiply by pi.

note: For shapes with straight sides, the distance around is called the perimeter.

def: the rule that in a right triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest
why: Builders, designers and navigators use it to find unknown distances and to check that corners are square.
ex: Using the Pythagorean theorem, Sofia worked out that a ladder 5 feet from the wall must be 13 feet long to reach 12 feet up.
Carpenters use the Pythagorean theorem with a 3-4-5 triangle to check that a corner is truly square.
Omar used the Pythagorean theorem to find that a TV 48 inches wide and 36 inches tall is 60 inches across diagonally.
On the geometry test, Keiko needed the Pythagorean theorem to find the missing side of a right triangle.

cloze.s: The ___ is usually written as a squared plus b squared equals c squared.

note: It works only for triangles that have one 90-degree angle.

def: a short way of writing very large or very small numbers as a number times a power of 10
why: Scientists, engineers and calculators use it to handle numbers like the speed of light without long strings of zeros.
ex: In scientific notation, 300,000,000 is written as 3 × 10⁸.
Fatima's calculator showed the answer in scientific notation because the number was too long for the screen.
Astronomers use scientific notation because distances between stars would take far too many zeros to write out.
Nadia's chemistry teacher wrote the mass of a tiny particle in scientific notation to save space on the board.

cloze.s: Writing 0.00045 as 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ is an example of ___.

note: The first number is usually at least 1 and less than 10.

def: a flat, closed shape made of three or more straight sides, such as a triangle or a square
why: Shapes like this are basic to geometry and are used to build the images in maps, video games and design software.
ex: A stop sign is an eight-sided polygon called an octagon.
Jamal explained that a circle is not a polygon because its edge is curved, not made of straight lines.
For art class, Samir cut out paper polygons, from triangles to hexagons, to build a mosaic.
Computer games often build 3D characters out of thousands of tiny polygons.

cloze.s: Triangles, squares, pentagons and hexagons are all types of ___.

note: The plural is polygons. A shape with any curved side does not count.

def: how far a number is from zero, ignoring whether it is positive or negative, so it is never negative
why: It measures size or distance when direction does not matter, such as the gap between two temperatures.
ex: The absolute value of −8 is 8, and the absolute value of 8 is also 8.
To find how many degrees the temperature changed, Olga took the absolute value of the difference.
Whether the elevator goes up four floors or down four floors, the absolute value of the change is 4.
On the number line, Yuki counted the steps from zero to show that the absolute value of −3 is 3.

cloze.s: Both 5 and −5 have a(n) ___ of 5, because each is five steps from zero.

note: It is written with vertical bars: |−3| = 3.

def: the number you get by dividing 1 by a given number; a number times this always equals 1
why: Dividing by a fraction is done by multiplying by this flipped version, a step used throughout math.
ex: The reciprocal of 4 is 1/4, and the reciprocal of 2/3 is 3/2.
Hannah remembered that to divide by a fraction, you multiply by its reciprocal.
Multiplying 8 by its reciprocal, 1/8, gives exactly 1.
Samir's calculator has a 1/x button that instantly shows the reciprocal of any nonzero number.

cloze.s: Flip 5/7 upside down and you get 7/5, its ___.

note: Zero has none, because you cannot divide by zero. As an adjective, the word also means given in return.

def: a computer or program that stores data or runs services and sends them to other computers over a network
why: Every website, email account and online game depends on these machines, usually kept in large data centers.
ex: When too many fans tried to buy concert tickets at once, the site's server crashed.
Priya's company keeps its files on a server so everyone in the office can reach them.
The online game went down for an hour while the company repaired its main server.
Ethan set up a small server at home to store family photos that every relative could reach.

cloze.s: When you open a website, your browser asks a distant ___ to send back the page you want.

def: a device that directs internet traffic between networks, such as linking the devices in a home to the internet
why: Restarting one or changing its default password is a basic step in fixing or securing home internet.
ex: When the Wi-Fi stopped working, Diego unplugged the router, waited a minute, and plugged it back in.
Moving the router to the middle of the house gave the upstairs bedrooms a stronger signal.
The blinking red light on the router told Leila that the internet connection was down.
Ben set a new password on the router so his neighbors could no longer use his Wi-Fi.

cloze.s: The ___ in the hallway sends the internet signal to every phone and laptop in our apartment.

note: A modem connects your home to your internet provider; this device shares that connection among your devices. Many boxes do both.

def: a small file a website saves in your browser to remember things like your sign-in, settings or the pages you visit
why: They keep you signed in and fill shopping carts, but they are also used to track people for advertising.
ex: A pop-up asked Hannah whether she would accept every cookie or only the ones the site needed to work.
Because of a saved cookie, the shopping site still remembered Malik's cart a week later.
Some ad companies use a cookie to track which websites you visit and then show you related ads.
Priya changed her browser settings to block any cookie from companies whose sites she never visited.

cloze.s: After Sofia cleared every ___ from her browser, she was logged out of all her accounts.

note: Cookies set by outside companies to follow you across many sites are called third-party cookies.

def: one of the tiny colored dots that together make up a digital image or a screen display
why: The number of them in a photo or screen sets how sharp it looks, as in a 1920 by 1080 display.
ex: When Jamal zoomed in too far on the photo, he could see each square pixel.
A 12-megapixel camera captures about twelve million pixels in every picture.
The old video game used such large pixels that the characters looked like stacks of colored blocks.
A dead pixel on Omar's new monitor showed up as a tiny black dot that never changed.

cloze.s: Each ___ on the screen mixes tiny red, green and blue lights to show one color.

note: A megapixel is one million of them.

def: a way of storing and sending information using only two symbols, 0 and 1
why: All digital devices, from phones to satellites, store text, pictures and sound this way.
ex: In binary code, the number 5 is written as 101.
Yuki's computer science class translated their names into binary code, letter by letter.
A computer turns every letter you type into binary code, a pattern of zeros and ones.
Malik showed his daughter that a light switch, either on or off, works like a single digit in binary code.

cloze.s: Deep inside a computer, every photo and song is stored as long strings of ones and zeros called ___.

note: Each 0 or 1 is called a bit.

def: an event in which private information, like passwords or card numbers, is stolen or exposed to the wrong people
why: After one, companies often must warn customers, who may need to change passwords or watch for fraud.
ex: After the data breach at the retailer, Tomás got a new credit card in the mail.
The hospital said a data breach had exposed thousands of patients' names and addresses.
After the data breach, the company offered its customers free credit monitoring for a year.
The hackers behind the data breach sold millions of stolen email addresses online.

cloze.s: The email warned that hackers had stolen customer records in a(n) ___, so everyone should reset their passwords.

def: a service that sends your internet traffic in secret code through another computer, hiding it from others on your network
why: People use one on public Wi-Fi or to reach their work network safely from home.
ex: Olga turns on her VPN whenever she uses the free Wi-Fi at the airport.
Employees had to connect through the company VPN before they could open files from home.
After Kofi started using a VPN, his internet provider could no longer see which websites he visited.
Before reporting from abroad, the journalist set up a VPN to keep her messages hidden from others on the network.

cloze.s: Working from a café, Liam logged in through a(n) ___ so his connection to the office files stayed private.

note: Short for virtual private network. It protects your connection but does not make you completely anonymous.

def: a basic unit of computer data made of eight bits, enough to store one letter of text
why: File sizes and storage are measured in larger units built from it, such as megabytes and gigabytes.
ex: The letter “A” takes up one byte of storage on a computer.
A gigabyte holds about a billion bytes, enough for hundreds of photos.
Each byte holds eight bits, and each bit is either a 0 or a 1.
A plain text message of 100 English letters takes up roughly 100 bytes of storage.

cloze.s: Kilobytes, megabytes and gigabytes are all multiples of the ___.

note: A bit is a single 0 or 1; eight of them make this unit.

def: a charter that English barons forced King John to accept in 1215, limiting the king's power
why: It became a lasting symbol of the idea that even rulers must obey the law.
ex: The Magna Carta was agreed to at Runnymede, a meadow beside the River Thames.
Fatima's history teacher said the Magna Carta influenced later ideas about fair trials and limits on government.
Hannah saw an original copy of the Magna Carta at the British Library in London.
The Magna Carta was written in Latin on a large sheet of parchment.

cloze.s: In 1215, rebellious nobles made King John accept the ___, which said the king was not above the law.

note: The name is Latin for “Great Charter.”

def: a deadly plague that swept through Asia, Europe and North Africa in the 1300s, killing tens of millions of people
why: It killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's people and changed its economy, religion and society.
ex: The Black Death reached Europe in 1347 and spread along trade routes by ship.
With so many workers killed by the Black Death, surviving peasants could demand higher pay.
Boccaccio's book The Decameron tells of young people who left Florence to escape the Black Death.
Yuki's history class compared the Black Death with modern outbreaks to see how diseases spread.

cloze.s: Caused by plague bacteria, the ___ wiped out entire villages in Europe in the mid-1300s.

note: It was an outbreak of bubonic plague, caused by bacteria.

def: a series of religious wars, from 1095 to the late 1200s, in which European Christians fought to control Jerusalem
why: They deepened lasting tensions between Christian Europe and the Muslim world and increased contact and trade between them.
ex: Pope Urban II called for the first of the Crusades in 1095.
Hannah's book on the Crusades described how the Muslim leader Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187.
Crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099, at the end of the first of the Crusades.
Castles built during the Crusades still stand today in Syria and Lebanon.

cloze.s: During the ___, armies from Europe traveled to the Middle East to try to capture the Holy Land.

note: In everyday English, a crusade can also mean any strong campaign for a cause.

def: the forced shipping of millions of Africans across the Atlantic to be sold as slaves in the Americas, 1500s to 1800s
why: It shaped the population, economies and racial history of the Americas, Africa and Europe.
ex: Historians estimate that about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships during the transatlantic slave trade.
Kwame visited a museum in Ghana that tells the story of the transatlantic slave trade.
Rosa's history class read letters from people who fought to end the transatlantic slave trade.
Britain banned its part in the transatlantic slave trade in 1807, and the United States banned importing enslaved people in 1808.

cloze.s: The terrible ocean crossing known as the Middle Passage was part of the ___.

def: a large South American state in the Andes mountains that Spanish soldiers took over in the 1500s
why: It was the largest empire in the Americas before Europeans arrived, known for its roads and mountain cities.
ex: The mountaintop city of Machu Picchu was built during the Inca Empire.
Without a written alphabet, officials of the Inca Empire kept records using knotted strings.
Runners in the Inca Empire carried messages along a vast network of mountain roads.
The capital of the Inca Empire was Cusco, a city high in the Andes of Peru.

cloze.s: Spanish forces led by Francisco Pizarro began the conquest of the ___ in 1532.

def: the Cold War contest between the United States and the Soviet Union to be first to reach major goals in space
why: It produced the first satellite, the first human in orbit and the first Moon landing, and pushed technology forward.
ex: The space race began in 1957 when the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite.
Many people say the United States won the space race when Apollo 11 landed on the Moon in 1969.
Leila's grandfather remembers watching rocket launches on a black-and-white TV during the space race.
The space race pushed both nations to pour money into rockets, satellites and science education.

cloze.s: Yuri Gagarin's flight in 1961, the first by a human into space, was a major Soviet win in the ___.

def: a guarded barrier that split the German city into East and West from 1961 to 1989
why: It was the clearest symbol of the Cold War division of Europe, and its fall led to German reunification.
ex: East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop its citizens from fleeing to the West.
Crowds celebrated and chipped away pieces of the Berlin Wall after it opened in November 1989.
Pieces of the Berlin Wall are now on display in museums around the world.
Many East Germans risked their lives trying to cross the Berlin Wall to reach the West.

cloze.s: When the ___ came down in 1989, families split for decades were finally able to cross freely.

def: a series of giant ocean waves usually caused by an earthquake or other sudden shift under the sea
why: They can flood coasts within minutes, so coastal towns post evacuation routes and warning sirens.
ex: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami struck coastlines in more than a dozen countries.
When the warning siren sounded, Yuki's family drove to higher ground in case a tsunami followed the earthquake.
Beaches in Hawaii have signs showing tsunami evacuation routes to higher ground.
The 2011 tsunami in Japan flooded towns far inland and damaged a nuclear power plant.

cloze.s: Minutes after the undersea earthquake, the sea pulled back from the beach, a warning sign that a(n) ___ was coming.

note: A Japanese word meaning “harbor wave.” Scientists avoid “tidal wave,” since these waves have nothing to do with tides.

def: a piece of land almost surrounded by water but connected to a larger land area on one side
why: Many famous places, such as Florida, Italy and Korea, take this shape, which shapes their climate and trade.
ex: Florida is a peninsula, with the Atlantic on one side and the Gulf of Mexico on the other.
Malik's family rented a cabin on a narrow peninsula, so they could see the lake from three sides.
Because the town is on a peninsula, the only road out runs along a thin strip of land joining it to the mainland.
Korea sits on a peninsula, bordered by sea on three sides and joined to the mainland in the north.

cloze.s: Italy is a boot-shaped ___ that juts out into the Mediterranean Sea.

note: An island is fully surrounded by water; this landform stays joined to the mainland.

def: a group or chain of islands close together in a sea or ocean
why: Whole nations, such as Indonesia, Japan and the Philippines, are spread across island groups like these.
ex: Indonesia, the world's largest island country, is an archipelago of thousands of islands.
Priya spent her vacation sailing between the small islands of a Greek archipelago.
Hawaii is an archipelago of eight main islands and many smaller ones.
The ferry hopped from island to island across the archipelago, stopping at a new harbor each morning.

cloze.s: The Philippines is a(n) ___ of more than 7,000 islands in the western Pacific.

def: the north–south line on maps that runs through London and is set as zero degrees for measuring east and west
why: It is the starting line for longitude and the reference point for the world's time zones.
ex: At the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, Hannah stood with one foot on each side of the prime meridian.
Places east of the prime meridian have east longitudes, and places west have west longitudes.
Heading south from England, the prime meridian crosses France, Spain and several countries in West Africa.
Ben's world map showed the prime meridian as a line running from the North Pole down through Greenwich in London.

cloze.s: Just as the equator is zero degrees of latitude, the ___ is zero degrees of longitude.

note: Chosen at an international conference in 1884.

def: the endless journey of water from land and sea up into the air, then back down as rain or snow
why: It delivers the fresh water that fills rivers, lakes and wells and drives the weather.
ex: In the water cycle, the sun heats lakes and oceans, and the rising vapor forms clouds.
Kwame's science project showed the water cycle with a sealed jar, a little water and a lamp.
Puddles drying in the sun are part of the water cycle, as the water rises into the air as vapor.
Amara's teacher said the water in a glass may once have fallen as rain, thanks to the water cycle.

cloze.s: Evaporation, condensation and rain are the main stages of the ___.

def: a stream or river that flows into a larger river instead of straight into the sea or a lake
why: Knowing how rivers join helps explain floods, water supply and how pollution travels downstream.
ex: The Missouri River is a tributary of the Mississippi, joining it near St. Louis.
After heavy rain, every small tributary poured muddy water into the main river and it overflowed.
Leila's kayak trip started on a small tributary and ended where it joined the wide river.
The Amazon River is fed by more than a thousand tributaries.

cloze.s: The creek behind Olga's house is a(n) ___ that feeds into the Ohio River.

def: an energy source such as coal, oil or natural gas, formed underground over millions of years from ancient plants and animals
why: Burning these fuels powers much of the world but releases the carbon dioxide that drives climate change.
ex: Gasoline is made from oil, a fossil fuel pumped from deep underground.
The city plans to replace its fossil fuel power plants with wind and solar farms.
Burning a fossil fuel like coal releases carbon dioxide into the air.
Aisha's family replaced their natural gas furnace with an electric heat pump to stop burning fossil fuel at home.

cloze.s: Coal is a(n) ___, made from swamp plants buried and pressed for millions of years.

note: It is called nonrenewable because people use it far faster than nature can replace it.

def: a system in which a king or queen is head of state but laws and elected leaders limit their power
why: Countries such as the United Kingdom, Japan, Sweden and Canada are governed this way.
ex: In a constitutional monarchy like Sweden, the king has mainly ceremonial duties.
Diego explained that Britain is a constitutional monarchy, so the prime minister, not the king, runs the government.
Spain became a constitutional monarchy under its 1978 constitution, which limited the king's role.
In a constitutional monarchy, the queen may open parliament, but elected lawmakers write the laws.

cloze.s: Japan has an emperor, but elected lawmakers make the decisions, which makes it a(n) ___.

def: the legal rule that a person accused of a crime is treated as not guilty unless the prosecution proves guilt
why: It is a basic protection in fair trials, putting the burden of proof on the government, not the accused.
ex: The judge reminded jurors that the presumption of innocence meant the defendant did not have to prove anything.
Because of the presumption of innocence, news reports describe arrested people as suspects, not criminals.
Nadia's civics teacher said the presumption of innocence puts the burden of proof on prosecutors, not on the accused.
Kai worried that online crowds ignore the presumption of innocence by condemning people before any trial.

cloze.s: “Innocent until proven guilty” is the everyday way of describing the ___.

def: a serious crime, such as robbery or murder, that in the US can be punished by more than a year in prison
why: A conviction for one can bring long prison terms and can cost a person rights such as owning a gun.
ex: Burglary is usually a felony, while shoplifting a candy bar is usually a less serious crime.
Fatima's law class compared how different states punish a felony like burglary.
Lying under oath in court, called perjury, is a felony in many states.
Under federal law, a person convicted of a felony generally loses the right to own a gun.

cloze.s: A minor crime is a misdemeanor, but armed robbery is a(n) ___ that can bring years in prison.

note: A misdemeanor is a less serious crime, usually punished by fines or up to a year in jail.

def: an official count of all the people in a country, usually with facts about their ages, homes and households
why: In the US it happens every ten years and decides how many House seats each state gets and how funding is shared.
ex: The US Constitution requires a census every ten years.
Liam filled out the census form online, listing everyone who lived in his apartment.
A census worker knocked on Wei's door because his household had not returned its form.
Families researching their ancestors often look through old census records to see where relatives lived.

cloze.s: After the 2020 ___, some states gained seats in Congress because their populations had grown.

def: a written direction from a president or governor telling government agencies how to act, without a new law
why: It lets leaders act quickly, but courts can block one, and a later leader can cancel it.
ex: The president signed an executive order directing federal agencies to buy more electric vehicles.
Because it was only an executive order, the next governor was able to reverse the policy on day one.
In 1948, President Truman signed an executive order calling for the desegregation of the U.S. armed forces.
The governor's executive order closed state offices for the day because of the snowstorm.

cloze.s: Rather than wait for lawmakers to pass a bill, the president issued a(n) ___ to change how the agency worked.

note: It must rely on powers the leader already has under the constitution or existing laws.

def: the person or group who starts a lawsuit in court against someone else
why: In civil cases this side must prove its claims, usually by showing they are more likely true than not.
ex: The plaintiff claimed the landlord had kept her deposit without any reason.
In the case, the plaintiff was a small bakery suing a supplier over spoiled flour.
As the plaintiff, the delivery driver had to prove that the company caused his injury.
The plaintiff asked the court for $50,000 to cover repairs after the builder's new roof leaked.

cloze.s: Jamal sued his former employer for unpaid wages, so he was the ___ in the case.

note: The side being sued, or charged with a crime, is the defendant.

def: the warnings US police must give people in custody before questioning, such as that they may stay silent and have a lawyer
why: If police skip the warning, what a suspect says in questioning may not be usable in court.
ex: The officer read the man his Miranda rights before asking him any questions.
In crime shows, the line “You have the right to remain silent” comes from the Miranda rights.
Before the detective questioned the teenager at the station, she explained his Miranda rights in plain words.
Because the woman was not under arrest and was free to leave, officers did not have to give her Miranda rights.

cloze.s: The confession was thrown out because detectives never told the suspect his ___.

note: Named after the 1966 Supreme Court case Miranda v. Arizona.

def: the price of one country's money measured in another country's money
why: It affects the cost of travel, imported goods and how well a country's products sell abroad.
ex: Before her trip to Mexico, Maria checked the exchange rate to see how many pesos she would get for each dollar.
A weaker exchange rate makes a country's exports cheaper for foreign buyers.
Hannah waited to buy euros for her trip until the exchange rate improved.
Thanks to a favorable exchange rate, Kwame's vacation in Japan cost less than he expected.

cloze.s: If the ___ is 1.10 dollars to the euro, a 100-euro hotel room costs about 110 dollars.

def: a share of a company's profits paid out to the people who own its stock
why: Many investors and retirees rely on these regular payments as income.
ex: Wei's shares in the power company pay a dividend every three months.
When profits fell, the company cut its dividend, and some investors sold their shares.
Some retirees choose stocks that pay a steady dividend to help cover their living expenses.
Aisha reinvests every dividend she receives to buy more shares of the same company.
