cloze.s: The company earned record profits, so it raised the ___ it pays to each shareholder.

note: Companies are not required to pay them; many growing firms keep their profits instead. In math, the same word names the number being divided.

def: a long period when stock prices keep rising and investors feel confident
why: News reports use the term to describe the mood of the market, often after prices rise 20% from a low.
ex: During the long bull market, Kwame's retirement savings grew every year.
Analysts said the bull market would end if company profits began to fall.
Investors felt cheerful during the bull market, as stock prices climbed month after month.
Even in a bull market, the shares of some individual companies still lose value.

cloze.s: Prices rose steadily for years in a(n) ___, and more first-time investors bought stocks.

note: A common way to remember it: a bull thrusts its horns up.

def: a period when stock prices fall sharply, commonly 20% or more from a recent high, and investors feel worried
why: These downturns test investors' patience and often come with or before economic slowdowns.
ex: When the market fell 25% from its peak, reporters said stocks had entered a bear market.
Hannah kept investing a little each month through the bear market instead of selling in a panic.
During the bear market of 2008, many people watched their retirement savings shrink.
Some investors see a bear market as a chance to buy good stocks at lower prices.

cloze.s: After stocks dropped more than 20% in a few months, experts declared a(n) ___.

note: A common way to remember it: a bear swipes its paws down.

def: the total value of everything a person or company owns minus everything they owe
why: It is a basic measure of financial health used by banks, planners and people tracking their own progress.
ex: Tomás owns a house worth $300,000 but owes $200,000 on it, so it adds $100,000 to his net worth.
By saving part of every paycheck, Aisha raised her net worth even though her salary stayed the same.
Fresh out of college with big student loans, Ana had a negative net worth for several years.
The magazine ranks business owners by net worth, adding up what they own and subtracting their debts.

cloze.s: If you own $50,000 in savings but owe $60,000 in loans, your ___ is negative $10,000.

note: Different from income, which is what you earn over time.

def: a system in which the government takes a larger share of income from people who earn more
why: The US federal income tax works this way, with higher rates on each higher band of income.
ex: Under a progressive tax, a doctor pays a higher share of income than a part-time cashier.
Priya learned that with a progressive tax, only the income above each cutoff is taxed at the higher rate.
Several states have a progressive tax on income, while others charge everyone the same flat rate.
The US federal income tax is a progressive tax, with rates rising in steps as income goes up.

cloze.s: In a(n) ___, the tax rate climbs as income rises, so high earners pay a bigger percentage.

note: A flat tax charges everyone the same rate; a regressive tax takes a larger share from lower earners.

def: the share of people in the workforce who have no job but are actively looking for one
why: It is one of the most watched signs of how healthy an economy is.
ex: When the factory closed, the town's unemployment rate jumped to 9%.
A low unemployment rate usually means employers must raise pay to attract workers.
Every month, the US government reports the unemployment rate based on a large survey of households.
Nadia's town saw its unemployment rate fall after a new hospital opened and hired hundreds of workers.

cloze.s: Retirees and full-time students who are not looking for work are not counted in the ___.

note: People who have stopped looking for work are left out, so the number can understate how many people lack jobs.

def: the total amount of money a country's central government owes from all its past borrowing
why: Interest on it takes up part of the government budget, and its size is a frequent topic in the news.
ex: Every year that the government spends more than it collects, the national debt grows.
Liam's economics teacher explained that selling government bonds is how the country borrows the money that makes up the national debt.
News reports often compare the national debt to the size of the whole economy to show how big a burden it is.
Part of every year's federal budget goes to paying interest on the national debt.

cloze.s: A deficit is the shortfall in a single year, while the ___ is the total piled up over many years.

note: Not the same as the deficit, which is one year's gap between spending and income.

def: the character or force in a story that works against the main character
why: Spotting who or what opposes the hero helps readers follow the main conflict of a plot.
ex: In the Harry Potter books, Lord Voldemort is the antagonist.
In some survival stories, the antagonist is not a person at all but a storm or the wilderness.
Every good mystery needs a clever antagonist who stays one step ahead of the detective.
Priya's writing teacher said a strong antagonist makes the hero's final victory feel earned.

cloze.s: The hero is the protagonist, and the villain who blocks her at every turn is the ___.

note: Not always evil; it only needs to oppose the main character's goal.

def: a figure of speech that gives human qualities or actions to animals, objects or ideas
why: Writers and poets use it to make descriptions vivid, and students learn to spot it in poems.
ex: “The wind whispered through the trees” is an example of personification.
Malik used personification in his poem, writing that the old house groaned and sighed at night.
The ad used personification, showing a cheerful toaster that “wanted” to make your breakfast.
Saying that a city never sleeps is personification, since only living things can actually sleep.

cloze.s: Saying “the sun smiled down on us” is ___, because the sun cannot really smile.

def: a hint or clue early in a story about something that will happen later
why: It builds suspense and makes endings feel earned, and readers enjoy spotting it on a second reading.
ex: The storm clouds gathering in the first chapter were foreshadowing of the tragedy to come.
Olga noticed the foreshadowing when the detective casually mentioned the locked drawer early in the film.
In the movie, a quick shot of a cracked dam is foreshadowing of the flood that comes an hour later.
Aisha loves rereading novels because she catches foreshadowing she missed the first time.

cloze.s: When a character says early on, “Nothing could go wrong on this trip,” it is often ___ that something will.

def: a word that sounds like the noise it describes, such as buzz, bang or splash
why: It adds sound to writing, and is common in poems, comics and ads.
ex: The comic book filled the fight scene with onomatopoeia like “POW!” and “CRASH!”
The children's poem uses onomatopoeia, with bees that buzz and bacon that sizzles.
Samir's toddler loves animal books full of onomatopoeia, like “moo,” “oink” and “quack.”
The sportswriter used onomatopoeia, describing the loud “thwack” of the ball leaving the bat.

cloze.s: Words like “hiss,” “splash” and “cuckoo” are examples of ___, since they copy real sounds.

note: The word comes from Greek for “making a name.”

def: a culture and music style that began in New York City in the 1970s, including rapping, record mixing, dance and street art
why: It grew into one of the most popular kinds of music and strongly influences fashion and language.
ex: Many trace hip-hop to block parties in the Bronx where DJ Kool Herc played the drum breaks of records.
Jamal's dance class teaches breaking, one of the original elements of hip-hop.
Hip-hop spread from the Bronx to cities around the world, from Paris to Seoul.
The museum's hip-hop exhibit shows graffiti art, turntables and videos of early breakdancers.

cloze.s: Rapping over beats made from old records became the heart of ___ music.

note: People often use it and “rap” to mean the same music, but hip-hop also names the wider culture.

def: a painting or drawing of objects that do not move, such as fruit, flowers, bottles or bowls
why: It is a classic subject in art classes and museums, from Dutch masters to Cézanne's apples.
ex: Paul Cézanne painted many a still life of apples and oranges on a tablecloth.
In art class, Yuki set up a still life with a vase, a lemon and a teacup to sketch.
Mateo painted a still life of sunflowers in a blue jar for his art portfolio.
The museum's Dutch gallery is full of still lifes showing lemons, oysters and silver cups on dark tables.

cloze.s: The painting showed only a bowl of pears, a jug and a folded napkin, a classic ___.

note: The plural is still lifes, not “still lives.”

def: paintings and sculptures that do not try to show real people, places or things, using shapes, colors and lines instead
why: It changed art in the 1900s and is common in museums, offices and public spaces today.
ex: Wassily Kandinsky is often called one of the first painters of abstract art.
Hannah's living room has a large piece of abstract art made of bold red and black stripes.
Kwame joked that his toddler's finger painting was abstract art, all colorful splashes and no real objects.
The museum's new room of abstract art features huge canvases covered in squares of pure color.

cloze.s: The painting had no people or objects at all, only swirls of blue and yellow, so it was ___.

note: Realistic art tries to show things as they actually look.

def: a serious play or story in which the main character suffers and usually falls to ruin or death
why: From ancient Greek theater to Shakespeare's Hamlet and Macbeth, it is one of drama's oldest forms.
ex: Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy, ending with the death of both young lovers.
Diego's drama class studied Greek tragedy, where heroes are often undone by a fatal flaw.
Samir's book club picked Macbeth, a tragedy in which ambition leads a Scottish lord to his doom.
The playwright's new tragedy ends with the proud hero losing his family, his fortune and his life.

cloze.s: Shakespeare's plays are often sorted into comedies, histories and ___, such as King Lear and Othello.

note: In everyday speech the word also means any very sad event, such as a deadly accident.

def: a way of thinking that centers on human worth, reason and achievement, rather than on religious teaching alone
why: It drove the Renaissance revival of learning and still shapes modern ideas about education and human worth.
ex: Renaissance humanism encouraged scholars to study ancient Greek and Roman writers again.
Wei describes her outlook as humanism: she believes people can lead good lives by reason and kindness.
Erasmus, a Dutch scholar of the 1500s, was a leading figure of Renaissance humanism.
The campus humanism club holds discussions about living ethically without relying on religious teachings.

cloze.s: Thinkers of the Renaissance revived interest in classical learning and human achievement, a movement called ___.

note: Renaissance humanists were mostly Christian; today the word often names a nonreligious worldview.

def: the view that whether God exists is unknown, or cannot be known
why: It is a common position in debates about religion, often confused with not believing in God at all.
ex: Thomas Huxley coined the word “agnostic” in 1869, and agnosticism soon became a common label for honest doubt about God.
Rather than claim God does or does not exist, Liam said his position was agnosticism.
Raised in a religious home, Sofia moved toward agnosticism in college, unsure whether any god exists.
Hannah's philosophy class debated whether agnosticism is a separate position or a kind of atheism.

cloze.s: The believer says God exists, the atheist says God does not, and ___ says we cannot be sure either way.

note: Different from atheism, which is not believing in any god.

def: the absence of belief in any god or gods
why: It is a widely held view in many countries and a frequent topic in discussions of religion and law.
ex: Surveys find that atheism is far more common in some countries than in others.
Fatima and her friend often discuss religion, since one is a Muslim and the other embraces atheism.
Diego's grandparents are devout Catholics, but they respect his atheism.
In his memoir, the scientist described his slow journey from religious faith to atheism.

cloze.s: While theism is belief in God, ___ is the lack of such belief.

note: Not the same as agnosticism, which says the question cannot be settled.

def: the principle that government and public institutions should be kept separate from religion
why: Debates over prayer in public schools or religious symbols in courts often turn on this principle.
ex: France's strong secularism limits religious symbols in public schools.
Supporters of secularism argue that keeping religion out of government protects people of every faith.
Under secularism, public schools may teach about many religions but do not lead students in prayer.
In debates about secularism, people ask whether city halls should display religious symbols at all.

cloze.s: Under ___, the state takes no side in religion and treats believers and nonbelievers equally.

note: It does not mean being against religion; many religious people support it.

def: openly and peacefully refusing to obey a law you believe is unfair, while accepting the punishment
why: Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. used it to win major political and social change.
ex: Henry David Thoreau wrote about civil disobedience after spending a night in jail for refusing to pay a tax.
When Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in 1955, it became a famous act of civil disobedience.
Gandhi led the Salt March in 1930 as an act of civil disobedience against Britain's salt laws in India.
The protesters practiced civil disobedience by sitting peacefully in the road and calmly accepting arrest.

cloze.s: Sitting peacefully at a whites-only lunch counter and waiting to be arrested was a form of ___.

note: It is public and nonviolent, which separates it from secret lawbreaking or riots.

def: the belief that war and violence are wrong and that conflicts should be settled peacefully
why: It shapes debates about military service, and some people refuse to fight in wars on these grounds.
ex: Because of his pacifism, Tomás chose to serve as a medic rather than carry a weapon.
Quakers are well known for their long tradition of pacifism.
In her ethics class, Rosa argued that pacifism is hardest to hold when one's own country is attacked.
His pacifism was tested when a classmate shoved him, but he calmly walked away instead of fighting back.

cloze.s: A person who refuses to fight in any war, even for their own country, holds a belief called ___.

def: the belief that each person's freedom, choices and interests matter more than the group's demands
why: It helps explain differences between cultures and shapes debates about personal freedom and community duty.
ex: Many observers see the United States as a culture of strong individualism and self-reliance.
Aisha's essay compared the individualism of her new city with the close family ties of her hometown.
The lone cowboy hero of old Westerns is a symbol of American individualism.
Diego's coach warned that too much individualism hurts a team, since players must work together to win.

cloze.s: A culture that tells people to follow their own dreams, even against family wishes, values ___.

def: a system in which property is shared by all rather than owned privately, aiming for a society without social classes
why: Inspired by Karl Marx, it became the stated goal of the ruling parties in the Soviet Union and China and a central force in the Cold War.
ex: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels set out the ideas of communism in The Communist Manifesto in 1848.
After the fall of communism in Eastern Europe, many state-owned factories were sold to private owners.
Under communism in the Soviet Union, the state owned the farms, the factories and most housing.
The museum's exhibit showed what daily life was like in East Germany under communism.

cloze.s: The Cold War was a long rivalry between capitalism, led by the United States, and ___, led by the Soviet Union.

note: In Marxist theory, socialism is often described as a stage on the way to it.

def: freedoms every person is believed to have simply by being human, which no government grants or can fairly take away
why: The idea, linked to John Locke, inspired the Declaration of Independence and modern human rights law.
ex: John Locke argued that natural rights include life, liberty and property.
The Declaration of Independence draws on natural rights when it speaks of “unalienable Rights.”
In her civics essay, Nadia explained that natural rights belong to everyone, whether or not a law lists them.
Thinkers in the 1600s and 1700s used the idea of natural rights to argue that kings could not rule without limits.

cloze.s: Because ___ come from being human, not from any law, a government cannot rightfully take them away.

note: Legal rights are those that a particular government's laws create and can change.

def: the splitting of the heavy center of an atom, such as uranium, into smaller pieces, releasing huge energy
why: It powers nuclear power plants and the first atomic bombs.
ex: The reactor heats water to steam using the energy released by nuclear fission of uranium fuel.
In physics class, Diego learned that nuclear fission splits one large nucleus into two smaller ones.
The first atomic bombs released their enormous energy through nuclear fission.
Nuclear fission produces no carbon dioxide, but it leaves radioactive waste that must be stored safely.

cloze.s: Every nuclear power plant now in commercial use makes electricity through ___, splitting uranium atoms apart.

note: Fission splits heavy atoms apart; fusion joins light atoms together. Both release energy.

def: the joining of the centers of light atoms, such as hydrogen, into a heavier atom, releasing huge energy
why: It is what makes the Sun and other stars shine, and scientists hope to use it for clean power.
ex: Deep inside the Sun, nuclear fusion turns hydrogen into helium and gives off light and heat.
Priya's lab is one of many teams trying to make nuclear fusion work as a practical source of electricity.
A hydrogen bomb gets much of its power from nuclear fusion.
Mateo's physics teacher said nuclear fusion needs temperatures of millions of degrees to force atoms together.

cloze.s: Stars shine because, in their hot cores, hydrogen atoms are pressed together into helium by ___.

note: Do not confuse with fission, which splits heavy atoms.

def: energy that is stored in an object because of its position or shape, ready to be released
why: It explains how dams, springs and roller coasters store energy and then turn it into motion.
ex: A boulder sitting at the top of a cliff has a lot of potential energy that would turn into motion if it fell.
When Yuki stretched the rubber band, she gave it potential energy that sent it flying across the room.
A heavy book on a high shelf has more potential energy than the same book lying on the floor.
As the roller coaster slowly climbed the first hill, it built up potential energy for the big drop.

cloze.s: Water held high behind a dam stores ___, which becomes motion when it rushes down through the turbines.

note: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion; this is the stored kind.

def: the tendency of an object to stay still, or keep moving the same way, unless a force acts on it
why: It is the idea behind Newton's first law and the reason seat belts save lives.
ex: When the bus braked hard, inertia kept the passengers moving forward until they grabbed the rails.
Malik pulled the tablecloth away so fast that inertia kept the dishes almost exactly in place.
Seat belts protect riders because inertia keeps their bodies moving forward when a car suddenly stops.
Rosa gave the heavy shopping cart a hard push, working against its inertia to get it rolling.

cloze.s: Because of ___, a soccer ball resting on the grass will not move until someone kicks it.

note: In everyday speech it also means a lack of energy or will to change.

def: a change in the genes of a living thing or virus, which may be harmful, helpful or harmless
why: Such changes are the raw material of evolution and the cause of some inherited diseases.
ex: A single mutation in one gene can cause a disease like sickle cell anemia.
Scientists track each new mutation in a virus to see whether it spreads more easily.
White tigers have white fur because of a mutation in a gene that controls coat color.
Most mutations in human cells are harmless, but some can lead to cancer.

cloze.s: The flu virus keeps changing, so a new ___ can make last year's vaccine less effective.

def: a method of finding out how old once-living material is by measuring how much carbon-14 is left in it
why: Archaeologists use it to date bones, wood and cloth up to about 50,000 years old.
ex: Radiocarbon dating showed that the wooden tools from the cave were roughly 9,000 years old.
Aisha explained that radiocarbon dating only works on things that were once alive, not on stone or metal.
Using radiocarbon dating on charcoal from an old fire pit, scientists estimated when people first camped there.
Radiocarbon dating can't measure the age of dinosaur fossils, because they are far too old for any carbon-14 to remain.

cloze.s: To learn the age of the ancient wooden boat, the museum sent a small sample of it for ___.

note: It cannot date dinosaur bones; they are far too old for this method.

def: a hormone the body releases in fear or stress that speeds up the heart and prepares you to react
why: It drives the fight-or-flight response, and doctors inject it to treat severe allergic reactions.
ex: Her heart pounded as adrenaline surged through her body when the car swerved toward her.
Tomás carries an adrenaline injector pen in case he has a severe allergic reaction to peanuts.
Skydivers often describe the rush of adrenaline they feel as they leap out of the plane.
When the fire alarm rang, a surge of adrenaline helped Omar carry his heavy suitcase down ten flights of stairs.

cloze.s: Right before his first big race, a rush of ___ made Liam's heart beat fast and his hands shake.

def: a natural chemical made by the body that eases pain and can create a feeling of well-being
why: It helps explain why exercise and laughter can make people feel better.
ex: Exercise raises the level of endorphins in the body, which can lift your mood.
Sofia says a good laugh with friends releases endorphins and eases her stress.
Samir's physical therapist said gentle exercise releases endorphins that can ease his back pain.
Endorphins act somewhat like pain medicine, which is why they are sometimes called the body's natural painkillers.

cloze.s: After a hard run, Olga felt calm and cheerful, partly because her body had released ___.

def: a condition in which the blood has too few healthy red blood cells to carry enough oxygen
why: It is a common cause of tiredness and weakness, and lack of iron is its most frequent cause.
ex: Fatima's blood test showed anemia, which explained why she had felt so tired for months.
Doctors often treat anemia caused by low iron with iron pills and iron-rich foods.
Before donating blood, Ben had a quick finger-prick test to make sure he did not have anemia.
Nadia's anemia left her short of breath when she climbed even one flight of stairs.

cloze.s: Her pale skin, shortness of breath and low red blood cell count all pointed to ___.

def: a substance or exposure that can cause cancer, such as tobacco smoke or strong sunlight
why: Knowing which substances cause cancer shapes health warnings, workplace safety rules and product labels.
ex: Tobacco smoke is a known carcinogen, linked to lung cancer and many other cancers.
Workers removing old insulation wear masks because asbestos is a powerful carcinogen.
Doctors urge people to wear sunscreen because ultraviolet light from the sun is a carcinogen.
The district tested the old school for radon, a natural gas that is a known carcinogen.

cloze.s: The label warned that the chemical was a known ___ that could raise the risk of cancer.

def: a sudden stop of the heart's pumping, usually from an electrical problem, causing death within minutes without help
why: Quick CPR and a defibrillator shock can save the life of someone in this emergency.
ex: A bystander started CPR right away when the runner collapsed in cardiac arrest near the finish line.
The airport keeps defibrillators on the walls so travelers in cardiac arrest can get a shock quickly.
Leila took a CPR class so she would know what to do if someone went into cardiac arrest.
Unlike a heart attack, which is a blockage of blood flow, cardiac arrest means the heart suddenly stops pumping.

cloze.s: When a person's heart suddenly stops pumping and they collapse, they are in ___ and need CPR right away.

note: Not the same as a heart attack, which is a blocked artery cutting off blood to part of the heart, though one can lead to the other.

def: a mineral, such as sodium, that carries an electric charge in body fluids and keeps nerves and muscles working
why: Losing too many through sweat, vomiting or diarrhea can cause cramps, weakness or heart rhythm problems.
ex: After the long hike in the heat, Diego drank a sports drink to replace the electrolytes he had sweated out.
The nurse checked the patient's electrolytes because very low potassium can affect the heartbeat.
During her stomach flu, Keiko sipped a drink with electrolytes to replace the salts she had lost.
The cyclist's muscle cramps were linked to low electrolyte levels after the long, hot race.

cloze.s: Sports drinks contain sodium and potassium to replace the ___ lost through heavy sweating.

def: live, helpful bacteria, eaten in foods or taken as pills, that support the healthy bacteria in your gut
why: They are found in foods like yogurt and are widely sold as supplements for digestion.
ex: Yogurt with live cultures is one of the most common sources of probiotics.
Hannah's doctor suggested a probiotic to help her stomach recover after a course of antibiotics.
Some fermented foods, such as kefir, are rich in probiotics that help balance the bacteria in your gut.
Tomás keeps his probiotic capsules in the fridge because heat can kill the live bacteria inside.

cloze.s: The yogurt label said each cup is packed with ___, live bacteria that help keep the gut healthy.

note: Antibiotics kill bacteria; this does the reverse, adding helpful ones. A few are yeasts rather than bacteria.

def: a rank showing what percent of a group scored lower; the 90th one means higher than about 90 percent
why: It is used for test scores and children's growth charts to compare one result with everyone else's.
ex: Priya's score was in the 85th percentile, so she did better than about 85 percent of test takers.
The pediatrician said the baby's height was in the 50th percentile, right in the middle for her age.
Rosa's typing speed put her in the 70th percentile of job applicants.
Ben's marathon time placed him in the 90th percentile for his age group, faster than about nine in ten men.

cloze.s: Scoring in the 99th ___ means you did better than almost everyone else who took the exam.

note: Not the same as percent correct: you could get 70 percent of answers right and still rank in the 95th.

def: an equation whose unknown is squared but raised to no higher power, as in x² + 3x + 2 = 0
why: It describes curved paths, such as a thrown ball's flight, and can have up to two answers.
ex: Because x appears squared, Malik knew he was solving a quadratic equation and might find two answers.
Engineers use a quadratic equation to describe the curved path of water shooting from a fountain.
Fatima used the quadratic formula to find both solutions to the quadratic equation on her homework.
To find a square patio's side length from its area of 50 square feet, Rosa solved the quadratic equation x² = 50.

cloze.s: Since the highest power of x in x² − 5x + 6 = 0 is two, it is called a(n) ___.

note: Its graph is a U-shaped curve called a parabola.

def: a number that tells how steep a line is: how much it rises for each step it goes across
why: It describes any steady rate of change, such as cost per hour or speed on a graph.
ex: A line that rises 2 units for every 1 unit it moves to the right has a slope of 2.
On the chart of her savings, Maria saw that the slope got steeper once she raised her monthly deposit.
Kwame's graph of his hiking distance had a slope of 3, meaning he covered 3 miles for each hour.
A line that falls as it moves to the right, like a shrinking bank balance over time, has a negative slope.

cloze.s: The flat line on the graph showed no change at all, so its ___ was zero.

note: Often described as rise over run.

def: a drawing of circles that partly cover each other, showing what groups share and what belongs to only one
why: It makes comparisons and the logic of overlapping groups easy to see at a glance.
ex: In a Venn diagram of cats and dogs, the overlap held traits both share, like fur and four legs.
Jamal drew a Venn diagram to show which students played soccer, which played music and which did both.
Before choosing a phone, Hannah drew a Venn diagram showing which features each model had and which both shared.
The math teacher shaded only the middle of the Venn diagram to show numbers that were both even and greater than 10.

cloze.s: To compare two novels, the teacher drew two overlapping circles, a(n) ___, with shared themes in the middle.

note: Named after the English logician John Venn, who described it in 1880.

def: any number, positive, negative or zero, that can be written as a fraction of two whole numbers, with the bottom not zero
why: It is the basic kind of number used for fractions and decimals that end or repeat.
ex: Because 0.75 equals three fourths, it is a rational number.
Wei showed that every whole number, like 5, is a rational number because it equals 5 divided by 1.
Since negative 2.5 can be written as -5 over 2, it counts as a rational number.
The square root of 2 is not a rational number, because no fraction of whole numbers equals it exactly.

cloze.s: The decimal 0.333... repeats forever, but it equals one third, so it is a(n) ___.

note: Numbers like pi, whose decimals never end or repeat, are irrational.

def: harmful software that locks a victim's files or computer and demands payment to unlock them
why: Attacks have shut down hospitals, schools and businesses, which is why regular backups matter.
ex: The hospital's computers were frozen for days after a ransomware attack demanded payment in cryptocurrency.
Because Sofia kept offline backups, the ransomware that hit her laptop did not cost her any files.
The school district trained teachers not to open strange email attachments that might carry ransomware.
After ransomware locked the company's payroll system, workers were paid late while experts restored the files.

cloze.s: A message popped up saying the city's files were locked and would be released only if it paid, a classic ___ attack.

note: A kind of malware; the 2017 WannaCry attack hit computers in over 150 countries.

def: a computer's short-term working memory, which holds what is in use now and is wiped when the power goes off
why: More of it lets a computer run many apps at once without slowing down.
ex: Priya's laptop slowed to a crawl with fifty browser tabs open because it ran out of RAM.
Unlike a hard drive, RAM loses everything stored in it when the computer is shut off.
Before buying a laptop for video games, Jamal checked that it had at least 16 gigabytes of RAM.
Phone makers advertise how much RAM a model has, since more of it lets the phone keep several apps open at once.

cloze.s: The video editor kept freezing, so Liam added more ___ to give the computer more short-term working memory.

note: Not the same as storage: files saved on a drive stay there after shutdown.

def: a store of copies of recently used data kept close at hand so it loads faster next time
why: Clearing it is a common fix when apps or websites show old information or act strangely.
ex: The website kept showing last week's prices until Jamal cleared his browser cache.
Phones keep a cache of images from apps so the pictures appear instantly when you reopen them.
Clearing the app's cache freed up space on Samir's phone and fixed the frozen screen.
Big websites keep a cache of their pages on servers around the world so they load quickly everywhere.

cloze.s: Pages loaded quickly the second time because the browser had saved copies of them in its ___.

note: Pronounced like cash. In everyday English it also means a hidden store of things.

def: digital money that is not issued by any government or bank and is tracked on a shared public record
why: Bitcoin, launched in 2009, was the first, and these coins are known for big swings in value.
ex: Bitcoin was the first cryptocurrency, and thousands of others have been created since.
Olga's cryptocurrency lost half its value in a month, so she decided to keep most of her savings in a bank.
Keiko keeps her cryptocurrency in a digital wallet protected by a long secret phrase.
The price of a cryptocurrency can swing wildly, sometimes rising or falling by a fifth in a single day.

cloze.s: Bitcoin is the best-known ___, a form of digital money that no central bank controls.

note: Most use a blockchain to record who owns which coins.

def: the movement of plants, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world after 1492
why: It brought potatoes and corn to Europe and horses to the Americas, but also deadly diseases like smallpox.
ex: Thanks to the Columbian Exchange, tomatoes from the Americas eventually became central to Italian cooking.
Diseases spread through the Columbian Exchange killed a vast number of Indigenous people in the Americas.
Chili peppers spread from the Americas to India and Thailand through the Columbian Exchange.
Through the Columbian Exchange, sugarcane and cattle from the Old World reshaped farming across the Americas.

cloze.s: Potatoes reached Europe and horses reached the Americas as part of the ___ that followed Columbus's voyages.

note: The term was coined by historian Alfred Crosby in 1972.

def: the 1919 peace agreement that ended World War I between Germany and the Allies, with harsh terms for Germany
why: It made Germany give up land and pay reparations, and its terms bred resentment that helped fuel World War II.
ex: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in the palace's Hall of Mirrors in June 1919.
Under the Treaty of Versailles, Germany had to accept blame for the war and pay large sums to the victors.
Many historians argue that anger over the Treaty of Versailles helped fuel the rise of the Nazis in Germany.
Olga's class debated whether the Treaty of Versailles punished Germany too harshly after World War I.

cloze.s: Signed in 1919, the ___ officially ended World War I and forced Germany to give up territory.

def: a tense 13-day conflict in October 1962 after the US found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba
why: It is often called the closest the world has come to nuclear war.
ex: During the Cuban Missile Crisis, US Navy ships blocked Soviet vessels from reaching Cuba.
The Cuban Missile Crisis ended when the Soviet Union agreed to remove its missiles from the island.
Omar's grandmother remembers how frightened her family felt watching the news during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
After the Cuban Missile Crisis, a direct hotline was set up between Washington and Moscow.

cloze.s: For thirteen days in October 1962, during the ___, the US and the Soviet Union stood on the edge of nuclear war.

note: In return, the US pledged not to invade Cuba and quietly removed its own missiles from Turkey.

def: the period from 1865 to 1877 when the US brought the South back into the Union and tried to protect freed slaves
why: It produced the 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments, but many of its gains were rolled back after it ended.
ex: During Reconstruction, formerly enslaved men voted and were elected to Congress for the first time.
Reconstruction ended in 1877 when federal troops were withdrawn from the South.
Our history teacher said the Freedmen's Bureau, which helped build schools for formerly enslaved people, was a key effort of Reconstruction.
Aisha's book club read a novel set in Georgia during Reconstruction, when the South was rejoining the Union.

cloze.s: After the Civil War, the years of ___ brought new amendments guaranteeing citizenship and voting rights.

def: the vast empire founded by Genghis Khan in 1206 that stretched across much of Asia and into Europe
why: It was the largest connected land empire in history and linked trade from China to Europe.
ex: At its peak in the 1200s, the Mongol Empire stretched from eastern Asia to Eastern Europe.
Trade along the Silk Road grew safer under the Mongol Empire, which controlled most of the route.
Riders of the Mongol Empire carried messages across Asia using a network of relay stations with fresh horses.
Samir's history class learned that the Mongol Empire eventually broke apart into several smaller states.

cloze.s: Founded by Genghis Khan, the ___ became the largest connected land empire the world has ever seen.

def: a legal order that requires a person to come to court to give evidence or to hand over documents
why: Courts and congressional committees use it to gather evidence, and ignoring one can bring a penalty.
ex: Priya received a subpoena ordering her to testify about what she saw on the night of the accident.
The committee issued a subpoena for the company's emails about the safety recall.
The landlord ignored the subpoena for his repair records and was warned he could be held in contempt of court.
The bank received a subpoena requiring it to hand over account records in the fraud case.

cloze.s: The witness did not want to appear in court, but the ___ legally required her to testify.

note: Pronounced suh-PEE-nuh. It can also be a verb: to subpoena a witness.

def: a deal in which a person accused of a crime admits guilt, often to a lesser charge, for a lighter sentence
why: Most criminal cases in the United States end this way instead of going to trial.
ex: Rather than risk a long trial, the defendant accepted a plea bargain and pleaded guilty to a lesser charge.
The prosecutor offered a plea bargain that would cut the sentence in half if he admitted the theft.
Facing strong video evidence, the driver's lawyer advised him to take a plea bargain and avoid a jury.
Most criminal convictions in the United States come from plea bargains, not jury verdicts.

cloze.s: Instead of going to trial, the accused man took a(n) ___, pleading guilty in exchange for a shorter sentence.

def: a group of citizens who meet in private to decide whether there is enough evidence to formally charge someone with a crime
why: The US Constitution requires one before a person can be tried for a serious federal crime.
ex: After hearing weeks of testimony in secret, the grand jury voted to charge the former mayor with fraud.
A grand jury does not decide guilt; it only decides whether a case should go to trial.
Mateo received a letter calling him to serve on a grand jury for three months.
Unlike a trial jury, a grand jury usually hears only the prosecutor's side of the case.

cloze.s: Prosecutors presented their evidence in a closed room to the ___, which then voted to bring charges.

note: A trial jury, which decides guilt or innocence, is sometimes called a petit jury.

def: the act of making false statements of fact about someone that harm their good name
why: People can sue over it, though in the US true statements and honest opinions are protected.
ex: The chef sued the website for defamation after it falsely claimed her restaurant had been shut down for rats.
Calling a movie boring is opinion, not defamation, because it is not a false statement of fact.
Before publishing the story, the editor checked every claim to avoid a lawsuit for defamation.
Leila deleted her angry post about the mechanic, worried that its untrue claims could count as defamation.

cloze.s: He sued the newspaper for ___, saying its false story about him had ruined his business.

note: Written defamation is called libel; spoken defamation is called slander.

def: a formal written charge that a person has committed a serious crime, usually issued by a grand jury
why: It starts a criminal case against someone, but it is not a finding of guilt.
ex: The indictment accused the three executives of stealing millions from their own company.
After the indictment, the businessman pleaded not guilty and the case was set for trial.
The newspaper published the full indictment, which listed twelve charges against the former official.
An indictment is only an accusation, so the defendant is still presumed innocent until proven guilty.

cloze.s: The grand jury returned a(n) ___, formally charging the official with bribery.

note: Pronounced in-DITE-ment; the c is silent. In everyday speech it can also mean a strong sign that something is wrong.

def: a vote in which a party's supporters choose which candidate will represent that party in the main election
why: In the US, these early contests narrow the field of candidates before the general election.
ex: Five candidates ran in the party's primary election, but only the winner made it onto the November ballot.
Hannah registered with a party so she could vote in its primary election.
Turnout in the spring primary election was low, so a small number of voters chose the party's nominee.
Diego volunteered for a mayoral candidate who lost the primary election and never reached the general election ballot.

cloze.s: Before facing the other party in November, each candidate first had to win their own party's ___.

def: the work of trying to persuade the people who make laws, or other officials, to support or block certain policies
why: Companies, unions and advocacy groups all do it; in the US it is legal, and paid lobbyists must usually report their work publicly.
ex: The farmers' association spent months lobbying state legislators to lower taxes on fuel.
Federal law requires paid lobbying of Congress to be reported in public records.
A group of parents met with the mayor as part of their lobbying for a new crosswalk near the school.
Students traveled to the state capitol for a day of lobbying in support of more school funding.

cloze.s: The tech companies hired former staffers for ___, sending them to meet senators and push for weaker rules.

note: The name comes from people waiting in the lobbies of lawmaking buildings to speak with members.

def: the profit made by selling something you own, such as stock or property, for more than you paid
why: In the US they are taxed, often at lower rates when the asset was held for more than a year.
ex: Liam bought the shares for $1,000 and sold them for $1,500, so he had $500 in capital gains.
When Fatima sold her rental house, she had to pay tax on the capital gains.
Rosa held her stock for more than a year, since long-term capital gains are taxed at a lower rate in the US.
The artist sold a painting she had bought cheaply years ago, and her capital gains paid for a new studio.

cloze.s: Selling the land for twice what she had paid left Aisha with large ___ to report on her taxes.

def: a general drop in prices across an economy over time, so money buys more than before
why: It sounds good but can be harmful, since people delay buying and debts become harder to repay.
ex: During the Great Depression, deflation pushed prices down sharply, making debts much harder to pay off.
Japan struggled with mild deflation for years, as shoppers waited for prices to drop even further.
During deflation, the same cart of groceries might cost less next year than it does today.
Central banks fear deflation because falling prices can lead to lower wages and fewer jobs.

cloze.s: Prices kept falling year after year, and economists worried this ___ would make people delay buying.

note: Not the same as disinflation, which means prices are still rising, just more slowly.

def: the gap when a country buys more goods and services from other countries than it sells to them
why: It comes up often in news and political debates about jobs, tariffs and trade deals.
ex: The country ran a trade deficit because it bought far more cars and phones from abroad than it sold.
Economists disagree about how much a trade deficit actually harms an economy.
Because the island imports most of its food and fuel but exports little, it runs a large trade deficit.
The evening news reported that the trade deficit narrowed last month as exports of airplanes rose.

cloze.s: Imports were worth much more than exports last year, so the nation had a large ___.

def: something valuable, such as a house or car, that a borrower agrees to give up if a loan goes unpaid
why: It lowers the risk for lenders, which is why loans backed by it usually have lower interest rates.
ex: The bank agreed to the business loan only after Jamal offered his delivery truck as collateral.
In a mortgage, the house itself serves as collateral for the loan.
Mateo used his savings account as collateral to get a small loan and build his credit.
The pawnshop holds a customer's guitar as collateral until the loan is repaid.

cloze.s: If Malik misses too many car payments, the lender can take the car, which he put up as ___.

note: Collateral damage is a different phrase, meaning harm to people or things that were not the target.

def: a private investment fund for wealthy people and large institutions that uses risky or complex ways to try to make money
why: These funds manage huge sums, face lighter rules than ordinary funds and usually charge high fees.
ex: The hedge fund made a fortune by betting that the company's stock would fall.
Most ordinary savers cannot join a hedge fund, since these funds are open only to wealthy investors and require large minimums.
After years as a trader, Ethan left the bank to start his own hedge fund.
Some university endowments put part of their money into a hedge fund to try for higher returns.

cloze.s: Only very wealthy investors could put money in the ___, which made big bets using borrowed money.

note: Despite the name, many do not hedge, or protect against, risk much at all.

def: a line on maps, roughly along 180 degrees longitude in the Pacific, where the calendar date changes by one day
why: Travelers crossing it westward skip ahead a day, and those crossing eastward repeat one.
ex: Flying from Los Angeles to Tokyo, Wei crossed the International Date Line and lost a whole day.
The International Date Line zigzags around some island nations so that each country keeps a single date.
Samoa moved to the other side of the International Date Line in 2011, skipping a whole day on its calendar.
Sailing east across the International Date Line, the cruise passengers lived through Sunday twice.

cloze.s: When the ship sailed west across the ___, the calendar jumped from Monday to Tuesday.

def: a warm, open land of grass with scattered trees and a long dry season, found mainly in Africa, Australia and South America
why: It supports famous herds of grazing animals, such as zebras and wildebeest in East Africa.
ex: Lions hunt zebras and antelope across the open savanna of the Serengeti.
During the dry season, the grass of the savanna turns brown and many animals travel in search of water.
On their safari in Kenya, Liam and Grace watched elephants cross the dry savanna at sunset.
Northern Australia's tropical savanna gets heavy summer rain and then months with almost none.

cloze.s: Giraffes eat from the few tall acacia trees that dot the grassy African ___.

note: Also spelled savannah.

def: a long, narrow arm of the sea between steep cliffs, carved out long ago by a huge, slow-moving river of ice
why: They are famous features of the coasts of Norway, New Zealand, Chile and Alaska.
ex: The cruise ship sailed slowly into the fjord, with waterfalls pouring down the cliffs on both sides.
Norway's coast is cut by hundreds of fjords left behind by glaciers in the last Ice Age.
Amara took a kayak tour of an Alaskan fjord and watched seals resting on floating ice.
New Zealand's Milford Sound is actually a fjord, carved by glaciers rather than by a river.

cloze.s: The ferry glided through a narrow ___, a deep inlet of the sea walled in by tall rock cliffs.

note: The word comes from Norwegian and is pronounced fee-ORD.

def: a very large natural area, such as a desert or tropical forest, with its own climate, plants and animals
why: Scientists use this idea to group the world's living environments and track how they change.
ex: The tundra is a cold biome where few trees grow and the ground below the surface stays frozen.
Malik's class built models of each biome, from tropical rainforest to hot desert.
The grassland biome of the American prairie once supported huge herds of bison.
Hiking up the mountain, Ethan passed from one biome to another, from forest into treeless alpine tundra.

cloze.s: Each ___ on Earth, from desert to grassland, has its own typical climate, plants and animals.

note: A biome is larger than an ecosystem and can contain many of them.

def: the process by which once-useful dry land turns into desert because of drought, poor farming or cutting down trees
why: It threatens the food and water supply of millions of people in dry regions such as Africa's Sahel.
ex: Planting trees along the edge of the Sahara is one way countries are fighting desertification.
Too many goats grazing the hills sped up the desertification of the valley.
Ben's report showed how desertification forces herders to move as their grazing land dries up.
Scientists use satellite photos to track desertification as grassland gives way to bare sand.

cloze.s: Years of drought and overgrazing turned the farmland into sand, a clear case of ___.

def: the high Rocky Mountain ridge that separates rivers flowing to the Pacific from those flowing east toward the Atlantic and Arctic
why: It decides which way the water of much of North America drains, and many hikers follow its trail.
ex: In Colorado, rain falling on the east side of the Continental Divide eventually flows to the Gulf of Mexico.
Tomás drove over the Continental Divide at a high mountain pass in Colorado.
Hikers on the Continental Divide Trail follow the mountain ridge all the way from Mexico to Canada.
Water managers built tunnels under the Continental Divide to send western snowmelt to cities like Denver.

cloze.s: Rivers west of the ___ in the Rockies drain toward the Pacific Ocean, while those east of it head the other way.

note: Any ridge that splits a continent's drainage can be called a continental divide; the Rocky Mountain one is the best known.

def: a situation in a story where the audience knows something important that a character does not
why: Writers use it to build tension, suspense or humor, as in Romeo and Juliet.
ex: The audience gasps in Romeo and Juliet because, through dramatic irony, they know Juliet is only sleeping.
In horror movies, dramatic irony builds fear as viewers see the monster behind the door before the hero does.
Readers feel dramatic irony when they know the letter is fake, yet the hero trusts it completely.
In the sitcom, dramatic irony makes us laugh because we can see the boss standing behind Mateo as he complains.

cloze.s: Viewers know the birthday guest is hiding in the closet but the character does not, an example of ___.

def: poetry that does not follow a fixed pattern of rhyme or regular beat
why: It became a major form of modern poetry, used famously by Walt Whitman in Leaves of Grass.
ex: Walt Whitman's long, flowing lines helped make free verse popular in American poetry.
Jamal prefers writing free verse because he does not have to force his lines to rhyme.
Keiko's teacher let students write in free verse, so they could focus on images instead of rhymes.
Most of the songs on the radio rhyme, but the poems in Omar's new book are all free verse.

cloze.s: Her poems have no rhyme and no steady rhythm; she writes only in ___.

note: Not the same as blank verse, which does not rhyme but keeps a regular beat.

def: a painting made on a wall or ceiling while its plaster is still wet, so the colors set into it
why: Many of the greatest works of the Renaissance, such as the Sistine Chapel ceiling, were painted this way.
ex: Michelangelo painted the fresco on the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512.
Hannah stood in the old church for an hour, studying the fading fresco above the altar.
Restorers spent years cleaning the fresco, removing centuries of candle smoke from the chapel wall.
Diego Rivera painted a famous fresco of auto workers on the walls of the Detroit Institute of Arts.

cloze.s: The artist had to work fast on the ___, painting each section of the wall before the plaster dried.

note: From the Italian word for fresh.

def: a style of building from medieval Europe with pointed arches, tall towers and huge stained-glass windows
why: It produced famous cathedrals such as Notre-Dame in Paris and Chartres, built roughly from the 1100s to the 1500s.
ex: Notre-Dame in Paris is a famous example of Gothic architecture, with pointed arches and a great rose window.
Builders of Gothic architecture used outside supports called flying buttresses so walls could hold more glass.
Leila's tour of France included Chartres Cathedral, a masterpiece of Gothic architecture.
Many American universities copied Gothic architecture for their libraries and chapels in the early 1900s.

cloze.s: With its pointed arches, soaring height and stained-glass windows, the cathedral is a classic example of ___.

note: Different from goth, the modern music and fashion style.

def: an art movement of the 1950s and 1960s that used images from ads, comics and everyday products
why: Artists like Andy Warhol and Roy Lichtenstein used it to blur the line between fine art and popular culture.
ex: Andy Warhol's paintings of Campbell's soup cans are among the most famous works of pop art.
Roy Lichtenstein's huge comic-strip paintings made pop art instantly recognizable.
The museum's pop art show filled a room with giant paintings of hamburgers, comic heroes and cereal boxes.
The café's walls were covered in pop art, with bright screen-printed portraits of movie stars and soda bottles.

cloze.s: Turning soup cans and comic strips into gallery paintings was the bold idea behind ___.

def: a piece of classical music for one instrument, or one instrument with piano, usually in several parts
why: It is a key form in classical music, with famous examples by Mozart and Beethoven.
ex: Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata is one of the most famous pieces ever written for piano.
For her recital, Olga played a violin sonata with her teacher on the piano.
Kwame practiced the slow middle movement of the sonata every evening before his music school audition.
Mozart wrote many piano sonatas, which piano students around the world still learn today.

cloze.s: The pianist performed a Mozart ___, a work in three parts written for solo piano.

note: A symphony is a similar large work, but for a full orchestra.

def: a passionate style of song, guitar music and dance from southern Spain, with stamping feet and sharp hand claps
why: It is closely tied to the Romani people of Andalusia and is on UNESCO's list of the world's intangible cultural heritage.
ex: In Seville, Sofia watched a flamenco dancer stamp out fast rhythms while a guitarist played.
Flamenco combines singing, guitar playing, dance and sharp rhythmic hand clapping.
Ethan's guitar teacher showed him the fast strumming patterns used in flamenco.
UNESCO lists flamenco as part of the world's cultural heritage.

cloze.s: The dancer's heels struck the floor in quick bursts as the guitarist played a fiery Spanish ___.

def: a famous puzzle asking whether you should send an out-of-control train car onto another track, killing one person instead of five
why: It is used to test moral ideas and now appears in debates about self-driving cars.
ex: The trolley problem forces students to ask whether causing one death to prevent five is right.
Engineers designing self-driving cars face a version of the trolley problem when planning for crashes.
In Professor Ahmed's ethics class, most students said they would pull the lever in the trolley problem.
One version of the trolley problem asks whether you would push a stranger off a footbridge to stop the runaway car.

cloze.s: Should you pull a lever to send the runaway tram toward one person instead of five? That is the ___.

note: Philippa Foot introduced it in 1967; Judith Jarvis Thomson gave it its name.

def: Aristotle's idea that a virtue is the balanced middle point between two extremes, too much and too little
why: It shapes ideas of moderation in ethics; courage, for example, lies between cowardice and recklessness.
ex: Following the golden mean, Aristotle said generosity lies between being stingy and wasting money.
Priya applies the golden mean to work, putting in steady effort without slacking off or burning herself out.
At the buffet, Ben aimed for the golden mean, eating neither too much nor too little.
Following the golden mean, the coach wanted her players confident but not arrogant, and modest but not timid.

cloze.s: Aristotle taught that courage is the ___, the balanced point between cowardice and recklessness.

note: In math, golden mean is also another name for the golden ratio, about 1.618; that is a different idea.

def: the debate over how much people are shaped by the genes they are born with versus how they are raised and live
why: It comes up in talk about intelligence, personality and health; most scientists now say both matter.
ex: Studies of twins raised apart are a classic way to explore nature versus nurture.
Whether musical talent comes from genes or practice is a typical nature versus nurture question.
Leila thought about nature versus nurture when her adopted son turned out to love cooking just as she does.
The documentary on nature versus nurture asked whether shyness comes from genes or from childhood experiences.

cloze.s: The twins grew up in different homes, so researchers used them to study the question of ___.

note: Francis Galton popularized the pairing of nature and nurture in the 1870s.

def: the argument that it is smarter to believe in God, since you lose little if wrong but gain everything if right
why: It is a famous argument from the French thinker Blaise Pascal about choosing under uncertainty.
ex: Pascal's wager treats belief in God like a bet with a small cost and a huge possible reward.
Critics of Pascal's wager ask which of the world's many religions a person should bet on.
Samir joked that he attends holiday services because of Pascal's wager, just in case.
Blaise Pascal, a French mathematician, set out Pascal's wager in notes that were published after his death.

cloze.s: "If God exists you gain everything, and if not you lose little" is the core of ___.

note: It appears in Pascal's notes published after his death as the Pensées.

def: caring about the well-being of others and acting to help them, even at a cost to yourself
why: Thinkers and scientists debate whether truly selfless behavior exists and how it could have evolved.
ex: Donating a kidney to a stranger is a striking act of altruism.
Biologists study altruism in animals, such as birds that give warning calls that put themselves at risk.
Leila showed real altruism when she gave up her seat on the last flight so a stranger could get home to a sick child.
The firefighters' altruism was clear when they spent their day off repairing an elderly neighbor's roof.

cloze.s: Out of pure ___, Diego spent his vacation rebuilding houses for families he had never met.

def: the way one cell divides to form two new cells that each have the same full set of chromosomes
why: It is how the body grows, heals cuts and replaces worn-out cells.
ex: When Diego scraped his knee, skin cells near the wound began dividing by mitosis to close the gap.
Under the microscope, the students watched an onion root cell go through mitosis and split into two.
A fertilized egg grows into a baby through countless rounds of mitosis.
Cancer develops when cells keep dividing by mitosis without the body's normal controls.

cloze.s: Each time a skin cell copies its chromosomes and splits into two identical cells, it is going through ___.

note: Often confused with meiosis, which makes egg and sperm cells with half the usual chromosomes.

def: the kind of cell division that makes egg and sperm cells, each with half the usual number of chromosomes
why: It explains why children inherit a mix of traits from both parents and why brothers and sisters differ.
ex: Because of meiosis, each sperm cell carries a different shuffle of the father's genes.
Hannah's biology teacher explained that meiosis halves the chromosome number so a fertilized egg ends up with the right total.
A mistake during meiosis can give an egg an extra chromosome, the cause of most cases of Down syndrome.
In meiosis, one cell divides twice, ending with four cells that each carry half the usual chromosomes.

cloze.s: Egg and sperm cells end up with only 23 chromosomes each because they are formed by ___.

note: Not the same as mitosis, which makes two identical cells with the full set of chromosomes.

def: a planet outside our solar system, usually one that circles a star other than our Sun
why: Thousands have been found, and scientists study them to learn how planets form and whether life could exist elsewhere.
ex: Astronomers spotted the exoplanet by noticing that its star dimmed slightly every time the planet passed in front of it.
Yuki's science club read about an exoplanet that may be the right distance from its star to hold liquid water.
The first exoplanet found circling a Sun-like star was announced in 1995.
Kwame's daughter wrote a story about astronauts landing on a rocky exoplanet with two suns.

cloze.s: The space telescope found a(n) ___ circling a small red star about 40 light-years away from our solar system.

def: the rule in physics that energy is never made or destroyed but only changes from one form to another
why: It explains why no machine can run forever without a power source and is used to solve countless physics problems.
ex: A roller coaster shows conservation of energy as height turns into speed on the way down and back into height on the next hill.
The engineer rejected the 'free energy' gadget because it broke the law of conservation of energy.
Because of conservation of energy, a dropped ball never bounces higher than where it started, since some energy turns into heat and sound.
In a power plant, the chemical energy in fuel becomes heat and then electricity, an example of conservation of energy.

cloze.s: A machine that keeps running forever with no fuel is impossible, because it would break the law of ___.

note: In physics this is a law of nature, not advice about saving electricity at home.

def: a link between two atoms that holds them together because they share one or more pairs of electrons
why: It holds together water, sugar, DNA and most of the molecules in living things.
ex: In a water molecule, each hydrogen atom is joined to the oxygen atom by a covalent bond.
Malik's chemistry quiz asked him to draw the covalent bond between two hydrogen atoms as a single line.
Diamond is so hard because each carbon atom is held to four others by a strong covalent bond.
Unlike table salt, where one atom gives an electron to another, the atoms in sugar are joined by covalent bonds.

cloze.s: When two atoms hold on to each other by sharing electrons rather than giving them away, they form a(n) ___.

note: In an ionic bond, by contrast, one atom gives electrons to another, as in table salt.

def: one of the different versions of the same gene, such as the versions that lead to different blood types
why: It explains how traits are passed down and why some traits can skip a generation.
ex: Sofia carries one allele for sickle cell disease and one typical allele, so she has sickle cell trait but not the disease.
Two parents with normal hearing can both carry a recessive allele linked to deafness and pass it to a child.
A dominant allele can hide a recessive one, so a parent may pass on a trait they never show.
Orange fur in cats comes from a particular allele of a coat-color gene on the X chromosome.

cloze.s: Each person inherits one ___ of the blood-type gene from each parent, which together decide whether the blood is type A, B, AB or O.

note: A gene is the general instruction; an allele is one particular version of it.

def: a hormone made by glands above the kidneys that rises during stress and helps control blood sugar and energy
why: Long-lasting high levels are linked to poor sleep, weight gain and weaker defenses against illness.
ex: The doctor explained that cortisol normally peaks in the morning and falls during the day.
During exam week, Jamal felt wired and couldn't sleep, which his coach blamed partly on high cortisol.
Weeks of overwork and poor sleep left Wei's cortisol levels high, so her doctor suggested ways to manage stress.
Steroid medicines like prednisone act much like cortisol, the body's natural hormone that calms swelling.

cloze.s: Often called the stress hormone, ___ floods the blood when we feel threatened and raises blood sugar for quick energy.

note: Adrenaline acts within seconds; this hormone works more slowly and lasts longer.

def: a life-threatening reaction in which the body's response to an infection starts damaging its own organs
why: It is a medical emergency, and fast treatment with antibiotics and fluids greatly improves survival.
ex: What began as a small kidney infection turned into sepsis, and Liam spent a week in intensive care.
Nurses watch for fever, a racing heart and confusion as early warning signs of sepsis.
Doctors gave Maria antibiotics within the first hour because every delay in treating sepsis raises the risk of death.
Even after surviving sepsis, Diego felt weak and tired for months as his body recovered.

cloze.s: Because an untreated infection can spread through the blood and set off organ failure, doctors treat ___ as an emergency.

note: Sometimes called "blood poisoning," but doctors say that older name is not accurate.

def: a problem with the heartbeat in which the heart beats too fast, too slow or in an uneven pattern
why: Some types are harmless, but others can cause fainting, stroke or sudden death and need treatment.
ex: A smartwatch alert led Wei to a cardiologist, who found an arrhythmia called atrial fibrillation.
Some people with a slow arrhythmia get a pacemaker to keep the heart beating at a steady rate.
After feeling her heart skip and race, Hannah wore a heart monitor for two weeks to check for an arrhythmia.
During the soccer match, a player collapsed from a dangerous arrhythmia, and a coach used a defibrillator to restore his heartbeat.

cloze.s: The heart monitor showed a fluttering, irregular beat, so the doctor diagnosed a(n) ___.

note: Atrial fibrillation is the most common lasting type.

def: a basic cell that has not yet taken on a job and can develop into many different kinds of cells
why: It is the basis of bone marrow transplants and much research into repairing damaged tissue.
ex: A stem cell transplant from his sister's bone marrow helped Tomás recover from leukemia.
Researchers are studying whether stem cells could be used to grow new heart muscle after a heart attack.
Blood from a newborn's umbilical cord is rich in stem cells that can be saved for future treatments.
In the lab, Yuki coaxed a stem cell to develop into a beating heart muscle cell.

cloze.s: Because a(n) ___ can turn into blood, muscle or nerve cells, scientists hope to use it to repair damaged organs.

def: the sorting of sick or injured people by how urgently they need care, so the most urgent cases are treated first
why: It decides who is seen first in emergency rooms and disasters, and the word is now used for any urgent sorting.
ex: At the crowded emergency room, the triage nurse sent the man with chest pain ahead of a patient with a sprained wrist.
After the earthquake, rescue teams set up triage tents to decide which victims needed surgery right away.
At the music festival's first aid tent, a nurse did triage, sending a fan who had fainted to the ambulance before treating blisters.
The clinic's phone triage line helps patients decide whether to come in today or wait for a regular appointment.

cloze.s: With dozens of people hurt in the bus crash, medics used ___ to decide who needed help first.

note: Also used outside medicine: "Aisha triaged her inbox, answering the urgent emails first."

def: a sudden, severe allergic reaction that can close the throat and drop blood pressure, and can kill within minutes
why: People with serious food or insect allergies carry epinephrine pens to treat it right away.
ex: When Fatima's lips swelled after eating a cookie with nuts, her friend used her epinephrine pen to treat the anaphylaxis.
A bee sting can trigger anaphylaxis in people who are badly allergic to the venom.
Restaurant staff are trained to call 911 at once if a diner shows signs of anaphylaxis after eating shellfish.
Some people have anaphylaxis after a dose of penicillin, so doctors ask about drug allergies first.

cloze.s: After a bee sting, Diego's throat began to swell and he struggled to breathe, a sign of ___ that needed emergency care.

note: Even after an epinephrine shot, the person should go to an emergency room.

def: medical care that aims to ease pain and other suffering and improve daily life for people with serious illness
why: It can begin at any stage of a serious illness and be given along with treatment meant to cure.
ex: While she continued chemotherapy, Maria's palliative care team helped her manage pain and nausea.
Palliative care also supports families as they make hard decisions about a loved one's treatment.
Palliative care can begin right at diagnosis, not just at the end of life.
The palliative care nurse adjusted Tomás's medicine so his breathing felt easier and he could sleep.

cloze.s: The goal of ___ is not to cure the disease but to keep the patient as comfortable as possible.

note: Not the same as hospice, which is for people near the end of life who have stopped treatment meant to cure.

def: a test of a treatment in which neither the patients nor the researchers know who received the real treatment
why: It keeps hopes and expectations from tilting the results, so it is the standard for testing new drugs.
ex: In the double-blind study, half the volunteers got the new pill and half got a sugar pill that looked identical.
Because the trial was not a double-blind study, critics said the doctors' hopes may have shaped the results.
In the double-blind study of the new pain cream, even the nurses handing out the tubes didn't know which ones were real.
Scientists trust a double-blind study more because no one's hopes can quietly sway the measurements.

cloze.s: To keep expectations from shaping the results, the drug was tested in a(n) ___ where even the doctors didn't know who got it.

note: In a single-blind study, only the patients don't know which treatment they got.

def: the branch of mathematics that studies how things change and how small pieces add up to a whole
why: It is the math behind physics, engineering and economics, and was developed by Newton and Leibniz in the 1600s.
ex: Engineers use calculus to work out how fast water drains from a tank as its level drops.
Aisha took calculus in her first year of college because her engineering degree required it.
Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz each developed calculus on their own in the late 1600s.
Economists use calculus to find the price at which a company earns the most profit.

cloze.s: To find the exact speed of a falling ball at one instant, physics students use ___, the math of change.

note: In medicine the same word means a hard stone, such as a kidney stone, or hardened tartar on teeth.

def: a quantity that has both a size and a direction, often drawn as an arrow
why: It is used to describe forces, wind and motion in physics, navigation and computer graphics.
ex: The pilot treated the crosswind as a vector, with both a speed and a direction, when planning her course.
In the game's code, each player's movement is stored as a vector pointing where they are heading.
The weather map showed each wind as a vector, with longer arrows for stronger winds.
When two people push a box in different directions, you add their pushes as vectors to find where it will move.

cloze.s: Speed alone is just a number, but velocity is a(n) ___ because it also tells you which way something is moving.

note: A quantity with size but no direction, such as temperature, is called a scalar.

def: a set of numbers arranged in a rectangle of rows and columns that can be added and multiplied by special rules
why: It is a basic tool in computer graphics, in solving many equations at once and in machine learning.
ex: Video game engines multiply each point in a scene by a matrix to rotate it on screen.
Kwame wrote the three equations as a matrix so the computer could solve them all at once.
Wei's statistics class treated each spreadsheet table of rows and columns as a matrix for its calculations.
Multiplying a 2-by-3 matrix by a 3-by-2 matrix gives a 2-by-2 matrix.

cloze.s: The math teacher wrote the numbers in a grid of three rows and three columns, a(n) ___ the class would multiply by another.

note: Plural: matrices. In everyday use it also means a setting or structure in which something grows.

def: one possible ordering of a set of items, used when counting arrangements in which order matters
why: It is used to count possible passwords, seating plans and race finishes.
ex: There are six permutations of the letters A, B and C, such as ABC, BAC and CAB.
Hannah figured out how many permutations of gold, silver and bronze winners were possible among eight runners.
Wei wondered which permutation of his three errands would get him home fastest.
The coach tried every permutation of her four relay runners to find the fastest order.

cloze.s: Because a lock code of 4-7-2 is different from 2-7-4, each code is a different ___ of the same digits.

note: A combination ignores order; a permutation counts each order separately.

def: a straight line that a curve on a graph gets closer and closer to as it stretches farther out
why: It shows up in graphs of limits, such as growth that levels off or values that shoot toward infinity.
ex: On the graph, the curve of y = 1/x hugs the x-axis, its asymptote, without ever reaching zero.
Malik said his test scores were approaching 100 like an asymptote: always closer, never perfect.
The graph of the cooling cup of coffee leveled off near room temperature, an asymptote it never quite reached.
The graph of y = 1/(x − 2) has a vertical asymptote at x = 2, a line the curve never touches.

cloze.s: No matter how far the graph was extended, the curve kept creeping toward the dotted line, its ___, without touching it.

def: a number, about 1.618, made when a line is cut so whole-to-longer-part equals longer-part-to-shorter-part
why: It appears in geometry and the Fibonacci numbers, and many artists and designers use it for pleasing proportions.
ex: Dividing each Fibonacci number by the one before it gives answers that get closer and closer to the golden ratio.
The designer shaped the logo's rectangle so its long side was about 1.6 times its short side, following the golden ratio.
The art teacher showed how to divide a canvas using the golden ratio, placing the horizon about 62 percent of the way up.
Some claims that famous buildings follow the golden ratio are exaggerated, since many fit it only loosely.

cloze.s: Often written with the Greek letter phi, the ___ equals about 1.618.

note: Claims that it appears in the Parthenon or the Mona Lisa are often repeated but not well supported.

def: a number that gives a negative result when multiplied by itself, written using i, the square root of -1
why: Despite the name, such numbers are essential in electrical engineering, physics and signal processing.
ex: No ordinary number squared gives -9, but the imaginary number 3i does.
Diego was surprised that engineers designing power grids use the imaginary number i every day.
Multiplying the imaginary number i by itself gives −1, a fact that puzzles many first-time algebra students.
The name "imaginary number" began as an insult from René Descartes, who doubted such numbers were real.

cloze.s: Because no real number times itself equals -1, mathematicians call its square root, i, a(n) ___.

note: Combined with ordinary numbers, as in 2 + 3i, they form complex numbers.

def: math in which numbers wrap around after reaching a set value, like hours on a clock
why: It is how clocks and calendars work and is a foundation of modern computer security.
ex: On a 12-hour clock, 10 o'clock plus 5 hours is 3 o'clock, a simple case of modular arithmetic.
Online banking relies on codes built from modular arithmetic with enormous numbers.
If today is Monday, modular arithmetic with 7 days tells you that 10 days from now is a Thursday.
Computer programmers often use modular arithmetic to check whether a number is even or odd.

cloze.s: Figuring out that 9 p.m. plus 6 hours lands on 3 a.m. is an everyday use of ___.

def: the easy-to-remember name of a website, such as wikipedia.org, which stands in for its number address on the internet
why: Businesses buy and protect these names, and scammers copy them with tiny spelling changes to trick people.
ex: Sofia registered a domain name for her bakery so customers could find its website easily.
The fake email used a domain name that swapped one letter in the bank's real address.
The startup paid extra for a short, catchy domain name that customers could easily type.
When Malik forgot to renew his domain name, someone else bought it and his blog went offline.

cloze.s: Because people can't remember long strings of numbers, each website has a(n) ___ like example.com that points to its address.

note: The system that turns these names into numeric IP addresses is called DNS.

def: a program that turns code written by people into the low-level instructions a computer can run directly
why: It lets programmers write in readable languages instead of the raw codes a processor understands.
ex: The compiler stopped with an error because Jamal had forgotten a semicolon on line 40.
Before the app can run on a phone, a compiler turns its source code into machine code.
The game studio's programmers waited several minutes for the compiler to build the new version.
Python code is usually run by an interpreter, while C programs are first turned into machine code by a compiler.

cloze.s: After writing the program, Hannah ran it through a(n) ___ to translate her code into instructions the processor could execute.

note: An interpreter runs code line by line instead of translating the whole program first.

def: the network of everyday objects, such as thermostats, doorbells and fridges, that connect online to send and receive data
why: It makes homes and factories easier to control, but each connected device can also be a security weak spot.
