ex: Malik's smart thermostat, door lock and lights are all part of the Internet of Things.
Farmers use soil sensors from the Internet of Things to water crops only when the ground is dry.
Security experts warn that cheap Internet of Things gadgets, like smart plugs, can be easy targets for hackers.
Hannah's fridge, part of the Internet of Things, texts her phone when the door is left open.

cloze.s: Smart speakers, fitness trackers and online security cameras are all examples of the ___, everyday devices linked to the web.

note: Often shortened to IoT.

def: information that describes other data, such as when and where a photo was taken or who wrote a file
why: It helps organize files, but it can also reveal private details like your location without you noticing.
ex: The photo's metadata showed it was taken in Lisbon at 6:42 p.m. on a Tuesday.
Even without reading messages, phone metadata can show who called whom and for how long.
The library's catalog stores metadata such as each book's author, publisher and year.
Kwame sorted his music by the metadata attached to each song, like artist and album.

cloze.s: Before posting the picture, Priya removed its ___, which recorded the exact GPS spot where it was taken.

note: Often explained as "data about data."

def: a realistic fake video, photo or voice clip, made with AI, of a real person doing or saying something they never did
why: They can spread false news and power scams, so people are urged to check sources before trusting clips.
ex: The video of the actor singing in Korean was a deepfake made with AI, not a real performance.
Scammers used a deepfake of a boss's voice on a phone call to trick an employee into sending money.
Before sharing the shocking clip, Hannah checked a fact-checking site and learned it was a deepfake.
The bank now asks callers a secret question, since a deepfake can copy a customer's voice.

cloze.s: Experts warned that the viral clip was a(n) ___, built by AI from old footage to put words in the senator's mouth.

def: technology that lays computer images over a live view of the real world, usually through a phone screen or glasses
why: It is used in games, shopping apps, navigation and training, letting digital objects appear in real places.
ex: With an augmented reality app, Fatima pointed her phone at the living room to see how a new sofa would look.
The game Pokémon Go uses augmented reality to show creatures on the street in front of you.
The museum's augmented reality app showed dinosaurs walking across the real floor when visitors held up their phones.
Mechanics wearing augmented reality glasses can see repair steps displayed right over the engine they are fixing.

cloze.s: Unlike virtual reality, which replaces your view entirely, ___ adds digital images on top of what you really see.

note: Virtual reality (VR) shuts out the real world; this technology adds to it.

def: steady winds that blow from the east toward the equator across the warm oceans of the tropics
why: Sailing ships relied on them to cross the oceans, and they still shape tropical weather and rainfall.
ex: Columbus sailed south to the Canary Islands to catch the trade winds that carried his ships west across the Atlantic.
On the Hawaiian islands, the trade winds bring cool breezes and rain to the eastern slopes.
The steady trade winds make many Caribbean beaches a favorite spot for kite surfing.
When the trade winds weaken, warm water drifts east across the Pacific, helping set off El Niño.

cloze.s: Old sailing ships crossing the Atlantic toward the Caribbean depended on the ___, which blew steadily from the east.

note: They blow from the northeast north of the equator and from the southeast south of it.

def: a strong, warm ocean current that flows from Florida up the east coast of the United States and then across the Atlantic
why: It affects weather and sea life along the Atlantic coast and has shaped shipping routes for centuries.
ex: Benjamin Franklin published one of the first maps of the Gulf Stream to help mail ships cross the Atlantic faster.
Hurricanes can grow stronger as they pass over the warm waters of the Gulf Stream.
Thanks partly to the Gulf Stream, western Europe has milder winters than places in Canada at the same latitude.
Sport fishers off North Carolina head out to the Gulf Stream, where warm water draws marlin and tuna.

cloze.s: Ships heading from America to Europe saved time by riding the ___, a warm current flowing northeast across the Atlantic.

def: the sinking of one of Earth's plates beneath another where they push together, deep into the hot layer below
why: It causes the world's deepest ocean trenches, biggest earthquakes and many volcanoes, such as those of the Andes.
ex: The Mariana Trench formed through subduction, as the Pacific Plate sinks beneath a smaller plate.
Subduction of the ocean floor under South America helped raise the Andes and feed their volcanoes.
Japan's frequent earthquakes come largely from subduction, as ocean plates dive beneath the islands.
Subduction off the coast of Washington and Oregon could one day cause a huge earthquake there.

cloze.s: Where a heavy ocean plate dives beneath a continent, a process called ___, deep trenches and chains of volcanoes form.

def: a huge, flat, dry area of grass with few or no trees, especially in eastern Europe and Central Asia
why: It was home to horse-riding peoples such as the Mongols and is a major region for grazing and grain.
ex: The Mongol armies rode across the steppe on hardy horses that could graze on its grass.
Kazakhstan's steppe stretches for hundreds of miles with hardly a tree in sight.
Nomadic herders on the steppe move their felt tents, called yurts, to find fresh grass for their animals.
In winter, icy winds sweep across the treeless steppe of Central Asia.

cloze.s: Travelers crossing Mongolia saw nothing but endless dry grassland, the open ___, stretching to the horizon.

note: Similar to the North American prairie. Not to be confused with "step."

def: the American program, begun in 1948, that gave billions of dollars to help Western Europe rebuild after World War II
why: It helped Western Europe recover quickly and tied it closely to the United States during the Cold War.
ex: Money from the Marshall Plan helped rebuild bombed factories, roads and railways across Western Europe.
The Marshall Plan was named after George C. Marshall, the US secretary of state who proposed it in 1947.
Aisha's grandfather in Italy remembered the new tractors that arrived through the Marshall Plan.
The Soviet Union refused Marshall Plan aid and pressured Eastern European countries to turn it down too.

cloze.s: After World War II, the United States sent more than $13 billion in aid to rebuild Western Europe under the ___.

def: the rush by European powers in the late 1800s and early 1900s to seize and divide nearly all of Africa into colonies
why: Borders drawn by outsiders during this period still shape many African countries and conflicts today.
ex: During the Scramble for Africa, leaders met in Berlin in 1884 and 1885 to set rules for claiming African land without any Africans present.
By 1914, after the Scramble for Africa, only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.
Many of today's straight African borders were drawn by Europeans during the Scramble for Africa.
Ethiopia's victory over Italy at Adwa in 1896 helped keep it free during the Scramble for Africa.

cloze.s: In the ___, countries like Britain, France and Belgium carved up almost an entire continent within a few decades.

def: the family of emperors that ruled China from 618 to 907, a time of great wealth, trade and poetry
why: It is often called a golden age of Chinese culture, producing famous poets like Li Bai and Du Fu.
ex: During the Tang dynasty, the capital Chang'an was one of the largest and most international cities in the world.
Wei's grandmother can still recite poems by Li Bai, who wrote during the Tang dynasty.
Tang dynasty pottery horses, glazed in green and amber, are prized by museums around the world.
Buddhism spread widely in China during the Tang dynasty, and many famous temples were built.

cloze.s: China's ___, which lasted from 618 to 907, is remembered as a golden age of poetry and Silk Road trade.

note: It came before the Song dynasty and long before the Ming.

def: direct rule by the military that replaces the normal government and courts, usually during an emergency or violent protests
why: It often suspends ordinary rights such as free movement, and it is a warning sign when used to keep leaders in power.
ex: After the riots, the government declared martial law, and soldiers enforced a strict nighttime curfew.
Under martial law, civilians can be tried in military courts instead of ordinary ones.
Under martial law, soldiers patrolled the streets and newspapers had to clear their stories with the army.
Hawaii was placed under martial law after the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941.

cloze.s: When the army took control of the capital and suspended the courts, the general announced that the country was under ___.

note: Not "marshal law." The word comes from Mars, the Roman god of war.

def: law built up over time from judges' earlier decisions in real cases, rather than only from written codes
why: It is the base of the legal systems of England, the United States, Canada, Australia and India.
ex: In a common law system, a judge looks at how earlier courts decided similar cases.
Many US rules about carelessness that causes injury come from judges' decisions in common law rather than from laws passed by lawmakers.
Common law, inherited from England, still shapes how courts in Australia and most of Canada decide cases.
Since no written law covered the dispute, the judge turned to common law and earlier rulings on similar contracts.

cloze.s: Because the US legal system grew from English ___, judges rely heavily on decisions made in past cases.

note: Most of Europe and Latin America use civil law, built mainly on written legal codes.

def: how much the amount people buy changes when the price of a product goes up or down
why: Businesses and governments use it to predict how price changes and taxes will affect sales.
ex: Gasoline has low price elasticity of demand, because people still need to drive even when prices rise.
Because restaurant meals have high price elasticity of demand, a small price hike sent many of Diego's customers elsewhere.
Since there are many brands of bottled water, its price elasticity of demand is high: raise the price and shoppers switch.
Before raising ticket prices, the theater studied the price elasticity of demand to predict how many seats would go empty.

cloze.s: Insulin sales barely fall when its price rises, a sign of very low ___.

note: Goods people need, like medicine, tend to be "inelastic"; luxuries with substitutes tend to be "elastic."

def: a market controlled by a small number of large companies, each able to affect prices
why: Airlines, mobile phone carriers and soft drinks are often cited examples, and regulators watch them for price-fixing.
ex: With only three big phone carriers, the country's wireless market is an oligopoly.
In an oligopoly, when one airline raises fares, the others often follow within days.
Critics say the movie theater business became an oligopoly once a handful of chains bought up most local cinemas.
In an oligopoly, a small company has a hard time breaking in, because the giants control most of the shelf space.

cloze.s: Because just four firms sell almost all the cereal in the country, economists describe the market as a(n) ___.

note: A monopoly has one seller; this has a few. From Greek for "few sellers."

def: the savings a business gets when making more of something lowers the cost of each item
why: It explains why big companies can often charge less and why many industries end up with a few giant firms.
ex: Thanks to economies of scale, the huge factory makes each phone case for far less than a small workshop can.
Priya's bakery lowered its flour costs by buying in bulk, a small example of economies of scale.
The small brewery couldn't match the big brand's prices, which benefit from economies of scale.
Carmakers chase economies of scale by building millions of cars on the same basic design.

cloze.s: Large warehouse stores can offer low prices partly because of ___: buying and selling in huge amounts cuts the cost of each item.

def: extremely fast and out-of-control rising prices that make a country's money nearly worthless
why: It wiped out savings in Germany in 1923 and in Zimbabwe in the 2000s and usually follows governments printing too much money.
ex: During Germany's hyperinflation in 1923, people carried cash in wheelbarrows to buy bread.
Zimbabwe's hyperinflation grew so severe that it printed a 100 trillion dollar note.
In a country hit by hyperinflation, a restaurant might raise its menu prices between breakfast and dinner.
Olga's grandmother remembers when hyperinflation made her life savings worth less than a loaf of bread.

cloze.s: When prices doubled every few days, workers rushed to spend their wages at once, a typical sign of ___.

note: Far more extreme than ordinary inflation of a few percent a year.

def: betting that a stock will fall by borrowing shares, selling them, and buying them back later at a lower price
why: It can expose overpriced or dishonest companies, but losses can be huge if the price rises instead.
ex: Through short selling, the fund profited when the struggling retailer's stock collapsed.
Short selling is risky because a stock's price can keep rising, so the possible loss has no upper limit.
Some countries temporarily banned short selling during the 2008 financial crisis to try to slow falling stock prices.
To start short selling, Lena's broker first had to find shares she could borrow.

cloze.s: Sure the company's stock would drop, Malik borrowed shares and sold them right away, a strategy called ___.

def: money that has value because a government declares it legal for payment, not because it can be swapped for gold
why: The US dollar and almost all modern currencies are this kind of money, which lets central banks control the supply.
ex: Since 1971, when the US stopped letting other nations trade dollars for gold, the dollar has been fiat money.
A paper bill is fiat money: the paper is nearly worthless, but people trust the government behind it.
Because fiat money isn't backed by gold, its value depends on public trust and careful management by the central bank.
In Wei's economics class, students compared fiat money with old coins made of real silver.

cloze.s: Unlike coins once made of real gold, today's paper bills are ___, valuable only because the government stands behind them.

note: From Latin "fiat," meaning "let it be done."

def: a bold design style of the 1920s and 1930s, known for clean lines, repeated shapes like zigzags, and shiny materials
why: It shaped buildings like New York's Chrysler Building as well as furniture, jewelry and posters of the era.
ex: Miami Beach is famous for its pastel Art Deco hotels from the 1930s.
The Chrysler Building's shining steel crown is one of the best-known examples of Art Deco.
Sofia's grandparents still have an Art Deco lamp with a chrome base and a fan-shaped glass shade.
The renovated train station kept its Art Deco lobby, with geometric tiles and gold sunburst patterns.

cloze.s: The old movie theater's zigzag patterns, sunburst designs and chrome trim are typical of 1920s ___.

note: The name comes from a 1925 design fair in Paris, though it was coined decades later.

def: a style of writing that follows a character's flowing thoughts and feelings as they pass through the mind, often without normal order
why: It is a key feature of modern novels such as James Joyce's Ulysses and Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway.
ex: Virginia Woolf used stream of consciousness to show a character's thoughts jumping from a London street to memories of her youth.
The last chapter of Ulysses is famous stream of consciousness, running for pages with very little punctuation.
Hannah tried stream of consciousness in her journal, writing every thought as it came without stopping to fix it.
William Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury uses stream of consciousness, which can make its opening section hard to follow.

cloze.s: The novel shows the character's thoughts as they rush along, one idea tumbling into the next, in a style called ___.

note: The phrase was made famous by the psychologist William James in 1890 to describe how thought flows.

def: a person telling a story in a book or film whose account can't be fully trusted, because they lie or are mistaken
why: Writers use this device to create surprise twists and make readers question what really happened.
ex: In Edgar Allan Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart," the unreliable narrator insists he is sane while describing a murder.
The film's twist reveals that its unreliable narrator has been hiding the truth from the audience all along.
Because the story is told by a young child who misreads the adults around her, Hannah called her an unreliable narrator.
Agatha Christie's The Murder of Roger Ackroyd shocked readers with an unreliable narrator who hid a key secret.

cloze.s: Halfway through the novel, readers realize the man telling the story has been lying to them; he is a(n) ___.

note: The term was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth in 1961.

def: in Indian classical music, a set pattern of notes and phrases that musicians use as a framework for building a melody
why: Each one is linked to a mood and sometimes a time of day, and performers like Ravi Shankar made them known worldwide.
ex: The sitar player spent nearly an hour exploring a single evening raga.
Priya explained that a raga is not a fixed tune but a set of rules a musician uses to create one.
Ravi Shankar's sitar concerts introduced many Western listeners to the raga.
Before improvising, the young singer learned which notes the raga allowed going up and coming down.

cloze.s: Before the concert began, the Indian musician announced which ___ he would play, a melodic framework traditionally performed at dawn.

note: Also spelled raag.

def: a drawing method that makes a flat picture look deep by making parallel lines seem to meet at one far point
why: Developed in Florence in the early 1400s, it changed Western painting and is still widely taught in drawing classes.
ex: Using linear perspective, the art student drew the railroad tracks meeting at a single point on the horizon.
Renaissance painters used linear perspective to make church walls look like they opened onto deep rooms.
Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper uses linear perspective, with the room's lines leading toward Jesus's head.
The Renaissance architect Brunelleschi is credited with working out the rules of linear perspective.

cloze.s: To make the long hallway seem to stretch away into the distance, the painter used ___, with all the lines leading to one vanishing point.

note: The architect Filippo Brunelleschi is credited with showing how it works in the early 1400s.

def: the view that being good means building a good character, such as honesty and courage, rather than just following rules
why: Going back to Aristotle, it asks "What kind of person should I be?" and is one of the three main approaches to ethics.
ex: A follower of virtue ethics would ask what an honest and kind person would do, not which rule applies.
Our philosophy class compared virtue ethics with utilitarianism, which judges actions only by their results.
Aristotle is the thinker most closely tied to virtue ethics, which focuses on building habits like courage and honesty.
Thinking in terms of virtue ethics, Sofia asked herself what a generous person would do with her year-end bonus.

cloze.s: Rather than asking which rule to follow, ___ asks what a person of good character, like a brave and fair friend, would do.

note: Aristotle argued that each good trait lies between two extremes: courage, for example, lies between cowardice and recklessness.

def: a thought test asking what rules for society you would pick if you did not know your own place in it
why: Named and made famous by John Rawls in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice, it is a widely used way to think about what makes a society fair.
ex: Behind the veil of ignorance, you might choose strong safety nets, since you could be born poor or sick.
Rawls's veil of ignorance asks you to design a society without knowing your race, sex, talents or wealth.
Diego cut the cake and let his sister choose her slice first, a simple version of the veil of ignorance.
Using the veil of ignorance, the class wrote school rules without knowing whether they would be students or teachers.

cloze.s: John Rawls asked people to imagine a(n) ___, choosing society's rules without knowing whether they would be rich or poor.

note: From John Rawls's book A Theory of Justice.

def: the Buddha's core teaching: life involves suffering, suffering comes from craving, it can end, and there is a path to end it
why: They are the basic teaching shared by all schools of Buddhism, one of the world's major religions.
ex: In his first sermon, the Buddha is said to have taught the Four Noble Truths to five companions.
Yuki's meditation teacher began the course with the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
After reading about the Four Noble Truths, Aisha began noticing how much of her stress came from wanting things.
The Four Noble Truths end with the path that Buddhists believe leads to freedom from suffering.

cloze.s: Buddhism's central teaching, the ___, says suffering is caused by craving and can be ended by following the Eightfold Path.

note: The fourth truth, the way to end suffering, is the Noble Eightfold Path.

def: a puzzle asking whether a ship that has had every old part replaced, one at a time, is still the same ship
why: It is a classic way to ask what makes something, or someone, stay the same over time.
ex: When the band had replaced every original member, fans joked that it had become a ship of Theseus.
The ship of Theseus puzzle comes from the ancient writer Plutarch, who said the Athenians kept repairing the hero's ship.
Museum experts called the old warship, rebuilt with mostly new timber, a real-life ship of Theseus.
Our philosophy class used the ship of Theseus to ask whether a person stays the same as the body's cells are replaced.

cloze.s: If every plank of a boat is swapped for a new one, is it still the same boat? This old puzzle is called the ___.

note: Also called Theseus's paradox.

def: the view that people seek meaning in a universe that offers none, and should live fully anyway rather than give up
why: It is closely linked to Albert Camus, who described life as the endless rock-pushing of Sisyphus.
ex: In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus explains absurdism by picturing a man pushing a rock uphill forever.
Kwame's favorite plays draw on absurdism, showing characters waiting for meaning that never arrives.
After losing his job, Kwame found comfort in absurdism: life might have no built-in meaning, but he would still enjoy it.
The professor said absurdism, unlike despair, urges people to keep living fully in a universe without meaning.

cloze.s: Camus argued that the clash between our hunger for meaning and a silent universe is the core of ___.

note: Not the same as nihilism, which says nothing has value; this view says we should keep living with spirit.

def: the rule in quantum physics that the exact position and exact momentum of a tiny particle cannot both be known at once
why: It shows that some limits on measurement are built into nature itself, not just into our tools.
ex: Priya explained that the uncertainty principle is not about clumsy equipment; even perfect tools could not pin down both values.
In the physics lecture, the uncertainty principle helped explain why electrons do not travel in neat, fixed orbits.
Kenji's textbook said the uncertainty principle limits how precisely anyone can know both where an electron is and how fast it moves.
Science fiction writers sometimes misuse the uncertainty principle to mean that anything at all can happen.

cloze.s: Werner Heisenberg stated the ___ in 1927, showing that measuring a particle's position more precisely makes its momentum less certain.

note: Stated by Werner Heisenberg in 1927. It applies to pairs of quantities, most famously position and momentum.

def: a link between particles in which measuring one instantly tells you about the other, no matter how far apart they are
why: It is central to research on quantum computers and on ultra-secure ways of sending information.
ex: Einstein disliked quantum entanglement, famously calling it "spooky action at a distance."
The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics honored experiments that confirmed quantum entanglement is real.
Kenji's physics teacher stressed that quantum entanglement cannot be used to send messages faster than light.
Researchers use quantum entanglement to build encryption systems that reveal any attempt to eavesdrop.

cloze.s: Because of ___, measuring the polarization of one photon told the lab team the polarization of its partner miles away.

note: It cannot be used to send messages faster than light, a common misunderstanding.

def: a tiny particle tied to an invisible field that gives many basic particles their mass, first detected in 2012
why: Its discovery confirmed the last missing piece of the Standard Model, physics' main theory of basic particles.
ex: Scientists at CERN cheered in July 2012 when they announced they had found the Higgs boson.
Diego read that the Higgs boson had been predicted in the 1960s, almost fifty years before anyone detected it.
The Large Hadron Collider near Geneva was built partly to search for the Higgs boson.
News reports sometimes called the Higgs boson the “God particle,” a nickname many physicists dislike.

cloze.s: Peter Higgs and François Englert won the 2013 Nobel Prize after the ___ they had predicted was finally found.

note: The nickname "God particle" came from a popular book; many physicists dislike it.

def: weak radiation left over from the early universe, which still reaches us almost evenly from every direction in the sky
why: It is among the strongest evidence that the universe began in a hot, dense state, as the Big Bang theory says.
ex: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background in 1965 while trying to remove a strange hiss from their antenna.
Maps of the cosmic microwave background show tiny temperature differences that later grew into galaxies.
Satellites such as Planck have mapped the cosmic microwave background across the entire sky.
Olga's astronomy professor described the cosmic microwave background as the oldest light we can detect.

cloze.s: Some of the static on an old analog TV set comes from the ___, the afterglow of the Big Bang.

note: Often shortened to CMB. Penzias and Wilson shared the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics for finding it.

def: the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, can ever escape
why: It marks where a black hole begins: the point of no return for anything that falls in.
ex: Once a star's gas crosses the event horizon, it is gone from view forever.
In the novel, Yuki's spaceship drifted dangerously close to the event horizon of a giant black hole.
The 2019 image of a black hole showed a dark center surrounded by glowing gas just outside the event horizon.
Sofia's physics teacher explained that an astronaut falling past the event horizon could never send a signal back out.

cloze.s: Light from inside the ___ can never reach us, which is why black holes look completely dark.

note: People also use it loosely for a point of no return in a situation.

def: the ability of certain materials, when cooled to extremely low temperatures, to carry electricity with zero resistance
why: It makes possible the powerful magnets inside MRI scanners and particle accelerators.
ex: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered superconductivity in 1911 when he cooled mercury close to absolute zero.
Engineers hope that superconductivity at room temperature could one day cut the energy wasted in power lines.
Japan's magnetic levitation trains use superconductivity to float above the track at high speed.
Wei's physics class watched a magnet float above a chilled disk, a dramatic demonstration of superconductivity.

cloze.s: The MRI scanner's magnet is chilled with liquid helium so that its wires show ___ and lose no energy as heat.

note: Claims of room-temperature versions make news often but have not held up to testing so far.

def: the idea that the energy-making parts inside complex cells began as free-living bacteria that other cells swallowed
why: It explains why mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own DNA, separate from the cell's main DNA.
ex: Lynn Margulis championed the endosymbiotic theory in 1967, when many biologists still rejected it.
The endosymbiotic theory suggests that nearly every cell in your body carries the descendants of ancient bacteria.
The endosymbiotic theory also explains chloroplasts, which plant cells use for photosynthesis and which still carry their own DNA.
In biology class, Tomás drew a cartoon of a large cell swallowing a bacterium to illustrate the endosymbiotic theory.

cloze.s: According to the ___, mitochondria were once separate bacteria that came to live inside larger cells.

note: Now widely accepted for mitochondria and for chloroplasts, the parts of plant cells that carry out photosynthesis.

def: the process by which unrelated living things develop similar features because they face similar challenges
why: It explains why sharks and dolphins share a body shape even though one is a fish and the other a mammal.
ex: Wings in birds, bats and insects are a classic case of convergent evolution.
Wei's biology teacher used the eyes of octopuses and humans to illustrate convergent evolution.
Because of convergent evolution, dolphins and sharks both have streamlined bodies and fins, even though dolphins are mammals and sharks are fish.
The extinct Tasmanian tiger looked remarkably like a wolf, though it was a marsupial, a striking case of convergent evolution.

cloze.s: Cactuses in the Americas and some unrelated plants in Africa look almost alike, a result of ___ in dry climates.

note: Similar features that arise this way are called analogous, not inherited from a shared ancestor.

def: harm or unpleasant side effects a person feels because they expect a treatment to hurt them
why: It helps explain why patients who read long lists of side effects sometimes report more of them.
ex: In the trial, some people taking sugar pills reported headaches, a likely sign of the nocebo effect.
Dr. Okafor worried that frightening warnings could trigger a nocebo effect in anxious patients.
After the nurse said the shot would hurt a lot, Liam felt more pain than usual, likely a nocebo effect.
Researchers study the nocebo effect to learn why patients warned about nausea are more likely to feel it.

cloze.s: After reading online that the drug causes dizziness, Malik felt dizzy even on a dummy pill, an example of the ___.

note: From Latin for "I will harm," the mirror image of the placebo effect, "I will please."

def: a wrongly folded protein that makes normal proteins fold wrongly too, causing rare, deadly brain diseases
why: It causes mad cow disease and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and cannot be destroyed by ordinary cooking.
ex: Stanley Prusiner won the 1997 Nobel Prize for his work showing that a prion can spread disease.
Unlike a virus, a prion has no genes; it is simply a protein with the wrong shape.
Because a prion is so tough, normal hospital sterilizing methods may not destroy it on surgical tools.
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a rare brain disorder in humans, is caused by a prion.

cloze.s: Mad cow disease spreads not through bacteria or a virus but through a misshapen protein called a(n) ___.

note: Coined by Stanley Prusiner in 1982 from "proteinaceous infectious particle."

def: a protective cap at each end of a cell's long threads of DNA, which gets shorter every time the cell splits
why: It is studied as a clue to aging, since cells usually stop dividing once these caps wear down.
ex: Scientists often compare a telomere to the plastic tip that keeps a shoelace from fraying.
The study measured telomere length to see whether long-term stress speeds up aging.
Elizabeth Blackburn shared the 2009 Nobel Prize for discoveries about how the telomere protects chromosomes.
Kenji's biology teacher explained that when a telomere becomes too short, the cell usually stops dividing.

cloze.s: Each time the cell divided, the ___ at the end of its chromosomes grew slightly shorter.

note: The 2009 Nobel Prize in Medicine honored the discovery of how these caps protect chromosomes and of telomerase, the enzyme that rebuilds them.

def: the planned, orderly self-destruction of a cell, which the body uses to clear out old or damaged cells
why: When this process fails, damaged cells can survive and multiply, which is one way cancer develops.
ex: Before birth, apoptosis removes the webbing between a baby's fingers.
Some cancer drugs work by pushing tumor cells into apoptosis.
When a cell's DNA is badly damaged, apoptosis can remove it before it turns cancerous.
A tadpole loses its tail as it becomes a frog, partly through apoptosis.

cloze.s: Every day the body clears out billions of worn-out cells through ___, a built-in program that makes them quietly break down.

note: Unlike necrosis, cell death from injury, it is tidy and does not cause inflammation.

def: a tight layer of cells lining the brain's blood vessels that keeps many substances in the blood from reaching the brain
why: It protects the brain from germs and toxins but also makes many medicines hard to deliver there.
ex: Many promising drugs for brain tumors fail because they cannot cross the blood-brain barrier.
Kwame learned that alcohol and caffeine slip easily through the blood-brain barrier.
Because the blood-brain barrier blocks many medicines, doctors sometimes inject drugs directly into the fluid around the spine.
Diego's pharmacology lecture explained how the blood-brain barrier protects the brain from toxins carried in the blood.

cloze.s: Researchers designed tiny particles that could sneak past the ___ and carry medicine directly to the brain.

def: describes an illness or injury caused by medical care itself, rather than by the patient's original condition
why: Hospitals track these harms, such as drug reactions or infections picked up during treatment, to make care safer.
ex: The patient's bleeding was iatrogenic, caused by a blood thinner given at too high a dose.
Hospital reviews look closely at iatrogenic infections, such as those linked to catheters.
The study found that some iatrogenic harm came from patients receiving the wrong medicine in the hospital.
Kwame's pharmacist warned that taking too many drugs at once can lead to iatrogenic problems, like falls in older adults.

cloze.s: Because the nerve damage came from the surgery, not the disease, doctors classified it as ___.

note: From Greek iatros, "physician": literally "brought about by a healer."

def: how many patients must receive a treatment for one more of them to benefit compared with not being treated
why: It turns study results into a plain count, making a drug's real benefit easier to judge than percentages.
ex: The number needed to treat was 50, so on average 50 people had to take the pill for one of them to avoid a stroke.
Hannah's doctor used the number needed to treat to explain how much the cholesterol drug might help her.
A drug with a number needed to treat of 5 helps far more patients than one with a number needed to treat of 200.
Malik's medical school class calculated the number needed to treat for a new flu vaccine using data from a large trial.

cloze.s: If 100 patients must take a drug to prevent one heart attack, the drug's ___ is 100.

note: A lower count means a more effective treatment; one means everyone treated benefits.

def: a long nerve running from the brain to the heart, lungs and gut that helps slow the heart and calm the body
why: It drives the body's "rest and digest" state and is involved in fainting, digestion and heart rate.
ex: Slow, deep breathing may help calm you by acting on the vagus nerve.
Fatima fainted at the sight of blood when her vagus nerve suddenly slowed her heart.
Splashing cold water on the face can stimulate the vagus nerve and slow a racing heart.
Doctors sometimes treat certain kinds of epilepsy with a small device that sends electrical pulses to the vagus nerve.

cloze.s: Its name comes from the Latin word for "wandering," because the ___ winds through the chest and belly.

def: a small area deep in the brain that controls body heat, hunger, sleep and the need to drink, and directs many hormones
why: It links the nervous system to the hormone system, keeping the body's inner balance steady.
ex: When you get too hot, your hypothalamus signals your body to sweat.
The hypothalamus tells the nearby pituitary gland when to release hormones.
After a long run, Wei's hypothalamus triggered her thirst, reminding her to drink water.
Damage to the hypothalamus can disrupt sleep, appetite and body temperature.

cloze.s: Fever happens when the brain's ___ raises the body's temperature setting to fight infection.

def: the equation e to the power of i times pi, plus one, equals zero, linking five of math's most important numbers
why: It is often called the most beautiful equation in mathematics because it ties together several separate branches.
ex: Sofia's math teacher wrote Euler's identity on the board and asked the class which five numbers it connects.
Some math fans have Euler's identity printed on T-shirts and coffee mugs.
Euler's identity is a special case of Euler's formula, which links powers of e to the sine and cosine functions.
Many mathematicians call Euler's identity beautiful because one short equation ties together addition, multiplication and powers.

cloze.s: The short equation e^(iπ) + 1 = 0, known as ___, joins e, i, pi, one and zero.

note: Named after the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler (1707–1783). Pronounced "OY-ler."

def: proofs from 1931 showing that any consistent set of math rules able to describe whole numbers has true statements it cannot prove
why: They ended the dream of building one complete set of rules from which all mathematical truths could be proved.
ex: Gödel's incompleteness theorems showed that some truths in math will always lie beyond proof within the system.
Jamal's philosophy seminar argued over what Gödel's incompleteness theorems mean for the limits of human knowledge.
Kenji's logic professor spent a whole lecture on Gödel's incompleteness theorems, which ended hopes of proving all of math from one set of rules.
Popular books about Gödel's incompleteness theorems often explain them using the puzzling sentence “This statement cannot be proved.”

cloze.s: Kurt Gödel shocked mathematicians in 1931 when his ___ showed that no set of rules for arithmetic can prove every true statement.

note: Often misused to claim that "nothing can be known"; the theorems apply only to formal systems of a certain kind.

def: a puzzle about a game show with three doors, where switching to the other closed door doubles your chance of winning
why: It is a famous example of how human intuition about probability can be badly wrong.
ex: When Marilyn vos Savant explained the Monty Hall problem in a 1990 magazine column, thousands of readers wrote in to say she was wrong.
Wei ran a computer simulation of the Monty Hall problem and found that switching won about two times in three.
Malik acted out the Monty Hall problem with three cups and a coin, and his friends finally believed switching was better.
The Monty Hall problem is named after the host of the TV game show Let's Make a Deal.

cloze.s: In the ___, after the host opens a door hiding a goat, you should switch, because switching wins two-thirds of the time.

note: Named after Monty Hall, host of the TV game show Let's Make a Deal. Switching helps only because the host knows where the prize is.

def: the pattern that in many real lists of numbers, about 30 percent start with 1 and very few start with 9
why: Auditors and investigators use it to spot made-up figures, since invented numbers often break the pattern.
ex: The auditor applied Benford's law and noticed too many expense claims starting with 7 and 8.
Benford's law holds for things like town populations and river lengths, which span many sizes.
Malik's statistics professor showed how Benford's law can help tax agencies spot invented numbers on tax returns.
Benford's law surprises most people, who guess that each first digit from 1 to 9 should appear equally often.

cloze.s: Faked sales figures were caught because their first digits did not follow ___.

note: Named after physicist Frank Benford (1938), though astronomer Simon Newcomb noticed it first in 1881.

def: the branch of math about features of shapes that stay the same when shapes are stretched or bent, but not torn
why: It is used throughout modern physics and data analysis, and explains why a coffee mug and a doughnut count as the same shape.
ex: In topology, a coffee mug and a doughnut are equivalent, since each has exactly one hole.
Olga's research in topology helps describe how strands of DNA knot and untangle.
Kwame's math club used topology to explain why you can't turn a ball into a doughnut without tearing a hole.
Subway maps use an idea from topology, keeping the order of connections while ignoring real distances.

cloze.s: Because ___ ignores size and exact shape, it treats a rubber band and a circle drawn on paper as the same.

note: Sometimes nicknamed "rubber-sheet geometry."

def: a famous claim from 1859, still not proved, about a special math function that would explain how prime numbers are spread out
why: It is one of math's most famous open problems, with a one-million-dollar prize offered for a proof.
ex: Many results in number theory are proved on the assumption that the Riemann hypothesis is true.
Liam joked that solving the Riemann hypothesis would pay off his student loans.
Computers have checked the Riemann hypothesis for trillions of cases, but no one has found a proof.
Sofia's number theory professor said that proving the Riemann hypothesis would reveal deep patterns in how primes are spaced.

cloze.s: The Clay Mathematics Institute will award one million dollars to whoever proves the ___, first proposed by Bernhard Riemann.

note: It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems named by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000.

def: the claim that a^n + b^n = c^n has no answers in positive whole numbers when n is greater than 2
why: It went unproved for over 350 years until Andrew Wiles solved it in the 1990s, a landmark of modern math.
ex: Pierre de Fermat wrote Fermat's Last Theorem in a book margin around 1637, saying the margin was too small for his proof.
Andrew Wiles first became fascinated by Fermat's Last Theorem as a ten-year-old in a library.
For over 350 years, mathematicians tried and failed to prove Fermat's Last Theorem.
Jamal's teacher showed that 3² + 4² = 5², but Fermat's Last Theorem says no positive whole numbers work that way for cubes or higher powers.

cloze.s: Andrew Wiles worked in secret for seven years before announcing a proof of ___ in 1993.

note: Wiles's first proof had a gap; the corrected proof was published in 1995.

def: a way of securing messages with two linked keys: a public key to lock and a private key to unlock
why: It lets strangers communicate safely online and underpins secure websites, digital signatures and online payments.
ex: Thanks to public-key cryptography, Aisha's browser can set up a secure link with her bank without sharing a secret first.
Digital signatures rely on public-key cryptography to prove who really sent a document.
Diego posted his public key online so friends could send him locked messages, a basic use of public-key cryptography.
Public-key cryptography was first publicly described in 1976 by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman.

cloze.s: With ___, you can publish one key openly while keeping its matching private key secret.

note: Introduced publicly by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman in 1976; the RSA system followed in 1977.

def: a formula that turns any data into a short code of set length, so that any tiny change gives a new code
why: It lets websites store passwords safely and lets computers check quickly that files have not been changed.
ex: Good websites store a hash function's output, not your actual password.
Changing one letter in the file made the hash function produce a completely different result.
To check that her download was not damaged, Priya compared its hash function result with the code on the website.
A good hash function for passwords makes it practically impossible to work backward from the code to the original data.

cloze.s: Each block in a blockchain stores a code made by a(n) ___, so any tampering with earlier blocks is easy to detect.

note: A good one works only one way: you cannot rebuild the original data from the code.

def: a system of reasoning with only two values, true and false, combined using AND, OR and NOT
why: Every digital circuit and computer program is built on it, and it powers advanced search filters.
ex: Typing "cats AND dogs NOT pets" into the library catalog is a simple use of Boolean logic.
Claude Shannon showed in 1937 that Boolean logic could be used to design electrical switching circuits.
The spreadsheet formula used Boolean logic, marking a row TRUE only if the order was paid AND shipped.
Priya's coding class practiced Boolean logic by predicting whether statements like “true OR false” would come out true.

cloze.s: Inside a computer chip, millions of tiny switches carry out ___, treating each signal as either 1 or 0.

note: Named after the English mathematician George Boole, who described it in the mid-1800s.

def: the internet service that turns website names people can remember into the number addresses computers use
why: Without it, you would have to type a string of numbers instead of a name to visit any website.
ex: When the domain name system failed, many popular websites seemed to vanish even though their servers were running.
The domain name system is often described as the phone book of the internet.
When Jamal's home internet acted up, the technician found that the router's domain name system settings were wrong.
Without the domain name system, people would need to type long strings of numbers to visit their favorite websites.

cloze.s: Typing a web address sends a request to the ___, which looks up the matching IP address.

note: Usually called DNS. It was introduced in 1983 to replace a single shared list of names.

def: sending data by breaking it into small pieces that travel separately across a network and are put back together at the end
why: It is the basic method the internet uses, letting many users share the same lines efficiently.
ex: Thanks to packet switching, pieces of Yuki's video call may travel by different routes and still be put back in the right order.
Paul Baran and Donald Davies developed packet switching independently in the 1960s.
Because of packet switching, data can travel around a broken cable by other routes instead of the whole message failing.
Unlike old telephone calls, which held one line open, packet switching lets many users share the same network links.

cloze.s: The early ARPANET used ___ rather than tying up one dedicated line for each conversation.

note: Old telephone networks used circuit switching, which keeps one line open for the whole call.

def: the idea that a network's value grows roughly with the square of its number of users
why: It helps explain why social networks and messaging apps grow more useful, and harder to compete with, as they get bigger.
ex: The investor cited Metcalfe's law to argue that the app would become far more valuable as more people joined.
Fax machines show Metcalfe's law at work: one is useless, but millions are very useful.
Metcalfe's law helps explain why a new social app with few users struggles to attract more.
Robert Metcalfe, a co-inventor of Ethernet, gave his name to Metcalfe's law about network value.

cloze.s: According to ___, doubling a network's users roughly quadruples its value.

note: Named after Robert Metcalfe, a co-inventor of Ethernet. It is a rule of thumb, not a precise law.

def: a computer design in which program instructions and data are kept in the same memory and handled by one processor
why: Most computers since the late 1940s follow this design, including the phones and laptops we use today.
ex: The von Neumann architecture made it possible to change what a computer does just by loading a new program.
Kwame's course explained how the von Neumann architecture differs from early machines that were rewired for each task.
Most laptops and phones today are still largely built on the von Neumann architecture, keeping programs and data in shared memory.
Engineers call the slow link between memory and processor the von Neumann bottleneck, a weakness of the von Neumann architecture.

cloze.s: Storing a program in memory alongside its data is the key idea of the ___, described by a mathematician in 1945.

note: Named after John von Neumann, though others working on early computers shared in the idea.

def: the open question of whether every problem whose answer can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly
why: The answer would affect online security, scheduling, medicine design and much more, and carries a million-dollar prize.
ex: If the P versus NP problem were solved in a surprising way, much of today's encryption could break.
Checking a finished sudoku is easy, but solving one is harder, which hints at the P versus NP problem.
The P versus NP problem is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, each with a one-million-dollar reward.
Liam's computer science class learned that the P versus NP problem asks whether puzzles that are easy to check are also easy to solve.

cloze.s: Computer scientists still do not know the answer to the ___, though most suspect that some problems are easy to check but hard to solve.

note: Also one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.

def: a 1494 agreement that split newly found lands outside Europe between Spain and Portugal along a line drawn on the map
why: It explains why Brazil speaks Portuguese while most of the rest of Latin America speaks Spanish.
ex: Under the Treaty of Tordesillas, lands west of the line went to Spain and lands east of it to Portugal.
Other European powers, such as England and France, simply ignored the Treaty of Tordesillas.
Because of the Treaty of Tordesillas, Brazil became Portuguese-speaking while most of South America speaks Spanish.
The Treaty of Tordesillas moved the pope's dividing line farther west, giving Portugal a larger share of the new lands.

cloze.s: Brazil's eastern bulge fell on Portugal's side of the line set by the ___ in 1494.

def: a set of about 280 laws issued by a king in ancient Iraq around 1750 BC and carved on a tall stone
why: It is one of the oldest and most complete written law codes, and it shows early ideas of fixed, public punishments.
ex: The Code of Hammurabi set penalties that depended on whether the victim was a noble, a commoner or a slave.
Visitors to the Louvre in Paris can see the black stone pillar carved with the Code of Hammurabi.
In world history class, Malik read laws from the Code of Hammurabi about builders whose houses collapsed.
The Code of Hammurabi is one of the oldest known written law collections, carved in wedge-shaped writing on stone.

cloze.s: The ancient Babylonian law "an eye for an eye" appears in the ___, written nearly 4,000 years ago.

note: Hammurabi ruled Babylon. The stone was found at Susa, in present-day Iran, in 1901–1902, where it had been carried off as war loot centuries later.

def: the roughly 200 years of relative peace and order across the Roman Empire, beginning with its first emperor
why: Safe roads and sea lanes in this period let trade, cities and ideas, including early Christianity, spread widely.
ex: During the Pax Romana, a merchant could travel from Spain to Syria on Roman roads with little fear of war.
Historians usually date the Pax Romana from 27 BC to AD 180.
Trade and city building flourished across the Mediterranean during the Pax Romana.
The Pax Romana was not perfectly peaceful, since Rome still fought wars along its frontiers.

cloze.s: The long calm known as the ___, Latin for "Roman peace," began under the first emperor, Augustus.

note: Writers now borrow the pattern, as in "Pax Americana," for a period of peace kept by one dominant power.

def: the military government that ruled Japan from 1603 to 1868, keeping long internal peace and limiting contact with foreigners
why: Its strict rule shaped traditional Japanese culture, and its fall opened the way to Japan's rapid modernization.
ex: Under the Tokugawa shogunate, the capital Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world.
The Tokugawa shogunate kept foreign trade to a few tightly controlled channels, such as a small Dutch trading post at Nagasaki.
Tokugawa Ieyasu founded the Tokugawa shogunate after winning the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600.
Hannah's history class studied how the Tokugawa shogunate required local lords to spend every other year in Edo.

cloze.s: The ___ ended in 1868, when power returned to the emperor in the Meiji Restoration.

note: Founded by Tokugawa Ieyasu. Edo, its capital, is today's Tokyo.

def: a medieval alliance of German and northern European trading cities that controlled much of the trade around the Baltic and North Seas
why: It shows how merchants, not kings, could build a powerful network that shaped the economy of northern Europe for centuries.
ex: Lübeck served as the leading city of the Hanseatic League.
Furs, timber, fish and cloth moved between Russia, Scandinavia and England through the Hanseatic League.
Merchants of the Hanseatic League ran a large trading base in London called the Steelyard.
Tomás toured the old wooden warehouses of Bergen, Norway, once a trading post of the Hanseatic League.

cloze.s: Hamburg still calls itself a "Hanseatic city," a reminder of its time in the ___.

note: It peaked in the 1300s and 1400s; its last general meeting was held in 1669.

def: a rich ancient trading state in what is now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, powerful from about AD 100 to the 900s
why: It was one of the first states anywhere to adopt Christianity, issued its own coins and linked Rome, Arabia and India by trade.
ex: Tall carved stone pillars raised by the Kingdom of Aksum still stand in northern Ethiopia.
King Ezana made Christianity the official religion of the Kingdom of Aksum in the 300s.
Aisha's history class studied the Kingdom of Aksum, one of the first states to put a cross on its coins.
Traders from the Kingdom of Aksum shipped ivory and gold through the Red Sea port of Adulis.

cloze.s: Gold coins from the ___ have been found as far away as India, showing the reach of its Red Sea trade.

def: a 1598 French law that granted Protestants the right to worship and helped end decades of religious war in France
why: It was an early, partial step toward religious tolerance in Europe; its reversal in 1685 drove many Protestants abroad.
ex: King Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes to bring peace between French Catholics and Protestants.
When Louis XIV canceled the Edict of Nantes in 1685, many skilled Protestant workers fled to England and the Netherlands.
Olga's history essay explained how the Edict of Nantes let French Protestants worship openly in many towns.
In class, Diego compared the Edict of Nantes with other early laws that granted religious tolerance.

cloze.s: The French Protestants known as Huguenots gained legal protection under the ___.

def: the guilty state of mind, such as intent or recklessness, that usually must be proved to find someone guilty of a crime
why: It is why the law treats an accident very differently from a planned act, even when the harm is the same.
ex: The defense argued there was no mens rea, since Diego truly believed the bike he took was his own.
Most serious crimes require both a harmful act and mens rea.
Jurors had to decide whether Tomás had mens rea, or whether he honestly forgot the bag was in his shopping cart.
Law students learn that some traffic offenses, like speeding, can be punished without proof of mens rea.

cloze.s: Prosecutors had to show ___, proving that the defendant knew the money was stolen when she took it.

note: Latin for "guilty mind." Its partner term, actus reus, means the guilty act itself.

def: a person or group, not part of a lawsuit, that offers a court information or arguments to help it decide
why: Major cases often draw many such briefs from experts and organizations hoping to shape the ruling.
ex: A group of doctors filed an amicus curiae brief explaining the medical facts to the court.
The judge allowed the university to appear as amicus curiae in the case about student data.
Several cities joined an amicus curiae brief asking the Supreme Court to consider the effect on local budgets.
As amicus curiae, a group of historians gave the court background on the old law at the center of the case.

cloze.s: Although it was not a party to the case, the trade association filed a brief as ___, Latin for "friend of the court."

note: Often shortened to "amicus," as in "an amicus brief." Plural: amici curiae.

def: the questioning of people called for jury duty by the judge and lawyers, to decide who will sit on the jury
why: It aims to remove jurors who might be biased, so that a trial is fair.
ex: During voir dire, Tomás was asked whether he had ever been the victim of a robbery.
The lawyers spent two full days on voir dire before the jury was finally chosen.
In voir dire, the defense lawyer asked each potential juror whether they had read news stories about the case.
Olga was dismissed during voir dire because she knew one of the witnesses personally.

cloze.s: Several people were excused during ___ after admitting they had already made up their minds about the case.

note: Pronounced "vwahr DEER" or "vor DIRE." It also refers to questioning a witness to test whether their evidence can be used.

def: a part of a law that makes the law end on a set date unless the legislature votes to extend it
why: It forces lawmakers to review a temporary measure instead of letting it run forever by default.
ex: The emergency powers came with a sunset clause, so they ended after one year.
Because of a sunset clause, the tax break will expire unless Congress acts again.
The city's trial program for free buses has a sunset clause, ending in two years unless the council renews it.
Lawmakers sometimes add a sunset clause to a new law so they can check whether it worked before keeping it.

cloze.s: Critics agreed to the new surveillance rules only after a(n) ___ was added requiring a fresh vote in five years.

def: the principle that decisions should be made at the most local level that can handle them well
why: It is a core principle of European Union law and a common argument in debates over national versus local power.
ex: Under subsidiarity, the EU should act only when a goal cannot be met well by member countries on their own.
The mayor appealed to subsidiarity, arguing that the town knew its own school needs best.
Following subsidiarity, the national sports federation let each local club set its own practice schedule.
The company applied subsidiarity by letting each store manager decide staffing rather than sending every choice to headquarters.

cloze.s: The principle of ___ suggests that a city, not the national government, should decide where to put its bus stops.

note: It also has deep roots in Catholic social teaching, notably a 1931 letter by Pope Pius XI.

def: the rule that a person becomes a citizen by being born on a country's land, whatever their parents' citizenship
why: Countries differ on it: many countries in the Americas grant citizenship this way, while most of Europe and Asia do not.
ex: Because of jus soli, Malik became a citizen simply by being born in the hospital in Toronto.
Most countries in Europe do not follow jus soli without conditions.
Many countries in the Americas, such as Brazil and Mexico, follow jus soli.
Yuki's law class compared jus soli, based on birthplace, with rules that pass citizenship from parents to children.

cloze.s: Latin for "right of the soil," ___ grants citizenship based on birthplace.

note: Its opposite, jus sanguinis ("right of blood"), passes citizenship through one's parents.

def: a way a U.S. president can kill a bill by not signing it while Congress is away and cannot get it back
why: Unlike a regular veto, it cannot be overridden by Congress, because the bill simply fails.
ex: The bill died by pocket veto when the president left it unsigned during the break.
Lawmakers sometimes avoid long breaks at the end of a session to prevent a pocket veto.
Sofia's civics teacher explained that, unlike a regular veto, a pocket veto cannot be overridden by Congress.
The senator worried that sending the bill to the president just before the holiday recess could invite a pocket veto.

cloze.s: Because Congress had adjourned, the president's silence on the bill counted as a(n) ___.

note: It applies when the president has not signed the bill within ten days, not counting Sundays, and Congress's adjournment prevents its return.

def: a side comment in a judge's ruling that is not needed to decide the case, so later courts need not follow it
why: Lawyers must tell these side comments apart from the core reasoning, which does set precedent.
ex: The judge's comment about free speech online was only an obiter dictum, so lower courts were not bound by it.
Law students learn to separate the ruling's key reasoning from any obiter dictum.
The lawyer quoted the judge's remark in court, but the other side called it an obiter dictum with no binding force.
In her case brief, Aisha labeled the judge's remark about future technology as obiter dictum, not part of the actual ruling.

cloze.s: Because the comment was a(n) ___, "something said in passing," later courts could ignore it.

note: Plural: obiter dicta. Such remarks can still be quoted as persuasive, just not as binding.

def: describes an action taken by a government body, official or company that goes beyond the powers it legally has
why: Courts can cancel such actions, which keeps agencies and officials within the limits set by law.
ex: The court ruled that the city council's new tax was ultra vires because only the state could impose it.
The shareholders argued that the board had acted ultra vires by selling the company's main asset.
The student council's decision to cancel classes was ultra vires, since only the principal had that power.
Hannah's law textbook explained that a rule issued ultra vires can be struck down even if it seems sensible.

cloze.s: Because the agency had no legal authority to issue the rule, the judge declared it ___.

note: Latin for "beyond the powers."

def: a situation in a strategic game where no player can do better by changing only their own choice
why: It is a core idea of game theory, used to study pricing, auctions, arms races and negotiations.
ex: Two gas stations both charging the same price can be a Nash equilibrium, since neither gains by changing alone.
In the prisoner's dilemma, both players confessing is the Nash equilibrium, even though both would do better staying silent.
Driving on the right is a Nash equilibrium in the United States, since no single driver gains by switching sides.
When every driver picks the fastest route given everyone else's choices, traffic settles into a Nash equilibrium.

cloze.s: Once each company's ad budget was its best response to the other's, the market had reached a(n) ___.

note: Named after mathematician John Nash, who described it in 1950 and shared the 1994 Nobel Prize in economics. His life inspired the film A Beautiful Mind.

def: the plan agreed in 1944, after World War II, that fixed world currencies to the U.S. dollar and the dollar to gold
why: It created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank and shaped the world economy until the early 1970s.
ex: Under the Bretton Woods system, foreign governments could swap dollars for gold at 35 dollars an ounce.
The Bretton Woods system broke down after the United States stopped exchanging dollars for gold in 1971.
Wei's history textbook explained that the International Monetary Fund was created as part of the Bretton Woods system.
Because the Bretton Woods system kept exchange rates mostly fixed, importers found their costs easier to predict.

cloze.s: Delegates from 44 nations met at a New Hampshire resort in 1944 to design the ___.

note: Named after Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, where the conference was held.

def: a graph showing a pattern in which lower unemployment tends to come with higher inflation, and the reverse
why: Central banks still debate it when deciding whether low unemployment will push prices up.
ex: The high inflation and high unemployment of the 1970s made many economists doubt the Phillips curve.
The economist argued that the Phillips curve had flattened, since prices barely rose as jobs grew.
The central bank's report used the Phillips curve to predict that falling unemployment would push prices higher.
The Phillips curve is named after economist A. W. Phillips, who studied British wages and unemployment in 1958.

cloze.s: According to the ___, pushing unemployment very low can lead to rising wages and prices.

note: Named after New Zealand economist A. W. Phillips, who published the pattern for Britain in 1958.

def: trying to gain wealth by getting special favors, such as rules that block rivals, rather than by creating new value
why: Economists see it as wasteful because the effort spent chasing favors produces nothing new for society.
ex: Critics called the industry's push for a license that only a few firms could obtain a clear case of rent-seeking.
Hiring armies of lobbyists to win a tariff is a classic example of rent-seeking.
The economist argued that some patent lawsuits were rent-seeking, aimed at collecting fees rather than inventing anything.
Maria's economics class discussed how rent-seeking wastes resources, since effort goes into winning favors instead of making things.

cloze.s: Instead of building better products, the firm spent millions on ___, lobbying for rules that kept new rivals out.

note: Here "rent" means income beyond what a free market would pay, not money for housing. The term was coined by Anne Krueger in 1974.

def: the process in which new products, firms and methods replace old ones, wiping out some jobs and businesses while creating others
why: It describes how economies grow and change, as when streaming replaced video rental stores.
ex: Digital cameras and then smartphones were creative destruction for the film photography business.
Hannah's economics professor used ride-hailing apps and taxi companies to illustrate creative destruction.
When streaming services spread, video rental stores closed while new jobs appeared in online entertainment, a case of creative destruction.
Some towns felt the pain of creative destruction when online shopping replaced local stores but created warehouse jobs.

cloze.s: Joseph Schumpeter called it ___ when innovation sweeps away older industries while building new ones.

note: Popularized by economist Joseph Schumpeter in his 1942 book Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy.

def: a luxury item that people want more of when its price rises, because a high price signals status
why: It breaks the usual rule that higher prices lower demand, which matters for pricing designer brands.
ex: When the handbag maker raised prices, sales went up, the classic pattern of a Veblen good.
Some rare whiskeys act like a Veblen good: cutting the price could make buyers think less of them.
The perfume brand refused to hold sales, fearing its Veblen good would lose appeal if it ever looked cheap.
Malik's economics teacher explained that a Veblen good breaks the usual rule that higher prices mean fewer buyers.

cloze.s: A luxury watch can behave as a(n) ___, selling better at 10,000 dollars than it would at 1,000.

note: Named after economist Thorstein Veblen, who coined "conspicuous consumption" in 1899.

def: the theory that stock prices already reflect all known information, so no one can consistently beat the market
why: It is a main argument for buying low-cost index funds instead of trying to pick winning stocks.
ex: Believers in the efficient-market hypothesis say a hot stock tip is usually already built into the price.
Market bubbles and crashes lead some economists to question the efficient-market hypothesis.
Citing the efficient-market hypothesis, Maria put her savings in a low-cost index fund instead of picking stocks.
Eugene Fama, who developed the efficient-market hypothesis, shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in economics.

cloze.s: Under the ___, good news about a company is reflected in its share price almost instantly.

note: Associated with economist Eugene Fama, who shared the 2013 Nobel Prize in economics.

def: the harm to a country's farming and factories that can follow a sudden boom in selling oil, gas or other resources
why: It explains why a resource discovery can make a country's other exports more expensive and less competitive abroad.
ex: Economists warned that the new oil fields could bring Dutch disease, hurting the country's farmers and factories.
Dutch disease happens when resource money pushes up the currency, so other exports become harder to sell.
Wei's economics class debated whether a country's new gold mines might cause Dutch disease by weakening its factories.
To avoid Dutch disease, Norway saves much of its oil income in a fund invested abroad.

cloze.s: The Economist coined the term ___ in 1977 after a gas boom in the Netherlands was followed by a decline in its factories.

note: Named after the Netherlands, whose large natural gas find in 1959 was followed by a decline in its manufacturing.

def: the pattern in which making a resource more efficient to use leads people to use more of it in total, not less
why: It matters in energy policy, since better fuel efficiency alone may not cut total fuel use.
ex: When LED bulbs made lighting cheap, people lit more spaces for longer, an example of the Jevons paradox.
The Jevons paradox warns that faster, cheaper computers can raise total energy use.
When cars got better gas mileage, people drove farther, and some economists pointed to the Jevons paradox.
The Jevons paradox comes from William Stanley Jevons's 1865 book The Coal Question.

cloze.s: Better steam engines used less coal each, yet Britain burned more coal overall, the original case of the ___.

note: Named after William Stanley Jevons, who described it in his 1865 book The Coal Question.

def: slow, regular changes in the shape of Earth's path around the Sun and in the angle and direction of its axis
why: They change how much sunlight reaches different parts of Earth and help set the timing of past ice ages.
ex: Over the past million years, Milankovitch cycles have helped set the rhythm of ice ages advancing and retreating.
Ice cores from Antarctica record temperature swings that match the timing of Milankovitch cycles.
Milankovitch cycles slowly change how much sunlight reaches each part of Earth during different seasons.
One of the Milankovitch cycles is a slow change in Earth's tilt, which swings between about 22 and 24.5 degrees over roughly 41,000 years.

cloze.s: Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković calculated how changes in Earth's orbit and tilt, now called ___, could trigger ice ages.

note: They work over tens of thousands of years or more, far too slowly to explain the warming seen since the 1800s.

def: the slow, worldwide movement of ocean water driven by differences in how warm the water is and how much salt it holds
why: It carries heat, oxygen and nutrients around the planet and plays a major part in Earth's climate.
ex: Scientists study whether melting Arctic ice could slow the thermohaline circulation in the Atlantic.
Water carried by the thermohaline circulation can take about a thousand years to travel the full loop.
Kenji's oceanography class learned that the thermohaline circulation carries heat from the tropics toward the poles.
Adding fresh water to the ocean's surface can slow the thermohaline circulation, because less salty water is less likely to sink.

cloze.s: Cold, salty water sinks near Greenland and drives the ___, often called the global ocean conveyor belt.

note: From Greek words for "heat" and "salt."

def: an invisible boundary through Indonesia that separates Asian wildlife to the west from Australian-type wildlife to the east
why: It was early evidence that animals' locations reflect Earth's history, supporting the theory of evolution.
ex: Bali and Lombok are only about 35 kilometers apart, yet they sit on opposite sides of the Wallace Line.
Tigers once lived on Bali, west of the Wallace Line, but never on nearby Lombok, just to the east.
On her trip to Indonesia, Yuki crossed the Wallace Line and noticed that many of the birds looked different.
The Wallace Line follows a deep ocean channel that stayed underwater even when sea levels dropped during the ice ages.

cloze.s: Naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace described the ___ in 1859 after noticing sharp differences in the animals of nearby islands.

note: Deep water between the islands stayed open even when ice-age sea levels dropped, keeping the animal groups apart.

def: land where water slowly eats away limestone or similar rock, leaving caves, holes in the ground and underground rivers
why: Many caves and much of Florida's sinkhole risk come from it, and it supplies drinking water to many people.
ex: The karst under central Florida is why sinkholes sometimes swallow roads and houses.
Mammoth Cave in Kentucky, the world's longest known cave system, formed in karst.
Hannah's cave tour guide explained that the whole region was karst, with rivers flowing through tunnels beneath the fields.
The towering limestone hills around Guilin, China, are a famous karst landscape.

cloze.s: Rainwater slowly ate away the limestone, creating a(n) ___ landscape full of caves and disappearing streams.

note: Named after the Kras region of Slovenia, where these landforms were first studied in detail.

def: a ring-shaped coral island or chain of islands around a shallow pool of sea water, often built on an old, sunken volcano
why: Countries such as the Maldives are made mostly of them, and their low height makes them very vulnerable to rising seas.
ex: From the plane, the atoll looked like a green ring around bright blue water.
Most of the land on the atoll stands only a meter or two above sea level.
Divers love the Maldives, where each atoll circles a calm lagoon full of fish.
Rising seas threaten island nations like Kiribati, where most people live on low atolls.

cloze.s: Charles Darwin proposed that a(n) ___ forms when coral keeps growing upward around a volcano that slowly sinks.

note: Darwin's explanation, published in 1842, was later confirmed by deep drilling in the Pacific.

def: a place where one of Earth's plates slides beneath another and sinks down into the hot layer below
why: It produces the world's largest earthquakes, deepest ocean trenches and many active volcanoes.
ex: The deadly 2011 earthquake in Japan struck along a subduction zone off the country's coast.
The volcanoes of the Andes formed above a subduction zone where an ocean plate dives under South America.
The Cascadia subduction zone off the Pacific Northwest could someday produce a very large earthquake.
Hannah's geology class built a clay model of a subduction zone, sliding one slab slowly under the other.

cloze.s: The Mariana Trench, the deepest point in the oceans, lies where the Pacific plate sinks beneath another plate at a(n) ___.

note: Most volcanoes in the Pacific Ring of Fire sit above them.

def: an area of land whose rivers drain into a lake or desert and never reach the ocean
why: Water leaves only by soaking in or drying up, which is why many such lakes, like the Dead Sea, are very salty.
ex: The Great Basin in Nevada and Utah is a huge endorheic basin with no outlet to the sea.
Because it is an endorheic basin, the Caspian Sea's level rises and falls with the balance between river inflow and evaporation.
The Dead Sea lies in an endorheic basin, so the Jordan River's water ends there instead of flowing to the ocean.
On the field trip, Hannah's geology class visited a dry salt flat at the bottom of an endorheic basin.

cloze.s: The Great Salt Lake is salty because it sits in a(n) ___, where water escapes only by drying up and leaves salt behind.

note: From Greek words meaning "flowing within."

def: the dry belt of grass and scattered bushes that stretches across Africa just south of the Sahara Desert
why: It is often in the news for droughts, hunger and efforts to stop the desert from spreading south.
ex: Farmers in the Sahel depend on a short rainy season that can fail in drought years.
The Great Green Wall project aims to restore land across the Sahel from Senegal to Djibouti.
Herders in the Sahel move their cattle with the seasons to find water and fresh grass.
The news report described how a long drought in the Sahel in the 1970s and 1980s caused widespread hunger.

cloze.s: Countries such as Mali, Niger and Chad lie partly in the ___, the dry zone between the Sahara and the wetter south.

note: From an Arabic word for "shore" or "coast," seeing the Sahara as a sea of sand.

def: a work that combines music, drama, poetry, design and other arts into one unified whole
why: Richard Wagner made the idea famous in his operas, and critics still use it for films, stage shows and buildings.
ex: Wagner designed his opera house in Bayreuth to present each opera as a Gesamtkunstwerk.
The reviewer called the immersive show a true Gesamtkunstwerk, blending music, light, dance and architecture.
Aisha, the architect, saw the new opera house as a Gesamtkunstwerk, designing its furniture, lighting and even door handles.
Students in the arts program spent a year on a Gesamtkunstwerk, composing the music, writing the script, and making the sets and costumes.

cloze.s: Richard Wagner wrote in 1849 about the ___, a "total work of art" uniting every art form.

note: German for "total work of art." A writer named Trahndorff used it first, in 1827, before Wagner popularized it.

def: a painting method of blending colors and tones so softly that edges seem to melt into each other like smoke
why: It gives the Mona Lisa her famously mysterious smile and is a hallmark of Leonardo da Vinci's style.
ex: Leonardo used sfumato to soften the corners of the Mona Lisa's mouth and eyes.
The art teacher showed how sfumato creates gentle shadows without any hard outlines.
Using sfumato in a digital painting app, Wei blurred the edges of the portrait until no hard lines remained.
The museum guide pointed out the sfumato around the eyes, where no clear outline separated skin from shadow.

cloze.s: Instead of sharp lines, the painter used ___, building up thin layers until the face seemed to fade into shadow.
