fix: Picture the choice as if both options were far in the future; if your answer changes, the nearness of one option is swaying you.

tests.s: Each January, Priya plans to start saving for retirement “next month,” but every month she spends that money on things she wants right away.
Asked on Monday, most gym members say they’ll choose a workout over sleeping in on Saturday, but when Saturday morning comes, most of them stay in bed.

def: when a researcher’s hopes, without meaning to, change how people in a study act or how results are recorded
scenario: A researcher who expects a new teaching method to work smiles and nods more at the students using it, and those students try harder on the test.
fix: Keep the people running a study unaware of which group is which, so their expectations can’t shape the results.
note: Classic case: the horse Clever Hans seemed to do arithmetic until Oskar Pfungst showed in 1907 that it was reading its questioners’ unconscious cues.

tests.s: A horse seems to count by tapping its hoof, but it gets answers right only when its questioner knows the answer and, without meaning to, relaxes as the horse reaches the right number.
Tasters prefer a chef’s new sauce when he serves it himself, sure that it’s better, but when an assistant who doesn’t know which sauce is which serves them, the preference disappears.

def: the mistaken pattern: A or B is true; A is true; so B must be false, even though both could be true
scenario: “The job requires a degree or five years of experience. Sofia has a degree, so she must not have five years of experience.”
fix: Check whether “or” allows both options to be true; usually it does, so one being true tells you nothing about the other.

tests.s: “To get into the lounge, you need a gold card or a first-class ticket. Yuki has a gold card, so she can’t have a first-class ticket.”
“You get the discount if you’re a student or a senior. Liam is a student, so he can’t be a senior.”

def: an argument that, if it worked, would also prove things that are clearly false, which shows something is wrong with it
scenario: Omar argues that homework should be banned because some students find it stressful. By that logic, exams, sports tryouts and job interviews should all be banned too.
fix: Apply the same reasoning to other cases; if it leads to absurd conclusions there, it is flawed here too.

tests.s: “Cars should be banned because people sometimes die in accidents,” Ana argues, though the same reasoning would also ban stairs, swimming pools and kitchen knives.
A student claims that since memories can be wrong, no eyewitness should ever be believed, an argument that would also rule out trusting his own memory of the study he is citing.

def: assuming an outcome had just one cause when several causes worked together to produce it
scenario: After a losing season, fans blame only the new coach, ignoring injuries to three starting players and a much tougher schedule.
fix: List all the factors that could have contributed, and ask how much each one likely mattered.

tests.s: A news report blames a bridge collapse entirely on one overloaded truck, without mentioning years of skipped repairs and a flaw in the bridge’s design.
Wei insists his restaurant closed only because of one bad online review, though his rent had doubled and a new highway had moved traffic away from his street.

def: trying to turn an audience against someone before they speak, so that nothing the person says will be taken seriously
scenario: Before Maria presents her budget plan, a coworker tells the room, “Keep in mind she’s always been bad with numbers.”
fix: Judge what the person actually says when they say it, not the warning someone gave beforehand.
note: A personal attack made in advance. The phrase in this sense comes from John Henry Newman’s 1864 book Apologia Pro Vita Sua.

tests.s: Introducing the next debater, the host says, “Our next speaker will probably just repeat the usual nonsense, but let’s hear him out anyway.”
Before the new manager’s first meeting, Kofi tells his teammates that she’ll only pretend to listen and that any idea she brings will be useless.

def: the uncomfortable feeling of holding two beliefs that clash, or of acting against a belief, often eased by changing the belief
scenario: Liam sees himself as a healthy person but smokes every day, so he starts telling himself that a few cigarettes aren’t really harmful.
fix: When you notice yourself changing a belief right after acting against it, ask whether the evidence changed or only your comfort did.
note: The theory was proposed by psychologist Leon Festinger in 1957.

tests.s: Members of a group that predicted the world would end on a certain date become even more devoted after the date passes, saying their faith is what saved the world.
Rafael always said cheating is wrong, but after copying a classmate’s homework, he decides that homework rules are silly and copying isn’t really cheating.

def: spending far too much time on small, easy matters while large, complicated ones get little attention
scenario: A school board approves a $5 million building budget in ten minutes, then argues for an hour about the color of the new sign out front.
fix: Give each item time in proportion to how much it matters, and save the longest discussion for the biggest decisions.
note: Comes from C. Northcote Parkinson’s 1957 example of a committee that quickly approves a nuclear reactor but argues at length over a bicycle shed.

tests.s: A software team’s review skims the security setup in five minutes but spends an hour debating which shade of blue the login button should be.
At the condo meeting, owners approve a costly roof replacement almost at once, then argue for most of the evening about where to put the new bike rack.

q: cygnet : swan :: leveret : ?
why: A cygnet is a young swan, and a leveret is a young hare. A young rabbit is called a kit or kitten, so rabbit is the tempting wrong choice.

q: codicil : will :: amendment : ?
why: A codicil is a later addition that changes a will; an amendment is a later addition that changes a constitution. A legislature may pass amendments, but it is not the document being changed.

q: teetotaler : alcohol :: vegan : ?
why: A teetotaler never drinks alcohol, and a vegan never eats or uses animal products. Vegetables are what a vegan does eat, the reverse of the relationship.

q: plagiarize : ideas :: embezzle : ?
why: To plagiarize is to steal someone else’s ideas or words; to embezzle is to steal money you were trusted to manage. A bank is a place it might happen, not the thing taken.

q: stanza : poem :: movement : ?
why: A stanza is one section of a poem, and a movement is one section of a symphony. An orchestra performs the symphony but is not made of movements.

q: cacophony : sound :: eyesore : ?
why: A cacophony is a harsh, unpleasant sound, and an eyesore is an ugly, unpleasant sight. Noise belongs with the first pair, not the second.

q: heretic : religious doctrine :: dissident : ?
why: A heretic openly rejects the official teaching of a religion; a dissident openly opposes the official policy of a government. Prison may be a dissident’s fate, not what they reject.

q: invulnerable : harm :: infallible : ?
why: Something invulnerable cannot be harmed, and someone infallible cannot make an error. Criticism is tempting, but an infallible person can still be criticized; they just are never wrong.

q: pedant : minor details :: hypochondriac : ?
why: A pedant worries too much about minor details, and a hypochondriac worries too much about having an illness. Doctors are people a hypochondriac visits, not what they fret about.

q: anesthetic : pain :: muffler : ?
why: An anesthetic blocks or dulls pain, and a muffler dulls an engine’s noise. Exhaust passes through a muffler, but the muffler’s job is to quiet the noise, not to stop the exhaust.

q: frugality : extravagance :: diligence : ?
why: Frugality (careful spending) is the opposite of extravagance (wasteful spending), and diligence (steady hard work) is the opposite of laziness. Effort and care are close to diligence, not opposite.

q: drought : famine :: spark : ?
why: A drought can cause a famine, and a spark can cause a fire. Flint and a match produce sparks, so they come before the spark rather than after it.

q: “The dinner began with friendly persiflage about Tomás’s terrible golf swing, but the mood turned serious once the talk shifted to the layoffs.” What does persiflage most likely mean?
options: a toast given in honor of someone
why: It is friendly and about a golf swing, and it contrasts with the serious talk that follows, so it means playful joking. A heated argument would not be described as friendly.

q: “The judge fined the contumacious witness after he refused, for the third time, to answer her questions or obey her orders to stop interrupting.” What does contumacious most likely mean?
why: He refuses again and again to follow the judge’s orders, so the word means stubbornly refusing to obey authority. Nothing suggests he was nervous; his refusals were deliberate.

q: “The editor cut the paragraph as otiose: it repeated points already made, added no new facts, and served no purpose in the story.” What does otiose most likely mean?
why: The paragraph only repeated earlier points and “served no purpose,” so the word means useless or unnecessary. It is not called wrong or confusing, only pointless.

q: “The guard dog gave a low, minatory growl, and the delivery driver backed slowly toward the gate.” What does minatory most likely mean?
why: The growl makes the driver back away, so it is threatening. Playful would not make someone retreat, and the similar-looking word “minute” (tiny) is a trap.

q: “Health officials had declared the outbreak over, so the recrudescence of cases in the spring caught them off guard.” What does recrudescence most likely mean?
options: a fresh outbreak after a quiet period
why: The outbreak was thought to be over, then cases appeared again, so the word means breaking out again after a lull. A disappearance is the opposite of what surprised the officials.

q: “Many friendships begin through simple propinquity: people who sit near each other at work or live on the same hall tend to become close.” What does propinquity most likely mean?
why: The examples are sitting near each other and living on the same hall, so the word means being physically close. Shared hobbies could also start friendships, but the sentence’s examples are all about location.

q: “Instead of answering the reporter’s simple question, the senator began to bloviate, talking for ten minutes in grand phrases that said almost nothing.” What does bloviate most likely mean?
options: to speak at length in a pompous, empty way
why: He talks for ten minutes in grand phrases that say almost nothing, so the word means to speak long-windedly and pompously. Refusing to speak is the opposite of what he does.

q: “The coach’s hortatory halftime speech, full of calls to ‘dig deeper’ and ‘leave everything on the field,’ fired up the tired players.” What does hortatory most likely mean?
why: The speech is full of calls to try harder and it fires the players up, so it means urging people to act. Nothing in it is described as angry or insulting.

q: “After the scandal, the once-admired mayor faced months of public obloquy, with newspapers and former allies condemning her in harsh terms.” What does obloquy most likely mean?
why: She is condemned harshly by newspapers and former allies, so the word means fierce public criticism and the shame that follows. Praise and support is the opposite.

q: “Street vendors importuned the tourists at every corner, following them and asking again and again until the visitors finally bought something.” What does importune most likely mean?
options: to ask someone persistently and annoyingly
why: The vendors follow the tourists and ask again and again, so the word means to pester with repeated requests. “Bring goods from abroad” comes from confusing it with “import.”

q: “After years of saving, Aisha booked a sybaritic week at a resort: silk sheets, daily massages, and champagne at every sunset.” What does sybaritic most likely mean?
why: Silk sheets, massages and champagne describe indulgence and comfort, so the word means given over to luxury and pleasure. Simple and strict is the opposite.

q: “Unwilling to approve or reject the plan, the director chose to temporize, asking for more studies and putting off the vote month after month.” What does temporize most likely mean?
options: to stall in order to avoid deciding
why: The director avoids saying yes or no and keeps delaying with requests for studies, so the word means to stall to gain time. Acting boldly is the opposite of what the director does.

q: At an online store, the share of orders that were returned rose from 4% last year to 6% this year. Which must be true?
options: The return rate rose by 2 percentage points, a 50% increase in the rate.
The number of returned orders rose by 50%.
Twice as many orders were returned this year.
The store sold fewer items this year.
Customers were less happy this year.
why: Going from 4% to 6% is a rise of 2 percentage points, or 50% of the old rate, so “rose by 2%” is wrong. The number of returns is unknown, since total orders aren’t given.

term: Inference: speed bumps on worst streets
q: A city added speed bumps to the 10 streets that had the most crashes last year. This year, crashes on those 10 streets fell by 30%. Which, if true, most weakens the claim that the speed bumps caused the drop?
options: The speed bumps cost more than the city expected.
Drivers complained that the bumps slowed their trips.
Crashes on the city’s other streets stayed about the same.
In past years, streets that had unusually many crashes saw them fall by about 30% the next year even without any changes.
The bumps were painted bright yellow so drivers would see them.
Most of the crashes happened at night.
why: Streets picked for an unusually bad year tend to drift back toward normal on their own, so a 30% drop is what would be expected anyway. Steady crash rates on other streets would, if anything, support the bumps.

q: Patients taking a certain heart drug are more likely to die within a year than patients with heart disease who don’t take it. Which, if true, best explains this without the drug causing harm?
options: The drug must be taken twice a day.
Patients taking the drug see their doctors more often.
Some patients forget to take the drug.
The drug was approved only a few years ago.
Doctors mainly prescribe the drug to patients whose heart disease is already severe.
why: If the sickest patients are the ones who get the drug, they would die more often even if the drug helps. Missed doses might weaken the drug’s effect but would not make users die more than nonusers.

q: A shop’s owner says, “Our new website brought in more business: since it launched, online orders have doubled.” The argument depends on which assumption?
options: The website was cheap to build.
The growth in online orders did not come mostly from customers who used to order by phone or in person switching to the web.
Online customers spend more per order than other customers.
The shop’s competitors have no websites.
The website will keep working without problems.
Most of the shop’s customers are young.
why: If the extra online orders were just old customers changing how they order, total business may not have grown at all. Spending more per order is not needed for the owner’s claim.

q: A magazine asked readers to mail in their views on a new law. Of the 5,000 replies, 80% opposed it. The editors conclude that most people in the country oppose the law. What is the biggest weakness in this reasoning?
options: 5,000 replies is too few to say anything at all.
80% is not a large enough majority.
Some replies may have arrived late.
The law may change in the future.
The people who chose to reply, all readers of one magazine, may not think like the country as a whole.
The magazine did not say who wrote the law.
why: The replies come from self-selected readers of one magazine, who may feel more strongly or differently than others. A well-chosen sample of 5,000 would be plenty, so the size is not the main problem.

q: Over five years, a drug lowers the risk of a heart attack from 2 in 1,000 people to 1 in 1,000. An ad says the drug “cuts your risk in half.” Which is best supported?
options: Half of the people who take the drug will avoid a heart attack.
About 1,000 people would need to take the drug for five years to prevent one heart attack.
The drug lowers risk by 50 percentage points.
Without the drug, most people will have a heart attack.
The drug prevents 500 heart attacks per 1,000 users.
why: The risk falls by 1 in 1,000, so about 1,000 people must take it to prevent one heart attack. The ad is technically true, since 1 is half of 2, but it hides how small the change is.

term: Inference: air filters and sick days
q: After a factory installed new air filters, workers’ sick days fell by 20% over the next year. Which, if true, most strengthens the claim that the filters caused the drop?
options: Workers said they liked the new filters.
The filters cost less than expected.
Sick days also fell by about 20% at most other factories in the region that year.
The factory hired more workers that year.
At the company’s other factory nearby, which got no new filters, sick days stayed the same that year.
The filters must be replaced every six months.
why: A similar factory without filters showed no change, which helps rule out a general cause such as a mild flu season. A region-wide drop would weaken the claim, not strengthen it.

q: Corals get most of their food from tiny algae that live inside them. When the water stays too warm for weeks, corals push out the algae and turn white, which is called bleaching. Bleached corals can recover if the water cools soon enough, but if the algae don’t return, the coral starves. Which is best supported?
options: A coral that has bleached is not necessarily dead.
Cold water is the main cause of bleaching.
The algae harm the coral they live in.
Corals get all of their food from algae.
Warm water helps the algae grow inside corals.
why: The passage says bleached corals can recover if the water cools soon enough, so bleaching does not always mean death. It says “most” of their food comes from the algae, not all.

q: Class A has 20 students, whose average test score was 80. Class B has 30 students, whose average was 70. What was the average score of all 50 students together?
why: The total is 20 × 80 + 30 × 70 = 1,600 + 2,100 = 3,700, and 3,700 ÷ 50 = 74. Simply averaging 80 and 70 gives 75, which ignores that Class B is larger.

q: A report finds that most car crashes happen within five miles of the driver’s home and concludes that driving near home is more dangerous than driving farther away. Which best explains the finding without that conclusion being true?
options: Roads near homes have more stop signs.
Crash reports are often filed late.
Drivers far from home use maps.
Most of the driving people do is within a few miles of home.
why: If most miles are driven near home, most crashes would happen there even if each mile is no riskier. Faster highway driving would, if anything, make far-from-home driving look more dangerous.

q: A town has 10,000 registered voters. In a recent election, 60% of them voted, and Candidate Reyes won 55% of the votes cast. Each voter cast one vote in this race. Which must be true?
options: Most of the town’s registered voters voted for Reyes.
Reyes received votes from 55% of the registered voters.
why: 6,000 people voted, and 55% of 6,000 is 3,300. The 5,500 figure wrongly applies 55% to all 10,000 registered voters, most of whom did not vote for Reyes.

q: Trees in cool climates usually add one growth ring each year, wider in good growing years and narrower in poor ones. The pattern of rings in a beam from an old barn exactly matches part of a dated record from local trees, and the beam’s outermost ring matches the year 1842. Which is best supported?
options: The tree was cut down before 1842.
The summer of 1842 was very dry.
The tree that the beam came from was still alive in 1842.
Every tree in the world adds exactly one ring per year.
why: A ring for 1842 means the tree was still growing that year. The barn need not date from 1842, since outer rings may have been trimmed off and the barn could have been built later.

q: Five people live on floors 1 to 5 of a building, one per floor. Dee lives on the floor directly above Ana. Eli lives below Bo, and Bo lives below Caz. Ana does not live on floor 1. Caz does not live on the top floor. Who lives on floor 3?
why: If Ana and Dee were on floors 2–3 or 3–4, Caz, the highest of Eli, Bo and Caz, would land on floor 5, which is not allowed. So Ana and Dee are on 4 and 5, and Eli, Bo and Caz fill floors 1, 2 and 3.

term: Logic: not the case that none
q: “It is not the case that none of the applicants speak French.” Which statement means the same?
options: All of the applicants speak French.
Most of the applicants speak French.
At least one applicant speaks French.
At least one applicant does not speak French.
why: Denying “none speak French” means at least one does. It doesn’t tell us that all, most or exactly one do, and it says nothing about whether anyone doesn’t.

q: Tara will join the trip only if Uri joins. Uri joins whenever the trip falls on a weekend. Tara joined the trip. Which must be true?
options: Uri joined, and the trip was on a weekend.
Nothing can be concluded about Uri.
The trip was on a weekday.
Uri may or may not have joined.
Whenever Uri joins, Tara joins too.
Uri joined, but the trip may not have been on a weekend.
why: Tara joining requires Uri, so Uri joined. A weekend guarantees Uri joins, but Uri might join on other days too, so we can’t tell when the trip was.

q: No reptiles have fur. Some pets have fur. Which must be true?
options: Every pet with fur is a dog or a cat.
why: The pets that have fur can’t be reptiles, so at least some pets are not reptiles. Nothing rules out other pets being reptiles, so “No pets are reptiles” does not follow.

q: Three boxes are labeled “Apples,” “Oranges” and “Mixed.” One holds only apples, one only oranges, and one both, but every label is wrong. You take one fruit from the box labeled “Mixed,” and it is an apple. What is in the box labeled “Oranges”?
options: Either only apples or only oranges
why: The “Mixed” box can’t really be mixed, so the apple shows it holds only apples. The “Oranges” box can’t hold oranges, and apples are taken, so it holds the mix.

q: Of 100 employees, 80 drink coffee, 70 drink tea and 60 drink juice. What is the smallest possible number who drink all three?
why: At most 20 skip coffee, 30 skip tea and 40 skip juice, so at most 90 people skip at least one drink. That leaves at least 10 who drink all three, and 10 is possible if no one skips two drinks.

q: Any student who earns all A’s makes the honor roll. A student makes the honor roll only if she has five or fewer absences. Ines earned all A’s. Which must be true?
options: Ines may have more than five absences.
Every student with five or fewer absences makes the honor roll.
Only students with all A’s make the honor roll.
Ines did not make the honor roll.
Ines has five or fewer absences.
Ines made the honor roll, but her absences can’t be judged.
why: All A’s puts Ines on the honor roll, and being on the honor roll requires five or fewer absences. “Every student with five or fewer absences makes the honor roll” reverses the “only if” rule and is not stated.

q: If the shop is open, then Ali or Bea is working. Bea works only on weekends. Today is Tuesday, and Ali is home sick and not working. Which must be true?
options: The shop is open, but no one is working.
why: Bea can’t work on a Tuesday and Ali isn’t working, so neither is working. An open shop would need one of them, so the shop is closed.

q: Which statement means the same as “Neither Jo nor Kim was at the party”?
options: Jo or Kim was not at the party.
Jo and Kim were not both at the party.
Jo was not at the party, and Kim was not at the party.
Jo was at the party, but Kim was not.
At least one of them was at the party.
If Jo was at the party, Kim was not.
why: “Neither…nor” means both were absent. “Not both were there” is weaker: it would still be true if one of them came.

q: Most of a club’s members are students. Most of the club’s members are under 25. Which must be true?
options: Most students in the club are under 25.
All students in the club are under 25.
Exactly half the members are students.
No member is both a student and under 25.
At least one member is both a student and under 25.
why: Each group is more than half the club, so the two groups must overlap in at least one person. They could overlap only slightly, so “most students are under 25” does not follow.

q: Ari, Ben, Cam and Dov each ordered a different drink: tea, coffee, juice or cocoa. Ari ordered neither tea nor coffee. Ben ordered either cocoa or juice. Cam did not order tea. Which must be true?
why: Ari and Ben use up juice and cocoa between them, though we can’t tell who has which. That leaves tea and coffee for Cam and Dov, and since Cam didn’t order tea, Dov did.

term: Logic: light if and only if
q: The light is on if and only if the switch is up and the power is on. Right now the light is off, and the switch is up. Which must be true?
options: Both the switch and the power are off.
why: With “if and only if,” the light is off exactly when at least one condition fails. The switch is up, so the power must be off. The rule as stated leaves no room for other causes, such as a burned-out bulb.

q: Which word is most similar in meaning to perspicuous (as in “a perspicuous explanation”)?
why: Perspicuous means clearly expressed and easy to understand. Insightful is the meaning of perspicacious, a different word that looks very similar.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of tenebrous?
why: Tenebrous means dark and shadowy, so luminous (full of light) is its opposite. Shadowy and gloomy are close in meaning, not opposite.

q: Which word is most similar in meaning to expatiate (as in “expatiate on a topic”)?
why: To expatiate is to speak or write about something at length and in detail, which is to elaborate. Emigrate comes from confusing it with “expatriate.”

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of laudatory (as in “a laudatory review”)?
why: Laudatory means expressing praise, so condemning is its opposite. Praising and approving mean nearly the same as laudatory.

q: Which word is the odd one out? obstinate, intransigent, obdurate, adamant, recalcitrant, pliant
why: The other five all describe someone who refuses to change their mind or give way. Pliant means easily bent or persuaded, the opposite.

q: Which word is the odd one out? sonnet, haiku, limerick, villanelle, ode, novella
why: Sonnets, haiku, limericks, villanelles and odes are all kinds of poems. A novella is a short novel, written in prose.

q: Which word is the odd one out? telescope, microscope, periscope, stethoscope, kaleidoscope, horoscope
why: All the others are instruments for looking or, in the stethoscope’s case, listening. A horoscope is not a device but a forecast that astrologers base on the positions of the sun, moon and planets.

q: Which pair does NOT show the same relationship as the others?
why: In every other pair, the first word is the young of the animal. A drake is an adult male duck, not a baby one; a young duck is a duckling.

q: Which word is most similar in meaning to inimical (as in “habits inimical to good health”)?
why: Inimical means harmful or working against something. Unique is the trap: it is close to inimitable, a different word that looks similar.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of diffident?
why: Diffident means shy and lacking confidence, so confident is its opposite. Shy is a synonym, and different only sounds similar.

q: Which word is the odd one out? corroborate, substantiate, confirm, verify, validate, refute
why: The other five all mean showing that something is true. To refute is to show that something is false.

q: Which pair does NOT show the same relationship as the others?
why: Each other instrument measures the amount of the thing named. A telescope lets you see faraway objects like stars but doesn’t measure them.

def: a pattern that shows up in every smaller group within the data but reverses when all the groups are combined into one
scenario: Treatment A works better than Treatment B for small kidney stones and also for large ones, yet B looks better overall, because A was used mostly on the harder, large stones.
fix: Before trusting a combined rate, check whether the groups being compared contain very different mixes of easy and hard cases.
note: Named for statistician Edward H. Simpson, who described it in 1951; Karl Pearson and Udny Yule had noted similar effects earlier.

tests.s: In each half of the season, Diego had a higher batting average than Malik, yet Malik’s average for the whole season was higher, because Diego got most of his at-bats in the half when everyone hit poorly.

In each of a college’s two departments, women were admitted at a higher rate than men, but overall the college admitted a smaller share of women, because most women applied to the department that turned away most applicants.

def: starting from how likely something seemed at first, then adjusting that belief by how strongly each new piece of evidence points one way
scenario: Hannah thinks there is about a 1 in 4 chance her flight will be delayed. When she learns a major storm is moving in, she raises her estimate to about even odds instead of jumping straight to certainty.
fix: Ask two questions: how likely was this before the evidence, and how much more likely is this evidence if the claim is true than if it is false?
note: A method, not a mistake: it avoids both ignoring the starting odds (base rate neglect) and ignoring the new evidence.

tests.s: A doctor first thinks a rash is most likely an allergy. When a fever appears, which is common with infections but rare with allergies, she shifts toward infection while still keeping allergy in mind.
Yuki puts a 20% chance on a rumor about her company being true. When a reliable reporter confirms part of it, she raises her estimate to about 60%, not all the way to 100%.

def: trying many different ways of analyzing data until one gives a “statistically significant” result, then reporting only that one
scenario: A researcher finds no link between coffee and test scores, so she splits the data by age, gender, time of day and type of coffee until one subgroup shows a significant result, and publishes just that.
fix: Trust studies that announced their exact analysis plan before collecting data, and ask how many comparisons were tried in total.

tests.s: After a sleep study shows no clear effect, the team drops a few “unusual” participants, tries three scoring methods, and stops collecting data the moment the result crosses the significance line.
An analyst runs the same statistical test on 40 customer groups, finds one where the ad’s effect is “significant,” and presents only that result to the board without mentioning the other 39.

def: assuming that a pattern found when comparing whole groups, such as countries or cities, also holds for the individual people in them
scenario: Countries that eat more chocolate per person win more Nobel Prizes per person, so a writer concludes that the individual people who eat the most chocolate are the ones winning prizes.
fix: Ask whether the data describe groups or individuals; group averages can’t tell you which people inside the group produce the pattern.
note: Different from the fallacy of division, which assumes each part shares a property of the whole; this one misreads statistical patterns measured across groups.

tests.s: Neighborhoods with higher average incomes have more gym memberships, so Sofia assumes the richest residents of her own neighborhood must be the ones who belong to gyms.
Counties where more households own cats report higher allergy rates, so a reporter writes that cat owners are more likely to have allergies than other people.

def: the principle that you should find out why a rule, custom or barrier exists before you remove it
scenario: A new manager wants to scrap the rule that every invoice needs two signatures. A colleague suggests finding out why it was added first; it turns out it was created after a costly fraud.
fix: Before getting rid of something that seems pointless, ask who put it there and what problem it was meant to solve.
note: From G. K. Chesterton’s 1929 book The Thing, which imagines a reformer who wants to clear away a fence without knowing why it was built.

tests.s: Before cutting down a row of bushes on his new property, Malik asks his neighbor about them and learns they keep the hillside from washing away in heavy rain.
A school board thinking of dropping an old rule about staggered pickup times first reads the old meeting notes and learns the rule keeps buses and parents’ cars from jamming the same driveway.

def: a false link between two qualities that appears only because the group being studied was picked for having one quality or the other
scenario: In a tough neighborhood, the surviving restaurants with the best food seem to have the worst locations, because places with bad food and bad locations closed, leaving only those strong in one way or the other.
fix: Ask how the group was selected; if getting in required one quality or another, the two will look opposed inside the group even when they’re unrelated outside it.
note: Named for Joseph Berkson, who described it in hospital data in 1946. It is a kind of selection bias, also called collider bias.

tests.s: Fatima notices that among famous actors, the most talented seem less good-looking, not realizing that people usually need talent or looks to become famous at all.
Studying only hospital patients, a researcher finds that people with one illness seem less likely to have a second, unrelated one, because people with neither illness were never admitted.

def: mistaking how rare a piece of evidence would be for an innocent person for the chance that the accused is innocent
scenario: An expert says only 1 in 10,000 people share the defendant’s rare blood type, and the prosecutor tells the jury that this means there is only a 1 in 10,000 chance he is innocent.
fix: Ask how many people in the whole pool of possible suspects would also match; in a city of millions, a 1-in-10,000 match fits hundreds of people.

tests.s: A lawyer argues that since only 1 in 50,000 shoes would leave a print like the one at the scene, there is just a 1 in 50,000 chance that her opponent’s client, whose shoes match, is innocent.
A reporter writes that because a random person’s DNA would match the crime sample only once in a million times, the suspect who matched is 99.9999% certain to be guilty.

def: moving some members from one group to another raises the average of both groups, even though no single member changed
scenario: A school moves its weakest honors students into the regular class. Their grades are still above the regular class’s average, so the average grade rises in both classes, though no one learned more.
fix: When averages in every group improve at once, check whether members were simply shifted from one group to another.
note: Named after a joke credited to humorist Will Rogers about people moving from Oklahoma to California; the credit is uncertain. The term dates from 1985.

tests.s: A sales manager moves the lowest seller on the top team to the second team, where she still outsells everyone; average sales per person go up on both teams.
After a more sensitive scan, some patients once labeled “early stage” are relabeled “late stage.” Survival rates rise for both stages, though no patient lives a day longer.

def: the false impression that finding a disease earlier helps people live longer, when it only starts the survival clock sooner
scenario: A new screening test finds a disease three years earlier. Survival after diagnosis rises by three years, but patients still die at the same age as before.
fix: Judge screening by whether fewer people die of the disease, not by how long people live after they are diagnosed.

tests.s: A clinic boasts that its patients live five years longer after diagnosis than patients elsewhere, yet they die at the same age; its tests simply catch the illness years sooner.
Two towns have the same death rate from a disease, but the town that screens heavily reports much better five-year survival, because its cases are found earlier in the illness.

def: building a rule or model so closely around past data that it copies random noise and then fails on new data
scenario: An analyst builds a stock-picking formula with 30 conditions that perfectly matches the last ten years of prices, but it loses money in its first year of real use.
fix: Test any rule on data it wasn’t built from; if it only works on the past it was tuned to, it learned noise rather than a real pattern.

tests.s: A hiring model trained on 50 past employees gives high scores to applicants who play chess, only because three past top performers happened to, and its picks turn out poorly.
A weather formula is tweaked until it matches every rainy day from last year exactly, yet this year it does worse than a simple forecast that ignores most of those tweaks.

def: concluding that a claim must be false just because someone argued for it badly
scenario: Jamal’s friend says exercise is healthy “because everyone knows it.” Jamal points out that this is a bandwagon argument and concludes exercise must not be healthy.
fix: A bad argument only fails to prove its claim; check the claim against better evidence before rejecting it.

tests.s: In a debate, a student shows that her opponent’s case for seatbelts relied on a slippery slope, then declares that seatbelts therefore don’t save lives.
Tomás learns that a supplement company used a fake expert to claim sleep improves memory, so he decides sleep has no effect on memory at all.

def: preferring to wipe out one small risk completely rather than make a bigger cut in the total risk
scenario: Plan A cuts a town’s yearly water-related illnesses from 10 to 0; Plan B cuts them from 100 to 50 at the same cost. Most residents prefer Plan A, though B prevents five times as many illnesses.
fix: Compare how much total harm each option prevents, not whether one of them gets a single risk down to zero.

tests.s: A factory spends its whole safety budget eliminating one rare kind of accident instead of halving a common one that injures far more workers, because “zero” sounds better.
Aisha pays to remove every trace of a tiny risk from one cleaning product rather than spend the same money cutting the much larger risk from her car’s worn brakes in half.

def: failing to change how much you care, or would pay, to match the size of a problem
scenario: Asked how much they would give to save 2,000 birds, people offered about the same amount as others asked about saving 200,000 birds.
fix: Ask whether your answer would change if the number were ten times bigger or smaller; if it wouldn’t, you’re ignoring the scale.

tests.s: Survey takers say they would pay about $50 to clean up one polluted river, and about the same $50 to clean up ten polluted rivers.
Volunteers feel exactly as strongly about a plan that would protect one small pond as about a plan that would protect every lake in the state.

def: the tendency to believe a statement more after hearing it many times, whether or not it is true
scenario: After hearing on several shows that people use only 10% of their brains, Diego starts repeating it as fact, though it is false.
fix: Notice when a claim feels true only because it’s familiar, and ask where you ever saw actual evidence for it.
note: First shown in a 1977 study; later research found repetition can sway people even when they already know the correct answer.

tests.s: A claim that a cereal “boosts brain power” appears in so many ads that shoppers start mentioning it as common knowledge, though no study supports it.
Fatima first dismissed a rumor about her company, but after seeing the same single post reshared in her feed every day for a month, she finds herself believing it, with no new evidence.

def: judging a past experience mostly by its most intense moment and by how it ended, rather than by the whole
scenario: A long, mostly pleasant vacation is remembered as awful because the last day ended with a miserable flight home.
fix: When judging an experience, try to recall all of it, including how long the good and bad parts actually lasted.
note: Proposed by psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Barbara Fredrickson.

tests.s: A patient whose procedure ended with a few extra minutes of only mild discomfort remembers it as less unpleasant than a shorter one that ended at its most painful point.
Kwame rates a three-hour concert as the best he has ever seen, mostly because of one thrilling encore at the end, though he was bored for much of the show.

def: believing you understand in detail how something works, until you are asked to explain it step by step
scenario: Priya rates her understanding of how a zipper works as “very good,” but when asked to explain it step by step she can’t, and lowers her rating.
fix: Before claiming you understand something, try explaining exactly how it works, step by step, to someone else.
note: Named by Yale psychologists Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil in 2002.

tests.s: Liam is sure he knows how a flush toilet works, but when his daughter asks him to draw the parts inside the tank and explain each one, he realizes he has only a vague idea.
Asked to explain step by step how a new tax plan would actually work, two friends who had argued about it confidently both stumble and become less certain of their views.

def: making decisions using only what is easy to count, and treating whatever can’t be counted as if it does not matter
scenario: A hospital judges its doctors only by how many patients they see per hour, and so ignores whether those patients actually get better.
fix: Ask what matters that the numbers don’t capture, and give it weight even when it is hard to measure.
note: Named after Robert McNamara, U.S. Secretary of Defense in the 1960s, whose Vietnam War planning leaned heavily on figures such as enemy body counts.

tests.s: A school board decides art classes are worthless because they don’t raise test scores, the only thing the board tracks.
A manager rates her team only by how many emails each person answers, then concludes that the engineer who spends weeks solving hard problems contributes nothing.

def: offering several excuses that cannot all be true at once, hoping that at least one will be accepted
scenario: Accused of returning a borrowed kettle damaged, a man says he returned it undamaged, that it was already damaged when he borrowed it, and that he never borrowed it at all.
fix: Check whether all the excuses could be true at the same time; if they can’t, at least one of them is false.
note: From a joke told by Sigmund Freud; the name was given later by the philosopher Jacques Derrida.

tests.s: Asked about the missing report, Kai says he already sent it, that his laptop crashed before he could finish it, and that nobody ever assigned it to him.
A teenager tells his parents he didn’t take the car, that he only drove it around the block, and that they had said he could use it anyway.

def: flooding a debate with so many quick, weak claims that the other side has no time to answer them all
scenario: In a five-minute debate, a speaker rattles off twenty doubtful claims. His opponent can answer only three, and the audience assumes the rest must be true.
fix: Don’t try to answer everything; name the tactic, then show that a few of the strongest-sounding claims are wrong.
note: Named in 1994 by anthropologist Eugenie Scott after Duane Gish, a debater known for the tactic.

tests.s: During a short call-in segment, a guest fires off a dozen half-true statistics in a row, then says, “See? My opponent couldn’t answer most of them.”
In a two-minute rebuttal, Olga’s opponent lists fifteen separate objections to her plan, none explained, knowing she has time to respond to only two or three.

def: arguing that because there is no exact point where one thing turns into another, there is no real difference between them
scenario: Since one more hair never turns a bare chin into a beard, Kai argues, there is no real difference between a clean-shaven face and a full beard.
fix: A fuzzy boundary doesn’t erase the difference between clear cases at either end.

tests.s: Since one extra cookie never turns a healthy diet into an unhealthy one, Olga argues, there is no such thing as eating too many cookies.
Because doctors can’t name the exact temperature at which a fever becomes dangerous, a parent decides there is no real difference between a mild fever and a very high one.

q: mycologist : fungi :: herpetologist : ?
why: A mycologist studies fungi; a herpetologist studies reptiles and amphibians. Insects are studied by an entomologist, a different specialist.

q: insipid : flavor :: callow : ?
why: Something insipid lacks flavor; someone callow lacks experience. Courage is tempting, but callow describes youthful inexperience, not cowardice.

q: ossify : bone :: petrify : ?
why: To ossify is to turn into bone; to petrify is to turn into stone. Fear is tempting because “petrified” can mean terrified, but that is not the parallel sense.

q: overture : opera :: preamble : ?
why: An overture is the opening piece of an opera; a preamble is the opening statement of a constitution or law. A conclusion comes at the end, the reverse position.

q: censorship : speech :: embargo : ?
why: Censorship restricts speech; an embargo is an official ban on trade with a country. Travel bans exist, but an embargo is specifically about trade.

q: antidote : poison :: rebuttal : ?
why: An antidote counters a poison; a rebuttal counters an argument. A verdict ends a case but does not answer an opposing claim.

q: eulogy : praise :: diatribe : ?
why: A eulogy is a speech full of praise; a diatribe is a speech or piece of writing full of bitter attack. Mourning goes with a eulogy’s setting, not with a diatribe.

q: amnesia : memory :: aphasia : ?
why: Amnesia is loss of memory; aphasia is loss of the ability to use or understand language, usually after brain injury. Hearing loss has a different name.

q: sonnet : fourteen lines :: limerick : ?
why: A traditional sonnet has fourteen lines; a limerick has five, rhyming AABBA. Four lines make a quatrain, a different form.

q: mercenary : money :: zealot : ?
why: A mercenary is driven by money; a zealot is driven by fierce devotion to a cause or belief. Orders drive an ordinary soldier, not a zealot.

q: abdicate : throne :: recant : ?
why: To abdicate is to formally give up a throne; to recant is to publicly take back a belief or statement. Breaking a promise is reneging, not recanting.

q: mutiny : ship :: coup : ?
why: A mutiny is a revolt by a ship’s crew against its officers; a coup is a sudden seizure of a government. Armies often carry out coups, but the government is what is seized.

q: “Liam’s talk of learning the cello was a mere velleity: he brought it up every few months but never rented an instrument or looked for a teacher.” What does velleity most likely mean?
options: a weak wish that never leads to action
a talent someone is born with
a fear of performing in public
why: He mentions the wish but never acts, so it is a faint, idle wish. A lifelong passion would show up in some effort, which the sentence says never happened.

q: “The court found the clause nugatory: because it conflicted with state law, it had no legal force, and the contract was read as if it weren’t there.” What does nugatory most likely mean?
why: A clause with “no legal force,” read as if absent, is worthless. Confusing language is tempting, but the sentence says the problem was conflict with the law.

q: “From the hammock, Priya could hear the susurrus of the pines, so faint that she had to stop talking to catch it.” What does susurrus most likely mean?
options: a soft rustling or whispering sound
why: She hears it, and it is faint, so it is a soft sound. A faint smell is tempting, but you smell a scent rather than hear it.

q: “The podcast host, a former sportscaster, had become an ultracrepidarian, confidently weighing in on vaccine research, tax law and nuclear physics without having studied any of them.” What does ultracrepidarian most likely mean?
options: giving opinions on matters beyond one’s knowledge
why: He speaks confidently on fields he never studied. “Gifted in many subjects” is the opposite: the point is that he lacks the knowledge.

q: “Villagers painted staring eyes on the bows of their boats and hung blue glass charms in their doorways, apotropaic customs that, the old fishermen said, kept storms and misfortune from finding them.” What does apotropaic most likely mean?
options: meant to ward off evil or bad luck
done to mark each boat’s owner
why: The customs are said to keep misfortune away, so they protect against evil. “Purely decorative” ignores the stated purpose.

q: “The philosopher’s lucubrations, written by candlelight over many sleepless winters, filled twelve dense volumes that few people have ever read.” What does lucubration most likely mean?
options: long, hard study or writing, especially late at night
why: Candlelight, sleepless nights and twelve dense volumes point to hard work done at night. Short sayings would not fill twelve dense volumes.

q: “The film’s oneiric scenes, with clocks melting, staircases leading nowhere and characters changing faces mid-sentence, left viewers feeling as if they had just woken up.” What does oneiric most likely mean?
why: Impossible images and the feeling of just waking up describe a dream. Nothing in the list suggests the scenes were funny.

q: “After three dry months, Kwame stepped onto the porch as the first drops hit the dusty yard and breathed in the petrichor, a scent he linked with every summer storm of his childhood.” What does petrichor most likely mean?
options: the earthy smell of rain on dry ground
the smell of freshly cut grass
why: It is a scent that comes as rain hits dry dirt. Distant thunder belongs to storms too, but it is a sound, not something breathed in.

q: “The movement proved fissiparous: within five years it had split into four rival factions, each accusing the others of betraying the cause.” What does fissiparous most likely mean?
options: tending to split into separate groups
why: Splitting into four rival factions shows a tendency to break apart. Rapid growth is the opposite of what the sentence describes.

q: “The hospital began as an eleemosynary institution, funded entirely by gifts and treating the poor free of charge.” What does eleemosynary most likely mean?
why: Funding by gifts and free care for the poor mark charity. Many charities were religious, but nothing in the sentence says this one was.

q: “Olga’s cachinnation over the cartoon echoed through the quiet library, loud and uncontrolled, and she couldn’t stop even when the librarian glared.” What does cachinnation most likely mean?
why: A loud, uncontrollable reaction to a cartoon is laughter. Sneezing can be uncontrollable too, but a cartoon doesn’t cause it.

q: “The anfractuous mountain road, doubling back on itself every few hundred yards, turned a ten-mile trip into an hour of white-knuckle driving.” What does anfractuous most likely mean?
why: A road that doubles back on itself again and again is winding. Steepness is common on mountain roads, but the clue given is the constant turning.

q: Hospital A: 430 of 600 patients survived (72%). Hospital B: 460 of 600 survived (77%). Among mild cases, A saved 190 of 200 and B saved 360 of 400. Among severe cases, A saved 240 of 400 and B saved 100 of 200. Which is best supported?
options: B gives better care, since its overall survival rate is higher.
The two hospitals perform equally well.
A did better with both mild and severe cases; its lower overall rate comes from treating a larger share of severe cases.
A did better with severe cases but worse with mild ones.
The figures must contain an error, since a hospital can’t be better in every group yet worse overall.
B should take more of the severe cases.
why: A’s rates are 95% vs. 90% for mild cases and 60% vs. 50% for severe ones; two-thirds of A’s patients were severe versus one-third of B’s. Judging by the overall rate alone gets the comparison backward.

q: 1 in 100 people in a town has a certain condition. A screening test catches 90% of people who have it, but it also flags 9% of people who don’t. Jun tests positive. Which is closest to the chance that he has the condition?
why: Out of 1,000 people, about 9 of the 10 who have it test positive, but so do about 89 of the 990 who don’t, so only about 9 of 98 positives are real. Picking 90% ignores how rare the condition is.

q: Across a city’s 40 neighborhoods, those with a higher share of dog-owning households have fewer burglaries per household. A security blogger concludes that owning a dog protects a home from burglary. Which is best supported?
options: Owning a dog cuts a household’s burglary risk.
The data can’t show whether the homes with dogs are the ones being spared, since the pattern is measured only across neighborhoods.
The pattern must be due to chance.
Neighborhoods with more dogs must have more police patrols.
Getting a dog would cut your own risk in half.
why: Neighborhood-level data can’t tell you which households inside a neighborhood avoid burglary. Concluding that each dog protects its own home reads a group pattern as an individual one.

q: A team tested each of 20 foods for a link to headaches, counting a result as “statistically significant” if it had under a 5% chance of appearing by luck alone. Only eggplant passed, and the team published just that finding. Which is best supported?
options: Even if no food affected headaches, about one of the 20 tests would be expected to pass by chance, so the eggplant result is weak evidence.
There is a 95% chance that eggplant causes headaches.
The other 19 foods were proven safe.
The study should have tested fewer people.
why: With a 5% false-alarm rate, 20 tests produce about one false alarm on average, and hiding the 19 misses makes it look stronger. The “95% chance” reading confuses the test’s cutoff with the chance the claim is true.

q: A company says its new interview method picks better employees: workers hired with it received higher performance ratings after one year than workers hired the old way. Which, if true, most weakens this claim?
options: The new method takes longer to carry out.
Some workers hired the old way also got high ratings.
The managers who gave the ratings designed the new method and knew which workers it had picked.
The company plans to use the method in other offices.
Applicants said they liked the new interviews better.
The new method costs less than the old one.
why: If the raters knew who was hired which way and had a stake in the method, their ratings could be biased in its favor. A few high-rated old-way hires don’t undercut an average difference.

q: Students who chose to join a summer reading program scored higher on fall reading tests than students who didn’t. So the district plans to require the program for everyone, expecting all students’ scores to rise by about the same amount. The plan depends on which assumption?
options: Every student enjoys reading in the summer.
The program will be cheaper if everyone joins.
Fall tests are harder than spring tests.
The students who chose to join weren’t already stronger or more motivated readers than those who didn’t.
Students who skipped the program read nothing all summer.
why: Because students picked themselves, the gap might reflect who joined rather than what the program did. Whether students read nothing at all is beside the point; the plan needs the gap to come from the program.

q: A college admits only students with either top grades or an outstanding athletic record, or both. Among its students, Professor Sato finds that star athletes tend to have lower grades than other students. She concludes that athletic training hurts grades. Which best explains the pattern without training hurting grades?
options: Students with neither strong grades nor strong athletics were never admitted, so among those admitted, weaker grades tend to go with stronger athletics.
Training leaves athletes too tired for class.
The college has more athletes than most colleges.
Grades at the college have risen in recent years.
Most students at the college play some sport.
why: The admission rule fills the student body with people strong in one way or the other, which creates an opposite-looking link even if the traits are unrelated outside. “Less study time” is just another way athletics would hurt grades.

q: After a new scan began detecting a certain cancer about two years earlier than before, the share of patients alive five years after diagnosis rose from 40% to 60%. Yet the number of deaths from that cancer per 100,000 people did not change. Which is best supported?
options: Earlier diagnosis may have lengthened the time people lived after diagnosis without making them live any longer overall.
The scan has saved many lives.
The cancer has become more common.
Treatment for the cancer has improved.
The death figures must be wrong.
Doctors should stop treating the cancer.
why: If the death rate is unchanged, starting the clock two years earlier can raise five-year survival on its own. “Saved many lives” is exactly what the unchanged death rate fails to show.

q: A country’s unemployment rate fell from 5% to 4%. Which must be true?
options: The rate fell by 20 percentage points.
The number of unemployed people fell by 20%.
The rate fell by 1% of its earlier value.
Twenty percent more people now have jobs.
The rate fell by one percentage point, which is a 20% drop in the rate.
why: Going from 5 to 4 is one percentage point, and 1 is 20% of 5. The number of unemployed people need not fall 20%, since the size of the workforce can change.

q: At a firm of 9 employees, the median salary is $50,000 and the mean salary is $80,000. Which must be true?
options: Exactly four employees earn more than $50,000.
Most employees earn more than the mean.
At least one employee earns more than $80,000.
The mean was pushed up by a data-entry error.
why: Not everyone can be at or below a mean of $80,000 when the middle salary is $50,000, so someone earns more. With 9 people the middle (fifth) salary is exactly $50,000, so “no one earns exactly $50,000” is false.

q: Drunk-driving crashes in Ashford fell 25% in the year after the city started a late-night bus route linking its bar district to residential areas. Officials credit the route. Which, if true, most strengthens their claim?
options: In nearby cities without new routes, such crashes held steady that year, and Ashford’s drop was concentrated along the route’s path.
The new buses run on electric power.
Riders said in a survey that they liked the route.
Police in Ashford also stepped up patrols that year.
Crashes of all kinds fell 25% statewide that year.
The route cost less to run than expected.
why: A comparison with similar cities, plus a drop clustered where the buses run, points to the route. More police patrols or a statewide drop would offer other explanations and weaken the claim.

q: A DNA profile from a crime scene would match about 1 in every million people. Police search a DNA database that holds profiles for only some of the city’s 5 million residents and find one match, a man with no other link to the crime. Which is best supported?
options: There is only a one-in-a-million chance that he is innocent.
The DNA test must be faulty.
No one else in the city could match.
About five people in the city would be expected to match, so the match alone doesn’t make his guilt nearly certain.
The match is worthless as evidence.
why: With 5 million people and a 1-in-a-million match rate, several people should match, so he is one of several possible sources. “Worthless” goes too far: the match does narrow the field a great deal.

q: The launch goes ahead only if the tests pass. The tests pass only if the server stays up. The launch went ahead. Which must be true?
options: The server stayed up, but the tests may have failed.
The tests passed, but the server may have gone down.
The tests passed and the server stayed up.
Any time the server stays up, the launch goes ahead.
Any time the tests pass, the launch goes ahead.
Neither the tests nor the server can be judged.
why: “Only if” sets a requirement: launch → tests passed, and tests passed → server up. The reversed rules (“server up → launch”) are not stated.

q: It is not true that every student who passed the exam attended every review session. Which must be true?
options: No student who passed attended every session.
At least one student who passed missed every review session.
At least one student who passed missed at least one review session.
Every student who failed attended every session.
Most students who passed skipped review sessions.
Attending review sessions doesn’t help students pass.
why: Denying “every” only requires one exception. That student missed at least one session, not necessarily all of them.

q: No member of the board owns shares in Vexo. Some members of the audit team are on the board. Which must be true?
options: No member of the audit team owns shares in Vexo.
Some members of the audit team own shares in Vexo.
Every board member is on the audit team.
Some members of the audit team don’t own shares in Vexo.
No one who owns Vexo shares is on the audit team.
Some board members are not on the audit team.
why: The audit members who sit on the board can’t own Vexo shares. Nothing is said about audit members who aren’t on the board, so “no member of the audit team” goes too far.

q: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Ava says, “Ben is a knave.” Ben says, “Ava and Cal are the same type.” Cal says, “Ava is a knave.” What are they?
options: Ava and Cal are knights; Ben is a knave.
Ava is a knight; Ben and Cal are knaves.
Ava is a knave; Ben and Cal are knights.
Ben is a knight; Ava and Cal are knaves.
why: If Ava is a knight, Ben is a knave, so Ava and Cal differ and Cal is a knave, whose claim “Ava is a knave” is indeed false. If Ava were a knave, Ben would be a knight and Cal a knave, but then Cal’s claim would be true, which a knave can’t say.

q: Exactly one of Ari, Bo, Cy and Di took the cash, and exactly one of these statements is true. Ari: “Bo took it.” Bo: “Di took it.” Cy: “I didn’t take it.” Di: “Bo is lying.” Who took the cash?
why: If Cy took it, only Di’s statement is true. If anyone else took it, at least two are true: Cy’s, plus Di’s (if Ari or Bo did it) or Bo’s (if Di did it).

q: Five friends sit in seats 1 to 5, left to right. Val sits next to Wen. Xia is not in an end seat. Yara sits exactly two seats to the right of Zoe. Wen sits somewhere to the right of Xia. Val is not in seat 5. Who sits in seat 3?
why: Testing each spot for Zoe and Yara (two apart) with Val and Wen side by side, Xia off the ends, Wen right of Xia and Val out of seat 5 leaves only Zoe, Xia, Yara, Val, Wen.

q: Which statement means the same as “No one gets a refund unless they have a receipt”?
options: Anyone with a receipt gets a refund.
If someone got a refund, they had a receipt.
If someone didn’t get a refund, they had no receipt.
Having a receipt guarantees a refund.
Only people without receipts are turned down.
Some people with receipts are always refused.
why: The rule makes a receipt necessary, not enough on its own: refund → receipt. “Anyone with a receipt gets a refund” reverses it.

q: Three of five people, P, Q, R, S and T, will form a committee. P and Q can’t both serve. If R serves, S serves. At least one of Q and T serves. P and S can’t both serve. Which must be true?
options: R and T don’t both serve.
why: The only possible committees are Q-R-S, Q-S-T and R-S-T, and S is in all three. Each other option fails in at least one of them, and R-S-T includes both R and T.

q: Every flight that was delayed had a crew change. No flight that had a crew change left from Terminal B. Flight 88 left from Terminal B. Which must be true?
options: Flight 88 was delayed but had no crew change.
Some delayed flights left from Terminal B.
Every flight without a crew change left from Terminal B.
Every flight that was not delayed left from Terminal B.
why: Flight 88 left from Terminal B, so it had no crew change, and without a crew change it can’t have been delayed. The last two options reverse the rules, which only run in one direction.

q: A person may enter the lounge only if they are a member or are with a member, and the rule is always enforced. Ana entered the lounge, and she is not a member. Which must be true?
options: Ana will soon become a member.
Everyone with a member may enter.
No member was in the lounge.
why: Entry requires membership or a member’s company; Ana isn’t a member, so she must have been with one. “Everyone with a member may enter” reverses the rule.

q: It is not the case that both the printer and the scanner are working. The scanner is working. Which must be true?
options: Nothing can be concluded about the printer.
why: At least one machine is down, and the scanner works, so the printer must be the one. “Neither is working” misreads “not both” as “neither.”

q: Four runners, Ana, Ben, Cara and Dev, finished a race with no ties. Ana finished ahead of both Ben and Cara. Cara finished ahead of Dev. Which CANNOT be true?
why: Ana must be first, and Dev must come after both Ana and Cara, so he can be no higher than third. Each other option happens in at least one possible order, such as Ana, Cara, Dev, Ben.

q: Which word is most similar in meaning to pertinacious?
why: Pertinacious means holding firmly to a goal or opinion; persistent matches. Relevant is the meaning of pertinent, a different word that only looks similar.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of evanescent?
why: Evanescent means fading away quickly; enduring means lasting a long time. Fleeting is a synonym, not an opposite.

q: Which word is most similar in meaning to taciturn?
why: A taciturn person says very little; uncommunicative matches. Tactless only looks similar, and talkative is the opposite.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of magnanimous?
why: Magnanimous means generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival; petty means small-minded and spiteful. Generous is a synonym.

q: Which word is the odd one out? tirade, harangue, diatribe, invective, broadside, panegyric
why: Every other word names an angry verbal attack; a panegyric is a speech or piece of writing full of praise. Broadside may look unrelated, but it also means a fierce spoken or written attack.

q: Which word is the odd one out? covert, clandestine, surreptitious, furtive, stealthy, overt
why: The others all mean done in secret; overt means done openly. Covert looks like overt but means the opposite.

q: Which choice is most similar in meaning to inveigh (as in “inveigh against”)?
why: To inveigh against something is to attack it with angry words. Luring with flattery is inveigle, a different word that looks alike.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of profligate?
why: Profligate means recklessly wasteful, especially with money; thrifty means careful with money. Wasteful is a synonym, and prolific only looks similar.

q: Which pair does NOT show the same relationship as the others?
why: In each other pair, the first word is a young stage of the second; a mare is an adult female horse. Foal : horse fits the pattern, since a foal is a young horse.

q: Which word is most similar in meaning to tendentious?
why: Tendentious writing pushes one side of a disputed issue; biased matches. Tedious and tentative only share opening letters.

q: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of pellucid?
why: Pellucid means very clear, whether water or writing; murky means cloudy or hard to see through. Lucid is a synonym.

q: Which word is the odd one out? nascent, incipient, inchoate, embryonic, budding, moribund
why: The others describe something just beginning to form; moribund describes something dying or near its end. Inchoate can also mean not yet organized, which still fits the beginning stage.

story: After the Greeks defeated the Persians at Marathon in 490 BC, a later legend said a runner carried the news about 25 miles to Athens, announced the victory, and died. The first modern Olympics, in 1896, honored the legend with a long race called the marathon.
def: a very long, tiring activity or event that takes great patience and energy to finish
ex: The budget meeting turned into a six-hour marathon, and nobody had time for lunch.
Wei and her roommates had a movie marathon, watching all eight films in one weekend.
Studying for the bar exam was a three-month marathon of reading and practice tests.
Saturday's cleaning marathon left Fatima's family exhausted, but the garage was finally spotless.

cloze.s: After a twelve-hour ___ of packing boxes, Kwame fell asleep on the floor of his new apartment.

note: Also the name of the running race of 26.2 miles (42.2 km).

term: the weight of the world on your shoulders
story: In Greek myth, Atlas was a Titan who fought against Zeus and was punished by being forced to hold up the sky forever. Later artists often showed him carrying a giant globe on his shoulders.
def: a feeling of being responsible for many heavy problems or worries all at once
ex: Since her father got sick, Fatima has been carrying the weight of the world on her shoulders.
Liam walked into the office looking like he had the weight of the world on his shoulders.
After the layoffs, Priya felt the weight of the world on her shoulders as she tried to support her family.
Exams, a sick parent, and two part-time jobs left Tomás with the weight of the world on his shoulders.

cloze.s: You don't have to solve every family problem alone, Diego; stop carrying ___.
cloze.a: the weight of the world on your shoulders

term: Rome wasn't built in a day
story: The proverb appears in a collection of medieval French sayings from around 1190 and was in English by 1545. Ancient Rome grew over many centuries from a small settlement into a great city.
def: great, lasting achievements take a long time, so be patient with slow progress
ex: Tomás was frustrated with his Spanish, but his teacher reminded him that Rome wasn't built in a day.
The new coach said Rome wasn't built in a day and asked fans to give the young team a few seasons.
Wei wanted to run a marathon after one month of training, but her coach said Rome wasn't built in a day.
City planners asked residents to be patient with the new bike lanes, saying Rome wasn't built in a day.

cloze.s: The business lost money in its first year, but Aisha told her partners, “___; let's keep going.”
cloze.a: Rome wasn't built in a day

term: when in Rome, do as the Romans do
story: The saying is traced to Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan in the 300s. Asked whether to fast on Saturday, as people did in Rome but not in Milan, he reportedly said he fasted on Saturday when in Rome but not when in Milan.
def: when you visit a place, follow the customs and habits of the people who live there
ex: In Japan, Malik took off his shoes at every door, saying, “When in Rome, do as the Romans do.”
Hannah usually skips dessert, but in Paris she decided that when in Rome, do as the Romans do.
At his new office everyone wore sneakers, so Kwame decided, “When in Rome, do as the Romans do.”
On the farm, everyone woke at 5 a.m., so the city visitors agreed that when in Rome, do as the Romans do.

cloze.s: Everyone at the dinner party in Madrid ate at 10 p.m., so Olga thought, “___,” and joined them.
cloze.a: When in Rome, do as the Romans do

note: Often shortened to just “when in Rome.”

story: In Scandinavian folklore, trolls are ugly, quarrelsome creatures that make trouble for travelers. Since the early 1990s the word has also named people who stir up trouble online; the fishing method called trolling, dragging bait behind a boat, may also have shaped this use.
def: a person who posts rude or annoying messages online on purpose to upset people and start arguments
ex: The players were told not to read the comments, because trolls posted cruel jokes after every loss.
Priya blocked the troll who kept insulting her cooking videos.
The museum's online forum banned a troll who posted insults under every article.
Kwame stopped replying to the troll, who only wanted to start fights about his favorite soccer team.

cloze.s: Ignore that ___; he only says outrageous things online to make people angry and get attention.

note: As a verb, “to troll” means to post such messages on purpose.

story: In Haitian folklore, a zombie is a dead person brought back to life by a sorcerer and controlled as a servant with no will of its own; the word likely traces back to Kimbundu, an African language. George Romero's 1968 film Night of the Living Dead created today's image of flesh-eating walking dead.
def: a person who moves and acts slowly and without thinking, usually because of being extremely tired
ex: After three nights with a crying newborn, Jamal was a zombie at work.
The students shuffled out of the final exam like zombies, too tired to talk.
After the overnight flight, Liam walked through the airport like a zombie.
Working double shifts all week left Maria a zombie by Saturday morning.

cloze.s: Sofia stayed up all night finishing her report and spent the next day like a(n) ___, staring blankly at her screen.

story: In hoodoo, an African American folk magic tradition, a mojo is a small cloth bag of charms carried for luck, love or protection; the word likely comes from Kikongo, a Central African language. Blues songs such as “Got My Mojo Working” spread the word, which came to mean personal power.
def: a person's special energy, confidence or skill that helps them succeed
ex: After two bad games, the pitcher finally got his mojo back and struck out ten batters.
Yuki lost her writing mojo for a while, but a trip to the mountains brought it back.
Liam wore his lucky sneakers to the interview, hoping they would give him some extra mojo.
Aisha says her morning run is where she finds the mojo for a long day of meetings.

cloze.s: The chef said cooking in her grandmother's old pan helped her get her ___ back after a slow, uninspired year.

story: In the 1920s, pilots in Britain's Royal Air Force invented gremlins, tiny imaginary creatures they jokingly blamed for unexplained problems with their aircraft. The idea spread widely during World War II, and Roald Dahl published a children's book called The Gremlins in 1943.
def: a hidden fault that makes a machine or system break down for no clear reason, jokingly blamed on a tiny made-up creature
ex: The printer jammed again, and Maria joked that gremlins had moved into the office.
Engineers spent all morning hunting the gremlin that kept crashing the website.
A gremlin in the car's wiring made the radio switch on by itself every morning.
Some gremlin in the school's new sound system cut off the microphone during every assembly.

cloze.s: Every time the video call froze, Diego blamed a(n) ___ in the computer instead of his slow internet.

story: The phrase comes from the King James Bible, where Paul praises early Christians for their “work of faith, and labour of love” (1 Thessalonians 1:3). It came to mean hard work done out of devotion rather than for reward.
def: hard work that someone does because they care about it, not for money or praise
ex: Restoring the old sailboat was a labor of love for Kwame, who worked on it every weekend for two years.
The free community cookbook was a labor of love for the volunteers who tested every recipe.
Grandma's handmade quilt, sewn over three winters for her new grandson, was a labor of love.
Coaching the kids' soccer team for free every Saturday is a labor of love for Diego.

cloze.s: Olga earns nothing from the town history website; building it is purely a(n) ___.

term: a leopard can't change its spots
story: In the Bible, the prophet Jeremiah asks whether a leopard can change its spots (Jeremiah 13:23), comparing this to people so used to doing wrong that they cannot easily start doing good.
def: people do not really change their basic character, especially their bad habits
ex: Hannah hoped her old business partner had become more honest, but a leopard can't change its spots.
Fans said the striker's angry outburst proved that a leopard can't change its spots.
The company said it had cleaned up its business, but critics replied that a leopard can't change its spots.
Sofia's roommate swore she would wash dishes daily, but the sink filled up again; a leopard can't change its spots.

cloze.s: He promised to stop lying, but within a week he was caught again; I guess ___.
cloze.a: a leopard can't change its spots

term: money is the root of all evil
story: The saying shortens a Bible verse: “For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1 Timothy 6:10). The original warns against greed, the love of money, rather than against money itself.
def: the desire for money is what leads people to do bad and harmful things
ex: When the brothers stopped speaking over their inheritance, their mother sighed that money is the root of all evil.
The documentary about the bank fraud opened with the line “money is the root of all evil.”
Grandma Olga often warned that money is the root of all evil and that greed ruins families.
In the movie, four friends find a bag of cash and turn on each other, showing that money is the root of all evil.

cloze.s: The friends' business fell apart in a bitter fight over profits, proving to Jamal that ___.
cloze.a: money is the root of all evil

note: Often misquoted: the Bible verse blames the love of money, not money itself.

story: In the Gospels, Jesus walks across the Sea of Galilee to reach his disciples in their boat (Matthew 14). Because no ordinary person could do this, saying someone can walk on water means people think they can do no wrong.
def: to be seen as perfect, as if able to do the impossible and never make mistakes
ex: The new manager's fans act like she can walk on water, but she makes mistakes like anyone else.
After his game-winning goal, the young striker could walk on water in the eyes of the fans.
Diego's grandmother thinks he can walk on water, even when he forgets her birthday.
New employees soon learned that the founder didn't walk on water; some of her plans failed badly.

cloze.s: Ever since Wei landed the big client, the boss acts as if she can ___ and never questions her ideas.

story: In the Gospel of Matthew, the Roman governor Pontius Pilate washes his hands in front of the crowd before handing Jesus over to be crucified, declaring that he is innocent of his death (Matthew 27:24).
def: to refuse to have anything more to do with someone or something, or to take responsibility for it
ex: After the third failed repair, Fatima washed her hands of the old car and sold it for parts.
The city council cannot simply wash its hands of the problem of crumbling bridges.
