After years of broken promises, Priya washed her hands of the business partnership.
The school can't wash its hands of bullying that happens on its buses.

cloze.s: Tired of his brother's risky schemes, Malik ___ the whole project and stopped answering his calls.

story: In the Gospels, Jesus carries the cross on which he will be crucified (John 19:17), and he tells his followers that they must carry their own cross (Luke 14:27). The phrase came to mean a hardship one must accept.
def: a lasting problem or burden that someone must put up with because it cannot be avoided
ex: Chronic back pain has been Aisha's cross to bear since the car accident.
Every team has its cross to bear, and ours is a stadium that floods in heavy rain.
Living next to the noisy train tracks is a cross to bear that Tomás accepts for the cheap rent.
Hannah's allergies are her cross to bear every spring, when pollen fills the air.

cloze.s: My neighbor's barking dog is my ___; I've complained for years, but nothing ever changes.

story: In medieval Christian thought, limbo (from the Latin limbus, “edge”) was an imagined place at the edge of hell for souls who were neither punished nor admitted to heaven. It was never official Catholic teaching, but the idea of being stuck in between gave the word its everyday meaning.
def: an uncertain state of waiting, when no decision has been made and nothing can move forward
ex: Diego's visa application has been in limbo for months while the office reviews it.
The stadium plan remains in limbo until the city finds the money to build it.
The house sale is in limbo until the buyer's bank approves the loan.
With the coach still undecided, Kwame's spot on the team stayed in limbo all week.

cloze.s: Until the company announces who will lead the new team, all our projects are stuck in ___.

term: a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step
story: The saying comes from chapter 64 of the Tao Te Ching, a classic Chinese text of Taoist thought traditionally credited to Laozi. More literally, it says a journey of a thousand li (a Chinese unit of distance) starts beneath one's feet.
def: even a very big goal is reached by starting with one small action
ex: Writing one page of her novel each day, Yuki reminded herself that a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
The charity's first well served only one village, but a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
Wanting to learn Spanish, Malik studied five words on day one; a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
Facing a mountain of debt, Fatima paid off one small bill first, because a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.

cloze.s: Running a marathon seemed impossible to Liam, but his coach said, “___; just run one mile today.”
cloze.a: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step

note: Often wrongly credited to Confucius.

story: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar (1599), the conspirator Casca reports that Cicero spoke in Greek and says, “for mine own part, it was Greek to me.” The line made the phrase famous as a way of saying something cannot be understood.
def: I cannot understand this at all; it is too confusing or strange to me
ex: My accountant explained the new tax rules twice, but honestly, it's Greek to me.
Sofia's brother showed her his computer code, but it was all Greek to her.
I've read the instructions for this baby car seat three times, and it's Greek to me.
Grandpa turned the new TV remote over in his hands and said, “It's Greek to me.”

cloze.s: The repair manual is full of technical diagrams and strange terms; ___.

term: all that glitters is not gold
story: In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, a prince who chooses a gold box hoping to win a bride finds a scroll inside that begins, “All that glisters is not gold.” The idea was already an old proverb, but Shakespeare's line made it famous.
def: something that looks attractive or valuable on the outside may not really be good
ex: The job offered a huge salary, but Kwame learned that all that glitters is not gold when he saw the 80-hour weeks.
That shiny new phone kept breaking, a reminder that all that glitters is not gold.
The used car looked spotless, but the mechanic found a cracked engine; all that glitters is not gold.
Hannah's grandmother reminded her that all that glitters is not gold when a charming stranger offered an easy way to get rich.

cloze.s: The hotel looked luxurious in the photos, but the rooms were dirty and noisy; ___.
cloze.a: all that glitters is not gold

story: In Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, Juliet says good night to Romeo at the end of the balcony scene: “Parting is such sweet sorrow / That I shall say good night till it be morrow.” The goodbye is sad, yet sweet because of their love.
def: saying goodbye to someone you love is painful, yet also sweet because of the love you share
ex: As her daughter left for college, Maria hugged her and whispered, “Parting is such sweet sorrow.”
On the last night of summer camp, the counselors joked that parting is such sweet sorrow.
After the long visit, Grandpa walked his grandkids to the car three times, joking that parting is such sweet sorrow.
As the band played the last song of its farewell tour, the singer told fans that parting is such sweet sorrow.

cloze.s: Hannah lingered at the train station with her boyfriend for an hour, saying goodbye again and again, because ___.

term: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears
story: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Mark Antony begins his speech at Caesar's funeral with these words, asking the crowd to listen. His speech then cleverly turns the people against the men who killed Caesar.
def: a joking or dramatic way to ask a group of people for their full attention
ex: Tomás tapped his glass at the wedding and said, “Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears.”
The coach opened the team meeting with “Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears,” and the players laughed.
Before reading the dinner specials, the waiter bowed and said, “Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears.”
Our science teacher quieted the noisy lab by calling out, “Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears!”

cloze.s: Standing on a chair at the family reunion, Uncle Jamal shouted, “___! I have an announcement.”
cloze.a: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears

story: In Carlo Collodi's Italian novel The Adventures of Pinocchio (1883), a wooden puppet comes to life, and his nose grows longer when he tells lies. Disney's 1940 film made the character known around the world.
def: a person who tells lies, especially obvious ones
ex: Stop being such a Pinocchio, Liam; I know you didn't finish your homework.
When the boy swore he hadn't eaten the cookies, his mother laughed and called him a little Pinocchio.
The reporter called the salesman a Pinocchio after every promise in his ad proved false.
“You say you didn't eat my fries, Pinocchio? There's ketchup on your chin,” Aisha laughed.

cloze.s: Every time my little brother fibs, his ears turn red, so we call him ___.

story: The phrase was already in use by the 1780s, but Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) made it famous with its grinning Cheshire Cat, which slowly fades away until only its grin is left.
def: to smile very widely, often looking very pleased with yourself, as if you know a secret
ex: Aisha came home grinning like a Cheshire cat after her job interview.
When the waiter brought out the surprise cake, Wei grinned like a Cheshire cat.
Priya sat grinning like a Cheshire cat, because she knew the surprise party was about to start.
Holding his first paycheck, Diego grinned like a Cheshire cat all the way home on the bus.

cloze.s: Malik walked in ___, and we knew right away he had won the concert tickets.

story: In the American children's story The Little Engine That Could, best known from a 1930 edition, a small train engine agrees to pull a heavy train over a mountain after bigger engines refuse. It succeeds by repeating, “I think I can, I think I can.”
def: a small or weak person or group that succeeds through determination and belief in itself
ex: The tiny school's robotics team was the little engine that could, beating schools ten times its size.
Olga's small bakery became the little engine that could, slowly winning customers from the big chain.
The small-town team was the little engine that could, reaching the state finals with only eleven players.
Diego was the slowest runner in his club, but like the little engine that could, he finished the marathon.

cloze.s: Nobody expected the underfunded startup to survive, but like ___, it kept pushing and finally made a profit.

story: In the 1765 English children's book The History of Little Goody Two-Shoes, a poor orphan girl who owns only one shoe is given a pair and happily tells everyone she has “two shoes.” She is rewarded for her goodness, and her name later became a teasing label.
def: a person who is annoyingly well-behaved and always follows the rules, often to look better than others
ex: Hannah was called a Goody Two-shoes for reminding the teacher to collect the homework.
Don't be such a Goody Two-shoes, Diego; nobody will mind if we leave five minutes early.
At the office, Malik was teased as a Goody Two-shoes for refusing to take even one extra break.
In the movie, the Goody Two-shoes student finally breaks a rule to help her friends.

cloze.s: My sister never broke a single rule growing up, and her friends teased her for being a(n) ___.

story: Medieval stories of chivalry, such as the legends of King Arthur, told of brave knights in armor who rescued people in danger. The phrase draws on that picture of a noble hero arriving just in time.
def: a person who comes to rescue someone from a difficult situation
ex: When Priya's car broke down at night, a passing tow truck driver was her knight in shining armor.
The investor saw himself as a knight in shining armor saving the failing company.
When the moving van never showed up, Diego arrived with his pickup truck like a knight in shining armor.
Sofia doesn't need a knight in shining armor; she fixed the leaking sink herself.

cloze.s: Kwame lent me his umbrella in the downpour and walked me to the station; he was my ___.

story: Writers had long described America as a place where immigrants were “melted” into a new people, and Israel Zangwill's 1908 play The Melting Pot made the term famous. A melting pot is a container in which different metals are melted together into one.
def: a place where people of many different cultures and backgrounds live together and blend into one community
ex: Queens is a melting pot where you can hear dozens of languages on one subway ride.
The university's dorms were a melting pot of students from over 80 countries.
The school cafeteria is a melting pot, with lunches from Korea, Nigeria, Mexico, and Italy on one table.
Over generations, the port city became a melting pot, and its food and music now mix traditions from three continents.

cloze.s: With families from Mexico, Vietnam, Somalia and Poland on one block, our neighborhood is a true ___.

note: Some prefer the image of a “salad bowl,” where cultures mix but keep their differences.

story: Writer James Truslow Adams made the phrase popular in his 1931 book The Epic of America. He described a dream of a land where life would be better, richer and fuller for everyone, with opportunity based on ability rather than birth.
def: the hope that anyone in the United States can succeed and live well through hard work
ex: For Tomás's parents, buying their first home felt like living the American Dream.
The documentary asks whether the American Dream is still within reach for young workers.
Malik's grandfather opened a small restaurant after immigrating, and his family sees it as the American Dream.
Owning a home with a yard is still part of the American Dream for many young families.

cloze.s: Fatima arrived with one suitcase, built a successful business, and now says she is living ___.

term: the pen is mightier than the sword
story: English writer Edward Bulwer-Lytton coined the line in his 1839 play Richelieu, in which a powerful French cardinal declares, “The pen is mightier than the sword.”
def: writing and ideas can change the world more than violence or force can
ex: The reporter's articles exposed the corrupt mayor, proving the pen is mightier than the sword.
Our history teacher believes the pen is mightier than the sword and assigns essays on great speeches.
Fatima's letter to the newspaper convinced the city to save the library, proof that the pen is mightier than the sword.
The debate coach told her students that the pen is mightier than the sword, so they should win with arguments.

cloze.s: The novel changed how millions of readers felt about the war, a reminder that ___.
cloze.a: the pen is mightier than the sword

story: English poet John Donne wrote “No man is an island, entire of itself” in a 1624 book of meditations written while he was recovering from a serious illness. He argued that all people are connected, so every death affects everyone.
def: no one can live completely alone; everyone depends on and is connected to other people
ex: After the flood, neighbors helped Jamal rebuild his house, and he realized that no man is an island.
The coach reminded her star player that no man is an island and that she needed her teammates.
Running her shop alone, Fatima learned that no man is an island and joined a group of local business owners.
The teacher reminded the class that no man is an island, so asking for help is a strength.

cloze.s: Wei always refused help from anyone, until a broken leg taught him that ___.

story: In his 1785 poem “To a Mouse,” Scottish poet Robert Burns, after turning up a mouse's nest with his plow, writes that “the best-laid schemes o' mice an' men / Gang aft agley,” meaning they often go wrong. John Steinbeck took the title Of Mice and Men from this poem.
def: even the most carefully prepared plans can fail
ex: The best-laid plans can fall apart, as Sofia learned when a storm hit her outdoor wedding.
Liam had a schedule for every hour of the trip, but the best-laid plans often go wrong.
We booked the tickets months ahead, but the best-laid plans fell apart when the concert was canceled.
The best-laid plans of the coaching staff collapsed when two starters got sick before the game.

cloze.s: Maria spent weeks organizing the surprise party, but her husband came home three hours early; so much for ___.

story: The earliest known version is in Anne Isabella Ritchie's 1885 English novel Mrs. Dymond: give a man a fish and he is hungry again in an hour, but teach him to catch fish and you do him a good turn. It is often called a Chinese proverb, but no early Chinese source has been found.
def: teaching people skills to help themselves is better than simply giving them what they need for now
ex: The charity follows the idea of “give a man a fish” and trains farmers instead of only handing out food.
When Priya asked her brother to fix her computer, he quoted “give a man a fish” and showed her how.
Rather than pay off her son's credit card again, Maria quoted “give a man a fish” and helped him build a budget.
Grandpa Kwame never simply paid for repairs; he believed in “give a man a fish” and taught his kids to fix things.

cloze.s: Instead of doing her son's math homework, Aisha remembered the saying “___” and taught him the method.

note: Full saying: “Give a man a fish, and you feed him for a day; teach a man to fish, and you feed him for a lifetime.”

term: God helps those who help themselves
story: Ancient Greek writers expressed the idea that the gods help those who help themselves. The modern English wording appeared in a 1698 book by Algernon Sidney, and Benjamin Franklin made it popular in Poor Richard's Almanack in 1736.
def: you should work hard to solve your own problems instead of just waiting for help
ex: Diego's grandmother told him God helps those who help themselves, so he started applying for jobs every day.
Rather than wait for the city to fix the playground, the parents agreed that God helps those who help themselves.
Instead of waiting for a lucky break, Yuki took night classes, believing God helps those who help themselves.
When the team blamed bad luck, their coach said God helps those who help themselves and ordered extra practice.

cloze.s: Stop hoping the problem will go away and start working on it; ___.
cloze.a: God helps those who help themselves

note: Many people think it is a Bible verse, but it is not in the Bible.

story: The princes in fairy tales such as Cinderella and Sleeping Beauty often have no name. In the 1600s, French writer Madame d'Aulnoy called one hero “King Charming,” and Andrew Lang's 1889 English retelling named a hero “Charming,” helping create the name Prince Charming.
def: an ideal romantic partner who seems perfect in every way
ex: Olga is tired of waiting for Prince Charming and has started enjoying life on her own.
On their first date, Malik was so polite and funny that Hannah wondered if she had found her Prince Charming.
Diego's sister has a long list for her Prince Charming: kind, funny, and great with dogs.
Fatima's friends kept setting her up on dates, hoping she'd finally meet her Prince Charming.

cloze.s: Real relationships take work; don't wait for a(n) ___ who will solve all your problems.

story: Many fairy tales told in English end with the words “and they lived happily ever after,” usually after the hero and heroine marry. The phrase came to stand for a perfect ending with no more trouble.
def: a perfect ending in which people stay happy forever and have no more problems
ex: Real marriages take effort; there is no automatic happily ever after.
The movie ends with the couple's wedding and the promise of happily ever after.
Winning the lottery didn't bring Malik a happily ever after; his money problems simply changed shape.
After the adoption was finally approved, the family hoped for their own happily ever after.

cloze.s: Kwame beat cancer and is healthy again, but he says life isn't a fairy tale with a guaranteed ___.

story: In the German fairy tale Hansel and Gretel, collected by the Brothers Grimm, Hansel drops breadcrumbs to mark the way home through the forest, but birds eat them and the children get lost.
def: a series of small clues or signs that lead someone toward something
ex: The detective followed a trail of breadcrumbs from the stolen credit card to the suspect's apartment.
Good websites leave a trail of breadcrumbs so visitors always know how to get back to the main page.
The historian followed a trail of breadcrumbs through old letters to learn who really wrote the famous song.
Hannah's online shopping left a trail of breadcrumbs, so her brother easily guessed what birthday gift she had bought him.

cloze.s: The mystery novel leaves ___, small hints that let careful readers guess the ending.

term: a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow
story: In popular legend, often linked with the leprechauns of Irish folklore, a pot of gold lies hidden at the end of the rainbow. Since no one can ever reach a rainbow's end, the treasure always stays out of reach.
def: a great reward or fortune that someone hopes for but that may never be reached
ex: Jamal kept switching jobs, always chasing the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow.
For many young athletes, a pro contract is the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow, but few ever get one.
Aisha stopped chasing a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow and took a steady job she enjoyed.
The ad for the online course promised a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow, but buyers got only a few basic videos.

cloze.s: Buying lottery tickets every week, Yuki still dreams of finding ___.
cloze.a: a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow

story: The saying comes from medieval Persian Sufi poetry, which tells of a king who asked his wise men for something to cheer him when he was sad; they gave him a ring engraved “This too shall pass.” Later versions told the story about King Solomon.
def: every situation, good or bad, is temporary and will eventually end
ex: During her hardest semester, Sofia kept a note on her mirror that said, “This too shall pass.”
Diego's father told him the pain of the breakup was real, but this too shall pass.
Stuck in traffic for two hours, Olga reminded herself that this too shall pass.
After the company's best year ever, the founder warned the staff not to get comfortable: this too shall pass.

cloze.s: When the team lost ten games in a row, the coach told the players to stay calm: “___.”

term: see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil
story: A famous 17th-century carving at the Tōshō-gū shrine in Nikkō, Japan, shows three monkeys covering their eyes, ears and mouth. The idea may come from a saying of Confucius about not looking, listening or speaking in ways that are improper.
def: choosing to ignore bad behavior, pretending not to notice it so you don't have to act
ex: Employees knew the manager was stealing, but everyone took a see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil approach.
The report blamed the league's see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil attitude toward cheating.
Everyone at the gym knew the trainer was selling fake supplements, but the owner's policy was see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil.
When the star player kept breaking curfew, the coaches went into see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil mode.

cloze.s: Neighbors heard the shouting every night but never did anything; it was a case of ___.
cloze.a: see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil

note: In Japan the saying means avoiding evil itself; in English it usually criticizes people who look the other way.

term: an apple a day keeps the doctor away
story: The earliest recorded version is an 1866 saying from Pembrokeshire, in Wales: “Eat an apple on going to bed, and you'll keep the doctor from earning his bread.” The modern wording appeared by the late 1800s.
def: eating healthy food regularly helps you stay well and avoid getting sick
ex: Wei packs fruit in her kids' lunches, saying an apple a day keeps the doctor away.
The school nurse hung a poster that said, “An apple a day keeps the doctor away.”
Diego joined a gym and started eating salads, joking that an apple a day keeps the doctor away.
When her son asked why he had to eat fruit, Priya smiled and said an apple a day keeps the doctor away.

cloze.s: Grandpa eats fruit every single morning and swears that ___.
cloze.a: an apple a day keeps the doctor away

story: SOS became the international distress signal under an agreement signed in Berlin in 1906; in Morse code it is a short, distinctive pattern of three dots, three dashes and three dots. The letters do not stand for words; “save our souls” was added later.
def: an urgent call or message asking for help
ex: The stranded hikers stamped a giant SOS in the snow, and a helicopter spotted it.
Kwame sent an SOS text to his roommate when he locked himself out in the rain.
When the party ran out of plates, the restaurant manager sent an SOS to the shop next door.
The crew of the sinking fishing boat radioed an SOS, and the coast guard arrived within an hour.

cloze.s: The school sent out a(n) ___ to parents, asking for volunteers after half the staff got sick.

story: A popular story links the name to Samuel Wilson, a meatpacker in Troy, New York, who supplied food to the U.S. Army during the War of 1812 in shipments stamped “U.S.” Historians doubt the story, but the name stuck, and James Montgomery Flagg's 1917 “I Want You” recruiting poster made the image famous.
def: a nickname for the United States government, often pictured as a tall man with a white beard and top hat
ex: Every April, Diego grumbles about how much of his paycheck goes to Uncle Sam.
The poster showed Uncle Sam pointing straight at the viewer, asking young people to join the army.
Thanks to the GI Bill, Uncle Sam helped pay for Grandpa's college degree after the war.
After four years in the Air Force, Kwame said he was ready to stop working for Uncle Sam.

cloze.s: When you win a big lottery prize, ___ takes a large share in federal taxes.

story: The British government designed a poster with this slogan in 1939 to raise spirits in case of heavy bombing in World War II, but it was almost never displayed. A bookstore owner in England found an original copy in 2000, and the design became hugely popular.
def: stay calm and continue with normal life, even during a crisis
ex: When the power went out during the exam, the teacher told everyone to keep calm and carry on.
The office flooded on Monday, but Olga put up a sign saying “Keep Calm and Carry On” and kept working from the hallway.
Their flight was delayed six hours, so Wei bought a book and decided to keep calm and carry on.
When the stock market dropped sharply, Fatima's financial adviser told her to keep calm and carry on.

cloze.s: The airport was chaos after the storm delays, but the pilot's message was simple: “___.”

story: From the 1400s to the 1700s, thousands of people in Europe and colonial America were accused of witchcraft and put to death; during the Salem witch trials in Massachusetts in 1692, nineteen people were hanged. The term now describes any unfair campaign to find and punish people.
def: an unfair campaign to find and punish people, based on fear, rumors or weak evidence rather than proof
ex: Employees said the search for whoever leaked the memo had become a witch hunt targeting anyone who complained.
The coach called the fans' online attacks on the young referee a witch hunt.
Neighbors started a witch hunt against the new family, blaming them for every broken mailbox without any proof.
Players said the league's drug investigation had become a witch hunt based on anonymous tips.

cloze.s: The new rules were meant to stop cheating, but students felt they were victims of a(n) ___ based on rumors.

story: When dominoes stand in a row, knocking over the first one makes all the others fall in turn. In 1954, U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower described a “falling domino” principle, the fear that one country after another would fall to communism, which made the image widely known.
def: a situation in which one event causes a chain of similar events, one after another
ex: When the main supplier closed, the domino effect shut down three factories that depended on it.
One canceled flight caused a domino effect of delays across the whole airline.
Missing one rent payment set off a domino effect of late fees, bad credit, and higher loan rates for Olga.
The star player's injury had a domino effect, forcing the coach to change three other positions.

cloze.s: Malik's late alarm set off a(n) ___: he missed the bus, got to work late, and missed his big meeting.

story: The Vandals were a Germanic people who captured and looted Rome in AD 455. In 1794, French bishop Henri Grégoire coined the word vandalisme for the destruction of art during the French Revolution, and the Vandals' name came to mean anyone who wrecks property, though they may have been no more destructive than other invaders of the time.
def: a person who deliberately damages or destroys public or private property
ex: Vandals spray-painted the new bus shelter the night after it opened.
The museum installed cameras after a vandal scratched one of its paintings.
A vandal carved initials into the old oak tree in the town park.
The school spent thousands of dollars repairing the gym after vandals broke in over the weekend.

cloze.s: Police are looking for the ___ who smashed the windows of every car on the street.

story: The Hail Mary is a Catholic prayer to Mary, the mother of Jesus. After a 1975 playoff game, Dallas Cowboys quarterback Roger Staubach said of his game-winning long pass, “I closed my eyes and said a Hail Mary,” making the term popular for desperate last-second tries.
def: a desperate, last-minute attempt that has only a small chance of working
ex: With the company nearly bankrupt, the CEO made a Hail Mary pitch to a major investor.
Down by four points with two seconds left, the quarterback threw a Hail Mary into the end zone.
With the deadline an hour away, Olga sent a Hail Mary email asking the client for one more day.
As a Hail Mary to avoid closing, the shop owner put everything in the store on sale.

cloze.s: Failing the class, Liam made a(n) ___ effort by begging the professor for extra-credit work the night before grades were due.

story: The term comes from English cricket: in 1858, H. H. Stephenson took three wickets with three balls in a row, and fans collected money to buy him a hat. It later spread to soccer and hockey, where it means one player scoring three goals in a game.
def: three goals scored by one player in a single game, or any three successes in a row
ex: Sofia scored a hat trick in the championship game, all three goals coming in the second half.
Winning the award for the third straight year gave the little bakery a hat trick.
Kenji was only seventeen when he scored his first hat trick for the city's professional soccer team.
Winning class president three years in a row gave Jamal a hat trick.

cloze.s: After two goals in the first period, fans threw their hats onto the ice when the center completed his ___.

story: Timbuktu, a city in Mali in West Africa, was a rich center of trade and Islamic learning, especially from the 1300s to the 1500s. Europeans heard tales of its wealth but found it very hard to reach, so its name became a symbol of a faraway place.
def: any place that is extremely far away or remote
ex: The new office is so far from downtown that it might as well be in Timbuktu.
Kwame's lost suitcase traveled everywhere from here to Timbuktu before it finally reached him.
Kwame's parents moved to a cabin so remote that his friends joke they live in Timbuktu.
The cheap flight had three layovers and seemed to route us through Timbuktu.

cloze.s: I'd follow my favorite band anywhere, from New York to ___.

story: Legends of magical water that brings back youth go back to ancient times. In 1535, a Spanish historian wrote that the explorer Juan Ponce de León had searched for such waters, though Ponce never mentioned it in his own writings.
def: something believed to keep people young or make them feel young again
ex: Hannah says swimming every morning is her fountain of youth.
Companies sell expensive creams as a fountain of youth, but most do little for wrinkles.
Travel ads call the island's hot springs a fountain of youth, but visitors mostly just come home relaxed.
Scientists study why some people stay healthy into old age, but no pill is a true fountain of youth.

cloze.s: At 85, Grandpa Tomás still dances every weekend and calls music his ___.

story: The word comes from tapu in the Tongan language of Polynesia, meaning sacred or forbidden. British explorer Captain James Cook recorded it in 1777 during his visit to Tonga, describing things that were forbidden to be eaten or used.
def: something people avoid doing or talking about because their culture sees it as wrong or deeply embarrassing
ex: In Priya's family, talking about money at dinner was taboo.
Mental health used to be a taboo subject at work, but many companies now discuss it openly.
In many American workplaces, asking a coworker about their salary is still taboo.
In the small town, divorce was once a taboo topic that families never discussed.

cloze.s: In many cultures, it is ___ to wear outdoor shoes inside someone's home.

term: low man on the totem pole
story: Totem poles are tall carved wooden poles made by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast of North America. The phrase was in use by the late 1930s and was made famous by H. Allen Smith's 1941 humor book Low Man on a Totem Pole; it assumes the top figure is most important, but many Native carvers did not rank figures that way, and some put the most important at the bottom.
def: the person with the least power or lowest rank in a group or organization
ex: As the newest nurse on the ward, Aisha was low man on the totem pole and got the holiday shifts.
Interns are usually low man on the totem pole, fetching coffee and making copies.
As the youngest cousin, Tomás was low man on the totem pole and got the folding chair at dinner.
Being low man on the totem pole at the law firm meant Yuki worked almost every weekend.

cloze.s: Since Wei had joined the band last, he was ___ and had to carry all the heavy speakers.
cloze.a: low man on the totem pole

note: The image comes from outsiders' assumptions about totem poles, not from Native tradition.

story: The phrase comes from the Chinese gōng hé, short for the name of Chinese worker cooperatives and understood to mean “work together.” U.S. Marine officer Evans Carlson made it his battalion's motto in World War II, and it spread into everyday English.
def: very eager and enthusiastic, sometimes too eager and not careful enough
ex: The new volunteers were gung-ho about cleaning the park and showed up an hour early.
Malik was so gung-ho about his new diet that he threw out every snack in the house.
Gung-ho new volunteers often sign up for every committee in their first month and burn out by spring.
Diego was gung-ho about learning guitar and practiced for three hours on his very first day.

cloze.s: Olga was so ___ about the camping trip that she bought every piece of gear in the store.

story: The English word is a translation of the Chinese xǐnǎo, “wash brain.” Journalist Edward Hunter brought it into English in 1950 to describe forceful ways of changing people's beliefs, and it spread during the Korean War, when some captured American soldiers cooperated with their captors.
def: to make someone believe something by pressuring them or repeating ideas until they stop thinking for themselves
ex: Jamal joked that the cartoon ads had brainwashed his kids into wanting the same cereal.
Former members said the group brainwashed them into cutting off contact with their families.
The coach joked that he had brainwashed his players into loving early-morning practice.
In the spy movie, enemy agents brainwash a soldier into following their orders without question.

cloze.s: After months of watching only one kind of online video, Diego worried that it had ___ his younger brother.

story: Honcho comes from the Japanese word hanchō, meaning “squad leader.” American servicemen picked it up in the mid-1900s and brought it home, where it came to mean the person in charge.
def: the person in charge; the boss or leader of a group or organization
ex: If you want a refund, you'll have to talk to the head honcho.
Maria became the head honcho of the hospital's nursing staff after twenty years there.
When the new head honcho took over the factory, she met every worker on the floor in her first week.
Liam's dad is the head honcho at the local hardware store, so he decides what goes on sale.

cloze.s: Everyone sat up straight when the ___ of the whole company walked into the meeting.

story: The boomerang is a curved throwing stick made by Aboriginal Australians, and the word comes from an Aboriginal language of the Sydney area, where it was recorded in 1822. Because some boomerangs fly back to the thrower, the word came to describe actions that come back to hurt the person who started them.
def: of a plan or action, to come back and harm the person who started it
ex: The rumor Liam spread about his rival boomeranged when people found out who started it.
Raising prices too fast can boomerang on a company if loyal customers leave.
Diego's plan to skip practice and blame the bus boomeranged when the coach checked the bus schedule.
The company's attack ads against its rival boomeranged, making shoppers trust the company less.

cloze.s: Hannah's plan to embarrass her coworker ___, and she ended up looking foolish in front of the boss.

story: The Bermuda Triangle is an area of the Atlantic Ocean between Florida, Bermuda and Puerto Rico where some ships and planes have vanished, including five U.S. Navy bombers in 1945. Writers in the 1950s and 1960s made it sound mysterious, but studies show accidents there are no more common than in other busy waters.
def: a place where things seem to disappear without any explanation
ex: Our laundry room is a Bermuda Triangle for socks.
Kwame's emails to the billing department vanish as if into the Bermuda Triangle.
The back seat of Hannah's car is a Bermuda Triangle for pens and hair ties.
Every spring the school's art budget seems to vanish into a Bermuda Triangle, and no one can explain where it went.

cloze.s: I've lost three umbrellas at that office; it's a(n) ___ for anything you leave by the door.

story: Guinea pigs, small rodents first tamed in the Andes of South America, have been used in scientific experiments since at least the 1600s. By the early 1900s, the name was being used for any person or thing that something is tested on.
def: a person used to test something new, such as a medicine, product or method
ex: Sofia volunteered to be the guinea pig for her friend's new haircut technique.
Our school was the guinea pig for the city's new four-day school week.
Kwame let his little sister use him as a guinea pig for her new pancake recipe.
Volunteers in the study agreed to be guinea pigs for a new allergy medicine.

cloze.s: Before launching the app to the public, the company used its own employees as ___ to find bugs.

story: The term came from a 1980s U.S. study of the AIDS epidemic in which one patient was labeled “Patient O,” for “Out of California.” Readers mistook the letter O for a zero, and the name stuck, though later research showed that patient had not started the epidemic.
def: the first person known to have a disease in an outbreak; also, the starting point of any spreading problem
ex: Health officials traced the measles outbreak back to patient zero, a traveler returning from abroad.
Wei was patient zero for the office flu, sneezing through Monday's meeting.
Liam's son was patient zero for the stomach bug that spread through the whole daycare.
The rumor spread across the whole school, and everyone wanted to know who was patient zero.

cloze.s: Investigators found that the virus that froze the bank's computers started on one laptop, the ___ of the attack.

story: The idea is linked to Hippocrates, the ancient Greek doctor; a medical work from his school tells doctors to help, or at least to do no harm. The exact wording “first, do no harm” is not in the Hippocratic Oath and is found only in much later writings.
def: before taking action, make sure you will not make the situation worse
ex: The new principal's motto was “first, do no harm,” so she made few changes in her first year.
When treating a patient, doctors weigh every risk, guided by the rule first, do no harm.
The new park manager's rule was first, do no harm, so she studied the wetland before cutting any trees.
When comforting a grieving friend, Malik follows the idea of first, do no harm and mostly just listens.

cloze.s: Before rewriting the whole software system, the engineer reminded the team of the rule “___” and asked what might break.

story: Litmus is a dye made from lichens that chemists use to test liquids: litmus paper turns red in an acid and blue in a base. Because the test gives one quick, clear answer, the phrase came to mean a single question used to judge something.
def: a single issue or question used to judge whether someone or something is acceptable
ex: For Fatima, how a date treats the waiter is a litmus test of his character.
The first big storm was a litmus test for the city's new flood barriers.
For Jamal, the quality of a restaurant's bread is a litmus test for the whole kitchen.
Investors saw the first three months of sales as a litmus test for the company's new phone.

cloze.s: How the company handled the product recall became a(n) ___ of whether customers could trust it.

story: In the 1960s TV series Star Trek, Captain Kirk often asked engineer Scotty to “beam” him back to the starship with a machine that sent people instantly through space. The exact words “Beam me up, Scotty” were never actually said on the show, though lines like “Scotty, beam us up” were.
def: a joking wish to escape right away from an unpleasant, boring or strange situation
ex: Stuck in a three-hour traffic jam, Liam muttered, “Beam me up, Scotty.”
When the party turned awkward, Yuki texted her sister one line: “Beam me up, Scotty.”
As the tent began to leak on the first night of their camping trip, Diego groaned, “Beam me up, Scotty.”
When her flight was delayed for the third time, Fatima posted a photo of the crowded gate: “Beam me up, Scotty.”

cloze.s: The meeting dragged on with no end in sight, and Aisha whispered, “___!”

term: with great power comes great responsibility
story: Spider-Man's first comic, Amazing Fantasy #15 (1962), ends with the caption “with great power there must also come great responsibility.” Later stories gave the line to Peter Parker's Uncle Ben, though similar ideas appear much earlier, in the Bible and in old political speeches.
def: people who have a lot of power or ability must use it carefully and for good
ex: When Priya became team captain, her coach told her that with great power comes great responsibility.
Tech companies hold huge amounts of personal data, and with great power comes great responsibility.
The new editor told her staff that with great power comes great responsibility, since millions read their stories.
Promoted to night supervisor, Hannah knew every patient on the floor now depended on her; with great power comes great responsibility.

cloze.s: Handing his teenage son the car keys for the first time, Jamal said, “Remember, ___.”
cloze.a: with great power comes great responsibility

story: Hakuna matata is a Swahili phrase meaning roughly “there are no worries.” Disney's 1994 film The Lion King made it famous worldwide through a song in which Timon the meerkat and Pumbaa the warthog share it with young Simba as a carefree motto.
def: no worries; a relaxed attitude of not letting problems bother you
ex: When the restaurant lost their reservation, Diego just shrugged and said, “Hakuna matata.”
Kwame's hakuna matata attitude helps him stay calm before big exams.
Rain canceled our beach day, but Grandma said “hakuna matata” and taught us card games instead.
Liam's hakuna matata approach to deadlines drives his more anxious coworkers crazy.

cloze.s: Missed the bus? ___! There's another one in ten minutes.

story: Homer Simpson, the father on the long-running cartoon The Simpsons, says “D'oh!” whenever he hurts himself or realizes he has done something stupid. Actor Dan Castellaneta created the sound, and the word entered the Oxford English Dictionary in 2001.
def: a word said when you suddenly realize you have made a silly mistake
ex: Hannah locked her keys in the car, slapped her forehead and said, “D'oh!”
“D'oh! I forgot the milk again,” Tomás groaned as he unpacked the groceries.
Kwame reached the airport, realized his passport was still on the kitchen table, and groaned, “D'oh!”
“D'oh! I studied the wrong chapter,” Yuki whispered as she read the first test question.

cloze.s: Malik realized he had sent the email without the attachment and muttered, “___”

term: May the Force be with you
story: In the 1977 film Star Wars, characters wish each other luck with these words. The Force is a mysterious energy that gives the Jedi knights their special powers.
def: a friendly, often joking way to wish someone good luck
ex: Before Olga's driving test, her brother saluted and said, “May the Force be with you.”
The professor ended the last class before finals with “May the Force be with you.”
Before Malik walked onstage for his first comedy show, the host gave him a thumbs-up and said, “May the Force be with you.”
Before the soccer final, the team captain texted everyone, “May the Force be with you.”

cloze.s: As Wei walked into her job interview, her best friend whispered, “___.”
cloze.a: May the Force be with you

story: In the 1984 film The Terminator, Arnold Schwarzenegger's robot killer is turned away at a police station's front desk and says, “I'll be back.” Moments later he drives a car through the front doors, and the line became one of the most quoted in film.
def: a joking or determined promise to return, often to try again after losing or failing
ex: After losing the chess tournament, Diego shook hands with the winner and said, “I'll be back.”
Leaving the store without the shoes she wanted, Aisha told the clerk, “I'll be back.”
After failing her driving test, Priya smiled at the examiner and said, “I'll be back.”
The champion lost her title this year, but she promised her fans, “I'll be back next season.”

cloze.s: The young boxer lost his first title fight but told reporters with a grin, “___.”

term: life is like a box of chocolates
story: In the 1994 film Forrest Gump, Tom Hanks's character says, “My mama always said life was like a box of chocolates. You never know what you're gonna get.”
def: life is full of surprises, and you can never be sure what will happen next
ex: Kwame never planned to become a chef, but life is like a box of chocolates.
When Sofia met her future husband during a canceled flight, she laughed that life is like a box of chocolates.
Priya moved to Denver for an office job and ended up opening a bakery; life is like a box of chocolates.
Hannah's grandfather says life is like a box of chocolates: he moved to Ohio for one year and stayed for fifty.

cloze.s: One week Liam lost his job, the next he got a better offer; as they say, ___.
cloze.a: life is like a box of chocolates

story: The line comes from the 1823 song “Home! Sweet Home!” (“Be it ever so humble, there's no place like home”). In the 1939 film The Wizard of Oz, Dorothy repeats it while clicking the heels of her ruby slippers to return to Kansas.
def: your own home is more comfortable and welcoming than anywhere else
ex: After two weeks in hotels, Maria flopped onto her own couch and sighed, “There's no place like home.”
The soldier's first words as he stepped off the plane were “There's no place like home.”
After her long hospital stay, Grandma Rosa smiled at her own garden and said there's no place like home.
Living abroad for a year taught Diego that there's no place like home.

cloze.s: Fancy resorts are fun, but Grandma always says ___ and sleeps best in her own bed.

story: In 1956, at a Louisiana Hayride show in Shreveport, the announcer told fans still screaming for Elvis Presley that he had left the building, so they would stop waiting and let the other acts perform. Announcers at Presley's concerts later used the line often.
def: it is over; the main event has ended and there is nothing more to wait for
ex: When the star player was traded away, one sad fan posted, “Elvis has left the building.”
The professor closed her laptop, smiled and said, “That's it, folks; Elvis has left the building.”
By the time Diego arrived at the big sale, the shelves were bare; Elvis had left the building.
When the chef closed the kitchen at ten, the waiter told late customers that Elvis had left the building.

cloze.s: The fireworks ended, the band packed up, and the host told the lingering guests, “___; time to go home.”

term: a picture is worth a thousand words
story: The saying grew out of American advertising in the early 1900s. Advertising man Fred R. Barnard used a version of it in 1921 and later called it a “Chinese proverb,” admitting he did so to make people take it seriously.
def: an image can explain an idea more quickly and clearly than a long description
ex: Instead of describing the flood damage, Priya sent a photo; a picture is worth a thousand words.
The teacher used a simple chart because a picture is worth a thousand words.
The real estate agent posted dozens of photos of the house, knowing a picture is worth a thousand words.
Instead of writing long directions, Kwame drew a quick map, since a picture is worth a thousand words.

cloze.s: The doctor showed Jamal the X-ray of his broken bone, since ___.
cloze.a: a picture is worth a thousand words

story: John Hancock was president of the Continental Congress in 1776 and signed the Declaration of Independence with a very large, bold signature. His name became an informal American word for a person's signature.
def: a person's signature, especially when signing a form or official paper
ex: The bank teller slid the form across and said, “Put your John Hancock right here.”
Yuki needed her landlord's John Hancock on the lease before she could move in.
The coach needed every parent's John Hancock on the permission slip before the field trip.
After buying the house, Diego joked that he had put his John Hancock on about fifty pages.

cloze.s: Before the rental company gives you the car keys, you'll need to put your ___ on the contract.

story: Mother Teresa (1910–1997) was a Catholic nun who spent decades caring for poor, sick and dying people in Kolkata, India. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and was declared a saint in 2016, and her name became shorthand for selfless kindness.
def: a person who is extremely kind and generous, always putting the needs of others first
ex: Malik volunteers at three shelters every week; he's a real Mother Teresa.
I'm no Mother Teresa, but I do carry my elderly neighbor's groceries every Saturday.
Mrs. Nguyen cooks for every sick neighbor on the street, so people call her the block's Mother Teresa.
You don't have to be a Mother Teresa to help; even one hour a month at the food bank matters.

cloze.s: Hannah gave her lunch, her coat and her bus fare to strangers today; she's a regular ___.

note: Often used in the negative: “I'm no Mother Teresa” means “I'm not perfectly good.”

term: carry the weight of the world on your shoulders
story: In Greek myth, the Titan Atlas fought against Zeus and lost, so he was punished by having to hold up the sky forever. Later art often showed him holding a globe, which is why people now picture the world on his shoulders.
def: to feel responsible for many heavy problems at once, often without help from anyone
ex: Since her father got sick, Aisha has been carrying the weight of the world on her shoulders at home and at the shop.
You don’t have to carry the weight of the world on your shoulders; let the rest of the team share the work.
As the oldest of five children, Malik carried the weight of the world on his shoulders after his mom lost her job.
Before the final game, the team captain felt she was carrying the weight of the world on her shoulders.

cloze.s: After the layoffs, the new manager looked tired and tense, as if he were ___.
cloze.a: carrying the weight of the world on his shoulders

note: In the original myth Atlas holds up the sky, not the earth.

story: The Greek philosopher Plato, writing around 360 BCE, described Atlantis, a rich and powerful island nation that sank into the sea in a single day and night. Most scholars believe he invented it as a moral tale about pride and power.
def: a lost world or place, often imagined as wonderful, that has disappeared and may never be found
ex: Divers called the flooded village under the reservoir a modern Atlantis, its church tower still visible in dry summers.
Treasure hunters have searched for the golden city for decades, but like Atlantis, it may never have existed.
To Grandpa, the record store of his youth is a lost Atlantis that no city map shows anymore.
For collectors, the band's unreleased first album is an Atlantis they keep searching for but never find.

cloze.s: When the lake was drained, the old town that had been flooded in 1950 rose from the mud like a sunken ___.

story: In the Book of Genesis, God places Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, a perfect garden that gives them everything they need. They are sent out after eating fruit that God had forbidden.
def: a perfectly beautiful, peaceful place where life seems easy and innocent
ex: With its fruit trees and quiet streams, the valley looked like the Garden of Eden to the tired hikers.
Diego remembers his grandmother’s farm as a Garden of Eden where summers never seemed to end.
The rooftop garden, full of flowers and birdsong, felt like a Garden of Eden above the noisy city.
After the long winter, Hannah's blooming backyard felt like her own Garden of Eden.

cloze.s: After weeks crossing the desert, the green oasis with its palm trees and cool springs felt like the ___.

story: In the Book of Genesis, Noah sends a dove out of the ark after the great flood, and it comes back with a fresh olive leaf, a sign that the waters are going down. The olive branch was also a sign of peace in ancient Greece and Rome.
def: an offer to make peace or end a fight or argument
ex: After their argument, Hannah held out an olive branch by inviting her brother to dinner.
The company offered the union an olive branch: a small raise while talks continued.
After the vote, the new club president extended an olive branch to the members who had opposed her.
Diego sent his former best friend a birthday card as an olive branch after years of silence.

cloze.s: The two rival coaches had not spoken in years until one of them held out a(n) ___ and asked to shake hands.

story: The phrase comes from the King James Bible, where the apostle Paul praises early Christians for their “work of faith, and labour of love” (1 Thessalonians 1:3).
def: hard work that someone does because they care about it, not for money or reward
ex: Restoring the old sailboat took Kwame six years, but it was a labor of love.
The free neighborhood newsletter is a labor of love for Sofia, who writes it every Sunday night.
Writing a cookbook of her grandmother's recipes was a labor of love for Priya.
The volunteer firefighters say their long unpaid nights are a labor of love for their town.

cloze.s: Olga earns nothing from running the community garden; tending it is purely a(n) ___.

story: The phrase comes from the King James Bible (Romans 13:1), which says that “the powers that be are ordained of God,” meaning the rulers who are in charge.
def: the people with authority who make the decisions, often far away or not named
ex: The powers that be have decided we’re moving offices in March, and nobody asked us.
Jamal hopes the powers that be at the league will finally change the replay rule.
The powers that be at the airline canceled our flight, and the gate staff couldn't tell us why.
Students asked the powers that be to keep the library open later during exam week.

cloze.s: We all wanted a four-day week, but ___ at headquarters said no.

note: Usually said with mild frustration or irony.

story: In the Bible, the apostle Paul warns some early Christians that they have “fallen from grace” (Galatians 5:4), meaning they have lost God’s favor. The phrase later came to mean any loss of standing.
def: a sudden loss of respect, power, or popularity, often because of a scandal or mistake
ex: The star chef’s fall from grace began when health inspectors shut down his flagship restaurant.
Once the league’s top scorer, the striker suffered a fall from grace after failing a drug test.
The once-beloved TV host's fall from grace came after his rude emails to staff were made public.
In the novel, the war hero's fall from grace begins when he lies to protect a friend.

cloze.s: The CEO went from magazine covers to a fraud trial in less than a year, a stunning ___.

story: The phrase grew out of Jesus’s words in the King James Bible: “strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life” (Matthew 7:14). “Strait” meant “narrow,” but people later heard it as “straight.”
def: an honest, law-abiding way of living that avoids crime and bad habits
ex: After his release from prison, Liam stayed on the straight and narrow, working two jobs and saving money.
The coach kept her young players on the straight and narrow with strict curfews and study hours.
After a few teenage run-ins with the police, Diego got back on the straight and narrow and opened his own shop.
Joining the boxing gym helped Andre stay on the straight and narrow while many of his friends got into trouble.

cloze.s: Her mentor helped her quit gambling and stay on ___ for good.

story: In the Book of Daniel, Daniel keeps praying to God despite a royal ban, so he is thrown into a den of lions as punishment. He survives the night unharmed, and the king sets him free.
def: a dangerous or hostile place where you must face people who are against you
ex: Presenting the budget cuts to the angry parents felt like walking into the lion’s den.
The visiting team stepped into the lion’s den: a stadium packed with 80,000 rival fans.
Knowing her future in-laws opposed the engagement, Ana walked into the lion’s den for Thanksgiving dinner.
The new manager stepped into the lion’s den when she met with workers furious about their lost overtime.

cloze.s: Knowing the reporters would be hostile, the spokesperson took a deep breath before entering ___.

story: The word comes from the Hindi paṇḍit, from Sanskrit paṇḍita, “learned man,” a title for a scholar of Hindu law, religion and philosophy. English borrowed it in the 1600s and later used it for any expert.
def: an expert who gives opinions on a subject in the media, especially politics or sports
ex: TV pundits predicted an easy win, but the underdog team took the title.
Before the vote, every pundit on the radio had a theory about what people wanted.
Health pundits on morning TV argued all week about whether the new diet actually works.
The election night broadcast featured a panel of pundits guessing which states would decide the race.

cloze.s: The game had barely ended when the ___ in the studio began arguing about the coach’s decisions.

note: Often slightly mocking, suggesting someone who talks with great confidence but may be wrong.

term: the blind men and the elephant
story: In a parable found in Buddhist, Jain, Hindu and Sufi texts, several blind men each touch one part of an elephant, such as the trunk, an ear, or a leg, and argue about what the animal is like. Each is partly right, but none grasps the whole.
def: a situation where people each know only part of the truth and wrongly believe it is the whole
ex: The three departments describing the customer problem were like the blind men and the elephant, each seeing only its own piece.
Without shared data, the research teams risked becoming the blind men and the elephant.
The doctors each studied one symptom, and like the blind men and the elephant, nobody saw the whole illness.
Each parent heard only one child's side of the fight; it was the blind men and the elephant all over again.

cloze.s: The witnesses each saw one corner of the crash and told completely different stories, like ___.
cloze.a: the blind men and the elephant

story: Kamikaze means “divine wind” in Japanese, the name given to storms that wrecked Mongol fleets invading Japan in 1274 and 1281. In World War II, Japan used the name for pilots who crashed their planes into enemy ships on purpose.
def: acting in a wild, reckless way without caring about your own safety or interests
ex: Kamikaze bike messengers weaved between buses during the morning rush hour.
Cutting prices that deeply was a kamikaze move that nearly put the store out of business.
The squirrel made a kamikaze dash across the busy highway.
Skiing straight down the expert slope on his first day was a kamikaze idea, and Diego knew it.

cloze.s: The ___ driver swerved across three lanes at full speed to reach the exit.

note: Some people find the casual use insensitive because of its wartime meaning.

story: The word comes from the Japanese taikun, “great lord,” a title used for the shogun, Japan’s military ruler, in dealings with foreigners. It entered English in 1857, and Abraham Lincoln’s aides jokingly called him “the Tycoon.”
def: a very rich and powerful business owner who controls a large company or industry
ex: The shipping tycoon donated a new wing to the city hospital.
Before she became a media tycoon, Hannah ran a single small-town newspaper.
The real estate tycoon owned half the buildings downtown and controlled the city's biggest construction firm.
Starting with one food cart, Wei grew into a restaurant tycoon with dozens of locations across the state.

cloze.s: Railroad ___ like Cornelius Vanderbilt built enormous fortunes in the 1800s.

story: In feudal Japan, ninja (also called shinobi) were hired agents trained in spying, sabotage and surprise attacks. Movies and comics later turned them into almost magical masters of stealth and fighting.
def: a person who is extremely skilled at a particular activity, often working quickly and quietly
ex: Olga is a spreadsheet ninja who can build a monthly report in ten minutes.
The kitchen staff moved like ninjas, clearing tables before the guests even noticed.
Grandma is a gift-wrapping ninja who can wrap twenty presents in an hour.
Priya is a parking ninja, sliding into the tiniest spaces on the first try.

cloze.s: Our IT ___ fixed the server crash before most of the office knew anything had gone wrong.

story: “Kumbaya” (“come by here”) is an African American spiritual, first recorded in 1926, asking God to come and help people in need. It became a popular campfire song and was sung in the civil rights movement in the 1950s and 1960s; later, people began using it to mock calls for easy harmony.
def: a simple, too-hopeful show of unity that ignores real conflicts between people
ex: The meeting was no Kumbaya moment; the two departments still blamed each other for the delay.
Malik rolled his eyes, saying the rival owners needed hard deals, not Kumbaya speeches.
The coach told the players to skip the Kumbaya hugs and settle their argument honestly.
After the merger, managers held a Kumbaya retreat, but the two teams still refused to share information.

cloze.s: The rivals smiled for the cameras, but nobody expected a(n) ___ moment once the tough negotiations restarted.

note: Usually sarcastic: it mocks the idea that everyone will simply get along.

story: In folklore around the world, the bogeyman is a monster with no fixed appearance that adults say will come for children who misbehave. Spanish-speaking countries have a similar figure called El Coco or El Cuco.
def: a person or thing that people are made to fear, often more than it deserves
ex: For years, video games were the favorite bogeyman of worried parents and talk shows.
Grandma used to warn that the bogeyman would get us if we didn’t go to bed.
For small shop owners, the new superstore became a bogeyman blamed for every slow week.
For many beginners, algebra is a bogeyman, but the first lessons are mostly simple puzzles.

cloze.s: Critics say the report turned social media into a(n) ___, blaming it for problems that have many causes.

note: Also spelled “boogeyman.”

story: The unicorn, a horse-like animal with a single horn, was described by the ancient Greek writer Ctesias and became a symbol of purity and magic in the Middle Ages. In 2013, investor Aileen Lee called startups worth over $1 billion “unicorns” because they were so rare.
def: something extremely rare and hard to find, especially a young company worth over $1 billion
ex: A cheap, sunny apartment near the subway is a unicorn in this city.
The app maker became a unicorn just three years after it was founded.
A plumber who answers the phone on a Sunday and charges fair prices is a true unicorn.
Investors poured money into the delivery startup, hoping it would become the next unicorn.

cloze.s: Recruiters call a candidate with ten years of experience who will accept a beginner’s salary a(n) ___.

story: In the nursery rhyme, first printed in 1797, Humpty Dumpty has a great fall, and in later versions “all the king’s horses and all the king’s men” cannot put him together again. The rhyme never says he is an egg, but he is usually pictured as one.
def: something broken or damaged so badly that it cannot be fixed or put back together
ex: Once trust is gone, a friendship can be a Humpty Dumpty that is very hard to put back together.
Economists warned that the collapsed bank was a Humpty Dumpty no rescue plan could save.
After the bitter fight, the band's partnership was a Humpty Dumpty that no manager could put together again.
Once the factory town lost its only employer, its economy became a Humpty Dumpty that years of grants couldn't repair.

cloze.s: After the scandal, the sponsors left one by one, and like ___, the deal could never be put back together again.

story: In Shakespeare’s The Tempest, Miranda cries, “O brave new world, that has such people in’t!” Aldous Huxley borrowed the phrase for his 1932 novel about a future society kept happy and obedient through technology and drugs.
def: a new age or situation created by change, often with a hint that it may be worse than it looks
ex: Remote work has created a brave new world of video meetings and kitchen-table offices.
Critics warned that editing the genes of babies could lead us into a brave new world we aren’t ready for.
At eighty, Kwame's grandmother stepped into the brave new world of online banking.
Driverless taxis are taking cities into a brave new world, and not everyone feels safe in it.

cloze.s: With robots taking orders and drones delivering meals, the restaurant business is entering a(n) ___.

note: In Shakespeare’s English “brave” meant “splendid”; today the phrase is often ironic.

story: In George Orwell’s novel Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), the Thought Police spy on citizens and punish them for “thoughtcrime,” having ideas that the ruling Party forbids.
def: people accused of trying to control what others are allowed to think or say
ex: Students joked that the strict debate judges had become the thought police.
Some users accuse the website’s moderators of acting like the thought police.
The novelist said she refused to let the thought police decide which characters she was allowed to write.
When the office banned complaining about schedules in group chats, workers grumbled about the thought police.

cloze.s: When the club banned any criticism of its president, members complained that the ___ had taken over.

note: Used as a criticism; it suggests someone wants to punish opinions, not actions.

story: In George Orwell’s Animal Farm (1945), farm animals overthrow their human owner under the rule “All animals are equal.” As the pigs take power, the rule becomes “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.”
def: getting special treatment while claiming that everyone is treated the same
ex: The company says all employees are equal, but managers with reserved parking are clearly more equal than others.
At the tennis club, some members seemed more equal than others when it came to booking courts.
The family rule was no phones at dinner, but Dad was apparently more equal than others.
Every dorm room had the same rules, though the senior students somehow seemed more equal than others.

cloze.s: Everyone was told to fly economy, yet the directors sat in first class; some staff were plainly ___.

story: In Herman Melville’s novel Moby-Dick (1851), Captain Ahab obsessively hunts the great white whale that bit off his leg, a chase that ends up destroying his ship and crew.
def: a goal someone chases for a long time and cannot stop thinking about, often one that seems impossible
ex: Winning the championship has been the veteran coach’s white whale for twenty years.
For the collector, a mint-condition 1952 baseball card was her white whale.
Solving one famous unproven math problem became the professor's white whale, consuming nearly thirty years of her career.
A table at the city's most popular restaurant has been Malik's white whale; he has tried to book one for years.

cloze.s: A perfect 300 game has been Jamal’s ___ ever since he joined the bowling league.

note: Because Ahab’s chase ends in disaster, the phrase can hint that the pursuit is unwise.

story: In Roald Dahl’s novel Charlie and the Chocolate Factory (1964), five golden tickets hidden in chocolate bars allow their lucky finders to tour Willy Wonka’s secret factory.
def: a rare chance or pass that opens the way to something very valuable or desirable
ex: For Sofia, the full scholarship was a golden ticket to a top university.
A job offer from the famous animation studio felt like a golden ticket.
For many young players, a spot on the national youth team is a golden ticket to a professional career.
Kwame's summer job at the hospital turned out to be his golden ticket into medical school.

cloze.s: Only twenty applicants win the fellowship each year, so landing one is seen as a(n) ___ into the film industry.

story: In Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar (1599), Casca says of a speech by Cicero, “it was Greek to me,” because he could not understand it. It may echo a medieval Latin saying used when scribes met Greek they could not read.
def: said when something is completely impossible for you to understand
ex: My accountant explained the new tax rules twice, but it’s all Greek to me.
Diego handed back the car manual with a shrug: “It’s all Greek to me.”
Kwame watched his first cricket match for an hour and finally admitted, “It's all Greek to me.”
Hannah's son tried to explain the rules of his video game, but it was all Greek to her.

cloze.s: Aisha stared at the contract full of long legal clauses and sighed that ___.

term: to thine own self be true
story: In Hamlet, the royal adviser Polonius gives his son Laertes a long list of advice before a trip, ending with “This above all: to thine own self be true.”
def: stay honest with yourself and act according to your own values
ex: When her friends pushed her toward law school, Hannah remembered the old line: to thine own self be true.
The graduation speaker closed with Polonius’s advice: to thine own self be true.
Liam's coach wanted him on the football team, but Liam chose the dance team instead; to thine own self be true.
When friends urged Aisha to hide her accent at work, her mother simply reminded her, “To thine own self be true.”

cloze.s: Malik turned down the high-paying job that clashed with his beliefs, deciding that the old line “___” mattered more than money.
cloze.a: to thine own self be true

note: Polonius is a long-winded, comic character, but the line is usually quoted seriously.

story: During World War II, millions of American women took factory jobs left by men who went to war. A 1942 song and a 1943 Norman Rockwell magazine cover named this working heroine Rosie the Riveter.
def: a symbol of strong, capable women doing work once done mostly by men
ex: Wearing a hard hat and rolled-up sleeves, Fatima looked like a modern Rosie the Riveter.
The museum honored the real-life Rosie the Riveters who built ships and planes during the war.
When the plant hired its first all-female welding crew, the local paper called them today's Rosie the Riveters.
As the first woman to lead the town's construction crew, Keisha proudly hung a Rosie the Riveter poster in her truck.

cloze.s: The welding program for women chose ___ as its symbol, since she stood for women building planes in World War II.

note: The famous “We Can Do It!” poster was linked to the name only in the 1980s.

story: In a 1946 speech in Fulton, Missouri, Winston Churchill said that “an iron curtain has descended across the Continent,” dividing Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe from the West. The divide lasted until 1989.
def: a strong barrier that stops people, information, or trade from passing between two sides
ex: Growing up behind the Iron Curtain, Olga’s parents could rarely buy Western records.
Fans complained of an iron curtain of secrecy around the new film’s plot.
A strict iron curtain around the factory kept rival companies from learning anything about the new design.
The company kept an iron curtain between its research team and its sales staff, so ideas rarely passed through.

cloze.s: Families on opposite sides of ___ were separated for decades during the Cold War.

story: President Harry Truman kept a sign reading “The Buck Stops Here” on his desk, a gift he received in 1945. It plays on “passing the buck” in poker, where a marker showed whose turn it was to deal, and meant he would not shift blame to anyone else.
def: said by someone who accepts final responsibility for decisions and their results
ex: When the product failed, the CEO told reporters, “The buck stops here,” and apologized.
As team captain, Aisha tells her teammates after every loss that the buck stops here, with her.
“I approved the trip, so the buck stops here,” the teacher told parents after the field trip bus broke down.
As head of the hospital, Dr. Nwosu says the buck stops here, so she answers personally for every serious error.

cloze.s: “Don’t blame my staff,” the principal said, insisting that ___ because she had approved the plan.

story: In the 1330s the Italian scholar Petrarch described the centuries after Rome’s fall as a time of “darkness” compared with the brilliant classical world. Historians now avoid the term, since that period had rich art, learning and trade.
def: a time when people seem to know little and progress seems to have stopped
ex: Before email, office communication was in the Dark Ages, with paper memos passed from desk to desk.
Without Wi-Fi at the cabin, the kids complained that they were living in the Dark Ages.
The town library still uses paper cards, and the young librarians feel stuck in the Dark Ages.
Our office's ancient computers make the whole team feel like it's working in the Dark Ages.

cloze.s: Grandpa still pays every bill by mailing a check, and his grandkids tease him for living in the ___.

story: The European Renaissance (roughly 1300–1600) prized people skilled in many fields. Leonardo da Vinci, a painter who also studied anatomy, engineering and flight, is the classic example.
def: a person who is talented and knows a lot about many different areas
ex: A surgeon, jazz pianist and published poet, Dr. Okafor is a true Renaissance man.
Wei is a Renaissance man who builds furniture, speaks four languages and writes code.
Our neighbor Mr. Haddad repairs engines, paints landscapes and teaches chemistry; he's a real Renaissance man.
The job ad seemed to want a Renaissance man, someone who could design, write, sell and manage accounts.

cloze.s: Benjamin Franklin, a printer, scientist, inventor, writer and diplomat, is often called America’s first ___.

note: Also “Renaissance woman” or “Renaissance person.”

story: After quickly defeating King Pharnaces II at the Battle of Zela in 47 BCE, Julius Caesar reported his victory in three Latin words: “Veni, vidi, vici,” meaning “I came, I saw, I conquered.”
def: said to show off about a fast, complete, and easy success
ex: Diego walked out of his driving test grinning and announced, “Veni, vidi, vici.”
The chess champion won in twenty moves, then posted just three words: veni, vidi, vici.
The underdog boxer knocked out the champion in the first round, and the next day's headline read “Veni, Vidi, Vici.”
Yuki fixed the broken printer in thirty seconds after the tech team had failed for days: veni, vidi, vici.

cloze.s: She toured the factory, spotted the problem and fixed it in one afternoon; her report could simply have read ___.

story: The saying is traced to St. Ambrose in the 300s. When St. Augustine and his mother asked whether to fast on Saturdays as people did in Rome, though their church in Milan did not, Ambrose replied that when he was in Rome he fasted on Saturday.
def: when you are in a new place, follow the customs of the people there
ex: Jamal doesn’t usually eat dinner at ten at night, but in Madrid he did: when in Rome.
Maria had never tried eating with her hands, but at the Ethiopian restaurant she said, “When in Rome,” and dug in.
At the Japanese inn, Diego took off his shoes at the door like everyone else; when in Rome.
Liam's new office goes out for karaoke every Friday, so, when in Rome, he grabbed the microphone.

cloze.s: Tomás had never used chopsticks, but at his friend’s family dinner in Seoul he gave them a try; after all, ___.

note: Short for “When in Rome, do as the Romans do.”

story: Under the gold standard, a country’s money was tied to a fixed amount of gold. Most countries left it in the 1930s and the U.S. cut the dollar’s last tie to gold in 1971, but the phrase lived on to mean the best measure of quality.
def: the best example of something, used to judge all the others
ex: Randomized studies that compare a drug with a fake pill are the gold standard for testing new medicines.
Her hotel’s customer service has become the gold standard in the industry.
The chef's tomato sauce became the gold standard that every new cook in the kitchen had to match.
For many teachers, that phonics program is the gold standard for teaching young children to read.

cloze.s: Among home cooks, this 1960s French cookbook is still the ___ that newer books are measured against.

story: Nostradamus was a French doctor and astrologer who published Les Prophéties (1555), a book of four-line poems said to predict the future. Fans still link his verses to later events, but scholars say they are vague enough to fit almost anything.
def: a person who claims, or seems, to be able to predict the future
ex: After correctly picking the last three champions, Kwame became the office Nostradamus.
No financial Nostradamus can tell you exactly when the stock market will fall.
Grandpa played Nostradamus at dinner, predicting which cousin would get married first.
After forecasting the snowstorm a week early, the local weather reporter was called the town's Nostradamus.

cloze.s: The analyst predicted the housing crash years ahead of time, and reporters called her a modern ___.

story: John Chapman, born in 1774 and known as Johnny Appleseed, planted apple tree nurseries across Pennsylvania, Ohio and Indiana as settlers moved west. Legend shows him scattering seeds, but he actually set up fenced nurseries and came back to tend them.
def: a person who spreads something good, such as an idea or project, from place to place
ex: Ms. Ruiz became the Johnny Appleseed of school gardens, helping start one at every school in the district.
Like Johnny Appleseed, the coach spread the sport by founding youth clubs in small towns across the state.
Like a modern Johnny Appleseed, Mei leaves free books in little neighborhood libraries everywhere she travels.
The retired nurse is a Johnny Appleseed of CPR training, teaching free classes in community halls across the county.

cloze.s: Libraries in twelve villages owe their start to Wei, who is known as the ___ of reading in the region.

story: In the 1750s, Benjamin Franklin promoted the lightning rod, a metal rod on a roof that catches lightning strikes and carries the electricity safely into the ground.
def: a person or thing that draws criticism or anger, often taking it away from others
ex: The new replay rule became a lightning rod for fan complaints all season.
As the public face of the merger, Priya became a lightning rod for employees’ anger.
The new toll on the bridge became a lightning rod, with drivers flooding city hall with complaints.
Uncle Jamal's loud opinions make him a lightning rod for arguments at every holiday dinner.

cloze.s: The giant modern sculpture in the town square became a(n) ___ for arguments about public art spending.

story: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. Physicist John Wheeler made the name popular in 1967.
def: something that keeps swallowing money, time, or effort and gives nothing back
