ex: The old stadium became a financial black hole, costing the city millions every year.
Sofia’s inbox is a black hole: messages go in and are never answered.
Kwame's old boat is a black hole for his paycheck, always needing new parts.
The meeting was a black hole of time: three hours and not one decision.

cloze.s: The failing mall had become a financial ___, eating up millions in repairs each year with nothing to show for it.

story: The line is spoken by NASA flight director Gene Kranz in the 1995 film Apollo 13, about the rescue of a damaged moon mission in 1970. Kranz never said it during the mission; the screenwriters created it, and he later used it as the title of his memoir.
def: a firm statement that a goal must be reached, no matter how hard it is
ex: With the hospital’s power down, the chief engineer told his crew that failure is not an option.
A sign in the locker room read “Failure is not an option” in big red letters.
The rescue leader told reporters that failure is not an option while the hikers remained trapped.
Kwame's parents worked two jobs to pay his tuition, so for him, failure is not an option.

cloze.s: Two days before the launch, the boss gathered the exhausted team and said that ___, so they would finish tonight.

story: The Roman writer Cicero tells of Damocles, a courtier who envied the tyrant Dionysius of Syracuse. Dionysius let him enjoy a royal feast in his place, but hung a sword above his head by a single horsehair to show how a ruler always lives in danger.
def: a constant threat of sudden disaster that hangs over someone, even when life seems good
ex: The unpaid tax bill hung over the family business like a sword of Damocles.
For months, the threat of layoffs was a sword of Damocles over everyone in the newsroom.
The threat of a pilots' strike hung over the airline like a sword of Damocles all summer.
For Diego, the coming medical test results were a sword of Damocles during an otherwise happy vacation.

cloze.s: The pending lawsuit was a(n) ___ over the startup: one bad ruling could wipe it out overnight.

story: According to legend, a fiendishly tangled knot in the city of Gordium was said to make whoever untied it the ruler of Asia. In 333 BC Alexander the Great is said to have simply sliced through it with his sword.
def: a very complicated problem, especially one best solved by a bold, direct action instead of slow, careful work
ex: The new manager cut the Gordian knot of overlapping committees by merging them into one.
Tax reform has become a Gordian knot that no lawmaker seems able to untie.
The family's tangle of shared bank accounts was a Gordian knot, so Priya closed them all and started fresh.
Lawyers argued for months over the Gordian knot of the property dispute before the judge cut through it with one ruling.

cloze.s: Instead of fixing the old software line by line, Wei cut the ___ and rebuilt the whole system from scratch.

note: Usually appears as “cut the Gordian knot,” meaning to solve a hard problem with one bold stroke.

story: In Virgil's Aeneid, the priest Laocoön warns the Trojans not to trust the giant wooden horse the Greeks left behind, saying he fears the Greeks even when they bring gifts. The Trojans ignored him, and the horse was full of soldiers.
def: be suspicious of a gift or favor from a rival, because it may hide a trick
ex: When the rival company offered free consulting, Aisha remembered to beware of Greeks bearing gifts.
The sudden friendly offer from the other team made the coach mutter, “Beware of Greeks bearing gifts.”
When the neighboring town that had fought us for years suddenly offered free help, the mayor said, “Beware of Greeks bearing gifts.”
The rival chess club offered to lend us their coach the night before the final, and Kwame muttered about Greeks bearing gifts.

cloze.s: Our biggest competitor wants to lend us its customer list for free? ___ — there must be a catch.

term: the face that launched a thousand ships
story: In Christopher Marlowe's play Doctor Faustus (late 1500s), Faustus sees the spirit of Helen of Troy and asks, “Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?” In Greek legend, the Greek fleet sailed to Troy to win Helen back.
def: a person of such great beauty that people would do huge things for them; often used jokingly
ex: Kwame grinned at his old school photo and said, “Behold, the face that launched a thousand ships.”
The movie poster called the lead actress the face that launched a thousand ships.
As his wife walked into the party, Wei joked, “Here comes the face that launched a thousand ships.”
Fans called the singer the face that launched a thousand ships after her photo sent ticket sales soaring.

cloze.s: In Marlowe's play, Faustus calls Helen of Troy “___” because a war fleet sailed for her sake.
cloze.a: the face that launched a thousand ships

story: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, the sculptor Pygmalion falls in love with the ivory statue of a woman he carved, and the goddess Venus brings it to life. George Bernard Shaw's 1913 play Pygmalion, the basis of My Fair Lady, retold it as a professor training a flower seller to speak like a lady.
def: a person who shapes and trains someone else into a polished, more refined version of themselves; also such a story
ex: The film is a modern Pygmalion story about a coach who turns a shy teenager into a confident champion.
Rosa played Pygmalion to her new assistant, teaching him how to dress, speak and run meetings.
The ballet director saw herself as a Pygmalion, molding raw young dancers into elegant stars.
Friends worried Leo was trying to be Ana's Pygmalion, constantly correcting her clothes, speech and taste.

cloze.s: In this ___ tale, a strict voice teacher transforms a street singer into an opera star.

note: The “Pygmalion effect” in psychology is the idea that higher expectations from others can lead people to perform better.

story: According to ancient Greek tradition, Thespis, a poet in Athens in the 500s BC, was the first person to step out of the chorus and speak lines as a character. That made him, in legend, the first actor.
def: an actor, especially a stage actor; often used in a joking or slightly grand way
ex: The school play drew budding thespians from every grade, even the shy seniors.
Diego, a lifelong thespian, still performs at the community theater every spring.
The local thespians are rehearsing a musical at the community center every evening this month.
Wei, an eager young thespian, auditioned for every college play and finally landed the lead.

cloze.s: Grandpa Tomás, a proud ___, has played King Lear in three different local theater productions.

note: Can also be an adjective: “thespian talents” means acting talents.

story: The Roman Empire built a vast network of roads spreading out from its capital, so travelers on almost any main road could eventually reach Rome. The idea became a well-known medieval proverb.
def: there are many different ways to reach the same result or end up in the same place
ex: Whether you study law or business first, all roads lead to Rome if you want to run the company someday.
Every argument in our family somehow ends with money; all roads lead to Rome.
Priya learned Spanish through songs while her brother used textbooks; all roads lead to Rome, and both became fluent.
Whether you start with healthier meals or with daily walks, all roads lead to Rome if the goal is better health.

cloze.s: You can learn by video, by book or by practice — ___, as long as you reach the same skill level.

story: The Kraken is a giant sea monster from Scandinavian folklore. The Clash of the Titans films placed it in a Greek myth, and in the 2010 version Zeus (Liam Neeson) bellows “Release the Kraken!”, a line that became a popular joke.
def: to send a powerful, scary force against an opponent; usually said as a joke
ex: Down by ten points, the coach decided to release the Kraken and sent in his best scorer.
When the landlord ignored her complaints, Priya released the Kraken: she called her lawyer.
With the score tied, fans chanted “Release the Kraken!” as the team's giant center jumped onto the ice.
The tech company released the Kraken in the price war, cutting its prices in half overnight.

cloze.s: The negotiation stalled, so the CEO joked it was time to ___ and bring in the company's toughest lawyer.

term: the meek shall inherit the earth
story: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says, “Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5), echoing Psalm 37. It promised that gentle, humble people would one day be rewarded.
def: gentle, humble people will be rewarded in the end; often used jokingly about quiet people winning
ex: The quiet intern ended up running the department — proof that the meek shall inherit the earth.
“The meek shall inherit the earth,” Fatima laughed, as the shyest player took home the chess trophy.
On the reality show, the quiet contestant outlasted all the loud ones; the meek shall inherit the earth after all.
The gentle tortoise beat the boastful hare, and the teacher joked that the meek shall inherit the earth.

cloze.s: The loud candidates fought each other until the calm, soft-spoken one won — I guess ___.
cloze.a: the meek shall inherit the earth

term: the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak
story: In the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus asks his disciples to stay awake and pray with him, but they keep falling asleep. He tells them, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41).
def: you truly want to do something, but your body or self-control is not strong enough to follow through
ex: I meant to go running at dawn and stayed in bed instead; the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak.
Malik promised to skip dessert all month; the spirit was willing, but the flesh was weak.
Grandpa wanted to dance all night at the wedding; the spirit was willing, but the flesh was weak.
Kwame planned to study after his night shift but fell asleep at his desk; the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak.

cloze.s: Hannah set her alarm for 5 a.m. to study, then hit snooze four times — ___.
cloze.a: the spirit is willing but the flesh is weak

story: When Jesus was asked whether people should pay taxes to Rome, he pointed to Caesar's image on a coin and said, “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Matthew 22:21).
def: give the government or worldly authority what it is owed, while keeping other duties, like faith, separate
ex: Jamal grumbled about his tax bill but paid it on time; render unto Caesar, he said.
The speaker argued that churches should render unto Caesar and obey building codes like everyone else.
Sofia keeps her faith private but obeys every city rule, believing you should render unto Caesar what is Caesar's.
The pastor reminded the church board to render unto Caesar and register the charity with the state.

cloze.s: “I don't like paying the city's parking fines,” Olga said, “but you have to ___.”

term: man does not live by bread alone
story: The saying comes from Deuteronomy 8:3. In the Gospels, when the devil tempts a hungry Jesus to turn stones into bread, Jesus answers with this line (Matthew 4:4).
def: people need more than food and material things; they also need meaning, beauty, love or faith
ex: The town cut its arts budget, but the mayor was reminded that man does not live by bread alone.
After years of long shifts, Yuki took up painting, because man does not live by bread alone.
The company added a music room and art classes for workers, saying man does not live by bread alone.
Priya earns a good salary but volunteers at the animal shelter, because man does not live by bread alone.

cloze.s: The refugee camp set up a library and music classes, since ___; people needed hope as well as meals.
cloze.a: man does not live by bread alone

note: Often said today as “we do not live by bread alone.”

story: In the Book of Revelation (chapter 6), four riders on white, red, black and pale horses bring disaster to the world at the end of time. They are often identified as conquest, war, famine and death.
def: a group of four things seen as signs or causes of great disaster or ruin
ex: The economist called debt, inflation, unemployment and a weak currency the four horsemen of the apocalypse.
Drought, fire, flood and disease were the four horsemen of the apocalypse for the region's farmers.
For the restaurant owner, rising rent, staff shortages, food costs and bad reviews became the four horsemen of the apocalypse.
The teacher jokingly called the flu, lice, snow days and broken heaters the four horsemen of the apocalypse for winter classes.

cloze.s: Critics described the team's injuries, bad trades, low morale and an aging roster as the ___ for the season.

note: Psychologist John Gottman uses “four horsemen” for criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling, which predict a failing relationship.

term: a house divided against itself cannot stand
story: Jesus says that “if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand” (Mark 3:25). Abraham Lincoln famously quoted it in an 1858 speech about a nation split over slavery.
def: a group whose members fight each other will fail; unity is needed to survive
ex: The coach told the feuding players that a house divided against itself cannot stand.
With the board split into two camps, investors feared that a house divided against itself cannot stand.
The family's inheritance fight threatened to ruin the farm, and Grandpa warned that a house divided against itself cannot stand.
The band members kept arguing on stage, and a critic noted that a house divided against itself cannot stand.

cloze.s: If the two founders keep fighting in public, the company will collapse; ___.
cloze.a: a house divided against itself cannot stand

note: Often shortened to “a house divided.”

story: In the Bible, the Israelites are warned that enemies left in the land would be “thorns in your sides” (Numbers 33:55), and Paul speaks of his own “thorn in the flesh” (2 Corinthians 12:7).
def: a person or thing that keeps causing trouble or bother over a long time
ex: The small rival shop has been a thorn in the big chain's side for years.
That leaky faucet is a thorn in my side; it drips all night.
The neighbor's barking dog has been a thorn in Hannah's side since the day she moved in.
The young chess player became a thorn in the champion's side, beating him in three straight tournaments.

cloze.s: “That reporter asks me hard questions at every press event,” the mayor complained. “He's been ___ for years.”

term: separate the wheat from the chaff
story: Farmers once tossed harvested grain into the air so the wind carried off the light, useless husks (chaff) while the heavy wheat fell. In the Gospels, John the Baptist uses this image for a coming judgment, when the wheat is gathered and the chaff is burned (Matthew 3:12).
def: to sort out what is valuable or useful from what is worthless
ex: The first interview round helps us separate the wheat from the chaff among 300 applicants.
A good editor can separate the wheat from the chaff in a messy first draft.
Teachers help students separate the wheat from the chaff when they look for trustworthy sources online.
The food critic visited forty new restaurants to separate the wheat from the chaff.

cloze.s: With thousands of online reviews, it's hard to ___ and find the honest ones.
cloze.a: separate the wheat from the chaff

story: The saying shortens Proverbs 16:18: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.”
def: people who are too proud or too sure of themselves are likely to fail or be humbled soon
ex: The champion bragged that he couldn't lose, and then lost in the first round; pride goes before a fall.
Sofia warned her brother not to mock the other team, because pride goes before a fall.
Jamal boasted he'd ace the exam without studying, then failed it; pride goes before a fall.
“Pride goes before a fall,” Grandma warned, as my cousin bragged that he never loses at cards.

cloze.s: The CEO boasted that no competitor could touch them, a month before sales collapsed — ___.

story: The idea comes from Paul's letter to the Galatians: “whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Galatians 6:7). A farmer harvests whatever seed he plants.
def: the results you get in life come from your own earlier actions, good or bad
ex: Liam skipped practice all season and then lost his starting spot; you reap what you sow.
Maria was kind to her coworkers for years, and they rallied around her when she needed help — you reap what you sow.
Wei studied a little every night all semester, and his top exam score showed that you reap what you sow.
After years of ignoring his car's warning lights, Malik faced a huge repair bill; you reap what you sow.

cloze.s: He cheated his business partners, and now no one will work with him; ___.

note: Close in meaning to “what goes around comes around” and to the everyday sense of “karma.”

term: like a lamb to the slaughter
story: The prophet Isaiah describes a suffering servant who “is brought as a lamb to the slaughter” without protest (Isaiah 53:7); Jeremiah uses a similar image. A lamb walks calmly to its death, not knowing what lies ahead.
def: going calmly and without resistance into great danger or harm, often without realizing it
ex: The young team walked onto the field like lambs to the slaughter against the defending champions.
Unaware of the layoffs, Kwame went to the meeting like a lamb to the slaughter.
Not knowing the test covered three chapters, Yuki walked into class like a lamb to the slaughter.
The rookie chess player sat down across from the grandmaster like a lamb to the slaughter.

cloze.s: The new hires, with no training, were sent to face the angry crowd ___.

term: the left hand doesn't know what the right hand is doing
story: Jesus told his followers to give to the poor quietly: “let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth” (Matthew 6:3). Over time the phrase came to describe confusion instead of secret kindness.
def: different parts of the same group are so poorly coordinated that they work against each other
ex: One department hired new staff while another was laying people off; the left hand doesn't know what the right hand is doing.
The airline sent me a refund and a bill on the same day — clearly the left hand doesn't know what the right hand is doing.
The school sent parents two different dates for the field trip; the left hand doesn't know what the right hand is doing.
When two nurses gave Malik different instructions for his medicine, the left hand clearly didn't know what the right hand was doing.

cloze.s: Sales promised a feature that engineering had already canceled; in this company, ___.
cloze.a: the left hand doesn't know what the right hand is doing

note: The original Bible verse praised giving in secret; the modern meaning is about disorganization.

story: The word comes from Turkish kısmet, from Arabic qisma, meaning “portion” or “lot” — the share of life given to each person. It reflects the Muslim belief in a fate decided by God, and it entered English in the 1800s.
def: fate or destiny, especially a lucky event that seems meant to happen
ex: Meeting her future husband on a delayed flight felt like kismet to Aisha.
Finding his grandfather's old shop for sale on the day he moved back seemed like kismet to Diego.
Sitting next to his childhood best friend on a plane after twenty years felt like kismet to Kwame.
The shelter dog walked straight into Fatima's arms, and she knew it was kismet.

cloze.s: They both reached for the last copy of the same book at the same moment; it had to be ___.

story: Dervishes are members of Sufi Muslim orders. The Mevlevi order, founded in Konya (in today's Turkey) by followers of the 13th-century poet Rumi, is famous for a ceremony in which members spin for long periods as a form of prayer.
def: a person who moves or works with fast, endless, spinning energy
ex: On moving day, Grandma was a whirling dervish, packing boxes faster than the movers.
The toddler turned into a whirling dervish after eating birthday cake.
In the final minutes of the match, the midfielder was a whirling dervish, chasing down every ball.
The night before the science fair, Kwame was a whirling dervish of glue, wires and poster board.

cloze.s: Before the dinner party, Wei was a(n) ___, cooking, cleaning and setting the table all at once.

note: The everyday phrase is lighthearted, but the original ceremony is a serious religious practice.

story: The Sherpa are a people of the Himalayan mountains of Nepal, famous as expert mountain guides. Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa, reached the top of Mount Everest with Edmund Hillary in 1953.
def: an expert guide or helper who does the hard early work that leads others to success
ex: Each country sends a sherpa to prepare the agenda weeks before the summit of world leaders.
Priya acted as our sherpa through the confusing loan application.
Ali was the sherpa for the product launch, booking venues and testing demos so the CEO could simply walk on stage.
Wei's older sister was her sherpa through college applications, handling forms and deadlines so Wei could focus on essays.

cloze.s: The senior engineer served as the team's ___, guiding the new hires through the company's huge codebase.

note: Capitalized for the people of Nepal; often lowercase “sherpa” for the general sense of a guide or summit aide.

story: Across the Mediterranean, the Middle East, South Asia and Latin America, many people traditionally believe an envious look can cause bad luck or illness. Blue eye-shaped charms, common in Turkey and Greece, are worn to block it.
def: a look believed to bring bad luck; also a hostile, angry stare at someone
ex: When Tomás took the last parking spot, the other driver gave him the evil eye.
Fatima's grandmother pinned a blue charm on the baby's blanket to protect her from the evil eye.
Hannah gave her brother the evil eye when he told her secret at the dinner table.
Some families never praise a newborn too loudly, afraid it might attract the evil eye.

cloze.s: The librarian gave the noisy students the ___ until they finally stopped talking.

term: may you live in interesting times
story: This is often called an old Chinese curse, but no Chinese source for it has ever been found. It shows up in English in the 1930s, attributed to China by British speakers.
def: an ironic wish or warning that someone will live through troubled, disordered times
ex: As the stock market swung wildly, Olga sighed, “May you live in interesting times.”
The professor opened his history lecture with “may you live in interesting times” and a smile.
After a week of snowstorms, power outages and a burst pipe, the principal emailed staff one line: “May you live in interesting times.”
The journalist ended her column about the chaotic year with the old line “may you live in interesting times.”

cloze.s: Wars, floods and a market crash in one year? Someone must have told us, “___.”
cloze.a: may you live in interesting times

note: Calling it a “Chinese curse” is a myth; the real origin is unknown.

story: The full saying, “it takes a village to raise a child,” is often described as an African proverb, though the exact source of the English wording is uncertain. It became very widely known in the United States in the 1990s.
def: raising children or doing big tasks needs help from a whole community, not one person
ex: With grandparents, neighbors and teachers all helping, Malik learned that it takes a village.
The food bank's success shows it takes a village: hundreds of volunteers keep it running.
When Liam's mom got sick, neighbors cooked meals and drove him to school; it takes a village.
Rebuilding the playground after the storm took parents, kids and local businesses; it truly takes a village.

cloze.s: Twin babies, two jobs and a move? We couldn't have done it without our friends — ___.

story: Czar (or tsar) was the title of the emperors of Russia, a word that comes from the Latin name Caesar. In the United States it came to be used for officials given broad power over one issue, such as a “drug czar.”
def: an official given broad power to manage one specific problem or area
ex: The city hired a housing czar to speed up construction of affordable homes.
Hannah became the company's safety czar after the factory accident.
The school district named a technology czar to manage every laptop, tablet and network problem.
The team's new nutrition czar banned soda from the locker room and planned every pregame meal.

cloze.s: To fight the opioid crisis, the governor appointed a drug ___ to coordinate every agency.

note: Also spelled “tsar.” Used informally; it is not an official job title.

story: Both the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union sent prisoners and political exiles to remote, freezing Siberia, far from family and power.
def: moved to a far-off, dull place or job as punishment or to get someone out of the way
ex: After arguing with the boss, Jamal was sent to Siberia — a desk in the basement next to the boiler.
The latecomers were sent to Siberia, the table by the kitchen door.
After complaining about the new boss, Olga was sent to Siberia: the company's tiny branch office in another state.
The noisy student was sent to Siberia: a desk alone in the back corner, far from all his friends.

cloze.s: The star player criticized the coach and was ___, benched for the rest of the season.

story: Godzilla, a giant monster that smashes cities, first appeared in the 1954 Japanese film Gojira. English speakers now add “-zilla” to words to describe someone who becomes a monster about one thing, like a “bridezilla.”
def: added to a word to describe a person who becomes a demanding monster about that thing
ex: The bridezilla screamed at the florist over the color of the napkins.
Sofia admits she turns into a momzilla on the day of her kids' school play.
Tired of the bridezillas on TV, Olga promised her wedding planner she would stay calm about every detail.
Our neighbor becomes a lawnzilla each summer, shouting at anyone whose dog steps on his perfect grass.

cloze.s: Before the wedding, Liam became a groom___, rewriting the seating chart for the tenth time.

story: A tale made famous by Mary Mapes Dodge's 1865 American novel Hans Brinker, or the Silver Skates (earlier versions had appeared in print) tells of a Dutch boy who plugs a leak in a dike with his finger all night, saving his town from a flood.
def: a small, temporary fix that holds back a much bigger problem for a short time
ex: The emergency loan was just a finger in the dike; the company still needed a real plan.
Hiring one more nurse is a finger in the dike when the whole hospital is understaffed.
Buying a space heater is just a finger in the dike; the house really needs a new furnace.
The coach's pep talk was a finger in the dike, and the team's deeper problems returned the next week.

cloze.s: Patching one pothole is like putting a(n) ___ when the whole road is falling apart.

note: Despite its Dutch setting, the story spread through English and American books; it is not a traditional Dutch folk tale.

story: A popular tale says a frog dropped into boiling water jumps out, but a frog in water heated slowly stays until it is cooked. Modern biologists say this is false: a healthy frog will try to escape as the water warms.
def: failing to notice a danger that grows slowly until it is too late to act
ex: Rising rents a little each year made Maria feel like the boiling frog, until she could no longer afford her home.
The analyst warned that slowly rising debt was a boiling frog problem for the city.
Doctors say rising blood pressure works like the boiling frog, since many people feel fine until it becomes serious.
Kwame's working hours crept up a little each month, and like the boiling frog, he didn't notice his burnout.

cloze.s: No single price increase seemed big, but we were like ___ and didn't notice our budget being ruined.

note: The lesson is used as a metaphor; the claim about real frogs is a myth.

story: In this fable attributed to Aesop, the grasshopper sings all summer while the ant stores food. When winter comes, the hungry grasshopper begs for food, and the ant tells it that it should have prepared.
def: the contrast between working and saving for the future and only enjoying the present
ex: Kwame saved part of every paycheck while his friends spent theirs — a real case of the ant and the grasshopper.
The teacher used the ant and the grasshopper to explain why students should start projects early.
While his neighbors partied all summer, Malik stacked firewood for winter; it was the ant and the grasshopper.
As a kid, Wei loved the story of the ant and the grasshopper, and now he plans every budget like the ant.

cloze.s: One sister put money aside each month, the other spent it all on trips; when the recession came, it was ___ all over again.

story: In the Brothers Grimm fairy tale “Rumpelstiltskin,” a miller boasts that his daughter can spin straw into gold, and the king demands she do it. A strange little man does it for her, first for her necklace and ring, and finally for a terrible promise: her first child.
def: to turn something cheap or worthless into something very valuable
ex: The chef can spin straw into gold, turning leftover vegetables into the best soup in town.
Investors hoped the new CEO could spin straw into gold with the failing brand.
Fatima can spin straw into gold, turning thrift-store furniture into pieces that sell for hundreds of dollars.
The coach managed to spin straw into gold, taking a team of unknown players to the championship.

cloze.s: With almost no budget, the film crew managed to ___ and made a movie that won major awards.

story: Camelot is the legendary castle and court of King Arthur. After President John F. Kennedy was killed in 1963, Jacqueline Kennedy compared his time in office to Camelot, quoting a popular musical, and the name stuck.
def: a time or place of ideal happiness, beauty and hope, often one that ended too soon
ex: Alumni remember the team's three championship years as the school's Camelot.
For the young couple, that first summer in Paris was a kind of Camelot.
For Hannah's family, the summers at the lake house before Grandma passed away were their Camelot.
The newsroom's early days, full of big ideas and loyal readers, now seem like a lost Camelot to the reporters.

cloze.s: The founders look back on the early, joyful startup days as their ___, before the company grew huge and serious.

term: abandon all hope, ye who enter here
story: In Dante's Inferno, written in Italian in the early 1300s, these words are written above the gate of Hell, which the poet passes through on his journey.
def: a joking warning that a place or task is awful, without hope, or impossible to escape
ex: Someone taped a sign reading “Abandon all hope, ye who enter here” on the door of the tax office.
Opening his teenage son's bedroom, Diego muttered, “Abandon all hope, ye who enter here.”
The haunted house greeted visitors with a spooky sign: “Abandon all hope, ye who enter here.”
Handing the new hire a 400-page rule book, Malik grinned, “Abandon all hope, ye who enter here.”

cloze.s: The line at the motor vehicle office was so long that a sign saying “___” would have fit perfectly.
cloze.a: abandon all hope, ye who enter here

story: In Samuel Beckett's play Waiting for Godot, first staged in Paris in 1953, two men wait day after day for someone named Godot, who never arrives.
def: waiting endlessly for something or someone that seems never to come
ex: Waiting for the landlord to fix the heat feels like waiting for Godot.
Fans of the delayed video game joked they were waiting for Godot.
Commuters on the cold platform joked that the late-night bus schedule meant waiting for Godot.
Hannah has been waiting for Godot since she asked the airline for a refund last spring.

cloze.s: We've expected that promised software update for three years; at this point we're ___.

story: Rudyard Kipling's The Jungle Book (1894) describes a “Law of the Jungle,” a code of rules the animals follow. Over time, the phrase came to mean the opposite: a world with no rules where the strongest win.
def: a situation where the strongest or toughest win and no one protects the weak
ex: Without a referee, the playground game turned into the law of the jungle.
Some critics say the unregulated market runs on the law of the jungle.
At the clearance sale, shoppers pushed and grabbed whatever they could; it was the law of the jungle.
Without rules on overtime, the warehouse ran by the law of the jungle, and the newest workers suffered most.

cloze.s: After the government collapsed, there were no police, and ___ took over the streets.

story: In Samuel Taylor Coleridge's poem The Rime of the Ancient Mariner (1798), a sailor shoots an albatross, a bird seen as a good sign. When bad luck follows, the crew hangs the dead bird around his neck as punishment.
def: a heavy burden, guilt or problem that you cannot get rid of
ex: The failed product launch became an albatross around the CEO's neck.
Yuki's huge student loan felt like an albatross around her neck for a decade.
The costly, unpopular stadium deal became an albatross around the city council's neck.
A single embarrassing video became an albatross around the young actor's neck, following him into every interview.

cloze.s: The senator can't escape that old scandal; it has been ___ in every campaign since.

term: 'tis better to have loved and lost
story: Alfred, Lord Tennyson wrote “'Tis better to have loved and lost / Than never to have loved at all” in his long poem In Memoriam A.H.H. (1850), mourning the death of his close friend Arthur Hallam.
def: loving someone is worth it, even if you later lose them and feel great pain
ex: After the breakup, Hannah's aunt hugged her and said, “'Tis better to have loved and lost.”
Grieving his old dog, Malik decided it's better to have loved and lost than never to have had him.
After her summer romance ended, Priya decided 'tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all.
The grief counselor quoted Tennyson: 'tis better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all.

cloze.s: The relationship ended badly, but she didn't regret it: ___ than never to have loved at all.
cloze.a: 'tis better to have loved and lost

story: Alexander Pope wrote “To err is human, to forgive divine” in his poem An Essay on Criticism (1711).
def: everyone makes mistakes, so we should be ready to forgive them
ex: When the new cashier gave the wrong change, the manager smiled and said, “To err is human.”
Our doctor admitted the scheduling mix-up; to err is human, and we appreciated her honesty.
My math teacher circles her own mistakes in red on the board, reminding us that to err is human.
The referee admitted his mistake after the game, and the coach accepted it: to err is human, to forgive divine.

cloze.s: Don't be so hard on yourself for missing one deadline; ___.

note: “Err” means to make a mistake.

story: Robert Frost's poem “The Road Not Taken” (1915) describes choosing between two paths in a wood. The speaker says he took “the one less traveled by,” though the poem notes both paths were worn about the same.
def: a choice you did not make, and the different life you wonder about because of it
ex: Sometimes Wei thinks about the road not taken: the music career he gave up for law.
The film follows the road not taken, imagining what if she had stayed in her hometown.
Looking at photos of the farm she almost bought, Olga sometimes wonders about the road not taken.
The podcast interviews retirees about the road not taken: the dreams they set aside for steady jobs.

cloze.s: At the reunion, everyone talked about ___ — the jobs, cities and partners they almost chose.

note: The poem is often read as praising bold, unusual choices, but many readers see it as gently ironic.

story: An old proverb made famous by Robert Frost's poem “Mending Wall” (1914). Two farmers repair the stone wall between their land each spring; the neighbor repeats the saying, while the speaker questions why the wall is needed.
def: clear boundaries between people help keep their relationship friendly and free of conflict
ex: The roommates agreed on separate shelves in the fridge; good fences make good neighbors.
Signing a clear contract with your friend's company is wise; good fences make good neighbors.
Before moving in together, the two friends wrote down who pays which bills; good fences make good neighbors.
The two coffee shops on the block agreed not to copy each other's specialty drinks; good fences make good neighbors.

cloze.s: We split the shared driveway with a painted line, and the arguments stopped — ___.

term: march to the beat of a different drummer
story: In Walden (1854), Henry David Thoreau wrote that if a man does not keep pace with his companions, “perhaps it is because he hears a different drummer,” and he should follow that music.
def: to live or act in your own way instead of following what everyone else does
ex: Aisha has always marched to the beat of a different drummer, wearing bright colors to formal events.
The inventor marched to the beat of a different drummer and ignored every expert who doubted him.
Hannah marches to the beat of a different drummer, so she spent her year off building wooden boats.
The coach let the quiet striker march to the beat of a different drummer, since her odd warm-ups worked.

cloze.s: While his classmates chose business degrees, Tomás chose to ___ and studied puppet-making.
cloze.a: march to the beat of a different drummer

note: Also said as “march to a different drummer” or “march to the beat of your own drum.”

term: reports of my death are greatly exaggerated
story: In 1897, when rumors spread that Mark Twain was gravely ill or dead, he told a reporter, “The report of my death was an exaggeration.” The line is now usually quoted in this smoother form.
def: a funny way to say that something thought to be finished or failing is still very much alive
ex: Asked if her bookstore was closing, the owner laughed that reports of its death were greatly exaggerated.
The aging rock band's new hit proved reports of their death were greatly exaggerated.
After rumors that he had quit tennis, the veteran won the tournament and joked that reports of his death were greatly exaggerated.
As subscriptions rose, the local newspaper ran a front page saying reports of its death were greatly exaggerated.

cloze.s: Experts said radio was dead decades ago, but ___: millions still tune in every day.
cloze.a: reports of its death are greatly exaggerated

note: Twain's actual words were “The report of my death was an exaggeration.”

story: Mark Twain made the phrase famous in his autobiographical writings (1906), crediting British Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli. No one has found evidence that Disraeli ever said it.
def: numbers and data can be used to make a weak or false argument sound convincing
ex: When both campaigns used the same poll to claim victory, the reporter muttered about lies, damned lies, and statistics.
The ad's “90 percent of users agree” claim reminded Olga of lies, damned lies, and statistics.
The diet ad promised users could lose “up to 50 pounds,” a classic case of lies, damned lies, and statistics.
In math class, Ms. Okoro showed how a tiny survey can mislead, then quoted the old line about lies, damned lies, and statistics.

cloze.s: The company picked one good month to show “huge growth” — a perfect example of ___.

term: he who must not be named
story: In J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter books, most witches and wizards are too afraid to say the name of the dark wizard Voldemort, calling him “You-Know-Who” or “He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named.”
def: a person or topic so feared, disliked or awkward that people avoid saying its name
ex: At family dinners, Liam's ex-girlfriend is now she who must not be named.
In the office, the failed project became the plan that must not be named.
Ever since his missed kick lost the final, fans have called the team's old kicker he who must not be named.
Since their bitter breakup, the band's former singer has become he who must not be named in interviews.

cloze.s: After the rival coach insulted the team, the players only referred to him as ___.
cloze.a: he who must not be named

term: the best of times, the worst of times
story: Charles Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities (1859), set during the French Revolution, opens with “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.”
def: a period that is full of great good and great bad at the same time
ex: For the new parents, the first year was the best of times, the worst of times.
The tech boom was the best of times and the worst of times for the city's longtime residents.
Starting a business during the recession was the best of times, the worst of times for Priya.
For the team, the season was the best of times, the worst of times: a championship, then their coach left.

cloze.s: Her first year of college brought new friends and heartbreak, success and failure — truly ___.
cloze.a: the best of times, the worst of times

story: In Nathaniel Hawthorne's novel The Scarlet Letter (1850), set in Puritan Boston, Hester Prynne is forced to wear a red letter A on her dress as public punishment for having a child outside her marriage.
def: a mark or label of public shame that follows someone everywhere
ex: The bankruptcy became a scarlet letter on Jamal's record for years.
Critics said posting the names of late payers online was like making them wear a scarlet letter.
Getting cut from the team became a scarlet letter for Tomás, who felt everyone at school stared at him.
Some parents feared a failing grade on the state report card would be a scarlet letter for the whole school.

cloze.s: For the athlete, the failed drug test became a(n) ___ that no later victory could erase.

term: the course of true love never did run smooth
story: In A Midsummer Night's Dream, the young lover Lysander says this to Hermia after her father forbids their marriage.
def: real love always meets problems and obstacles along the way
ex: Their wedding was postponed twice, but the course of true love never did run smooth.
Sofia's grandparents met during a war and were separated for years; the course of true love never did run smooth.
Diego and Ana survived two moves and a long-distance year; the course of true love never did run smooth.
When the bride's flight was canceled the night before the wedding, her father laughed, “The course of true love never did run smooth.”

cloze.s: His job moved him overseas a month after they got engaged — well, ___.
cloze.a: the course of true love never did run smooth

term: neither a borrower nor a lender be
story: In Hamlet, the old adviser Polonius gives his son Laertes a list of advice before he leaves for France, including this line, because lending money often loses both the money and the friend.
def: avoid borrowing or lending money, especially with friends, because it causes trouble
ex: When his cousin asked for another loan, Kwame remembered: neither a borrower nor a lender be.
Grandpa's rule about money was simple: neither a borrower nor a lender be.
When a coworker asked to borrow fifty dollars until payday, Fatima politely said no: neither a borrower nor a lender be.
The money advice column quoted Shakespeare: neither a borrower nor a lender be, especially with family.

cloze.s: After lending her roommate rent money she never got back, Priya adopted a new motto: “___.”
cloze.a: neither a borrower nor a lender be

story: In Richard III, the king loses his horse during the Battle of Bosworth and cries, “A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!” He is killed soon after.
def: said when you would give almost anything for something simple you badly need right now
ex: Stranded on a muddy farm road after his car broke down, Diego groaned, “My kingdom for a horse!”
Halfway through the marathon, Hannah thought, “My kingdom for a glass of water.”
Lost in the huge parking garage with three heavy bags, Grandma sighed, “My kingdom for a shopping cart!”
The last bus pulled away without him, and Kwame laughed, “A horse, a horse, my kingdom for a horse!”

cloze.s: Trapped in a meeting with a dead phone, Wei sighed: “___ — or at least a charger!”

note: People usually swap “horse” for whatever they need: “My kingdom for a coffee!”

story: In Macbeth, one of the three witches says, “By the pricking of my thumbs, / Something wicked this way comes,” just before Macbeth arrives. Ray Bradbury used the line as the title of a 1962 novel.
def: a warning that something evil or dangerous is about to arrive
ex: As the storm clouds rolled over the hills, Maria whispered, “Something wicked this way comes.”
The film's trailer used dark music and the line “something wicked this way comes.”
When the principal walked in holding the test results, Diego whispered, “Something wicked this way comes.”
As the undefeated rival team's bus pulled into the parking lot, the coach muttered, “Something wicked this way comes.”

cloze.s: The dog growled, the lights flickered, and Fatima joked, “By the pricking of my thumbs, ___.”

story: In Twelfth Night, the self-important servant Malvolio reads a fake letter that says, “Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon 'em.” It was written to fool him.
def: people become important in different ways: by birth, by their own effort, or by chance
ex: Malik never wanted to be team captain; some are born great, and some have greatness thrust upon them.
The professor said of the accidental hero: some are born great, but he had greatness thrust upon him.
Born into a famous acting family, Tomás was told, “Some are born great,” but he still had to earn his roles.
Ana never wanted the spotlight, but when her video went viral she joked that some are born great, and some have greatness thrust upon them.

cloze.s: She became mayor only after the others dropped out; ___, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon them.

story: Much Ado About Nothing is a Shakespeare comedy (around 1598–99) in which a great deal of trouble grows from lies, tricks and misunderstandings.
def: a lot of excitement and worry over something that turns out not to matter
ex: The rumored merger turned out to be much ado about nothing.
All that arguing over the paint color was much ado about nothing; nobody noticed the difference.
The neighbors' loud fight over a few fallen leaves on their property line was much ado about nothing.
The news hyped the giant storm for days, but it was much ado about nothing; we barely got rain.

cloze.s: Everyone panicked about the system warning, but it was ___ — just a test message.

note: “Ado” means fuss or trouble.

term: speak softly and carry a big stick
story: Theodore Roosevelt called this a West African proverb (there is little evidence it is one) and used it in 1900. He made it famous in a 1901 speech, and it came to describe his foreign policy of calm talks backed by military strength.
def: be calm and polite in dealing with others, while keeping strength ready in case you need it
ex: In tough contract talks, Aisha's style was to speak softly and carry a big stick.
The new principal spoke softly and carried a big stick, rarely raising her voice but enforcing every rule.
The quiet store manager seemed easygoing, but she spoke softly and carried a big stick when suppliers broke their contracts.
In the dispute over the fence, Kwame decided to speak softly and carry a big stick, smiling politely while his lawyer stood by.

cloze.s: Our negotiator stayed friendly but made sure the other side knew we had other offers; she believes you ___.
cloze.a: speak softly and carry a big stick

term: the only thing we have to fear is fear itself
story: President Franklin D. Roosevelt said this in his first inaugural address on March 4, 1933, during the Great Depression, to calm a panicked nation.
def: panic and fear can do more harm than the danger itself, so stay calm and act
ex: Before the big exam, the coach reminded the nervous students that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.
As markets dropped, the bank's chief told customers the only thing to fear was fear itself.
When shoppers emptied store shelves over rumors of a shortage, the mayor said the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.
In 1933, President Franklin Roosevelt told a frightened nation that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.

cloze.s: When rumors caused a rush to empty the bank, the manager said, “___; your money is safe.”
cloze.a: the only thing we have to fear is fear itself

story: On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, saying, “That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” He later said he meant to say “a man.”
def: a simple action that marks a huge advance or turning point; often used as a joke
ex: When the baby took her first step, Dad announced, “One small step for man, one giant leap for our family!”
Opening its first overseas office was one small step for man and a giant leap for the tiny company.
When Grandpa finally sent his first emoji, he proudly announced, “One small step for man!”
When the shy toddler finally waved hello to the mail carrier, her mom whispered, “One small step for man.”

cloze.s: The first test drive of the self-driving bus was, as the engineer joked, “___, one giant leap for transit.”

term: the shot heard round the world
story: Ralph Waldo Emerson's poem “Concord Hymn” (1837) praised the farmers who “fired the shot heard round the world” at Concord, Massachusetts, in 1775, at the start of the American Revolutionary War.
def: a single event whose effects spread very far beyond where it happened
ex: The small bank's collapse was the shot heard round the world that started the financial crisis.
Sports fans still call that famous home run the shot heard round the world.
One chef's angry video about food waste became the shot heard round the world, sparking changes in restaurants everywhere.
The first battles at Lexington and Concord in 1775 are remembered as the shot heard round the world.

cloze.s: The student's protest video became ___, sparking similar marches in dozens of countries.
cloze.a: the shot heard round the world

note: Also used for Bobby Thomson's 1951 pennant-winning home run for the New York Giants.

story: Fort Knox, Kentucky, is home to the United States Bullion Depository, built in the 1930s, which stores a large share of the nation's gold behind heavy security.
def: a place that is extremely well guarded and very hard to get into
ex: Getting into the concert's backstage area was like breaking into Fort Knox.
Mom keeps the holiday cookies locked up like Fort Knox.
With three locks, an alarm and a barking dog, Olga's apartment is like Fort Knox.
The hospital's newborn unit is a Fort Knox of security, with locked doors and ID bracelets for every baby.

cloze.s: The tech company guards its new phone designs like ___, with guards, cameras and fingerprint locks.

term: standing on the shoulders of giants
story: Isaac Newton wrote to fellow scientist Robert Hooke, “If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of Giants.” The image is much older; it was credited to the French scholar Bernard of Chartres in the 1100s.
def: making progress by building on the discoveries and work of people who came before
ex: The young researcher said her cancer breakthrough came from standing on the shoulders of giants.
Every new app is standing on the shoulders of giants who built the internet.
Isaac Newton wrote that if he had seen further, it was by standing on the shoulders of giants.
Today's rocket engineers are standing on the shoulders of giants who did the math with pencils and slide rules.

cloze.s: The Nobel winner thanked her teachers, saying she was only ___.
cloze.a: standing on the shoulders of giants

story: Neanderthals were an early human species named after the Neander Valley in Germany, where fossils were found in 1856. They were long pictured as brutish, though scientists now know they made tools, controlled fire and hunted large animals.
def: an insulting word for a person with crude manners or very old-fashioned, narrow-minded views
ex: Rosa called the coworker who made rude jokes about women a Neanderthal.
Some fans behaved like Neanderthals, throwing cups onto the field.
Malik was called a Neanderthal after he yelled at the waiter and refused to say please or thank you.
Anyone who thinks bullying makes kids tougher has Neanderthal ideas about raising children, the school counselor said.

cloze.s: His belief that only men should handle money made him seem like a(n) ___ to his daughters.

note: The insult is unfair to real Neanderthals, who were skilled and intelligent.

story: In the 1800s, people used “missing link” for an imagined creature halfway between apes and humans. Scientists now see human evolution as a branching tree, not a single chain with one gap.
def: a missing piece of information or a step needed to complete an explanation or connect two things
ex: The detective believed the stolen car was the missing link between the two robberies.
Good bus service was the missing link between the new housing and the jobs downtown.
The historian believed the old letters were the missing link in the story of how the town was founded.
For the startup, a reliable delivery partner was the missing link between its great product and happy customers.

cloze.s: Investigators found the bank records they needed — the ___ that tied the CEO to the fraud.

story: In nuclear physics, critical mass is the smallest amount of material, such as uranium, needed for a chain reaction that keeps itself going.
def: the size or number needed for something to grow and keep going on its own
ex: The new social app never reached critical mass, so people stopped using it.
Once enough parents joined, the carpool group reached critical mass and ran itself.
The recycling program only became cheap to run once it reached critical mass across the whole city.
The book club struggled until it hit critical mass, and now new members join every week without any advertising.

cloze.s: The protest grew slowly until it hit ___, and suddenly thousands filled the streets.

term: you're gonna need a bigger boat
story: In Steven Spielberg's 1975 film Jaws, police chief Brody (Roy Scheider) gets his first close look at the huge shark and tells the boat's captain, “You're gonna need a bigger boat.”
def: a funny way of saying a problem is much bigger than the plan or tools prepared for it
ex: When the caterer saw 300 guests instead of 50, she told her assistant, “You're gonna need a bigger boat.”
Looking at the pile of tax forms, Tomás joked that he was gonna need a bigger boat.
The plumber looked at the flooded basement, then at the homeowner's tiny bucket, and said, “You're gonna need a bigger boat.”
Seeing the line of hungry campers stretch past the little grill, Sofia told her brother, “You're gonna need a bigger boat.”

cloze.s: The IT team saw the flood of support tickets after the outage and said, “___.”
cloze.a: you're gonna need a bigger boat

note: Often misquoted as “We're gonna need a bigger boat.”

term: if you build it, they will come
story: In the 1989 film Field of Dreams, an Iowa farmer (Kevin Costner) hears a voice whisper, “If you build it, he will come,” and builds a baseball field in his cornfield.
def: the belief that if you create something good, people will show up to use it
ex: The town built a big skate park, hoping that if you build it, they will come.
Too many startups assume that if you build it, they will come, and skip marketing.
The library added a room with 3D printers and sewing machines, trusting that if you build it, they will come.
Hannah opened a bakery on a quiet street, believing that if you build it, they will come, and soon there was a line.

cloze.s: The city opened a huge stadium with no train line nearby, betting that ___.
cloze.a: if you build it, they will come

note: The actual film line is “he will come”; “they will come” is the popular version.

story: In the 1992 courtroom film A Few Good Men, a Marine colonel (Jack Nicholson), pushed by a young lawyer demanding the truth, shouts, “You can't handle the truth!”
def: a dramatic reply claiming someone is not ready to hear a harsh fact; often used jokingly
ex: When Liam asked how bad his haircut really was, his sister grinned: “You can't handle the truth!”
Asked how many cookies he ate, Grandpa boomed, “You can't handle the truth!”
When her roommate asked what was really in the mystery casserole, Aisha laughed, “You can't handle the truth!”
Whenever his kids ask what's really in his famous chili, Dad just says they can't handle the truth.

cloze.s: “Do you really want to know what the critics said?” the director asked. “Trust me, ___.”

story: In the 1942 film Casablanca, a police captain who knows exactly who fired the shot tells his officers to “round up the usual suspects,” so the real culprit can go free.
def: to blame or call on the same expected people or things as always, without looking deeper
ex: Whenever sales drop, management rounds up the usual suspects: weather, prices and the competition.
The guest list for the panel just rounded up the usual suspects from past years.
When the cookies disappeared, Mom rounded up the usual suspects: the twins and the dog.
Every time the office printer breaks, the tech team rounds up the usual suspects instead of finding the real problem.

cloze.s: Instead of studying the real cause of the delays, the report simply ___ — bad weather and staff shortages.

note: “The usual suspects” alone means the familiar, predictable people or things.

story: In Charles Schulz's comic strip Peanuts, Lucy repeatedly promises to hold a football for Charlie Brown to kick, then pulls it away at the last second. He trusts her again and falls flat on his back every time.
def: a promise that keeps being broken at the last moment, fooling someone who trusts it again and again
ex: Every year the landlord promises repairs and backs out; it's Lucy and the football.
Fans felt like Charlie Brown with Lucy and the football when the star's comeback was canceled again.
Each time the airline promised our delayed flight would leave within the hour, it felt more like Lucy and the football.
Each time his brother swears he'll repay the loan next month, Diego feels like he's falling for Lucy and the football.

cloze.s: The company keeps promising raises and then cancels them — it's ___ all over again.

story: MacGyver was an American TV series (1985–1992) about a secret agent who avoids guns and escapes danger by building clever devices out of everyday items like a pocketknife, tape and paper clips.
def: to fix or build something cleverly using whatever ordinary objects happen to be nearby
ex: When the car's belt snapped, Grandma MacGyvered a fix with a pair of stockings.
Kwame MacGyvered a phone stand out of a binder clip and a credit card.
When the tent pole snapped, Diego MacGyvered a new one from a tree branch and duct tape.
Fatima MacGyvered a baby gate out of a laundry basket and two kitchen chairs.

cloze.s: With no tools at the campsite, Yuki managed to ___ a coffee filter out of a sock and a cup.

note: Used as a verb (“MacGyvered”) or a noun (“a real MacGyver”).

story: On February 3, 1959, a plane crash in Iowa killed rock stars Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and J. P. “The Big Bopper” Richardson. Don McLean's 1971 song “American Pie” called it “the day the music died.”
def: the moment when something loved or exciting suddenly came to a sad end
ex: For local fans, the day the old jazz club closed was the day the music died.
When the team's star player retired, Sofia said it was the day the music died.
For many fans, the day their favorite comedy show was canceled was the day the music died.
When the town's summer fair was canceled for good, the kids called it the day the music died.

cloze.s: The town's beloved theater burned down in 1985; residents still call it ___.

story: In the 1987 film Wall Street, the ruthless investor Gordon Gekko (Michael Douglas) tells shareholders that “greed, for lack of a better word, is good.” The line became a shorthand for the money-chasing spirit of the era.
def: a famous line claiming that chasing money and serving yourself is a good thing
ex: The documentary showed how the greed is good attitude led to reckless lending.
Critics said the bank's bonus culture still ran on greed is good.
In business class, the professor asked whether greed is good or whether it just leads to scandals.
The influencer's videos preached that greed is good, urging teenagers to chase quick riches at any cost.

cloze.s: The trader's motto came straight from the 1980s: “___” — and he didn't care who got hurt.

note: Usually quoted with irony or disapproval.

story: In the 1939 film The Wizard of Oz, the dog Toto pulls back a curtain to reveal that the mighty Wizard is an ordinary man working machines. He cries, “Pay no attention to that man behind the curtain!”
def: the hidden person who is really in control, often less impressive than the image they project
ex: The famous chef is the face of the restaurant, but his business partner is the man behind the curtain.
Reporters wanted to know who was the man behind the curtain running the senator's campaign.
The famous online store turned out to have one teenager as the man behind the curtain, running everything from his bedroom.
When the so-called robot tutor turned out to be a tired student typing replies, users finally met the man behind the curtain.

cloze.s: The company's powerful image hid a simple truth: one nervous founder was ___, making every decision alone.

story: Legend said that whoever untied a famously tangled knot in the city of Gordium would rule Asia. When Alexander the Great came there in 333 BC, he is said to have simply sliced through it with his sword.
def: to solve a hard, messy problem with one bold, direct action instead of slow careful work
ex: After months of failed talks, the new manager cut the Gordian knot by merging the two rival teams into one.
Rather than fixing every old rule one by one, the city council cut the Gordian knot and wrote a new code from scratch.
Unable to settle years of family arguments over the old house, the siblings cut the Gordian knot and sold it.
The airline cut the Gordian knot of confusing fares by offering one simple price for every seat.

cloze.s: The paperwork was so tangled that Aisha decided to ___ and simply cancel the old account and open a new one.

story: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, Morpheus is a son of Sleep who appears to people in dreams, taking on human shapes; his name comes from the Greek word for shape. The painkiller morphine was named after him because it brings sleep.
def: fast asleep, in a deep and peaceful sleep
ex: By nine o'clock the tired children were in the arms of Morpheus.
After the overnight flight, Hannah was in the arms of Morpheus before the taxi left the airport.
Grandpa was in the arms of Morpheus in his armchair before the movie's opening credits ended.
After her long night shift at the hospital, Aisha was in the arms of Morpheus by noon.

cloze.s: The long hike wore Kwame out, and minutes after dinner he was ___ on the couch.

note: A literary, slightly playful phrase.

story: In the Gospel of Matthew, Judas Iscariot agrees to hand Jesus over to the chief priests in return for thirty pieces of silver.
def: the money or reward someone takes for turning against a friend, a cause, or their own beliefs
ex: Fans said the star had sold out his hometown team for thirty pieces of silver.
She refused the bribe, saying she would not trade her coworkers' trust for thirty pieces of silver.
The spy sold his country's secrets for thirty pieces of silver and spent the rest of his life in shame.
The witness refused to change her story for thirty pieces of silver, even when offered a new car.

cloze.s: The former partner leaked the plans to a rival, and everyone knew he had done it for ___.

note: Strongly negative: it implies a shameful betrayal for gain.

story: In the Gospel of John, Lazarus of Bethany has been dead and in his tomb for four days when Jesus calls him out, alive again.
def: a person or thing that makes a surprising comeback after seeming to be dead, ruined or finished
ex: The old brand pulled off a Lazarus act, returning to store shelves after ten years away.
With a goal in the last minute, the team staged a Lazarus-like comeback to stay in the league.
The singer's Lazarus comeback album topped the charts twenty years after her last hit.
Nearly torn down twice, the old downtown theater became the city's Lazarus when a film festival brought crowds back.

cloze.s: Written off after two failed launches, the company rose like ___ when its third product became a hit.

note: Usually in phrases like "a Lazarus act" or "a Lazarus-like comeback."

story: In the Book of Genesis, God destroys the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah with fire and brimstone from heaven because of their great wickedness.
def: a place thought of as full of sin, wild behavior, and lack of morals
ex: The preacher described the casino strip as a modern Sodom and Gomorrah.
Grandpa jokingly called the college party scene Sodom and Gomorrah.
Strict Aunt Olga called the beach resort, with its all-night parties, a modern Sodom and Gomorrah.
Early visitors described the boomtown's saloons and gambling halls as a Sodom and Gomorrah of the West.

cloze.s: To the strict old headmaster, the noisy festival looked like ___, a place of pure sin.

note: Often used with humor or exaggeration today.

term: the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse
story: The Book of Revelation describes four riders on white, red, black and pale horses who bring disaster at the end of the world; the last is named Death. They are commonly understood as conquest, war, famine and death.
def: a set of four major disasters or threats that arrive together, or that signal great ruin
ex: The economist called high debt, inflation, unemployment and slow growth the four horsemen of the apocalypse.
For the farmers, drought, pests, floods and falling prices were the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse.
For the small ski town, warm winters, rising costs, closed roads and fewer tourists were the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse.
Researcher John Gottman calls criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling the four horsemen of the apocalypse for couples.

cloze.s: The coach joked that injuries, fatigue, bad luck and the referee were ___ of his team's season.
cloze.a: the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse

note: The psychologist John Gottman used the phrase for four habits that predict divorce: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling.

term: hide your light under a bushel
story: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says no one lights a candle and puts it under a bushel, a basket used to measure grain, but on a stand so it gives light to everyone.
def: to keep your talents or good qualities hidden because you are too modest or shy
ex: Priya is a gifted singer but hides her light under a bushel and never joins the choir.
Don't hide your light under a bushel; put your awards on your résumé.
Kwame is a brilliant cook, but he hides his light under a bushel and lets his friends do all the grilling.
The coach told the quiet rookie to stop hiding her light under a bushel and take the final shot.

cloze.s: Her manager urged her to share her ideas in meetings instead of trying to ___.
cloze.a: hide her light under a bushel

term: by the sweat of your brow
story: In the Book of Genesis, God punishes Adam for eating the forbidden fruit by telling him that from now on he will eat bread only by the sweat of his face, meaning through hard labor.
def: through your own hard work and effort, rather than by luck or someone else's help
ex: My grandparents built that farm by the sweat of their brow.
Jamal paid for college by the sweat of his brow, working nights at a warehouse.
Aisha built her cleaning business by the sweat of her brow, scrubbing floors herself for the first five years.
Every stone wall on the ranch was built by the sweat of Diego's brow.

cloze.s: No one gave Tomás his restaurant; he earned it ___, cooking sixteen hours a day.
cloze.a: by the sweat of his brow

story: In Hamlet's "To be or not to be" speech, he says death might be like sleep, but "to sleep, perchance to dream, ay, there's the rub," since no one knows what dreams may come. "Rub" meant an obstacle that blocks a bowling ball.
def: that is the main difficulty or catch that makes something harder than it first seems
ex: We could finish the project early if we hired more people, but there's the rub: we have no budget.
Moving to the country sounds wonderful, but there's the rub: the commute would be two hours each way.
I'd love to adopt a dog, but there's the rub: my lease doesn't allow pets.
The new medicine works well, but there's the rub: Fatima's insurance won't pay for it.

cloze.s: The plan works only if everyone agrees on a date, and ___: no one ever agrees.

term: the fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars
story: In Julius Caesar, Cassius tries to persuade Brutus to act against Caesar, telling him, "The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, but in ourselves, that we are underlings."
def: people are responsible for their own situation; they should not blame fate or bad luck
ex: When the team blamed bad luck for another loss, the coach replied that the fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars.
Wei stopped blaming the economy for his failing shop and admitted the fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars.
Sofia blamed the rain for failing her driving test, but her instructor gently said, “The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars.”
When profits fall, the business columnist reminds owners that the fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars.

cloze.s: "Stop blaming the weather for missed deadlines," the boss said. "___, but in ourselves."
cloze.a: The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars

note: John Green's novel title The Fault in Our Stars plays on this line.

story: In Hamlet, the prince arranges for actors to perform a play that copies his father's murder, saying, "The play's the thing wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king," so he can watch his uncle's guilty reaction.
def: used to say that the play or the work itself matters most, more than the fame or fuss around it
ex: Forget the fancy costumes and big stars; for this director, the play's the thing.
Our drama teacher always ended rehearsal with "Remember, the play's the thing!"
The school's tiny theater had no fancy lights or sets, but for the students, the play's the thing.
When reporters kept asking about her famous co-star, the actress smiled and said the play's the thing.

cloze.s: The theater critic ignored the celebrity gossip and wrote about the acting and script, since for her ___.

term: Lord, what fools these mortals be!
story: In A Midsummer Night's Dream, the mischievous fairy Puck watches confused human lovers chase and quarrel in the forest and laughs at them with this line.
def: a laughing comment about how silly and foolish people can behave
ex: Watching shoppers fight over discount TVs, Kwame shook his head: "Lord, what fools these mortals be!"
As her friends argued over a board game for an hour, Olga sighed, "Lord, what fools these mortals be."
Reading about people camping in line for days for new sneakers, Priya laughed, “Lord, what fools these mortals be!”
As drivers honked and argued in the stalled traffic, the old taxi driver chuckled, “Lord, what fools these mortals be.”

cloze.s: Seeing grown adults scream at a youth soccer game, the old referee muttered, "___"
cloze.a: Lord, what fools these mortals be!

story: In Othello, the hero says goodbye to the "pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war." Edward Elgar named his marches Pomp and Circumstance; the first, from 1901, is now played at many American graduations.
def: grand formal ceremony and fancy display at an official event
ex: The royal wedding was full of pomp and circumstance, from golden carriages to trumpets.
Maria wanted a small ceremony without all the pomp and circumstance.
The new judge was sworn in with little pomp and circumstance, just a short oath in a quiet office.
The state dinner had all the pomp and circumstance of a royal visit, including a military band.

cloze.s: The new museum opened with full ___: a parade, speeches, and a brass band.

story: In Edmond Rostand's 1897 play Cyrano de Bergerac, a brilliant poet who thinks his huge nose makes him unlovable secretly writes the love letters that a handsome but tongue-tied friend sends to Roxane, the woman Cyrano loves.
def: a person who secretly supplies the romantic words that someone else uses to win a partner
ex: Jamal played Cyrano, texting his shy roommate exactly what to write to his crush.
The dating app's message helper was called a digital Cyrano by reviewers.
Stuck for words, Liam asked his poet friend to be his Cyrano for the anniversary card.
Fatima became the office Cyrano, quietly helping coworkers write sweet notes to their partners for Valentine's Day.

cloze.s: The heartfelt wedding speech was so good that guests suspected the groom's poet sister had been his ___.

story: In George Orwell's 1949 novel Nineteen Eighty-Four, the ruling Party invents Newspeak, a shrunken language designed to remove words needed for free or rebellious thought.
def: misleading official language that twists or hides the truth and limits what people can easily say or think
ex: Calling the job cuts "rightsizing" struck many workers as corporate Newspeak.
The essay mocked the agency's Newspeak, in which a price increase became "a value adjustment."
The airline's Newspeak called a canceled flight an “involuntary schedule change.”
Students rolled their eyes when the school renamed detention “reflection time,” calling it pure Newspeak.

cloze.s: Critics said renaming the tax hike a "revenue enhancement" was pure ___.

note: Related to Orwell's "doublethink"; "doublespeak" is a later word built on the same idea.

story: In Harper Lee's 1960 novel To Kill a Mockingbird, Atticus Finch is a small-town Alabama lawyer who calmly defends a Black man falsely accused of a crime, despite anger from much of the town.
def: a person, especially a lawyer, admired for calm courage and fairness in standing up for what is right
ex: Law students often name Atticus Finch as the reason they wanted to become lawyers.
The public defender was called the county's Atticus Finch for taking unpopular cases.
Grandpa, a small-town lawyer, was the family's Atticus Finch, calmly defending poor clients whom others refused to help.
When the teacher calmly defended the bullied new student before an angry school board, parents called her an Atticus Finch.

cloze.s: Facing a hostile crowd, the young attorney stayed polite and principled, a true ___.

note: Harper Lee's later book Go Set a Watchman (2015) shows a more troubling version of the character.

story: In Charles Dickens's novel Oliver Twist (1837–39), Jack Dawkins, known as the Artful Dodger, is a clever young pickpocket in a gang of child thieves run by Fagin.
def: a clever, tricky person who is good at fooling others and at escaping blame or trouble
ex: The senator was an artful dodger who never gave a straight answer to reporters.
Our cat is an artful dodger who always slips out the door before we can stop her.
The smooth con man was an Artful Dodger who slipped out of three towns before the police caught up with him.
My little brother is an Artful Dodger; whenever the dishes need washing, he suddenly has homework to finish.

cloze.s: Every time the teacher asked about missing homework, Leo had a clever excuse; he was a real ___.

note: Often written in lowercase when used as a general description.

story: In Arthur Conan Doyle's 1892 story "Silver Blaze," Sherlock Holmes points to "the curious incident of the dog in the night-time": the dog did nothing. Its silence showed the thief was someone the dog knew.
def: an important clue that comes from something that did not happen when you would expect it to
ex: The dog that didn't bark in this case is that no money was ever withdrawn from the missing man's account.
Investors noticed the dog that didn't bark: the company stopped mentioning its biggest product.
The doctor noticed the dog that didn't bark: despite the bad cough, the patient never had a fever.
The dog that didn't bark was the burglar alarm: it stayed silent, so police suspected someone who knew the code.

cloze.s: Analysts saw the lack of any complaint from the rival company as ___, a silence that suggested a secret deal.

story: In Samuel Taylor Coleridge's 1798 poem "The Rime of the Ancient Mariner," a sailor shoots an albatross, a bird thought to bring good luck. When bad luck strikes the ship, the crew hangs the dead bird around his neck as punishment.
def: a burden, often caused by a past mistake, that you cannot get rid of and that keeps holding you back
ex: The failed merger became an albatross around the CEO's neck for the rest of her career.
That old loan was an albatross around his neck for a decade.
The embarrassing video from his twenties became an albatross around Liam's neck whenever he applied for jobs.
The badly built gym became an albatross around the school district's neck, costing money in repairs every year.

cloze.s: For years the mayor's unpopular stadium deal was ___, following him into every election.

story: Xanadu was the summer capital of the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan. Samuel Taylor Coleridge's poem "Kubla Khan" begins, "In Xanadu did Kubla Khan / A stately pleasure-dome decree," making the name stand for dreamlike luxury.
def: an imagined place of great beauty, luxury and pleasure
ex: The resort sold itself as a tropical Xanadu of pools, gardens and spas.
For a kid who loved books, the giant library felt like Xanadu.
After years in a tiny apartment, Fatima's new house with a garden felt like her own Xanadu.
The chocolate factory in the movie is a candy lover's Xanadu, with a chocolate river and gardens of sweets.

cloze.s: The billionaire's island estate, with marble palaces and private beaches, was a modern ___.

note: In the 1941 film Citizen Kane, Xanadu is the name of Kane's huge estate.

term: not with a bang but a whimper
story: T. S. Eliot's 1925 poem "The Hollow Men" ends, "This is the way the world ends / Not with a bang but a whimper."
def: ending in a weak, quiet, disappointing way instead of a big dramatic finish
ex: The famous band's final tour ended not with a bang but a whimper, in half-empty halls.
The long-hyped product line ended not with a bang but a whimper when it was quietly removed from stores.
The long-awaited TV series ended not with a bang but a whimper, with a confusing final episode.
The summer heat wave ended not with a bang but a whimper, fading into a week of gray drizzle.

cloze.s: After years of headlines, the investigation closed ___, with a short notice that no charges would be filed.
cloze.a: not with a bang but a whimper

story: In Walden (1854), Henry David Thoreau, who lived simply in a cabin near Walden Pond, wrote, "The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation."
def: a way of living with hidden, silent unhappiness, feeling stuck but never complaining out loud
ex: The novel follows office workers living lives of quiet desperation in a gray city suburb.
Hannah quit her job, saying she refused to lead a life of quiet desperation.
