Ana's grandfather spent forty years in a job he hated, living a life of quiet desperation without one complaint.
Thoreau wrote that most men lead lives of quiet desperation, and the line still rings true for many commuters.

cloze.s: Behind their neat lawns and polite smiles, many of the neighbors were leading ___.

story: In Leviathan (1651), the English philosopher Thomas Hobbes argued that without government, people would live in a constant war of everyone against everyone, and life would be "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short."
def: describing a life or event that is harsh, cruel and quickly over
ex: For sailors in the 1700s, life at sea was often nasty, brutish, and short.
The boxing match was nasty, brutish, and short, ending in the first round.
The philosopher Thomas Hobbes described life without any government as nasty, brutish, and short.
The kitchen argument between the two chefs was nasty, brutish, and short, over in two shouted minutes.

cloze.s: Without clean water or doctors, life in the camp was ___.

note: Often used jokingly about things like meetings or games.

story: Arcadia is a real mountain region of Greece, home of the god Pan in myth. The Roman poet Virgil and later Renaissance writers turned it into a dream of peaceful country life where shepherds sing and live simply.
def: an imagined place of simple, peaceful and happy country life, free from the troubles of the modern world
ex: The ad showed the small farm town as a sunny Arcadia of orchards and friendly neighbors.
Retiring to the mountains, Olga hoped to find her own Arcadia far from city noise.
The novel's hero dreams of a lost Arcadia where families farmed together and nobody locked their doors.
After a week of camping by the lake, the city kids called the quiet green valley their own Arcadia.

cloze.s: The painting shows shepherds resting under olive trees in a calm, green ___.

note: The adjective "Arcadian" means simple, peaceful and rural.

term: the nail that sticks out gets hammered down
story: This is an English version of a Japanese proverb that compares a person who stands out to a nail or stake that sticks up. It expresses a cultural pressure to fit in with the group and not stand out.
def: people who stand out or act differently from the group will be pushed back into line
ex: In that old-fashioned office, the nail that sticks out gets hammered down, so new ideas rarely survive.
Yuki said she learned early that the nail that sticks out gets hammered down.
At the strict boarding school, new students learned quickly that the nail that sticks out gets hammered down.
Some young artists reject the idea that the nail that sticks out gets hammered down and dress boldly anyway.

cloze.s: Kenji hid his bold proposal, fearing that ___ in a company that prized fitting in.
cloze.a: the nail that sticks out gets hammered down

note: Compare "tall poppy syndrome," a similar idea from Australia and New Zealand.

story: The Roman historian Livy tells how King Tarquin, asked by his son's messenger for advice, silently struck off the heads of the tallest poppies in his garden; the son understood and killed the leading men of the town he controlled. The phrase became common in Australia and New Zealand.
def: the habit of disliking, attacking or cutting down people who are very successful or stand out
ex: The singer said tall poppy syndrome made her hometown turn on her after she became famous.
Some managers suffer from tall poppy syndrome and quietly block their best workers' promotions.
When Priya was promoted ahead of her friends, tall poppy syndrome turned their congratulations into gossip.
Some students hide their good grades to avoid tall poppy syndrome from their classmates.

cloze.s: As soon as the young chef won national praise, local critics started attacking her, a clear case of ___.

story: In this well-known children’s folk tale, a hen asks the other farm animals to help her plant wheat, harvest it, and bake bread, and each refuses. When the bread is ready they all want some, and she eats it herself.
def: a person who does all the work alone while others who refused to help still expect to share the reward
ex: Nobody helped plan the reunion, but everyone wanted credit; Fatima felt like the Little Red Hen.
The professor joked that group projects always have one Little Red Hen.
Wei planted and weeded the community garden alone, then everyone showed up for tomatoes; he felt like the Little Red Hen.
On every group trip, Aisha plays the Little Red Hen, booking everything while the others just show up.

cloze.s: Maria cooked the whole holiday meal alone, and when her brothers rushed to eat, she felt like ___.

story: A popular fable says a frog dropped into hot water will jump out, but one in water heated slowly will stay until it is cooked. Some 1800s experiments seemed to support this, but modern biologists say real frogs try to escape as water warms.
def: a person or group that fails to notice a danger because it grows slowly, until it is too late
ex: Rising costs crept up so gradually that the company was a boiling frog until it ran out of cash.
Critics warned that slow changes to privacy rules could make users into boiling frogs.
Hannah's credit card debt grew a little each month, and like a boiling frog, she didn't notice until it was huge.
The workers were boiling frogs, as their shifts crept up by a few minutes every month for years.

cloze.s: Each year the town lost a few shops, and like a(n) ___, no one reacted until Main Street was empty.

note: The image is a metaphor only; it is not true of real frogs.

story: Theodore Roosevelt liked to quote what he called a West African proverb: "Speak softly and carry a big stick; you will go far." As president, his "big stick" foreign policy meant calm talks backed by the threat of military force.
def: a show of power or the threat of force used to back up talks or demands
ex: The regulators used the big stick of heavy fines to make banks follow the new rules.
The union carried a big stick into negotiations: a vote to strike.
The teacher kept detention as her big stick, but she rarely needed to use it.
Parents found that the big stick of taking away video games got homework done fast.

cloze.s: The landlord spoke politely, but the eviction notice in his hand was a clear ___.

note: Little evidence shows the saying is really West African.

story: The phrase first described medieval German lords who charged travelers illegal tolls to cross their land or sail the Rhine. In the 1800s Americans applied it to rich industrialists like Cornelius Vanderbilt, and Matthew Josephson's 1934 book The Robber Barons made it famous.
def: a very rich and powerful business owner thought to have gotten rich through cruel or unfair methods
ex: The documentary portrayed the railroad tycoons of the 1800s as robber barons.
Protesters called the tech billionaires the robber barons of our time.
Students debated whether the steel and oil tycoons of the Gilded Age were robber barons or builders of the nation.
In the board game, players act as robber barons, buying up railroads and driving rivals out of business.

cloze.s: The novel's villain is a(n) ___ who crushed small rivals and paid his miners almost nothing.

note: Negative; "captain of industry" is a more admiring term for the same kind of person.

story: The American writer O. Henry coined the term in his 1904 book Cabbages and Kings, inspired by his time in Honduras, a country whose economy depended on banana exports.
def: a weak, corrupt country run for the benefit of a few powerful people or foreign companies
ex: Critics warned that rigged courts and bribed officials would turn the nation into a banana republic.
The journalist described the island's dictator as the ruler of a banana republic.
In history class, students learned how foreign fruit companies once ran parts of Central America as banana republics.
The novel is set in a made-up banana republic where the president's family owns every bank and newspaper.

cloze.s: When the leader jailed his opponents and gave his cousins every top job, observers called it a(n) ___.

note: Insulting; avoid applying it lightly to real countries.

story: Two families on the West Virginia–Kentucky border carried on a violent feud from the 1860s to about 1891, with killings, a court fight over a hog, and a doomed romance between a Hatfield son and a McCoy daughter.
def: two families or groups locked in a long, bitter fight that neither side will give up
ex: The two neighbors have fought over the fence for so long that people call them the Hatfields and McCoys.
The rival pizza shops were the Hatfields and McCoys of Main Street.
The two chess clubs in town have been the Hatfields and McCoys for decades, refusing to share a tournament hall.
Fans of the two high school football teams act like the Hatfields and McCoys every homecoming week.

cloze.s: The two sides of the family haven't spoken in twenty years; they're like the ___.

note: Usually used with humor about everyday rivalries.

story: In June 1876, U.S. Army officer George Armstrong Custer attacked a large camp of Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho people at the Little Bighorn River in Montana. Custer and every soldier with him were killed.
def: a final fight against impossible odds that ends in total defeat
ex: The tiny bookstore's protest against the giant chain felt like Custer's last stand.
Down by forty points, the team's fourth-quarter push was a Custer's last stand.
The old video store refused to close as streaming took over, and its final half-price sale was its Custer's last stand.
Sure she would fail the final exam, Olga called her all-night study session Custer's last stand.

cloze.s: With nearly every vote against him, the senator's long speech was his ___.

note: Often stresses that the defeat came from overconfidence or poor planning.

story: The Scottish explorer David Livingstone had not been heard from for years in Africa when journalist Henry Morton Stanley found him in 1871 at Ujiji, in present-day Tanzania. Stanley reported greeting him with these calm, formal words.
def: a joking hello to someone you have finally found or met after a long search or absence
ex: When Diego finally found his friend at the crowded festival, he grinned and said, "Dr. Livingstone, I presume?"
After hours in the huge hospital, Hannah found her father's room and joked, "Dr. Livingstone, I presume?"
When his roommate finally came out after a week of studying for exams, Kwame said, “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?”
Spotting her pen pal at the train station after years of letters, Yuki smiled and asked, “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?”

cloze.s: Spotting his long-lost cousin at the far end of the airport, Malik walked up and said, "___"

note: Humorous; historians doubt Stanley really said it, since pages of his diary for that day are missing.

story: In the 1930s, France built a long line of strong forts along its border with Germany, named after war minister André Maginot. In 1940 the German army simply went around it through Belgium and the Ardennes forest, and France fell within weeks.
def: a defense that people trust completely but that is useless because an attack comes from another direction
ex: The company's firewall was a Maginot Line; hackers got in by tricking employees with fake emails.
Relying only on height, the basketball team built a Maginot Line that quick guards easily went around.
Our tall fence was a Maginot Line against the raccoons, who simply climbed the tree and dropped into the yard.
In the war novel, the huge sea wall proves a Maginot Line when the invaders arrive by air.

cloze.s: The castle-like gate was a(n) ___, since thieves entered through the unguarded back door.

story: Gulag was the short name of the Soviet government agency that ran a huge network of forced-labor prison camps, especially under Joseph Stalin. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn's book The Gulag Archipelago (1973) made the word known worldwide.
def: a harsh prison camp for political prisoners, or any brutal system that punishes people for their beliefs
ex: The historian interviewed survivors of the Soviet gulag about their years of forced labor.
Human rights groups warned that the new detention camps were a modern gulag.
Her grandfather survived five years in a Soviet gulag and rarely spoke about it.
The novel describes a made-up nation where critics of the king disappear into a gulag in the mountains.

cloze.s: The dissident writer spent ten years in a frozen ___ for criticizing the government.

note: Sometimes used jokingly for a strict place, but the real history is very grim.

term: Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds
story: J. Robert Oppenheimer, who led the building of the first atomic bomb, said in a 1965 TV documentary that this line from the Hindu scripture the Bhagavad Gita came to his mind at the first test explosion in 1945. In the Gita, the god Krishna speaks it.
def: a serious line expressing horror at having created something with terrible power to destroy
ex: Watching the new weapon tested, the scientist quietly quoted, "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds."
The film about artificial intelligence opens with Oppenheimer's words, "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds."
Horrified by the deadly virus he had created, the novel's scientist whispered, “Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.”
The professor ended her lecture on nuclear weapons by quoting, “Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.”

cloze.s: Remembering the first atomic test, Oppenheimer recalled the words, "___."
cloze.a: Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds

term: the unexamined life is not worth living
story: At his trial in Athens in 399 BC, as told in Plato's Apology, the philosopher Socrates refused to stop questioning people about how to live, saying that a life without such questioning is not worth living for a human being.
def: people should think deeply about their beliefs, choices and values instead of living without reflection
ex: Before changing careers, Priya spent a month journaling, believing the unexamined life is not worth living.
Our philosophy teacher began every year by writing on the board: "The unexamined life is not worth living."
Before accepting the promotion, Ravi asked himself whether he truly wanted it, since the unexamined life is not worth living.
The first-year seminar opens with Socrates' line, “The unexamined life is not worth living,” to start talks about values.

cloze.s: The retreat invites guests to reflect on their goals, since, as Socrates said, "___."
cloze.a: the unexamined life is not worth living

story: In Jean-Paul Sartre's 1944 play No Exit, three dead strangers are locked together forever in an ordinary-looking room in hell. There are no torture tools; they slowly realize they will torment one another by watching and judging each other.
def: a saying that being stuck with others, and always judged by them, can be the worst suffering of all
ex: After six hours in a crowded airport line, Liam muttered that hell is other people.
The novel's family vacation chapter proves that sometimes hell is other people.
Stuck on a group project where everyone argued and judged each other's ideas, Malik joked that hell is other people.
Sartre's famous line “hell is other people” came to Hannah's mind during the endless office group chat.

cloze.s: Trapped in a tiny cabin with three quarreling relatives all weekend, Yuki finally understood the line "___."

note: Often quoted as simple dislike of people; Sartre meant how others' judgments trap us.

story: In early-1900s Germany, a horse named Hans seemed to solve math problems by tapping his hoof. In 1907 the psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed Hans was reading tiny, unconscious body cues from questioners and failed when he could not see them.
def: a case in which an animal, person or machine seems to understand a task but is really picking up hidden clues
ex: Researchers feared their test was a Clever Hans case, with the dog reacting to the trainer's glances.
The AI looked brilliant at spotting disease in X-rays, but it was a Clever Hans, using hospital labels on the images instead.
The teacher realized her “star” student was a Clever Hans, watching her face to guess the right answer.
Psychologists make sure the person giving a test can't see the answers, to avoid a Clever Hans problem.

cloze.s: The parrot only answered correctly when its owner was watching, which made the scientists suspect a(n) ___ effect.

note: The "Clever Hans effect" is why many experiments are run so testers cannot accidentally give hints.

story: The Roman poet Juvenal described something rare as “a rare bird on earth, very like a black swan,” since Europeans believed all swans were white. In 1697 Dutch explorers found black swans in Western Australia. Writer Nassim Nicholas Taleb's 2007 book The Black Swan made it a term for rare, shocking events.
def: a rare, unexpected event with huge effects that people later claim they should have seen coming
ex: The sudden market crash was a black swan that no economist had predicted.
Insurance companies try to plan for black swans like rare mega-storms.
For the small bakery, a road closure that lasted a whole year was a black swan that nearly ended the business.
Good engineers design bridges with black swans in mind, not just the ordinary storms they expect.

cloze.s: No model had predicted the volcano that closed every airport in the region; it was a true ___ event.

story: In 1990, the American lawyer Mike Godwin stated a rule about early online discussion groups: the longer an online argument goes on, the closer to certain it becomes that someone will compare someone or something to Hitler or the Nazis.
def: the joking rule that any long online argument will sooner or later include a comparison to Hitler or Nazis
ex: The forum thread about parking rules proved Godwin's law within two hours.
When her uncle compared the city's recycling plan to the Nazis, Sofia said he had just proved Godwin's law.
The online debate about dog parks lasted three hundred comments before Godwin's law finally kicked in.
The gaming forum bans Nazi comparisons, partly to stop Godwin's law from ruining every heated thread.

cloze.s: Sure enough, the comment war over pizza toppings ended with a Nazi comparison, another win for ___.

note: Often used to suggest that whoever makes the Nazi comparison has lost the argument.

story: After World War II, some Pacific island groups in Melanesia built fake runways and control huts, hoping planes would return with the goods soldiers had brought. Physicist Richard Feynman's 1974 Caltech speech used "cargo cult science" for research that copies the look of science but not its methods.
def: copying the surface look of something successful without understanding what actually makes it work
ex: Buying beanbags and a ping-pong table to act like a tech startup is cargo cult management.
The team's cargo cult coding copied other programs line by line without knowing why they worked.
Students who copy the top scorer's highlighter colors without actually studying are practicing cargo cult learning.
Critics called it cargo cult planning: the city built a shiny tech park but gave companies no real reason to move there.

cloze.s: The school copied the famous academy's uniforms and slogans but none of its teaching methods, a classic ___.

note: Some anthropologists criticize the term for oversimplifying real island movements.

term: we're gonna need a bigger boat
story: In Steven Spielberg's 1975 film Jaws, police chief Martin Brody gets his first close look at the huge shark they are hunting, backs away in shock, and tells the boat's captain, “You're gonna need a bigger boat.”
def: a joking way of saying a problem is far bigger than expected and needs much more than you have
ex: When the caterer saw three hundred guests instead of fifty, she said, "We're gonna need a bigger boat."
After the server crashed from all the traffic, the IT chief joked that we're gonna need a bigger boat.
Seeing twenty kids arrive for the sleepover instead of five, Kwame turned to his wife: “We're gonna need a bigger boat.”
When the volunteers saw how much trash covered the beach, Priya laughed, “We're gonna need a bigger boat.”

cloze.s: Seeing the mountain of laundry after vacation, Jamal sighed, "___."
cloze.a: We're gonna need a bigger boat

note: The film line is "You're gonna need a bigger boat"; people commonly say "we're."

story: "Winter is coming" is the family motto of House Stark in George R. R. Martin's fantasy novels A Song of Ice and Fire and the HBO series Game of Thrones, a warning to always be ready for hard times ahead.
def: a warning that hard or dangerous times are on the way, so people should get ready now
ex: With sales falling, the CEO told staff that winter is coming and froze all new hiring.
Before exam season, our teacher wrote on the board: "Winter is coming."
As the baby's due date approached, friends teased Malik, “Winter is coming,” and told him to sleep while he could.
Hearing that the landlord was selling the building, Tomás told his roommates, “Winter is coming,” and started saving for a deposit.

cloze.s: As layoffs spread across the industry, workers updated their résumés, saying, "___."

story: In the Road Runner cartoons, Wile E. Coyote often chases the bird right off a cliff. He hangs in midair, fine, until he looks down, realizes there is nothing under him, and only then falls.
def: the moment someone suddenly realizes there is nothing supporting their situation, just before it collapses
ex: Economists warned of a Wile E. Coyote moment when investors finally notice the company has no profits.
The band had a Wile E. Coyote moment when they saw the empty ticket sales for their tour.
Diego had a Wile E. Coyote moment halfway through his speech when he realized his notes were gone.
Sofia's Wile E. Coyote moment came when she checked her bank balance after a month of carefree spending.

cloze.s: The housing market kept rising on borrowed money until a(n) ___, when buyers looked down and prices fell fast.

note: Common in finance and economics writing.

story: In William Styron's 1979 novel Sophie's Choice, later a 1982 film, a Polish mother arriving at the Auschwitz death camp is forced by a Nazi officer to choose which one of her two children will be allowed to live.
def: a very painful choice between two options that are both terrible, or between two things you love equally
ex: Choosing between caring for her sick mother and keeping her dream job felt like Sophie's choice to Fatima.
Asking a parent which child they love more is an unfair Sophie's choice.
Picking which of her two rescue dogs to give up before the move felt like Sophie's choice to Hannah.
With only one spot left on the roster, the coach faced a Sophie's choice between two equally loyal players.

cloze.s: Forced to cut either the children's program or the senior meals, the charity faced a true ___.

note: Often used lightly ("choosing a dessert is a Sophie's choice"), but the source is very dark, so use with care.

story: In Lewis Carroll's 1871 book Through the Looking-Glass, the Red Queen tells Alice, "It takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place." Biologists later named the Red Queen hypothesis after it.
def: a situation where you must keep working harder and harder just to stay in the same place as rivals
ex: In the phone market, constant new features are a Red Queen's race, since every rival adds them too.
Bacteria and medicines are locked in a Red Queen's race, each changing to keep up.
Small online shops are in a Red Queen's race, lowering prices every week just to match the big sites.
For students applying to top colleges, piling on more activities has become a Red Queen's race.

cloze.s: Each year the farm had to buy better equipment just to keep up with its neighbors, an endless ___.

note: In biology, the "Red Queen effect" describes species that must keep evolving to survive against rivals.

story: In Lewis Carroll's 1865 book Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice eats a cake and suddenly grows enormously tall. So amazed that she forgets proper English, she cries, "Curiouser and curiouser!"
def: a funny way of saying a situation keeps getting stranger and more puzzling
ex: First the lights flickered, then the cat vanished; curiouser and curiouser, thought Hannah.
As the reporter dug into the missing funds, the story got curiouser and curiouser.
The scientist's data got curiouser and curiouser: the plants kept growing faster in the dark than in the light.
First new locks, then covered windows, then a camel in the yard; our neighbor's house got curiouser and curiouser.

cloze.s: The package had no stamp, no return address, and a key inside; ___, Wei thought.

note: Deliberately bad grammar, used for humor.

story: In Greek myth, Princess Ariadne of Crete gave the hero Theseus a ball of thread to unwind as he entered the Labyrinth. After killing the Minotaur inside, he followed the thread back out.
def: a clue or method that guides someone step by step through a confusing problem or situation
ex: The detailed project log was the Ariadne's thread that helped Kwame trace where the budget errors began.
Old tax records gave the historian an Ariadne's thread through the family's tangled past.
In the huge hospital, the colored lines on the floor were Ariadne's thread, leading patients to each clinic.
The detective's notebook of dates and names became her Ariadne's thread through the confusing case.

cloze.s: Lost in hundreds of pages of contract rules, Sofia used the index as her ___, following it from one clause to the next.

story: In Greek myth, the Styx was a dark river of the underworld, the gloomy land of the dead. The word first meant 'of the Styx' and came to describe deep, frightening darkness.
def: extremely dark and scary, like the land of the dead
ex: When the power failed, the subway tunnel was plunged into stygian darkness.
Hannah's flashlight barely cut through the stygian gloom at the back of the cave.
The hikers' headlamps died, leaving them in stygian blackness on the forest trail.
During the blackout, the hospital hallway was stygian until the backup generators kicked on.

cloze.s: The basement had no windows, and once the door shut, the room was ___, so dark she could not see her own hand.

note: Often capitalized (Stygian). Usually paired with 'darkness' or 'gloom.'

story: Cerberus was the many-headed dog that guarded the entrance to the Greek underworld. In Virgil's Aeneid, a priestess gets the hero past him by tossing the dog a drugged honey cake, which he gulps down before falling asleep.
def: a small gift or favor given to quiet or calm someone who could cause trouble
ex: The free parking passes were a sop to Cerberus, meant to calm neighbors angry about the new stadium.
Diego's boss gave the complaining client a discount as a sop to Cerberus.
The free dessert was a sop to Cerberus after the waiter spilled soup on an already angry customer.
The airline handed out meal vouchers as a sop to Cerberus to passengers furious about the long delay.

cloze.s: To keep the angry union leader from walking out, management offered a small bonus as a(n) ___.

note: Often shortened to just 'a sop.' A sop was originally a piece of bread soaked in liquid.

story: In Plato's Republic, Glaucon tells of a shepherd in Lydia who finds a gold ring that makes him invisible. He uses it to seduce the queen, kill the king, and take the throne, raising the question of whether anyone would stay honest if never caught.
def: the power to do anything without being seen or punished, used to ask whether people would still act rightly
ex: Anonymous accounts give internet users a kind of ring of Gyges, and some of them behave badly.
In ethics class, Aisha asked what she would do with a ring of Gyges, knowing no one would ever find out.
Working from home with no manager watching felt like a ring of Gyges, testing whether Diego would still work hard.
A store with no cameras or cashiers offers a small ring of Gyges: would shoppers still pay for everything?

cloze.s: The professor asked: if you owned the ___ and could steal with no chance of being caught, would you still be honest?

story: At Delphi in ancient Greece, a priestess of the god Apollo gave prophecies that were famously unclear. Herodotus says King Croesus was told that if he attacked Persia he would destroy a great empire; the empire he destroyed was his own.
def: deliberately unclear or mysterious, so it can be understood in more than one way
ex: The CEO's Delphic remark that 'changes are coming' left employees guessing about layoffs.
Malik's grandmother gave Delphic advice that he understood only years later.
The fortune cookie's Delphic message, “Change comes from within,” could mean almost anything.
When Mei asked if she had gotten the job, the recruiter's Delphic “we'll be in touch” could have meant yes or no.

cloze.s: Asked whether he would run again, the senator gave a(n) ___ answer that both sides took as a yes.

story: Croesus was the last king of Lydia, in what is now Turkey, in the 500s BC. His wealth was legendary, and he is credited with issuing some of the first gold coins of fixed purity.
def: extremely wealthy, with far more money than anyone could need
ex: After selling her app, Priya was rich as Croesus but still drove her old car.
Tourists assume everyone in the resort town is rich as Croesus, but many residents struggle to pay rent.
Malik isn't rich as Croesus, but he saved enough to pay for his kids' college.
The old oil baron was rich as Croesus and owned mansions on three continents.

cloze.s: The lottery jackpot left the retired teacher ___, with more money than his family could spend in three lifetimes.

note: Often said as 'as rich as Croesus.' Croesus is pronounced KREE-sus.

story: According to Roman tradition, in 458 BC the farmer Cincinnatus was called from his plow and made dictator to rescue a trapped Roman army. He won, then gave up his total power after about two weeks and went back to his farm.
def: a leader who takes power in a crisis and then willingly gives it up to return to ordinary life
ex: Historians often call George Washington an American Cincinnatus for retiring to his farm instead of seeking more power.
The interim director played Cincinnatus, fixing the charity's finances and then quietly stepping aside.
After leading the town through the flood recovery, the retired engineer stepped down like Cincinnatus and went back to fishing.
Fans hoped the legendary coach would play Cincinnatus, rescuing the team for one season and then retiring again.

cloze.s: After steering the club through its money crisis, Olga refused a second term and went back to coaching kids, a true ___.

story: After Hannibal crushed Roman armies, the Roman commander Fabius Maximus, made dictator in 217 BC, avoided big battles and wore the enemy down with delay and small attacks. He was nicknamed Cunctator, 'the Delayer.'
def: a plan to beat a stronger opponent slowly by avoiding direct battle and wearing them down over time
ex: The small startup used a Fabian strategy, avoiding a price war and slowly winning customers the big firm ignored.
The underdog boxer adopted a Fabian strategy, dodging for ten rounds until his opponent tired.
Knowing she couldn't outrace the champion head-on, the cyclist used a Fabian strategy, staying behind him until he tired.
The tenants used a Fabian strategy against the huge landlord company, filing small complaints for months until it gave in.

cloze.s: Outmatched in money and staff, the small legal team chose a(n) ___: no head-on fights, just patient, steady pressure over many months.

note: The British Fabian Society took its name from this slow, patient approach to change.

story: Lucullus was a wealthy Roman general of the first century BC who retired to a life of famous luxury. Plutarch says that when his cook served a simple meal because he was dining alone, he scolded him: 'Today Lucullus dines with Lucullus.'
def: very rich, fancy, and costly, especially describing a meal or feast
ex: The wedding guests enjoyed a Lucullan dinner of seven courses and rare wines.
Jamal's idea of a Lucullan weekend was a stack of novels and endless room service.
For their anniversary, the couple splurged on a Lucullan tasting menu of twelve courses.
The tech company's Lucullan holiday party featured an oyster bar and a chocolate fountain.

cloze.s: The cruise advertised ___ banquets every night, with lobster, caviar, and ice sculptures on every table.

story: In the 300s BC, the Athenian speaker Demosthenes gave a series of fiery speeches attacking King Philip II of Macedon. Centuries later, Cicero called his own furious speeches against Mark Antony 'Philippics.'
def: a long, angry speech or piece of writing that bitterly attacks someone
ex: The coach delivered a ten-minute philippic against the referees after the loss.
Her newspaper column was a philippic against the city's failure to fix the water pipes.
At the town meeting, one resident delivered a philippic against the noisy new airport flight paths.
Grandpa's letter to the cable company was a three-page philippic about dropped channels and rising bills.

cloze.s: Instead of a calm review, the critic wrote a furious ___ that tore apart every scene of the film.

term: Caesar's wife must be above suspicion
story: In 62 BC a man named Clodius sneaked, disguised as a woman, into a women-only religious festival at Julius Caesar's house. Caesar divorced his wife Pompeia though nothing was proved against her, saying his wife should not even be suspected.
def: people close to power must avoid even looking guilty, not just avoid doing wrong
ex: The judge sold her shares in the company before the trial, since Caesar's wife must be above suspicion.
Our treasurer won't even borrow the club's van; she says Caesar's wife must be above suspicion.
The referee turned down free tickets from the home team, saying Caesar's wife must be above suspicion.
The new mayor handed her business to an outside manager because Caesar's wife must be above suspicion.

cloze.s: The mayor's brother withdrew his bid for the city contract, explaining that ___.
cloze.a: Caesar's wife must be above suspicion

story: Rome fought three wars with the city of Carthage and, in 146 BC, destroyed it completely. In 1919 the economist John Maynard Keynes called the treaty forced on Germany after World War I a Carthaginian peace.
def: a peace deal so harsh that it crushes the losing side completely
ex: Critics warned that the merger terms were a Carthaginian peace that would leave the smaller company with nothing.
Historians still debate whether the treaty was a Carthaginian peace or a fair settlement.
Some historians argue that the Treaty of Versailles was a Carthaginian peace for Germany.
The older brother's terms for ending the fight were a Carthaginian peace: he kept the bedroom, the game console and the TV.

cloze.s: The winners took the land, the factories, and the army, imposing a(n) ___ that left the defeated nation helpless.

note: The popular story that the Romans salted Carthage's soil has no ancient evidence.

story: The Roman poet Juvenal asked 'Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?' (who will guard the guards themselves?) in a satire about locking up a wife, since a clever wife could win over the guards themselves. It is now asked about holding powerful people accountable.
def: a question asking who will check and control the people whose job is to check and control others
ex: When the review board turned out to be run by the officials it was meant to review, reporters asked: who watches the watchmen?
The auditors were caught hiding their own errors, which raised the old question, who watches the watchmen?
If the hospital's safety committee only ever reviews itself, patients may fairly ask, who watches the watchmen?
The referees' union picked the officials who judge the referees, leading fans to ask, who watches the watchmen?

cloze.s: If the safety inspectors can't be trusted either, then ___?

note: Also quoted in the original Latin: quis custodiet ipsos custodes?

story: In Homer's Iliad, the Myrmidons were the fierce warriors who followed Achilles into battle at Troy. A later myth, told by Ovid, said Zeus created them from ants.
def: a loyal follower who carries out a leader's orders without question, even harsh ones
ex: The dictator's myrmidons rounded up anyone who criticized him.
The tech billionaire arrived surrounded by myrmidons who blocked every reporter's question.
The coach's myrmidons enforced his harsh training rules, even on players who were clearly injured.
In the film, the cruel queen sent her myrmidons to seize the farmers' grain, and not one of them protested.

cloze.s: The landlord sent his ___ to change the locks, and they obeyed without asking whether it was legal.

note: Usually negative.

story: In Norse myth, Ragnarök is the final battle in which the gods are destroyed and the world burns. Richard Wagner's 1876 opera Götterdämmerung ('Twilight of the Gods') ends with Valhalla, the gods' hall, going up in flames.
def: a violent, total collapse of a powerful regime, group, or way of life
ex: The final months of the war were a Götterdämmerung for the regime.
Fans described the band's chaotic farewell tour as a rock-and-roll Götterdämmerung.
The company's final year was a Götterdämmerung of lawsuits, firings and bankrupt factories.
The fantasy series ends in a Götterdämmerung, with the old kingdom destroyed in one last battle.

cloze.s: As the empire's leaders turned on each other and its cities burned, observers spoke of a(n) ___.

story: In ancient China, the Zhou dynasty, which overthrew the Shang around the 11th century BC, taught that Heaven gives rulers the right to govern only while they rule justly. Famine, disaster, or revolt was taken as a sign that the mandate had been lost.
def: the right to rule or lead, which people believe is lost when a leader rules badly
ex: After three losing seasons and a cheating scandal, the coach seemed to have lost the Mandate of Heaven.
Business writers joke that a CEO keeps the Mandate of Heaven only as long as profits keep rising.
After the school board ignored parents' complaints for years, many felt it had lost the Mandate of Heaven.
In history class, Wei learned that Chinese dynasties claimed the Mandate of Heaven, which bad rule could take away.

cloze.s: When floods and riots followed one another, people believed the emperor had lost the ___.

story: In Zen Buddhism, which began in China as Chan, a koan is a riddle or short story a teacher gives a student to break ordinary logical thinking. A famous one from the Japanese master Hakuin asks: 'Two hands clap and there is a sound; what is the sound of one hand?'
def: a puzzling question or statement that cannot be solved by ordinary logic and makes you think deeply
ex: 'How do you plan for a surprise?' sounded like a koan, and the team argued about it for an hour.
Grandpa answered every question with a koan, leaving Wei to work out the meaning herself.
Ms. Okafor opened the philosophy class with a famous koan: 'What is the sound of one hand clapping?'
Diego's toddler asked, 'Where does the dark go when you turn on the light?', a koan that kept him thinking.

cloze.s: The meditation teacher handed each student a(n) ___, a riddle with no logical answer, to think about all week.

story: Tikkun olam is Hebrew for 'repairing the world.' The phrase appears in early Jewish law and prayer, and in modern times it came to mean the duty to improve society through justice and kindness.
def: the idea that people have a duty to help heal and improve the world through good acts
ex: For Hannah, volunteering at the food bank every Sunday is her small act of tikkun olam.
The synagogue's tikkun olam committee organizes tree planting and tutoring programs.
Their family's tikkun olam project is collecting winter coats for neighbors who can't afford them.
Rabbi Levin urged the teenagers to practice tikkun olam by volunteering at the local animal shelter.

cloze.s: Inspired by the Jewish value of ___, the youth group spent its summer cleaning parks and tutoring refugee children.

story: In the One Thousand and One Nights, a king marries a new bride each day and has her killed the next morning. Scheherazade marries him and tells a story each night, stopping at an exciting point, until after 1,001 nights he spares her.
def: a gifted teller of stories who keeps people eager to hear more, often to put something off
ex: Our tour guide was a Scheherazade, ending each stop with a cliffhanger so we hurried to the next.
Every night the kids begged their dad, a true Scheherazade, for one more chapter.
The camp counselor was a Scheherazade, stretching one ghost story over five nights so the kids would beg for more.
The podcast host is a Scheherazade, always ending each episode just before the big reveal.

cloze.s: The novelist was a modern ___, ending every chapter on a cliffhanger that kept readers up past midnight.

story: In a tale from the One Thousand and One Nights, a rich nobleman of the Barmecide family invites a starving beggar to a grand feast, then serves only empty dishes and describes imaginary food. The beggar plays along, and the host finally serves a real meal.
def: something that looks generous or rich but turns out to be empty or not real
ex: The 'unlimited' phone plan was a Barmecide feast once the hidden limits kicked in.
The job offer was a Barmecide feast: a fancy title with no salary and no staff.
The new park plan was a Barmecide feast, with beautiful drawings but no money to build anything.
The cheap hotel's fancy menu was a Barmecide feast, since most of the dishes were never actually available.

cloze.s: The brochure promised free meals and shows, but the resort turned out to be a(n) ___ of locked doors and empty buffets.

term: if the mountain won't come to Muhammad
story: In his 1625 essay 'Of Boldness,' Francis Bacon told a story, of unknown origin, that Muhammad called a hill to come to him. When it did not move, he said that he would go to the hill instead.
def: if things will not change to suit you, you must adapt and go to them yourself
ex: The client refused to travel, so Maria flew to Tokyo: if the mountain won't come to Muhammad, Muhammad must go to the mountain.
My son never visits, so I'll visit him; if the mountain won't come to Muhammad, I'll go to it.
The bookstore couldn't attract young readers, so it opened a stand on campus; if the mountain won't come to Muhammad, Muhammad must go to the mountain.
The doctor began visiting elderly patients at home, saying, “If the mountain won't come to Muhammad, Muhammad must go to the mountain.”

cloze.s: The investors wouldn't come to the small town, so the founders went to the big city: ___, Muhammad must go to the mountain.
cloze.a: if the mountain won't come to Muhammad

note: Usually finished with '...Muhammad must go to the mountain.' Bacon spelled the name Mahomet.

story: Visitors to Blarney Castle near Cork, Ireland, lean backward over a high wall to kiss a stone built into it. Legend says the Blarney Stone gives whoever kisses it the gift of charming, persuasive talk.
def: smooth, charming talk or praise that is not sincere, used to win someone over
ex: The salesman's blarney about 'once-in-a-lifetime deals' didn't fool Fatima.
Liam talked his way out of the parking ticket with pure blarney.
Jamal's blarney about Grandma's cooking earned him a second slice of pie.
The candidate's blarney charmed the hiring panel, but his references told a different story.

cloze.s: Don't believe his ___ about how talented you are; he flatters everyone he wants a favor from.

story: Spanish conquerors in South America in the 1500s heard of 'el dorado,' 'the golden one,' a ruler said to cover himself in gold dust and wash it off in a sacred lake. The legend grew into a lost city of gold that explorers searched for in vain.
def: an imagined place of great wealth or opportunity that people search for but rarely find
ex: For many young programmers, Silicon Valley seemed an El Dorado of quick fortunes.
The mining town was no El Dorado; most prospectors left poorer than they arrived.
The explorers spent years in the jungle searching for El Dorado and found only hunger.
To the young actor, Hollywood looked like El Dorado, but most auditions led nowhere.

cloze.s: Investors rushed into the new market as if it were a(n) ___, sure they would all strike it rich.

story: In an American folk legend from the railroad-building years after the Civil War, John Henry, a powerful steel-driving man, raced a steam-powered drill while cutting a tunnel. He won the contest but died soon after, hammer in hand.
def: a person who tries to beat a machine with pure human effort, often at great personal cost
ex: The veteran typist went John Henry against the new software and actually finished first.
Kwame refused to use the spreadsheet formulas, playing John Henry with a calculator all night.
Like John Henry, the warehouse worker raced the new sorting robot all day and ended his shift exhausted.
When the bank brought in a coin-counting machine, old Mr. Novak played John Henry, sorting coins by hand until his wrists ached.

cloze.s: Like a modern ___, the chess champion insisted on facing the computer again, though it was clearly faster and stronger.

term: don't throw me in the briar patch
story: In African American folktales published by Joel Chandler Harris in 1881, the trickster Brer Rabbit, caught by Brer Fox, begs not to be thrown into a thorny briar patch. Fox throws him in, and Rabbit, who was born and raised in briars, escapes easily.
def: a pretend plea against a punishment that is secretly exactly what the person wants
ex: When his boss threatened to send him to the beach office, Diego joked, 'Please, don't throw me in the briar patch.'
Told she might have to work from home, Yuki sighed dramatically: 'Oh no, don't throw me in the briar patch.'
When his mom threatened to leave him at the library all afternoon, the young bookworm cried, “Oh, don't throw me in the briar patch!”
The chef pretended to dread her move to the pastry kitchen, but her “don't throw me in the briar patch” grin gave her away.

cloze.s: Threatened with a transfer to the quiet Hawaii branch, the manager grinned and said, 'Please, ___!'
cloze.a: don't throw me in the briar patch

note: The Brer Rabbit tales grew largely from African trickster stories carried to America by enslaved people.

story: In a European folktale, hungry travelers tell stingy villagers they can make soup from a stone and need only a few extras. Each villager adds something, and soon there is a rich soup that everyone shares.
def: a project that succeeds because many people each add a small part, often after a clever start
ex: The community garden was stone soup: one woman brought seeds, and soon the whole block pitched in.
Our film project became stone soup, with each friend adding a camera, a song, or a scene.
The school fundraiser became stone soup when one parent's bake sale grew into a whole carnival run by families.
The free software project began as stone soup: one coder shared a simple tool, and hundreds of volunteers improved it.

cloze.s: The library began with one donated shelf, and like ___, neighbors kept adding books until it filled a room.

note: In some versions the soup is made from a nail or an axe instead of a stone.

story: In this fable, a scorpion asks a frog to carry it across a river, arguing it won't sting since both would drown. Midway it stings anyway and explains that it is its nature. The earliest known version is in a 1933 Russian novel.
def: a story about someone who harms others, even at their own cost, because that is simply their nature
ex: When the con artist cheated his own partner, Hannah thought of the scorpion and the frog.
The rival firm betrayed them even though it hurt both companies, just like the scorpion and the frog.
The office gossip kept spreading rumors even when it cost her friends and promotions; it was the scorpion and the frog.
Fatima thought of the scorpion and the frog when her cousin sabotaged the family business he depended on.

cloze.s: Everyone warned Sam that his old business partner would cheat again; it was ___ all over, because cheating was who he was.

note: It is not one of Aesop's fables. Orson Welles made it famous in English in his 1955 film Mr. Arkadin.

story: In Thomas Morton's 1798 play Speed the Plough, Dame Ashfield constantly worries about what her neighbor Mrs. Grundy will think, though Mrs. Grundy never appears on stage. Her name came to stand for the judgment of prim, narrow-minded society.
def: a narrow-minded, very proper person who objects to anything that breaks the rules of polite behavior
ex: Don't let the Mrs. Grundys of the neighborhood stop you from painting your door purple.
The new principal turned out to be a Mrs. Grundy who banned dancing at the prom.
Every office seems to have a Mrs. Grundy who complains when someone wears jeans on a Monday.
The Mrs. Grundy of the book club objected to every novel that contained a single swear word.

cloze.s: Ignoring the local ___ who frowned at everything modern, the couple held their wedding on roller skates.

story: In Genesis, hungry Esau sells his birthright, his rights as the older son, to his brother Jacob for a bowl of lentil stew. The phrase 'mess of pottage' comes from old English Bible chapter headings, not from the Bible text itself.
def: something of small, short-term value accepted in exchange for something far more valuable
ex: Selling the family farm to a developer for quick cash felt like trading it for a mess of pottage.
Olga later realized she had given up her pension for a mess of pottage: a slightly higher salary.
Trading your personal privacy for a free phone game is giving it away for a mess of pottage.
The town sold its public beach for a mess of pottage: a one-time payment that was spent within a year.

cloze.s: The player gave up his college scholarship for a small signing bonus, a(n) ___ he regretted within a year.

note: 'Mess' here means a serving of food, and 'pottage' means a thick soup or stew.

story: In the Gospels, Jesus drives demons into a herd of pigs, which rush down a steep bank into the water and drown. In the King James Bible, Mark and Luke place the event in 'the country of the Gadarenes.'
def: rushing together wildly toward disaster, like a crowd in a panic
ex: Analysts warned of a Gadarene rush into risky stocks just before the crash.
The Gadarene stampede to buy the new digital coin ended with most buyers losing money.
Critics warned of a Gadarene rush by companies to adopt the untested technology.
The Gadarene charge of homebuyers into overpriced houses ended in a painful crash.

cloze.s: When rumors spread, depositors made a(n) ___ rush to pull out their money, and the bank collapsed.

story: In the Book of Revelation, the church in the city of Laodicea is scolded for being 'neither cold nor hot' but lukewarm. Its name became a word for halfhearted commitment.
def: not caring strongly either way, especially about religion, politics, or a cause
ex: Most voters were Laodicean about the zoning measure, and turnout was tiny.
The coach couldn't stand Laodicean players who didn't care whether they won or lost.
The charity struggled because most of its members had grown Laodicean, giving neither time nor money.
Raised in a devout family, Tomás became Laodicean about faith in college, neither believing nor rejecting it.

cloze.s: Her once-passionate interest in the club had become ___; she paid her dues but never showed up or cared what happened.

story: In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says, 'Ye cannot serve God and mammon' (Matthew 6:24, King James Version). The word comes from an Aramaic term for wealth and came to mean money treated as a false god.
def: money and wealth seen as an evil force that people worship or chase above all else
ex: The documentary showed how mammon had corrupted a once-honest sport.
Tomás left banking, saying he was tired of serving mammon instead of his community.
The film's villain gave up every friendship he had in his endless service to mammon.
Critics complained that the sports league now bows to mammon, moving games wherever the money is.

cloze.s: The preacher warned that people who worship ___ end up caring more about their bank accounts than their families.

note: Sometimes capitalized as Mammon, pictured as a demon or god of greed.

story: In the Gospels of Mark and Luke, Jesus watches rich people give large sums at the Temple, then sees a poor widow put in two tiny coins called mites. He says she gave more than all of them, because she gave everything she had.
def: a small gift from a poor person that means more than big gifts from the rich because it costs more
ex: The ten dollars from the retired janitor was a widow's mite, worth more than the big corporate checks.
Each child gave a widow's mite from their allowance to help the flood victims.
The old farmworker's widow's mite, a jar of coins he had saved for months, moved the whole congregation.
At the school fundraiser, the true widow's mite came from a student who gave up her lunch money for a week.

cloze.s: The charity's director said the most moving donation was a(n) ___: five dollars from a man who lived in the shelter.

term: weighed in the balance and found wanting
story: In the Book of Daniel, a mysterious hand writes on the wall at King Belshazzar's feast. Daniel explains one of the words: 'Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting,' and the king is killed that night.
def: tested or judged and shown to be not good enough
ex: The new manager was weighed in the balance and found wanting after the product launch failed.
Many of the old safety rules were weighed in the balance and found wanting after the storm.
The cheap umbrella was weighed in the balance and found wanting during the first strong gust of wind.
After a semester of lost assignments, the new grading app was weighed in the balance and found wanting by teachers.

cloze.s: Every promise the airline had made was ___ when thousands of passengers were stranded for days.
cloze.a: weighed in the balance and found wanting

term: law of the Medes and Persians
story: In the Book of Daniel, King Darius signs a decree and then cannot cancel it, because 'the law of the Medes and Persians' could never be changed. As a result, Daniel is thrown into the lions' den.
def: a rule or decision that cannot be changed or broken under any circumstances
ex: In Grandma's house, dinner at six o'clock was the law of the Medes and Persians.
Treat the deadline like the law of the Medes and Persians; the publisher won't extend it.
At the hospital, the hand-washing rule is the law of the Medes and Persians: nobody ever skips it.
For our soccer coach, showing up ten minutes early to practice was the law of the Medes and Persians.

cloze.s: The school treated its no-phones rule as the ___, refusing every exception, even for emergencies.
cloze.a: law of the Medes and Persians

story: The apostle Paul wrote, 'For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face' (1 Corinthians 13:12). The 'glass' was a mirror, which in his day gave only a dim, unclear image.
def: seeing or understanding something only partly and unclearly, not fully
ex: Early astronomers saw the planets through a glass, darkly, guessing at what they could not measure.
We know the ancient city only through a glass, darkly, from a few broken clay tablets.
Doctors once understood the brain only through a glass, darkly, before modern scans showed it at work.
Looking back, Maria remembers her grandmother's village only through a glass, darkly, in a few faded scenes.

cloze.s: With only rumors and a few blurry photos, the reporters were seeing the secret project ___.

story: In Genesis, after Cain kills his brother Abel, God asks him where Abel is. Cain replies, 'I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?'
def: a question used to deny that you are responsible for another person's welfare, or to ask whether you are
ex: When asked why he ignored his struggling coworker, Mark shrugged: 'Am I my brother's keeper?'
At the town meeting about the flooded farms, one speaker insisted the answer to 'Am I my brother's keeper?' was yes.
Asked why he hadn't warned his teammate about the coach's anger, Leo snapped, “Am I my brother's keeper?”
The documentary about homelessness asks viewers an old question: “Am I my brother's keeper?”

cloze.s: Told that his neighbor's house had been robbed, the man just shrugged, asked '___', and went back inside.

story: The prophet Isaiah foresaw a time when nations 'shall beat their swords into plowshares,' the cutting blades of farm plows, and not learn war anymore (Isaiah 2:4). The same words appear in the Book of Micah.
def: turning weapons, armies, or war industries to peaceful, useful purposes
ex: The old missile base became a solar farm, a true case of swords into plowshares.
The program melted down guns and made garden tools, turning swords into plowshares.
The town turned its old army barracks into a public library, a modern case of swords into plowshares.
The artist welded collected guns into park benches, a project she proudly called swords into plowshares.

cloze.s: After the war, the tank factory began building tractors, beating ___.

note: British spelling: ploughshares.

term: a voice crying in the wilderness
story: The prophet Isaiah described 'the voice of him that crieth in the wilderness,' calling people to prepare the way of the Lord. All four Gospels apply the words to John the Baptist.
def: a lone person whose warnings or ideas are ignored by almost everyone
ex: For years she was a voice crying in the wilderness, warning that the bridge was unsafe.
Before the crash, the economist was a voice crying in the wilderness about the housing bubble.
Nobody listened when the young nurse called for better hand-washing; she was a voice crying in the wilderness.
The scientist who first warned about the polluted river was a voice crying in the wilderness until the fish began dying.

cloze.s: Dr. Okafor had warned about the virus for a decade, but she was ___ until the outbreak began.
cloze.a: a voice crying in the wilderness

story: In the Book of Job, three friends visit Job after he loses his children, wealth, and health. Instead of consoling him, they insist he must have sinned, and Job calls them 'miserable comforters.'
def: someone who tries to comfort you but makes you feel worse, often by blaming you
ex: Aunt Rosa was a Job's comforter, telling Priya her breakup was probably her own fault.
Don't be a Job's comforter; he needs support, not a list of his mistakes.
When Kwame lost his job, his brother played Job's comforter, asking why he hadn't worked harder.
Visiting her in the hospital, Hannah's neighbor was a Job's comforter, saying the illness came from her bad diet.

cloze.s: After the loss, the assistant coach acted like a(n) ___, reminding each player of every error they had made.

note: Job is pronounced JOHB, rhyming with robe.

story: In Shakespeare's King Lear, the old king, wandering in a storm after his daughters have turned him out, cries, 'I am a man / More sinned against than sinning.'
def: having been wronged by others more than you have done wrong yourself
ex: By the end of the trial, the jury saw the young driver as more sinned against than sinning.
In the bitter divorce, Aisha felt she was more sinned against than sinning.
The worker had been late a few times, but after his boss stole his ideas, he was more sinned against than sinning.
In the history book, the queen who was forced from her throne appears more sinned against than sinning.

cloze.s: The whistleblower had broken a few rules, but after years of threats from her bosses, most people saw her as ___.

term: uneasy lies the head that wears a crown
story: In Shakespeare's Henry IV, Part 2, the sleepless King Henry envies his poorest subjects, who can rest easily, and ends, 'Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.'
def: people with great power or responsibility carry heavy worries that rob them of peace
ex: The new CEO hasn't slept well since taking over; uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.
Being team captain means constant pressure, and Malik learned that uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.
The school principal, facing budget cuts and angry parents, knew that uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.
The young king in the novel couldn't sleep for fear of rebels; uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.

cloze.s: The champion admitted she worried every day about losing her title; ___.
cloze.a: uneasy lies the head that wears a crown

note: Often misquoted as 'the head that wears the crown.'

story: In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Caesar tells Mark Antony that he distrusts Cassius: 'Yond Cassius has a lean and hungry look; / He thinks too much: such men are dangerous.' Cassius soon leads the plot to kill him.
def: the appearance of an ambitious person who seems to be secretly plotting to take power
ex: The ambitious young lawyer had a lean and hungry look that made the senior partners nervous.
Keep an eye on the vice president; he has a lean and hungry look.
The new intern had a lean and hungry look, quietly studying how every manager made decisions.
Before the club elections, the president didn't trust the treasurer's lean and hungry look.

cloze.s: The coach noticed the backup quarterback's ___ and suspected he was quietly campaigning for the starting job.

story: In Shakespeare's Othello, Iago pretends to be Othello's loyal friend while secretly convincing him that his wife, Desdemona, is unfaithful. Driven by Iago's lies, Othello kills her.
def: a false friend who secretly tricks and turns against someone while seeming loyal
ex: The office Iago praised Kwame to his face while spreading rumors behind his back.
In the drama series, the king's most trusted advisor turns out to be an Iago.
On the reality show, the friendliest contestant turned out to be an Iago, secretly voting off his closest allies.
Fatima's coworker played Iago, cheering her promotion while whispering doubts about her to the boss.

cloze.s: She never suspected that her charming best friend was a(n) ___ who had been turning everyone against her for years.

term: the quality of mercy is not strained
story: In Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice, Portia, disguised as a lawyer, urges Shylock to show mercy: 'The quality of mercy is not strain'd; / It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven.' 'Strained' here meant forced.
def: true mercy must be given freely and willingly, never forced
ex: The judge reminded the court that the quality of mercy is not strained and reduced the sentence.
When Hannah forgave her brother without being asked, her mother smiled: 'The quality of mercy is not strained.'
Pardons granted only under public pressure ring hollow, the columnist wrote, because the quality of mercy is not strained.
When the teacher freely let the whole class retake the quiz, she smiled and said, 'The quality of mercy is not strained.'

cloze.s: Forced apologies mean little, and forced forgiveness means less; as Portia said, ___.
cloze.a: the quality of mercy is not strained

story: In Shakespeare's Henry V, the king rallies his tired soldiers to attack a gap blasted in the walls of a French town: 'Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more.'
def: a call to try again at a hard, tiring task or to fight one more time
ex: It was 2 a.m., the code still crashed, and Yuki said, 'Once more unto the breach.'
Facing a third round of tax forms, Liam sighed, 'Once more unto the breach, dear friends.'
With the in-laws arriving for the third holiday dinner, Maria tied on her apron and said, 'Once more unto the breach.'
After failing his driving test twice, Jamal gripped the wheel for a third try: once more unto the breach.

cloze.s: The volunteers had already filled 500 sandbags, but the river kept rising, so their leader shouted, '___!'

note: Often misquoted as 'once more into the breach.'

term: discretion is the better part of valor
story: In Shakespeare's Henry IV, Part 1, the cowardly Falstaff plays dead in battle to avoid being killed, then gets up and declares, 'The better part of valour is discretion.'
def: being careful and avoiding danger you don't need to face is often smarter than being bold
ex: Seeing the icy trail, Sofia turned back; discretion is the better part of valor.
The lawyer chose not to argue with the judge, deciding discretion was the better part of valor.
Seeing the long, angry line at the store, Kwame decided discretion was the better part of valor and shopped online.
Rather than argue with his furious boss, Diego decided discretion was the better part of valor and stayed quiet.

cloze.s: When the bear appeared on the trail, the hikers decided that ___ and quietly backed away.
cloze.a: discretion is the better part of valor

note: Often said jokingly to excuse avoiding a fight.

story: In Voltaire's 1759 novel Candide, the tutor Dr. Pangloss insists that all is for the best in 'the best of all possible worlds,' even as war, earthquake, and disease strike. Voltaire was mocking blind optimism.
def: always sure that things are good or will turn out fine, even when the facts clearly show they are bad
ex: His Panglossian forecast ignored three straight years of falling sales.
Diego's Panglossian belief that the leaky roof would 'fix itself' cost him a new ceiling.
Despite a hurricane warning, Uncle Ray kept a Panglossian faith that the beach picnic would go ahead.
The doctor warned that a Panglossian attitude toward his rising blood pressure could put his health at risk.

cloze.s: The minister's ___ speech claimed the economy was perfect, even as factories closed across the country.

note: Close to Pollyanna, but Panglossian stresses insisting that everything already happens for the best.

story: In Charles Dickens's David Copperfield (1850), Mr. Wilkins Micawber is always in debt yet always cheerfully sure that 'something will turn up.' He is even sent to debtors' prison.
def: a person who keeps believing luck will solve their money problems instead of taking action
ex: Like a Micawber, Uncle Jim never kept a budget, always expecting a lottery win to save him.
The company took a Micawber approach to its debt, assuming some buyer would eventually appear.
Jamal was a real Micawber, ignoring his overdue rent and insisting that a lucky break was coming soon.
The bakery owner acted like a Micawber, letting her debts pile up while waiting for one big order to rescue her.

cloze.s: Deep in credit-card debt, he kept spending like a(n) ___, certain that something would turn up.

note: The adjective is Micawberish.

story: In Charles Dickens's novel Hard Times (1854), Thomas Gradgrind, a wealthy man who controls a local school, demands, 'Now, what I want is, Facts,' and crushes children's imagination. His own children's lives are damaged by his cold system.
def: a cold, hard person who values only facts and numbers and ignores feelings and imagination
ex: The new administrator was a Gradgrind who cut art and music to raise test scores.
Don't be a Gradgrind about the vacation budget; leave some room for fun.
The Gradgrind accountant canceled the office birthday parties because they didn't show up as profit.
Our math teacher was no Gradgrind; she made fractions fun with stories and games.

cloze.s: Our ___ of a manager judged workers only by spreadsheets and never once asked how they were doing.

note: Also used as an adjective: a Gradgrind approach to schooling.

story: In Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726), Gulliver visits Brobdingnag, a land of giants as tall as church steeples, where he himself is tiny. It is the opposite of Lilliput, the land of tiny people.
def: enormous; huge in size, like something from a land of giants
ex: The new stadium's Brobdingnagian video screen could be seen from the highway.
Grandpa served Brobdingnagian portions of pasta at the family reunion.
The bakery's Brobdingnagian cinnamon rolls are as big as dinner plates.
In the Brobdingnagian new office, the small team felt lost among hundreds of empty desks.

cloze.s: Next to the tiny dog, the Great Dane looked ___, almost as tall as the children.

story: In Molière's comedy Tartuffe (first staged in 1664), a con man pretends to be deeply religious and wins the trust of a rich man, Orgon. He then tries to seduce Orgon's wife and seize his property.
def: a fake who pretends to be very religious or moral to gain power or money
ex: The TV preacher was exposed as a Tartuffe who spent donations on mansions.
The town's loudest moralist turned out to be a Tartuffe with a secret gambling habit.
The charity director, praised for his goodness, was a Tartuffe who kept most of the donations for himself.
The self-help guru turned out to be a Tartuffe, lecturing fans on kindness while cheating his own staff.

cloze.s: He lectured everyone about honesty while cheating his own customers, a modern ___.

story: In Victor Hugo's 1862 novel Les Misérables, police inspector Javert spends years hunting Jean Valjean, a former convict who broke his parole and became a good man, because Javert believes the law allows no exceptions.
def: a person who hunts someone down without ever stopping and enforces rules with no mercy
ex: The parking officer was a Javert, ticketing an ambulance driver who stopped for one minute.
The auditor chased the tiny accounting error like Javert, for months on end.
The homeowners' association president was a Javert, measuring every lawn and fining anyone a half inch over.
Like Javert, the reporter chased the runaway businessman across three countries for ten years.

cloze.s: The landlord chased one late rent payment from years ago with the grim, merciless zeal of ___.

story: In W. W. Jacobs's 1902 story 'The Monkey's Paw,' an old couple wish on a cursed paw for 200 pounds. They receive it as compensation after their son dies in an accident at work, and their next wish brings even worse horror.
def: a wish that comes true in a terrible, unexpected way, so that getting it brings disaster
ex: The promotion turned into a monkey's paw: more pay, but eighty-hour weeks and no time for family.
For Raj, winning the lottery was a monkey's paw that tore his family apart.
Hannah's wish for a day off came true like a monkey's paw: she got one through a bad case of flu.
The city got its wish to host the championship, but like a monkey's paw, the stadium costs nearly bankrupted it.

cloze.s: She wished for a quiet house, and like a(n) ___, the wish came true only when her kids moved across the country and stopped calling.

story: In Goethe's 1797 poem, an apprentice uses magic to make a broom carry water but cannot stop it. When he splits it with an axe, each half becomes a new broom, and both keep fetching water until his master returns. Disney's Fantasia (1940) made it famous.
def: someone who starts a powerful process they do not understand and then cannot control it
ex: The engineers felt like the sorcerer's apprentice as their trading program bought and sold faster than they could stop it.
The farmer who released the fish to eat weeds became the sorcerer's apprentice; now they fill every lake.
Like the sorcerer's apprentice, the city planted fast-growing vines for shade, then watched them choke the native trees.
Liam set up an automatic email system, then felt like the sorcerer's apprentice when it sent thousands of messages he couldn't stop.

cloze.s: Starting the online prank seemed fun until it spread to millions, leaving the teenager feeling like ___.

story: The ancient Greek poet Archilochus wrote that 'a fox knows many things, but a hedgehog knows one big thing.' In a 1953 essay, Isaiah Berlin used the line to divide thinkers into those with one big idea and those with many.
def: the contrast between people who explain everything through one big idea and those who draw on many small ones
ex: Reading about the hedgehog and the fox, Wei realized she was a fox, curious about everything.
Researchers who study forecasting often sort experts using the hedgehog and the fox.
Our debate coach used the hedgehog and the fox to explain why Malik always argued from one big theory.
Choosing team leaders, the manager thought about the hedgehog and the fox: one grand vision, or many practical ideas?

cloze.s: In the old contrast of ___, the specialist with one grand theory faces the generalist who knows a little about many things.

story: The Russian writer Anton Chekhov advised in an 1889 letter that one must never put a loaded rifle on the stage if it isn't going to go off. Writers now use his name for the rule that every important detail should pay off.
def: the writing rule that every important detail shown early in a story should matter later
ex: The mysterious key in chapter one was a Chekhov's gun that unlocked the final twist.
Screenwriting teachers say a close-up on a knife is a Chekhov's gun the audience expects to see used.
Readers noticed the locked attic in the first chapter and knew it was a Chekhov's gun.
My writing teacher circled the mysterious letter in my opening scene, calling it a Chekhov's gun I had never used.

cloze.s: The film lingered on the broken elevator in its first scene, a(n) ___ that became the key to the ending.

story: Grub Street was a real London street, renamed Milton Street in 1830, known in the 1700s as a home of poor writers who turned out cheap work for money. Samuel Johnson's dictionary said it was 'much inhabited by writers of small histories, dictionaries, and temporary poems.'
def: the world of poorly paid writers who produce quick, low-quality work just to earn money
ex: Before her novels sold, Maria survived on Grub Street, writing product reviews for pennies.
The website's Grub Street writers churned out three articles a day each.
Many famous authors started out on Grub Street, writing cheap articles to pay the rent.
Jamal called his job writing hundreds of rushed product descriptions a modern Grub Street.

cloze.s: Desperate for rent money, the young poet joined ___, writing gossip columns and cheap romance stories.

story: In the 1950s, science fiction writer Theodore Sturgeon answered critics who sneered at his field by saying that 'ninety percent of everything is crud,' so science fiction was no worse than anything else.
def: the idea that most of what is made in any field, about 90 percent, is poor quality
ex: Scrolling through the streaming service's new shows, Aisha was reminded of Sturgeon's law.
By Sturgeon's law, most apps in the store aren't worth downloading, but the good ones are great.
The art fair had hundreds of booths, and as Sturgeon's law predicts, only a few paintings were memorable.
Hannah reminded the frustrated editor about Sturgeon's law after he read fifty weak manuscripts in a row.

cloze.s: Don't judge all podcasts by the bad ones; ___ says ninety percent of everything is junk anyway.

story: The saying 'Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity' was printed in a 1980 book of Murphy's-law jokes, credited to a Robert J. Hanlon. Similar ideas appeared earlier, including in Robert Heinlein's fiction.
def: the rule of thumb that you should blame foolishness or mistakes before you blame evil intent
ex: Before accusing the IT team of sabotage, apply Hanlon's razor: they probably just made a typo.
Hanlon's razor kept Jamal from assuming his neighbor had stolen his package; it had simply been misdelivered.
Hanlon's razor reminded Sofia that her friend's late reply was probably forgetfulness, not anger.
The teacher applied Hanlon's razor when half the class missed the deadline, deciding the instructions had been unclear.

cloze.s: When the email went to the wrong client, the manager applied ___ and assumed carelessness, not a plot.

note: A 'razor' is a rule for cutting away unlikely explanations, as in Occam's razor.

story: Philosophers imagined a donkey standing exactly between two equal piles of hay that cannot choose either one and so starves. It is named after the 14th-century French thinker Jean Buridan, though the example does not appear in his writings.
def: someone stuck, unable to choose between two equally good options, and losing out as a result
ex: Torn between two equally good job offers, Tomás became Buridan's ass and missed both deadlines.
Faced with forty nearly identical cereals, I stood like Buridan's ass in the grocery aisle.
Like Buridan's ass, the hungry family stood debating between two great pizza places until both had closed.
Unable to choose between two equally good designs, the committee became Buridan's ass and built nothing at all.

cloze.s: Unable to pick between two perfect apartments, the couple waited so long they lost both, like ___.

note: 'Ass' here means donkey.

story: In 1847, Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis showed that having doctors wash their hands in a chlorine solution sharply cut deaths of new mothers from childbed fever in a Vienna hospital. Many doctors rejected his findings, which won wide acceptance only after his death.
def: the automatic rejection of new evidence because it goes against established beliefs or habits
ex: The Semmelweis reflex delayed the hospital's switch to a safer surgery checklist for years.
When the intern's data showed the old method failed, the senior staff's Semmelweis reflex kicked in.
When a new study showed his favorite treatment didn't work, the veteran surgeon's Semmelweis reflex made him refuse to read it.
Jamal's coach showed a Semmelweis reflex, rejecting new research on rest days because he had always trained daily.

cloze.s: The board dismissed the young engineer's proof of the design flaw without even reading it, a textbook ___.

story: Soviet biologist Trofim Lysenko rejected genetics and made false claims about growing crops, and Stalin backed him. Leading geneticist Nikolai Vavilov was arrested in 1940 and died in prison in 1943; from 1948 genetics was effectively banned, and thousands of biologists lost their jobs.
def: forcing science to fit political beliefs, and punishing researchers whose honest results disagree
ex: Historians describe the ban on unwelcome research as a clear case of Lysenkoism.
Any company that fires scientists for inconvenient findings is practicing a corporate Lysenkoism.
In history class, students learned how Lysenkoism silenced Soviet geneticists and badly hurt the country's farming.
The scientist warned that cutting funds for every study whose results officials dislike is a slide toward Lysenkoism.

cloze.s: When officials ordered biologists to publish only results that matched the party line, critics called it ___.

story: In 1935 the Soviet government announced that coal miner Alexei Stakhanov had dug 102 tons of coal in under six hours, about fourteen times his quota. Officials used him to push workers to produce more; later reports said other miners had helped him.
def: an extremely hard-working, productive worker, especially one held up as a model for others
ex: Emma worked with Stakhanovite energy, finishing a month of reports in a single week.
The warehouse's Stakhanovite workers were praised in every company newsletter.
During harvest season, the farm's Stakhanovite pickers filled twice as many baskets as anyone else.
Management held up Rosa as a Stakhanovite example, but her coworkers just wanted reasonable hours.

cloze.s: The new intern's ___ effort, sixteen hours a day without complaint, made the rest of the team look lazy.
