story: During the Spanish Civil War in 1936, a general on the Nationalist side, usually said to be Emilio Mola, reportedly claimed that four columns of troops were marching on Madrid and a 'fifth column' of supporters inside the city would rise to help them.
def: a hidden group inside a country or organization that secretly works to help its enemies
ex: During the war, the government feared a fifth column of spies working in its factories.
The CEO suspected a fifth column inside the company was leaking plans to a rival.
The chess club suspected a fifth column was secretly passing their opening plans to the rival school.
Spy novels often feature a fifth column of ordinary-looking neighbors who secretly work for a foreign power.

cloze.s: The rebels counted on a(n) ___ of secret supporters inside the capital to open the gates.

note: Who first said it is uncertain; the original remark has never been found.

story: A 12th-century chronicle says Cnut, king of England in the 1000s, set his throne on the shore and ordered the tide to stop. When the waves soaked him, he declared that the power of kings is worthless next to God's.
def: someone who foolishly tries to stop something that cannot be stopped
ex: By banning smartphones from the office, the old boss was playing King Canute against the tide of technology.
Critics called the record label a King Canute, fighting online music instead of adapting to it.
Trying to keep the kids from hearing how the show ends is playing King Canute; their friends will spoil it.
Ordering employees never to discuss the merger online, the CEO was playing King Canute with the office gossip.

cloze.s: Trying to stop teenagers from using slang is like being ___, commanding the waves to go back.

note: In the original story, Cnut was showing he could not command the tide, not claiming he could.

story: In January 1077 the German king Henry IV, cut off from the Church by Pope Gregory VII, stood for three days in the snow outside the castle of Canossa, Italy, begging forgiveness. The pope finally lifted the ban.
def: to humble yourself and admit you were wrong to someone you had opposed
ex: After the boycott hurt sales, the company's founder had to go to Canossa and apologize publicly.
The star striker went to Canossa, asking the coach he had insulted to let him back on the team.
After insulting the club's founder, the new member had to go to Canossa and apologize at the next meeting.
Rather than go to Canossa and admit her mistake, the stubborn author let her book deal fall apart.

cloze.s: After months of attacking the new rules, the union leader was forced to ___ and accept them in public.

note: Germany's leader Otto von Bismarck famously vowed in the 1870s, 'We will not go to Canossa.'

story: This French saying, meaning 'after me, the flood,' is credited to King Louis XV, or in the form 'après nous' to his favorite, Madame de Pompadour, in the 1750s. Who said it, if anyone did, is uncertain.
def: an attitude of not caring what disaster comes after you are gone, as long as you are fine now
ex: The executives' après moi, le déluge approach left the next team with huge debts.
Spending the whole budget right before retiring was pure après moi, le déluge.
The landlord skipped every repair before selling the building, a classic après moi, le déluge move.
Economists worry that some leaders take an après moi, le déluge view of the nation's long-term debt.

cloze.s: The departing manager signed every expensive contract on his last day with a careless ___ attitude.

story: Screenwriter Angus MacPhail coined the term, and director Alfred Hitchcock made it famous for the secret papers or object that drives a spy plot. Hitchcock said it is the thing the spies are after, but the audience doesn't care.
def: an object or goal that drives a story's plot but matters little in itself
ex: In the heist movie, the stolen diamond is just a MacGuffin; the real story is the friendship.
The missing briefcase was a MacGuffin, and we never even learn what's inside.
In many spy thrillers, the secret computer chip is a MacGuffin that simply keeps the chase going.
Wei's writing teacher said the treasure map in her story was a MacGuffin, so she shouldn't spend pages describing it.

cloze.s: The secret formula was the film's ___: everyone chases it, but the audience never learns what it does.

story: In the film Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan (1982), the Kobayashi Maru is a training test that no cadet can win. James Kirk, as a cadet, secretly reprogrammed the simulation so that he could beat it.
def: a no-win situation, or a test designed so that no one can succeed
ex: With every option losing money, the budget meeting felt like a Kobayashi Maru.
The interview question was a Kobayashi Maru meant to see how candidates handle failure.
Choosing between caring for a sick parent and a dream job abroad felt like a Kobayashi Maru to Yuki.
The video game's final level is a Kobayashi Maru, built so that no player can ever win it.

cloze.s: The training exercise was a(n) ___: no matter what the students chose, the virtual patient could not be saved.

note: Sometimes used for Kirk's move instead: changing the rules of a test you can't win.

story: Lake Wobegon is the made-up Minnesota town on Garrison Keillor's radio show A Prairie Home Companion, 'where all the women are strong, all the men are good-looking, and all the children are above average.'
def: the common tendency of most people to rate themselves as better than average
ex: Thanks to the Lake Wobegon effect, most drivers believe they are better than average behind the wheel.
When every employee rated their own work as excellent, HR blamed the Lake Wobegon effect.
Ask parents whether their child is above average, and the Lake Wobegon effect means nearly all will say yes.
The Lake Wobegon effect explains why most students in the class expected an A on the very hard exam.

cloze.s: In the survey, 80 percent of staff ranked their own work in the top 20 percent, a clear case of the ___.

note: Not the same as the Dunning-Kruger effect, which is about the least skilled overrating themselves the most.
